docs.title: Neuro Scutbook
docs.text:
A bedside neurology reference for MDs, NPs, PAs, and medics — how to work up and manage a patient with neurological symptoms in the clinic, ER, or on the wards, the way a neurology consult would. Every topic pairs a prescriptive consult workflow with a plain-language evidence brief and a standardized military-medicine layer.

By presentation TRICARE prior authorization Deployment by disease and medication

This site is educational clinical decision-support. It is not a substitute for professional clinical judgment, formal consultation, or individual medical advice, and it does not establish a provider–patient relationship. Dosing, protocols, and military standards change — verify everything against current guidelines, product labeling, and the governing regulation before acting on it. Use reflects your own professional responsibility.

Site-wide evidence/policy review: 21–22 November 2026. All 59 pages in the initial review were read, with material corrections checked against accessible primary guidelines, FDA labels, trials and official military/TRICARE sources. The six new presentation guides list their own sources and review dates.

This is an AI-assisted evidence review, not clinician certification of every claim. See review scope and source limits, TRICARE PA/MN requirements, and deployment — disease AND medications. Some specialty PA criteria and controlled policy procedures still need current-source confirmation.

docs.title: Acute myelopathy
docs.text:
Last reviewed: November 2026

One-liner: acute spinal cord dysfunction — a syndrome, not a diagnosis. The first job is to exclude a compressive, vascular, or infectious cause that needs a surgeon or antibiotics now; only then does it become an inflammatory-myelitis problem. For the on-call provider seeing new weakness, a sensory level, or sphincter dysfunction: image the cord first, and do not give empiric steroids for "transverse myelitis" before the MRI.

🚩 Red flags — escalate immediately

Pattern Worry Do now Rapidly progressive weakness, new sphincter dysfunction Compressive lesion needing surgical decompression Emergent MRI whole spine; neurosurgery/spine surgery now Fever, IV drug use, bacteremia, recent spinal instrumentation, CRP often >100 mg/L, ESR >60 mm/h Spinal epidural abscess Blood cultures, then empiric antibiotics immediately; emergent decompression if deficit Known cancer with new back pain (pain precedes myelopathy by weeks in most patients) Malignant spinal cord compression Dexamethasone on suspicion, even before imaging; surgery and/or radiotherapy Anticoagulation, coagulopathy, or recent procedure/surgery Epidural hematoma Reverse coagulopathy; urgent decompression Apoplectic onset with tearing back or chest pain Aortic dissection or spinal cord infarction Aorta imaging (CTA if dissection possible); support perfusion Ascending level in a cervical lesion, respiratory compromise Rising cervical edema, ventilatory failure ICU; monitor vital capacity; airway plan Worsening after steroids Dural AV fistula, or lymphoma steroids may obscure Stop and rethink; spinal angiography; do not re-dose blindly

docs.title: Diagnosis / classification
docs.text:
Tempo is the first classifier — and it beats any single test:

Tempo Think first Hyperacute — nadir in minutes to hours Spinal cord infarction, epidural hematoma, aortic dissection Acute/subacute — nadir in hours to days, under 3 weeks Inflammatory myelitis (MS, NMOSD, MOGAD, sarcoid, SLE/Sjögren, Behçet), infectious myelopathy, epidural abscess Progressive beyond 3 weeks Tumor, compression, dural AV fistula, metabolic causes, sarcoid — transverse myelitis is unlikely here

Anatomic compartment on MRI is the second classifier: an extradural or intradural extramedullary process deforming the cord is compressive until proven otherwise; an intramedullary lesion is inflammatory, infectious, vascular, or neoplastic. Categories overlap — an epidural abscess is both infectious and compressive.

Syndromes (localize before you image): complete cord syndrome, anterior cord syndrome (dissociated sensory loss — pain/temperature lost, vibration/proprioception spared), Brown-Séquard syndrome (ipsilateral weakness + proprioception loss, contralateral pain/temperature loss), central cord syndrome, and conus/cauda equina syndrome. Early cord injury is often flaccid and areflexic — neither absent hyperreflexia nor an initially indistinct sensory level excludes myelopathy, and flaccidity alone is not Guillain–Barré syndrome.

Pitfalls that mislead: enhancement, CSF pleocytosis, and raised protein do not reliably separate myelitis from mimics — spondylotic myelopathy can show pleocytosis in 12.5% of cases and enhancement in up to 80%. Spinal cord infarction makes up 14–16% of cases labeled "transverse myelitis," and an early MRI can be normal in infarction.

docs.title: Rapid approach
docs.text:
1. Stabilize and localize. Protect ventilation (cervical lesions) and perfusion — avoid hypotension, especially if infarction is possible. Record a reproducible baseline: exact onset and time to worst deficit, strength in all four limbs, tone, reflexes, plantars, sensory level by pinprick/light touch plus vibration/proprioception, perineal sensation, voluntary anal contraction, and bladder/bowel symptoms. Re-examine serially, including before and after transport or intervention.
  2. Image emergently — assume compression until proven otherwise. MRI of the spine without and with IV contrast, centered on the clinical level; image the whole spine if cancer is suspected, because compression is often multilevel. If MRI is impossible, use CT myelography. Notify neurology early and involve neurosurgery/spine surgery immediately when compression, hematoma, instability, or rapidly progressive deficits are suspected — those discussions proceed while the workup continues. If MRI or spinal surgery is unavailable, arrange urgent transfer.
  3. Labs before MRI (do not let them delay it): CBC, ESR/CRP, blood cultures if any infection risk, coagulation studies, glucose, electrolytes. B12/copper come later for subacute cases.
  4. Treat the cause, in cause order: compression → surgery/steroids/antibiotics per Step 1 below; infarction → perfusion + aorta; fistula → angiography, never steroids; inflammatory → IVMP, then PLEX early where indicated.
  5. Support and dispose: bladder scan/catheter for retention, respiratory monitoring (vital capacity) in cervical lesions, DVT prophylaxis once bleeding risk allows, spinal cord unit, and rehabilitation once stable.

docs.title: The prescriptive flow (what I want done, in order)
docs.text:
1. ABCs + neuro baseline + sensory level (above). Admit; ICU for high cervical lesions or rising edema.
  2. Emergent MRI whole spine (with contrast) — plus brain MRI with gadolinium once compression is excluded, and orbits if there are visual symptoms.
  3. If compressive, infectious, or vascular — treat that first (Step 1). Obtain urgent MRI to exclude compression/hematoma and assess infection/vascular mimics before empiric myelitis steroids. MRI alone cannot exclude early infarction or every DAVF; pursue DWI/repeat imaging/angiography when indicated without creating an unnecessary delay in a convincing inflammatory emergency. Malignant compression is the exception: steroids start on suspicion.
  4. If inflammatory — IVMP 1,000 mg IV daily × 3–5 days (Step 2), with disease-specific escalation and taper (table below). In NMOSD, do not wait: add PLEX early, ideally within 2 days.
  5. Second-tier workup in parallel once compression is excluded (CSF, antibodies, systemic screen — see Workup).
  6. Supportive care + disposition + rehabilitation (see Disposition). Re-image and reconsider the diagnosis if the course breaks the tempo rules — progression beyond 3 weeks, or enhancement that persists, points away from demyelinating myelitis, toward sarcoidosis in particular.

docs.title: Workup
docs.text:
Imaging: MRI spine without and with IV contrast (whole spine if cancer suspected); MRI brain with gadolinium; orbits if visual symptoms. Spinal angiography (DSA) is the gold standard for dural AV fistula. CTA of the aorta if dissection is possible. CT myelography only if MRI is impossible. For infarction: DWI — restricted diffusion appears before T2 change, in an anterior or watershed distribution, with no early enhancement; early enhancement argues against infarction. Associated vertebral body infarction or an adjacent arterial dissection/occlusion supports infarction.

CSF (after imaging excludes compression): cell count and differential, protein, glucose, paired oligoclonal bands/IgG index, cytology. Add Gram stain and culture plus viral PCR (HSV, VZV, enterovirus) when infection is possible.

Serum antibodies — cell-based assays, drawn before steroids/PLEX where feasible: AQP4-IgG by live cell-based assay (sensitivity >80%, specificity >99%; ELISA can give false-positive low titers — confirm on a cell-based assay if the picture is atypical; false negatives occur during immunosuppression or after PLEX, so retest off treatment or during a relapse; CSF AQP4 testing adds little) and MOG-IgG (live assays more specific than fixed; low-positive titers require phenotype/MRI support and exclusion of a better diagnosis; titers fluctuate and can be negative outside attacks in up to 57% of patients). Coexistence of both antibodies is rare.

Systemic screen: ANA, ENA (SSA/SSB), dsDNA, antiphospholipid antibodies, ACE, chest CT or PET for sarcoidosis, B12/copper (a normal B12 does not exclude deficiency — check MMA and homocysteine; nitrous oxide inactivates B12), HIV, syphilis; paraneoplastic panel if suspected. For infarction: echocardiography, lipids, diabetes workup.

docs.title: Inflammatory myelitis — MS vs NMOSD vs MOGAD
docs.text:
The three diseases that dominate inflammatory myelitis, distinguished by lesion length and position, CSF oligoclonal bands, and cell-based antibody assays. Full disease pages: NMOSD, MOGAD, MS.

2015 NMOSD criteria (Wingerchuk et al.): AQP4-IgG positive — one core clinical characteristic plus exclusion of other diagnoses is enough; a single attack can establish the diagnosis. AQP4-IgG negative or unknown — two or more different core characteristics (dissemination in space; dissemination in time is not required), at least one of which must be optic neuritis, myelitis with LETM, or area postrema syndrome with a dorsal medulla lesion, plus the additional MRI requirements, and exclusion of alternatives. Up to 40% of patients who were AQP4-negative turn out MOG-IgG positive and are now classified as MOGAD.

2023 international MOGAD panel criteria — all three required: (1) one core clinical event — optic neuritis, myelitis, ADEM, cerebral monofocal or polyfocal deficits, brainstem/cerebellar deficits, or cortical encephalitis; (2) positive MOG-IgG on a cell-based assay — a clear positive (fixed-assay titer ≥1:100, or live-assay positive at its standard cutoff) needs no further support, while a low-positive, titer-unavailable, or CSF-only result requires at least one supporting clinical or MRI feature; (3) exclusion of better explanations, especially MS. For MS, apply the McDonald criteria once a typical clinically isolated syndrome is established and alternatives are unlikely.

Feature MS AQP4+ NMOSD MOGAD Cord lesion length Under 1 segment, rarely more than 3; often several LETM (≥3 segments) LETM common; short lesions also occur Axial / location Peripheral (dorsal/lateral), wedge-shaped; cervical Central, cord swelling, bright spotty lesions; cervicothoracic Gray matter only (H-sign); conus/caudal cord Enhancement / evolution Focal or ring enhancement Prominent, sometimes ring; lesions persist and cause atrophy Often none; lesions often resolve Brain MRI Periventricular, juxtacortical, Dawson fingers, inferior temporal lesions Near ventricles and aqueduct, hypothalamus, dorsal medulla ADEM-like fluffy lesions, deep gray matter, cerebellar peduncles, leptomeningeal enhancement CSF Oligoclonal bands 90–95% Oligoclonal bands 20–30%; pleocytosis ~35%, sometimes neutrophils/eosinophils Oligoclonal bands 10–20%; pleocytosis ~35% Demographics / course Relapsing, can progress Female:male ~9:1; severe attacks, incomplete recovery Female:male ~1:1; ~50% monophasic; better recovery

Other inflammatory causes:

Cause Cord MRI Distinguishing clues Neurosarcoidosis LETM (short lesions less often); long-lasting subpial/leptomeningeal enhancement, "trident sign" (dorsal subpial + central canal enhancement, axial) Subacute or progressive course beyond 3 weeks; low CSF glucose, raised CSF ACE, sometimes normal CSF; systemic disease SLE LETM with swelling, can span whole cord and medulla; gray-matter vs white-matter myelitis forms Antiphospholipid-related myelopathy (thoracic, patchy, little enhancement); check AQP4 — overlap occurs Sjögren syndrome LETM, mostly cervical, can extend to medulla; confluent, enhancing Frequently overlaps with AQP4+ NMOSD; sicca/parotid/systemic disease, neuropathy; anti-SSA positivity alone does not prove Sjögren caused the lesion; no validated pathognomonic Sjögren MRI signature Behçet disease Cervical or thoracic LETM (short lesions less often); "bagel sign" (T2 center darker than a bright rim); enhancement uncommon Recurrent oral/genital ulcers, uveitis/retinal vasculitis, characteristic skin disease; CSF neutrophilic, lymphocytic, or mixed pleocytosis, OCBs usually absent; HLA-B51 is neither diagnostic nor exclusionary

docs.title: Management
docs.text:
Step 1 — treat the surgical, infectious, or vascular cause first (before any myelitis therapy)

  • Malignant spinal cord compression with neurological symptoms/signs — dexamethasone 16 mg PO (or equivalent parenteral dose) promptly, then 16 mg/day while awaiting surgery/radiotherapy (NICE NG234). Start on suspicion, even before imaging; taper after definitive treatment. Stop if compression/metastasis is excluded. Monitor glucose and provide gastric protection. Steroids are a bridge to surgery and/or radiotherapy. In unexplained epidural lesions, possible lymphoma is a reason for caution — hold steroids if lymphoma is possible and the patient is stable enough to wait for tissue, because chemosensitive tumors are managed differently.
  • Spinal epidural abscess — blood cultures first, then vancomycin + ceftriaxone immediately. Use cefepime instead of ceftriaxone for people who inject drugs, surgical-site infection, sepsis, or substantial neurologic deficits. Dosing (verify renal function; pharmacy to dose): vancomycin 15–20 mg/kg IV q8–12h by actual body weight in normal renal function; cefepime 2 g IV q8h when CrCl >60 mL/min, reduced or interval-extended in renal impairment. Urgent decompression for new/progressive deficits or significant compression — consult immediately. Do not wait 48–72 hours; neurological status and delay to source control affect recovery. Withholding antibiotics until image-guided biopsy is reasonable only when the patient is neurologically intact, not septic, has no cord compression on MRI, and can be closely monitored.
  • Epidural hematoma — reverse the coagulopathy and decompress urgently.
  • Disc herniation / spondylosis (the commonest extrinsic compression, mostly cervical) — decompression per spine surgery; contributing factors include malalignment, instability, and a congenitally narrow canal.
  • Spinal cord infarction — support perfusion and find the cause. No established universal reperfusion/antithrombotic regimen. Use neurology/vascular assessment and the suspected mechanism; an observational aspirin-plus-LMWH regimen is not a standard prescription. Evaluate the aorta (CTA if dissection possible). Avoid hypotension.
  • Dural AV fistula — do NOT give steroids (rapid deterioration in about half of patients). DSA is the gold standard; treatment is embolization or surgical disconnection. Surgery is permanent; embolization is not possible if the feeder also supplies the anterior spinal artery.

→ Urgent imaging and clinical assessment support inflammatory myelitis, with compression excluded and infection/vascular mimics addressed → Step 2.

Step 2 — inflammatory myelitis: IVMP, then disease-specific escalation and taper

  • IVMP — methylprednisolone 1,000 mg IV daily for 3–5 days (children: 30 mg/kg/day, maximum 1 g). Equivalent high-dose oral steroids may work about as well as IV.
  • AQP4+ NMOSD — IVMP plus early or upfront PLEX for myelitis; myelitis responded better to PLEX than to IVMP in one study. Start PLEX first-line or within days, ideally within 2 days. Then prednisone 1 mg/kg/day, tapered to 10–15 mg/day over 2–3 weeks, with low-dose maintenance for 3–6 months to prevent early relapse until long-term immunotherapy takes effect. Untreated NMOSD attacks leave only 21.6% fully recovered — do not wait.
  • MOGAD — IVMP; add early PLEX for severe or inadequately responding attacks. Rescue with PLEX or IVIG (IVIG 2 g/kg total over 2–5 days); apheresis within 4.5 days improved recovery, and early escalation was linked to fewer relapses in children. Slow taper over up to 6 months is common — relapses cluster below about 10 mg prednisone and within 2 months of stopping. MOGAD usually responds well to steroids.
  • MS — IVMP alone in about 93% of cases; usually no taper. PLEX for severe attacks that do not respond to steroids. MS attacks are usually milder than NMOSD attacks.
  • PLEX regimen — about 5 exchanges, daily or every other day; up to 10 have been used (pediatric reviews describe 5–7 exchanges over 2 weeks). Timing matters most: earlier is better, and in steroid-refractory cases PLEX gave moderate to marked improvement in 42% vs 6% with sham.
  • IVIG — 2 g/kg total over 2–5 days, as rescue when steroids fail and as an alternative to PLEX mainly in MOGAD and children. Its role in adult NMOSD or MS myelitis is limited.

Step 3 — mimics and refractory disease

  • B12 / copper deficiency myelopathy — replace urgently; it halts or improves with replacement, and delayed treatment leaves residual deficits. Check MMA and homocysteine when B12 is normal, and copper, ceruloplasmin, and zinc (zinc excess, e.g. denture cream, drives copper deficiency). B12 deficiency shows dorsal-column sensory ataxia and spasticity, often with neuropathy, and symmetric posterior or lateral column T2 signal, usually thoracic, rarely enhancing. Copper deficiency looks identical. Replacement dosing was not pinned in this research round — use local protocol and verify before prescribing.
  • Infectious myelopathy — HSV, VZV, CMV, EBV, West Nile virus, Borrelia, TB, syphilis, histoplasma, HIV, HTLV-1. Clues: fever, immunosuppression, CSF pleocytosis, positive serology/PCR. Treat the organism; do not anchor on steroids.
  • Sarcoid / SLE / Sjögren / Behçet — disease-specific workup and rheumatology; see the table above. Worsening beyond 3 weeks or persistently enhancing lesions should re-open the sarcoid question.
  • Other mimics to exclude: intramedullary neoplasm or lymphoma, paraneoplastic myelopathy (tract-specific lesions; Hu, CRMP5, amphiphysin antibodies), delayed radiation myelopathy, hematomyelia, hereditary myeloneuropathies (chronic presentations).
  • Refractory inflammatory myelitis — if appropriately delivered therapies repeatedly fail, reconsider the diagnosis before adding more immunotherapy.

Avoid

  • Empiric steroids for "transverse myelitis" before MRI — compression, abscess, hematoma, and ischemia must be excluded first (malignant compression on suspicion is the exception). Steroids can blur the diagnosis and, in DAVF, cause rapid, lasting worsening.
  • MS disease-modifying drugs in NMOSD — interferon-β, natalizumab, fingolimod and other S1P modulators, alemtuzumab, and dimethyl fumarate have been reported to trigger severe attacks. Do not start an MS DMT until AQP4-IgG is back. Glatiramer acetate is a different case: it is ineffective at preventing NMOSD attacks rather than a reported exacerbation trigger.
  • Anchoring on enhancement or CSF pleocytosis to call something myelitis — see Pitfalls above.

TRICARE — verified rules and the current form

Urgent MRI, surgery and inpatient rescue treatment should not wait for routine outpatient PA. Continuing immune treatment, outpatient PLEX/infusions and rehabilitation require their own benefit/site review. Use the cause-specific diagnosis and evidence; “myelopathy” alone does not establish every drug indication.

Current PA/MN details, benefit routing and packet · Live Formulary Search. Check the exact product, beneficiary and venue on the prescribing date.

docs.title: Disposition
docs.text:
Admit with neurosurgical access; ICU for high cervical lesions or rising edema. Neuro checks must include respiratory function (vital capacity) in cervical lesions. Transfer early if surgery is unavailable. After stabilization, a dedicated spinal cord unit plans care for respiration, mobility, voiding and bowel, spasticity, autonomic dysfunction, and pressure-injury prevention.

  • Bladder and bowel: check the post-void residual or place an indwelling catheter for retention in the acute phase; move to intermittent catheterization (or suprapubic catheter when needed) plus a scheduled laxative and bowel program. (Specific PVR thresholds and timing of catheter removal were not addressed in the sources used here.)

  • DVT prophylaxis: use mechanical prophylaxis while bleeding risk prohibits anticoagulant prophylaxis, then start LMWH when the spine/surgical team judges it safe. Adjust for renal function, weight, procedures, and bleeding. Select duration with the spinal cord rehabilitation team according to mobility and VTE risk; do not prescribe an extended course from an incompletely captured research regimen.

  • Rehabilitation: start mobilization and rehabilitation once the patient is medically and surgically stable, ideally during the acute admission in a spinal cord unit, then move to secondary rehabilitation. Specific timing trials for non-traumatic myelopathy are limited.

Cause Prognosis Epidural abscess Emergency spine/ID assessment and prompt source control; do not use a 48–72h window as permission to wait Metastatic compression Prompt treatment prevents paralysis; function before treatment drives outcome Spinal cord infarction Outcome varies with initial severity and cause; substantial late recovery is possible. Avoid applying a single cohort’s outcome percentage to every patient Dural AV fistula Treatable; strength and gait improve more than pain or sphincter function; delay causes permanent deficit B12 / copper deficiency Halts or improves with replacement; delayed treatment leaves residual deficits

Military medicine — duty, retention and deployment

  • Profile / function: A new cord syndrome requires urgent care/transfer. Subsequently document mobility, hand function, bladder/bowel, sensation and respiratory support.
  • Retention / MEB–MAR2: Retention depends on cause, residual function and recovery; inflammatory demyelination, trauma, tumor and permanent paralysis invoke different standards. Use the retention framework; permanent P3/4 does not by itself select DES versus MAR2.
  • Deployment / medications: Assess recurrence, need for assistance, autonomic risk and access to rehabilitation/specialty care. Immunotherapy and anticoagulation create separate medication issues. See the disease AND drug screen for the current CENTCOM rules and waiver packet.
  • Special duty: flight, diving and other special assignments have separate standards and waiver authorities; a general duty profile does not clear them.
  • LOD / EPTS: document onset, duty status, exposures and aggravation objectively. The designated authority determines LOD/EPTS; neither in-service diagnosis nor a genetic finding settles it automatically.

docs.title: 📚 Discover — evidence brief
docs.text:
Written from primary guidelines and trials; source articles are a reading list, not copied.

  • Compression first, always. The 2026 ACR Appropriateness Criteria update keeps extrinsic cord compression as the first thing to exclude in acute-onset myelopathy, with MRI of the spine without and with IV contrast as the key study — and the whole spine when cancer is suspected, because multilevel compression is common.
  • Tempo + compartment beats any single test. Hyperacute onset points vascular; hours-to-days under 3 weeks points inflammatory; beyond 3 weeks it is almost never transverse myelitis. Enhancement and CSF pleocytosis do not separate myelitis from spondylotic mimics.
  • NMOSD is the time-critical inflammatory myelitis. Untreated attacks leave only 21.6% fully recovered, and PLEX belongs first-line or within days — ideally within 2 — not as a salvage after weeks of steroids. MOGAD is the mirror image: steroid-responsive, slow taper over up to 6 months, relapses clustering below ~10 mg prednisone.
  • Steroids are dangerous in the wrong myelopathy. Empiric steroids before MRI risk masking lymphoma and worsening a dural AV fistula (rapid deterioration in about half); malignant cord compression is the one setting where steroids start on suspicion.
  • Antibody assay quality decides the diagnosis. Live cell-based AQP4-IgG (sensitivity

    80%, specificity >99%) and MOG-IgG with the ≥1:100 clear-positive threshold — ELISA low titers and off-attack MOG titers mislead in both directions.

  • Supportive care is outcome care. Bladder/bowel programs, LMWH within 72 hours when safe, a spinal cord unit, and rehabilitation starting once stable — with prognosis set by cause and by function before treatment, especially in metastatic compression and infarction (severity at nadir strongly influences recovery; a single cohort percentage is not a universal prognosis).

Key sources: ACR Appropriateness Criteria Myelopathy 2026 Update; Wingerchuk et al. 2015 NMOSD criteria; 2023 international MOGAD panel criteria (Banwell et al., Lancet Neurology); JAMA Neurology 2019 MOG myelitis comparison; Ciccarelli et al., Lancet Neurology 2019; Cortese et al., Neurology 2023; MENACTRIMS NMOSD consensus (CNS Drugs 2026); NEJM spinal epidural abscess review (April 23, 2026); Essibayi et al., spinal dural AV fistulas (Neurology 2023).

docs.title: CIDP & IVIG Order Set
docs.text:
Last reviewed: November 2026

One-liner: the prescriptive approach to chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP) under the 2021 EAN/PNS criteria — how to make the diagnosis and not miss its mimics, first-line IVIG vs steroids vs plasma exchange with exact doses, the practical IVIG order set (labs, rates, adverse-effect plan), subcutaneous immunoglobulin and efgartigimod for maintenance, and what to do when CIDP is refractory. For the neurologist, or the PCP/internist admitting a patient with progressive symmetric weakness and demyelinating nerve-conduction studies. Educational clinical decision-support, not medical advice — verify doses and eligibility against current labeling and guidelines before ordering.

🚩 Red flags — reconsider CIDP, or act now

Pattern Worry Do now Rapidly progressive weakness Consider GBS, acute-onset CIDP and other mimics. Classic GBS usually reaches nadir within four weeks. Further worsening beyond eight weeks or three or more treatment-related fluctuations should prompt reassessment for acute-onset CIDP. Use the acute weakness pathway for urgent respiratory and bulbar assessment and syndrome-specific treatment. Respiratory or bulbar weakness Ventilatory failure — rare in CIDP, dangerous whenever present Admit, forced vital capacity / negative inspiratory force, ICU triage Marked asymmetry, severe pain, or stepwise deficits Vasculitic neuropathy or multifocal CIDP mimics (vasculitis, HNPP, multifocal motor neuropathy) Urgent vasculitis workup; do not default to "CIDP" on asymmetry alone IgM paraprotein, especially with distal sensory-predominant disease Anti-MAG neuropathy — no longer classed as CIDP, and it responds poorly to standard CIDP therapy Anti-MAG antibody; reframe the diagnosis before escalating immunotherapy Sensory ataxia/pseudoathetosis with normal motor studies Sensory neuronopathy, CISP, or sensory CIDP — distinguish by sensory conduction and the clinical distribution Dorsal-root-ganglion / paraneoplastic workup; sensory CIDP requires the pattern below Upper-motor-neuron signs, fasciculations with pure motor disease Motor neuron disease mimicking motor CIDP EMG + neurology review before committing to chronic immunotherapy Nodal–paranodal antibody clues (e.g. severe ataxia, tremor, poor IVIG response) Autoimmune nodopathy — a separate entity, not CIDP Nodal–paranodal antibody panel; nodopathies may need rituximab rather than IVIG

docs.title: Diagnosis / classification (2021 EAN/PNS)
docs.text: CIDP is a clinical phenotype + electrodiagnostic diagnosis. There are only two certainty levels — "CIDP" and "possible CIDP". The old "definite/probable/possible" scheme was dropped: without a gold standard, definite and probable performed no differently. Diagnostic and many sequencing recommendations rest on low-certainty evidence; IVIG efficacy versus placebo has high-certainty support, and real-world validation found more than a third of patients meeting electrodiagnostic criteria fit no defined phenotype — so phenotype first, numbers second.

docs.title: Typical CIDP — all of the following must be present
docs.text:
• Symmetric weakness affecting proximal and distal muscles of the upper and lower limbs
  • Sensory involvement in ≥2 limbs
  • Progressive or relapsing course developing over ≥8 weeks in typical CIDP. Acute-onset CIDP can initially resemble GBS.
  • Reduced or absent tendon reflexes throughout the limbs

For a variant, the distribution or modality differs as below; reflexes may remain normal in unaffected limbs.

docs.title: Variants
docs.text:
Variant Defining clinical pattern Classic mimics to exclude Distal CIDP (formerly DADS) Distal sensory loss + gait instability; weakness if present is distal, worse in legs Anti-MAG / IgM paraprotein (~2/3 of the phenotype), diabetic, hereditary, amyloid Multifocal CIDP (Lewis–Sumner / MADSAM) Asymmetric sensory + motor involvement in ≥2 limbs, usually starting in the arms; cranial nerves more often involved Vasculitis, HNPP, multifocal motor neuropathy Focal CIDP Sensory + motor involvement confined to 1 limb Same as multifocal, localized Motor CIDP Motor symptoms/signs only, with normal sensory studies Multifocal motor neuropathy, motor neuron disease Motor-predominant CIDP Clinically motor presentation, with sensory abnormalities detected on nerve-conduction studies As for motor CIDP Sensory CIDP Sensory symptoms/signs only (motor conduction must be normal) Sensory neuronopathy, CISP, anti-MAG neuropathy Sensory-predominant CIDP Sensory presentation with minor motor involvement As for sensory CIDP

No longer classed as CIDP: autoimmune nodopathies (nodal–paranodal antibodies), anti-MAG neuropathy, and chronic immune sensory polyradiculopathy (CISP). Calling them CIDP misdirects therapy.

docs.title: Electrodiagnostic criteria — motor conduction (strongly supportive of demyelination)
docs.text:
Study >4 nerves, add proximal stimulation in the upper limbs, keep limbs warm (palm ≥33 °C, malleolus ≥30 °C), and repeat later if criteria are not met the first time. At least one of the following, with nerve counts by phenotype:

  • Distal motor latency ≥50% above the upper limit of normal (ULN) in 2 nerves (median nerve with carpal tunnel syndrome excluded)
  • Conduction velocity ≥30% below the lower limit of normal (LLN) in 2 nerves
  • F-wave latency ≥20% above ULN in 2 nerves (≥50% if distal CMAP <80% LLN)
  • Absent F-waves in 2 nerves (only if distal CMAP ≥20% LLN) plus ≥1 other demyelinating parameter in ≥1 other nerve
  • Motor conduction block — proximal/distal CMAP amplitude reduction ≥30% (distal CMAP ≥20% LLN) in 2 nerves, or 1 nerve + another demyelinating parameter in another nerve
  • Abnormal temporal dispersion in ≥2 nerves
  • Distal CMAP duration prolongation in ≥1 nerve + ≥1 other demyelinating parameter in another nerve

Sensory conduction abnormalities are now required: typical CIDP needs them in ≥2 nerves.

docs.title: Certainty — how the pieces combine
docs.text:
• Typical CIDP = "CIDP" if motor criteria are met in ≥2 nerves and sensory abnormalities in ≥2 nerves; "possible" if motor criteria in only 1 nerve.
  • If the clinical picture fits but minimal electrodiagnostic criteria are not met, possible typical CIDP may be supported by objective treatment response plus at least one other supportive criterion, following the guideline’s specific pathway.
  • Distal / multifocal / focal / motor variants follow the same structure: "CIDP" when ≥2 nerves meet criteria, "possible" when 1 does; the nerves must fit the phenotype pattern (distal criteria are especially strict — the main source of misdiagnosis).
  • Pure sensory CIDP has a maximum certainty of possible sensory CIDP. Focal CIDP can meet CIDP criteria when motor criteria occur in ≥2 nerves in one limb and sensory abnormalities in ≥2 affected-limb nerves; one qualifying motor nerve supports possible focal CIDP.

docs.title: Supportive criteria — upgrade "possible" → "CIDP" (two needed, or one + objective treatment response in some pathways)
docs.text:
• Raised CSF protein with WBC <10/µL
  • Nerve ultrasound enlargement of the proximal median nerve, cervical roots, or brachial plexus
  • MRI gadolinium enhancement or hypertrophy of roots/plexus
  • Objective improvement after treatment on validated scales
  • Nerve biopsy (sural, occasionally superficial peroneal) showing demyelination/remyelination — a positive biopsy is not specific, and a negative biopsy does not exclude CIDP

docs.title: Rapid approach
docs.text:
1. Exclude the dangerous thing first: rapidly progressive weakness, respiratory/bulbar involvement, or severe pain/asymmetry → acute weakness or vasculitis pathway, not routine CIDP workup.
  2. Classify the phenotype from the table above — the phenotype decides which electrodiagnostic counts apply and which mimic to chase.
  3. Order the required workup (below) and the baseline IVIG labs in the same visit — paraprotein and antibody results change the diagnosis, and serologies must be drawn before any immunoglobulin infusion.
  4. Route to the tiered management below and fix an objective baseline (INCAT, grip strength, I-RODS) before the first dose — without it, you cannot judge response, remission, or failure.

docs.title: The prescriptive flow (what I want done, in order)
docs.text:
1. Confirm the phenotype and the electrodiagnostic criteria; complete the required workup (paraprotein screen, anti-MAG if IgM, nodal–paranodal antibodies, CSF, ultrasound/MRI as indicated).
  2. Start Step 1 first-line therapy, matched to the patient (table below) — IVIG 2 g/kg induction for most, pulsed steroids when cost/access or lasting remission is the priority, PLEX for severe disease or first-line failure.
  3. Measure response objectively at the same scale points. IVIG non-response after one course is not failure — give a second course or 1 g/kg every 3 weeks × 2–5 doses before calling it.
  4. If Step 1 fails or is not tolerated, switch to another first-line option before adding anything else — and reconsider the diagnosis first, because misdiagnosis is common in "refractory" CIDP.
  5. Maintenance: lowest dose holding maximal improvement; try reducing every 6–12 months in the first 2–3 years, then every 1–2 years, to test for remission.
  6. Refractory disease (Step 3): PLEX induction, then rituximab / cyclophosphamide / cyclosporine with a 3–6 month stop rule; efgartigimod as a maintenance alternative for IgG-mediated disease.

docs.title: Workup
docs.text:
Required CIDP workup — order at diagnosis

  • Monoclonal gammopathy screen in every patient (serum/urine immunofixation + free light chains)
  • Anti-MAG antibody if an IgM paraprotein is present
  • Nodal–paranodal antibodies when clinically indicated (e.g., atypical features or poor response): (neurofascin, contactin, Caspr1 and related targets per local panel)
  • CSF when needed for support or exclusion of mimics: protein + cell count (raised protein with WBC <10/µL is supportive)
  • Supportive imaging when needed: nerve ultrasound (proximal median nerve, cervical roots, brachial plexus) or MRI of roots/plexus with gadolinium, where available
  • Nerve biopsy only when the diagnosis remains uncertain after the above — sural, occasionally superficial peroneal
  • Baseline objective scales before treatment: INCAT disability score, grip dynamometry, I-RODS, MRC sum score, timed walking
  • Draw any needed serologies BEFORE the first immunoglobulin infusion — passively transferred antibodies cause false positives, including a positive Coombs test

docs.title: Management
docs.text:
Step 1 — first-line (start here for most)

  • IVIG — 2 g/kg total, split over 2–5 days (usual daily cap ≤80 g/day). Fastest response, fewer long-term side effects than steroids; ~76% of treatment-naive patients respond. High-certainty evidence vs placebo. Then maintenance 1 g/kg every 3 weeks (given in 1 day, or 0.5 g/kg on 2 consecutive days), titrating over time to the lowest effective dose, typically 0.4–1 g/kg every 2–6 weeks.
  • OR corticosteroids (regimens appear equally effective — pick one): prednisone/prednisolone 60 mg/day orally, tapered slowly over 6–8 months; OR pulsed dexamethasone 40 mg/day × 4 days every 4 weeks × 6 months; OR pulsed IV methylprednisolone 500 mg/day × 4 days each month × 6 months (or 1,000 mg weekly or monthly). Pulsed regimens have fewer side effects and act faster than daily oral (low–moderate certainty). Add calcium + vitamin D, consider a bisphosphonate; watch gastric ulceration, diabetes, hypertension, cataracts, avascular necrosis.
  • OR plasma exchange — 5–10 exchanges on alternate days over 2–4 weeks for severe disease or when IVIG/steroids are unsuitable. Similarly effective for induction, but invasive, needs venous access and specialist facilities, and is rarely used for maintenance.
  • Non-response rule: after a first IVIG course, give either 1 g/kg every 3 weeks for 2–5 doses or a second 2 g/kg course a few weeks later before calling IVIG failure. In ProCID, 56% improved 3 weeks after the loading dose alone; maintenance response was 65% at 0.5 g/kg, 80% at 1.0 g/kg, and 92% at 2.0 g/kg every 3 weeks (only 0.5 vs 2.0 differed significantly).
  • → Inadequate, intolerable, or contraindicated → Step 2.

Step 2 — switch first-line, then maintenance alternatives

  • Switch to another first-line option before adding anything else. After IVIG failure, 67% responded to PLEX and 59% to steroids; ~75% who then failed PLEX/steroids responded to the remaining option. Involve the patient in the choice.
  • Subcutaneous immunoglobulin (SCIg) for maintenance — FDA-approved for adult CIDP maintenance since 2018: 0.2 or 0.4 g/kg/week (split 2–3 infusions/week for induction-style loading where used: 0.4 g/kg/week × 5 weeks, limited evidence). In PATH, both doses beat placebo (absolute relapse reduction 25% at 0.2 g/kg, 30% at 0.4 g/kg). Good candidates: poor venous access, headache/systemic IVIG side effects, long distance to an infusion centre, frequent travel. More injection-site reactions; fewer systemic effects; no venous access or premedication needed.
  • Efgartigimod alfa–hyaluronidase (Vyvgart Hytrulo) — subcutaneous once weekly as a maintenance alternative: 1,000 mg efgartigimod alfa + 10,000 units hyaluronidase in a prefilled syringe (patient/caregiver-administered), or 1,008 mg + 11,200 units from a vial. FDA-approved for adults with CIDP June 2024 (also EMA-approved) on the ADHERE trial — see Discover. The approval is not restricted to patients who have failed IVIG, and it applies to the subcutaneous combination product (IV Vyvgart remains labeled for generalized myasthenia gravis). No head-to-head vs IVIG and no established superiority to IVIG; treat as an alternative maintenance option, not a replacement for established first-line therapy. Reasonable when maintenance IVIG/SCIg is burdensome, poorly tolerated, or contraindicated, when IVIG supply/access is a problem, or when the patient prefers weekly home self-injection. Caution: response was lower in previously IVIG-treated patients, and FcRn blockade acts on IgG, so presumed IgM- or IgA-mediated disease may not respond. How best to transition from IgG therapy is not yet defined, and a switch from effective IVIG requires careful monitoring — the current label reports worsening CIDP signs/symptoms during transition from IVIG. Establish objective baselines and a monitoring/rescue plan, and reassess continuation if neurological symptoms worsen.
  • → Still refractory after all three first-line options → Step 3.

Step 3 — refractory CIDP

  • Plasma exchange induction first: 5 exchanges over 10 days.
  • Second-line (EAN/PNS, case-series evidence only): rituximab, cyclophosphamide, or cyclosporine — stop if no objective benefit within 3–6 months.
  • Steroid-/IVIG-sparing agents: azathioprine, mycophenolate, cyclosporine — take >6 months to work; evidence for azathioprine and methotrexate is not robust.
  • Investigational / last resort (flagged as such, not routine): riliprubart (C1s inhibitor) remains investigational; the MOBILIZE phase 3 refractory-CIDP study was stopped in June 2026. Earlier phase-2 response percentages do not establish phase-3 efficacy. Other FcRn inhibitors (nipocalimab, batoclimab) are in trials; small phase 2 rozanolixizumab was negative. Autologous haematopoietic stem-cell transplant has been reported to benefit selected patients. Not supported: alemtuzumab, natalizumab, fingolimod, methotrexate, and others.
  • Before escalating any "refractory" label: specialty referral and diagnostic reconsideration — many patients labeled IVIG-refractory improve when maintenance is increased (e.g. every-2-week dosing), and misdiagnosis is common.

docs.title: Choosing first-line therapy
docs.text: Patient / situation Preferred agent Why Pure motor CIDP IVIG Avoid steroids — they can worsen motor CIDP Severe or rapidly progressing disease IVIG (or PLEX) Fastest response Osteoporosis, diabetes, or other steroid contraindication IVIG / SCIg Avoids long-term steroid toxicity Need for fast response IVIG Weeks vs months for steroids Cost/access matters, no steroid risk factors, lasting remission is the goal Corticosteroids, pulsed preferred Cheap; pulsed regimens may give more and longer remissions at 6 months Severe disease, or IVIG/steroids failed or unsuitable Plasma exchange Similarly effective induction; invasive and facility-dependent Maintenance burden, poor venous access, IVIG intolerance, or home-therapy preference SCIg, or efgartigimod weekly SC See Step 2 doses

docs.title: Tapering — test for remission, don't just continue
docs.text:
• IVIG: once stable, try reducing the dose (e.g. by 25% per infusion), lengthening the interval, or stopping — every 6–12 months for the first 2–3 years, then every 1–2 years. Fix end-of-dose wearing-off first by raising the dose or shortening the interval; do not mistake wearing-off for treatment failure.
  • Steroids: taper daily prednisolone slowly over 6–8 months, guided by response and side effects; pulsed regimens run 6 months, daily prednisolone up to 15 months.
  • All therapies: separate active disease from fixed axonal deficits, which will not improve with more immunotherapy. Treatment failure means failure of an adequate trial on objective scales — not persistent numbness, pain, or fatigue alone.

Avoid

  • Steroids in pure motor CIDP — use IVIG first.
  • Labeling IVIG failure after a single course — a second course or 1 g/kg every 3 weeks × 2–5 doses is required first.
  • Escalating immunotherapy for fixed axonal deficits — more drug will not recover dead axons; reassess the diagnosis instead.
  • Routine premedication for every IVIG infusion — reserve it for high-risk patients or prior reactions (see order set).
  • Routine anti-IgA testing — low IgA alone is not a contraindication (see order set).

docs.title: IVIG order set — practical prescribing
docs.text:
IVIG order set for CIDP (adult, first infusion)

  • Dose: 2 g/kg total induction, split over 2–5 days (usual cap ≤80 g/day); maintenance 1 g/kg every 3 weeks, titrating to the lowest effective dose (0.4–1 g/kg every 2–6 weeks).
  • Pre-infusion labs / screening: BUN + creatinine before the first infusion and periodically after; confirm the patient is not volume-depleted. CBC + ABO blood group (non-O groups carry higher hemolysis risk, highest in AB then A); baseline haemoglobin as the reference for post-infusion monitoring. Clot-risk review: age >65, prior VTE/arterial events, atherosclerosis/cardiovascular disease, diabetes, hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia, immobility, dehydration, heart failure, kidney failure. Viscosity at baseline when hyperviscosity is possible (monoclonal gammopathy, cryoglobulins, markedly high triglycerides). Migraine history (raises aseptic-meningitis risk). IgA: low IgA alone is NOT a contraindication — IVIG is contraindicated only in IgA-deficient patients who have anti-IgA antibodies plus a prior hypersensitivity reaction; routine anti-IgA testing adds little.
  • Premedication: routine premedication NOT required. After a prior reaction: acetaminophen or ibuprofen + diphenhydramine or a non-sedating H1 blocker, with or without hydrocortisone, 1 hour before infusion. Hydration (oral or IV) before infusion helps prevent hypotension, renal injury, and aseptic meningitis — limit volume in heart failure/kidney failure. Keep epinephrine at the bedside for every infusion.
  • Infusion rates (10% product; Gamunex-C CIDP label): 2 mg/kg/min (0.02 mL/kg/min) for the first 30 minutes, then step up as tolerated to a maximum of 8 mg/kg/min (0.08 mL/kg/min). Use the minimum practical rate with kidney or clot risk. Other brands are product-specific (e.g. ASCENIV starts at 0.5 mg/kg/min); brands differ in approved indications, excipients, contraindications and rates; do not infer CIDP approval or interchangeability from class membership. A specialist-directed switch may improve tolerability. Reactions are most likely during the first infusion of a given product and less likely after 3 treatments with the same product.
  • Monitoring during infusion: vital signs; watch for anaphylaxis, fluid overload, and TRALI (respiratory distress, hypoxaemia, fever 1–6 hours after starting).
  • Monitoring after infusion: creatinine + urine output in at-risk patients; haemoglobin, reticulocytes, LDH, bilirubin, and direct antiglobulin test if haemolysis is suspected — haemolysis typically occurs 5–10 days after a high-dose course; consider routine checks in that window for non-O patients receiving 2 g/kg. Watch clot symptoms and headache/meningism for up to 48 hours. Sodium: distinguish true hyponatraemia from pseudohyponatraemia from high serum protein — restricting water in pseudohyponatraemia worsens viscosity/clot risk. Track efficacy objectively with INCAT, grip strength, and I-RODS.

docs.title: IVIG adverse effects — prevention and management
docs.text:
Adverse effect When / who Prevention Management Infusion reactions (headache, flushing, chills, myalgia, BP changes) During infusion; 5–15% of infusions; headache was the most common adverse event in ProCID Slow titration, hydration, premedicate after a prior reaction Slow or stop 15–30 min, then restart at the last tolerated rate Anaphylaxis / IgA-related Seconds to hours; IgA deficiency with anti-IgA IgE After a serious reaction, stop and obtain allergy/immunology + neuromuscular review; a low-IgA product or SCIg is not automatically safe, and exact product contraindications apply Stop infusion; epinephrine, oxygen, antihistamines, IV steroids Acute kidney injury Pre-existing CKD, volume depletion, older age, diabetes, sucrose-stabilized products Hydrate, avoid sucrose products, minimum rate, check creatinine first Stop IVIG if kidney function worsens Thrombosis (MI, stroke, DVT/PE) Usually at the end of or after infusion; CV risk factors, age >65, hyperviscosity, immobility Hydrate, minimum rate, check viscosity if at risk, consider splitting doses over more days Standard clot management; reassess benefit vs risk Haemolysis 5–10 days after; blood group AB/A, dose ≥2 g/kg, first course Know the ABO group, products with reduced isoagglutinins, lower doses/splitting where possible Confirm with labs; supportive care; transfusion if needed Aseptic meningitis Hours to 2 days; dose ≥2 g/kg, rapid infusion, migraine history Acetaminophen, hydration, slow rate Lumbar puncture to exclude infection; analgesia; stop IVIG if possible; resolves within days with no lasting effects

TRICARE — verified rules and the current form

Vyvgart Hytrulo 1,000 mg/5 mL prefilled syringe has a pharmacy PA flag; HyQvia/Hizentra have 365-day prior-use/history rules. IVIG products and clinician-administered therapies may use medical-benefit authorization. Obtain the current CIDP form, objective diagnostic/response measures and renewal criteria; payer failure counts were not independently verified.

Current PA/MN details, benefit routing and packet · Live Formulary Search. Check the exact product, beneficiary and venue on the prescribing date.

docs.title: Disposition
docs.text:
• Admit for rapidly progressive weakness, respiratory/bulbar involvement, severe pain/asymmetry suggesting vasculitis, or a first PLEX course requiring central access and monitoring.
  • Outpatient for stable, confirmed CIDP on maintenance therapy, with neurology follow-up tied to infusion intervals and objective-scale reassessment at each taper decision.
  • Follow-up: reassess INCAT/grip/I-RODS at every maintenance interval change; formal taper attempts every 6–12 months in the first 2–3 years, then every 1–2 years.

Military medicine — duty, retention and deployment

  • Profile / function: Document strength, gait, hand function, falls and measurable treatment response; restrict tasks affected by weakness or sensory loss.
  • Retention / MEB–MAR2: Use the applicable neuropathy/functional standards, including DoDI V2 5.26.i and Army Chapter 3; do not infer a board solely from receiving IVIG. Use the retention framework; permanent P3/4 does not by itself select DES versus MAR2.
  • Deployment / medications: Weekly SC therapy, home administration or improved gait is not deployment clearance. Evaluate injections, immunomodulation, rescue needs, resupply and objective deterioration if treatment is delayed. See the disease AND drug screen for the current CENTCOM rules and waiver packet.
  • Special duty: flight, diving and other special assignments have separate standards and waiver authorities; a general duty profile does not clear them.
  • LOD / EPTS: document onset, duty status, exposures and aggravation objectively. The designated authority determines LOD/EPTS; neither in-service diagnosis nor a genetic finding settles it automatically.

docs.title: 📚 Discover — evidence brief
docs.text:
Written from primary guidelines and trials; source articles are a reading list, not copied.

  • The 2021 EAN/PNS guideline rebuilt CIDP diagnosis around phenotype + electrodiagnostics and dropped "definite/probable" — a patient is "CIDP" or "possible CIDP," and pure sensory CIDP has a possible-only ceiling; focal CIDP can meet full criteria. The practical consequence is diagnostic discipline: distal CIDP criteria are strict because that phenotype is where misdiagnosis concentrates, and anti-MAG disease, nodopathies, and CISP are now separate diagnoses, not CIDP subtypes.
  • First-line therapy is a three-way tie on efficacy, not a ladder: IVIG, steroids, and PLEX each help roughly 50–80%, and switching between them rescues most "failures" — which is why the guideline insists on an adequate trial of each (including a second IVIG course) before declaring refractory disease.
  • Maintenance is where the field moved: SCIg (PATH) made home maintenance routine, ProCID defined the dose–response curve for IVIG maintenance (0.5 → 1.0 → 2.0 g/kg every 3 weeks), and ADHERE added weekly subcutaneous efgartigimod as a maintenance alternative — with a 61% reduction in relapse risk vs placebo in the randomized-withdrawal phase, but no head-to-head against IVIG.
  • The order set is the safety story: most IVIG harm is preventable — hydration and slow titration for kidney injury and meningitis, ABO awareness for haemolysis at days 5–10, and clot-risk review before every high-dose course.

Key sources: 2021 EAN/PNS CIDP guideline; ProCID IVIG dose-ranging trial; PATH SCIg trial; ADHERE efgartigimod trial; Gamunex-C and Privigen labeling; Ontario IVIG Infusion Guide.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Van den Bergh PYK, et al. European Academy of Neurology/Peripheral Nerve Society guideline on diagnosis and treatment of chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy: Report of a joint Task Force of the European Academy of Neurology and the Peripheral Nerve Society. Eur J Neurol. 2021. — anchors the diagnostic criteria, phenotypes, first-line choices, and refractory pathway on this page.
  2. ProCID trial — IVIG dose-ranging in CIDP (0.5 vs 1.0 vs 2.0 g/kg every 3 weeks; loading-dose response). Dose–response figures on this page.
  3. PATH trial — subcutaneous immunoglobulin for CIDP maintenance (0.2 and 0.4 g/kg/week vs placebo; relapse reduction). SCIg maintenance doses on this page.
  4. ADHERE trial — efgartigimod alfa–hyaluronidase in CIDP (Stage A open-label response 214/322, 66%; Stage B relapse 27.9% vs 53.6%, HR 0.39; FDA approval June 2024). Efgartigimod dosing and positioning on this page.
  5. Gamunex-C prescribing information (CIDP label) — IVIG infusion-rate titration (2 → 8 mg/kg/min) and daily cap context.
  6. Privigen prescribing information; Ontario IVIG Infusion Guide and Adverse Reaction Chart v3.0; Payne et al., Hospital Pharmacy 2025, IVIG administration protocol review — order-set, premedication, and adverse-effect details.

  7. Official TRICARE sources, retrieved forms and access limits.

  8. HyQvia — FDA-approved facilitated SC immunoglobulin for adult CIDP maintenance.

  9. Vyvgart Hytrulo — current label, including transition-worsening reports.

docs.title: Adding or updating a topic
docs.text: Use the migraine page as a style reference and includes/topic-template.md as a starting skeleton. Keep the bedside action easy to find. A reader should know what to do now, what can wait, what defines failure and who needs a call.

docs.title: Clinical structure
docs.text:
1. Title, owner-approved review date, one-liner and intended reader. Record the evidence audit separately.
  2. Red flags and immediate action; diagnosis/classification with the important exclusions.
  3. Rapid approach, workup and a numbered management flow.
  4. Dosed adult first-line options, escalation criteria, contraindications and disposition. Label pediatric or off-label regimens explicitly; do not imply that every listed alternative belongs in one combined order set.
  5. A short condition-specific military assessment, linked to retention, deployment/medications and TRICARE.
  6. A plain-language evidence brief and matching primary references. State what is uncertain when it changes the decision.

docs.title: Evidence and tone
docs.text:
Follow the evidence and update policy. Use current issuing-society guidance, original trials, FDA labeling and official policy. Separate a clinical recommendation from a payer requirement and from deployment eligibility. Record actual form/version dates and distinguish PA, MN, quantity limits and medical-benefit authorization.

Write in your own words. Dry humor is welcome when it makes the point memorable; give the useful action first and keep emergencies, doses and patients out of the punchline. Avoid presenting an AI answer or a review stamp as proof that every claim was independently verified.

Do not publish patient details, Army restricted material or personnel information. Common abbreviations belong in includes/abbreviations.md.

docs.title: Preview and publication
docs.text:
Add the page to mkdocs.yml, preview it, and build with mkdocs build --strict into a separate preview directory. Check internal links and mobile readability. Have a clinician review material clinical changes and resolve or visibly bound source gaps.

Obtain the site owner’s explicit approval before pushing or publishing. This repository updates a public website. Keep a reviewable change log with the source and reason for each material correction.

docs.title: What “reviewed” means here
docs.text:
The text was read for dangerous instructions, internal contradictions, outdated guidelines, drug-label changes, unsupported comparative claims and military/coverage assumptions. Material corrections were checked against accessible primary guidelines, trials, FDA labels and official DoD/TRICARE sources. Evidence briefs distinguish trial findings, observational data and clinical interpretation where those distinctions change a decision.

This is an AI-assisted editorial/clinical evidence review, not independent clinician certification of every sentence or a systematic review of every drug on the site. Some cited papers were accessible only as abstracts or partial full text. An automated FDA-label screen supported, but did not replace, manual review; it does not validate every dose, combination or off-label regimen. Historical statements that every dose had been “verified” through AI answer services have been removed.

docs.title: Independent correction pass — 22 November 2026
docs.text:
The first proposal was not ready to publish unchanged. A second pass corrected regulatory status, device/dose distinctions, stroke-selection recommendations, safety instructions, indication-specific coverage examples and references that resolved to unrelated papers. New approvals were checked against current FDA labeling; trial statements were checked against primary reports where accessible. The dated correction record is in review/site-wide-2026-11-22/50-changelog.md, with source mapping and its limits in 40-ledger.md.

Research-identifier checks establish that the citation names the intended paper; they do not verify every assertion on the page. Many legacy quantitative statements still lack an individually adjudicated entry in the claim ledger. Current specialty-drug PA forms were not all obtainable, and this review cannot determine an individual patient’s benefits or deployment clearance. Those gaps remain explicit rather than being filled with assumed criteria. Page footers dated 21 November identify the initial pass; original owner review stamps were preserved.

docs.title: How to use a clinical page
docs.text:
• Start with red flags and the first actions. Drug doses are generally adult unless a pediatric regimen is explicitly identified; do not scale an adult order set to a child.
  • Check indication, route, organ function, pregnancy, interactions and local administration protocol before ordering. A table is not an individualized prescription.
  • New or conflicting safety information should prompt review of the current product label and relevant specialist guidance.
  • Use the TRICARE page for the exact coverage scope and forms retrieved. A missing form is marked as unresolved; clinical step therapy is not invented.
  • Use the deployment guide for the CENTCOM-specific snapshot and the retention guide for the separate Service framework.

docs.title: Updating the site
docs.text:
For each material recommendation, record the source/version, applicable population, action, important exclusions and review date. Prefer the issuing society, trial report, FDA label or official policy over summaries of summaries. Cite the source beside the recommendation or in a clearly matching reference entry.

When a new guideline differs from an older trial, explain which population or decision changed. Do not label a negative study as supportive, a pending application as approval, or a single observational comparison as proof of superiority. Replace a definitive instruction with a bounded recommendation when uncertainty matters.

For humor, aim at bureaucracy and clinical absurdity. Keep doses, resuscitation instructions, uncertainty and vulnerable patients out of the punchline. Put the useful action before the joke; the person reading this may be holding a pager and a sandwich of uncertain provenance.

Before publication: a clinician should review the clinical changes, the remaining source limits and any locally applicable policy. Preview the pages and check links. Publishing requires the site owner’s explicit authorization; pushing the repository updates the public site.

docs.title: Hypercoagulable workup
docs.text:
Last reviewed: November 2026

One-liner: For the on-call neuro, ED, or clinic clinician seeing a young adult with unprovoked VTE, arterial thrombosis, or unusual-site thrombosis — which thrombophilia tests to order, which to skip (MTHFR is out), when to send them, and when the result actually changes management.

🚩 Red flags — don't let the workup delay the treatment

Pattern Worry Do now Arterial thrombosis (stroke, MI, limb ischemia) in a patient <50 y with no atherosclerotic explanation Antiphospholipid syndrome Use the acute stroke/arterial-ischemia pathway; send the full APS panel when indicated. Do not automatically heparinize acute ischemic stroke for suspected APS; antithrombotic choice/timing depends on the event, imaging, and specialist review Cerebral venous thrombosis or splanchnic-vein thrombosis APS, JAK2-positive MPN, PNH Venous imaging now (MRV/CTV for CVT; contrast CT for splanchnic); anticoagulate — see Cerebral venous thrombosis Recurrent VTE, or VTE + thrombocytopenia / livedo racemosa / valve disease APS (often triple-positive) Anticoagulate; send the APS panel; do not start a DOAC until APS is excluded — triple-positive APS needs warfarin Thrombosis + cytopenias, hemolysis, or unexplained erythrocytosis/thrombocytosis PNH, JAK2-positive myeloproliferative neoplasm CBC, LDH, haptoglobin, reticulocytes; JAK2 V617F; PNH flow cytometry — hematology Any acute thrombosis The workup itself Treat the event first. VTE usually needs anticoagulation; arterial stroke follows its own pathway. Do not delay indicated treatment to draw the panel — DNA and antibody tests can be sent anytime; functional tests (protein C/S, antithrombin, lupus anticoagulant) are unreliable acutely and on anticoagulation, so they wait

docs.title: Diagnosis / classification
docs.text: "Thrombophilia" here means two buckets — inherited and acquired. The inherited defects are factor V Leiden (FVL), prothrombin G20210A, and antithrombin, protein C, and protein S deficiency. The acquired one that matters is antiphospholipid syndrome (APS). Inherited thrombophilias are principally venous — their association with arterial stroke, MI, and peripheral arterial thrombosis is weak and inconsistent, so do not order them for arterial events.

docs.title: The valid panel — order these, and only these
docs.text: Test What it is Notes Antithrombin activity Physiologic anticoagulant deficiency Functional — send later, off anticoagulation (see timing) Protein C activity Physiologic anticoagulant deficiency Functional — send later; warfarin falsely lowers it Protein S (free antigen preferred) Physiologic anticoagulant deficiency Functional — send later; warfarin falsely lowers it; pregnancy lowers activity Factor V Leiden (PCR) DNA test Valid anytime, on or off anticoagulation Prothrombin G20210A (PCR) DNA test Valid anytime, on or off anticoagulation Lupus anticoagulant (LA) APS — functional/clot-based Most anticoagulant-sensitive test in the panel; send off anticoagulation if possible Anticardiolipin IgG/IgM (aCL) APS — ELISA Generally valid anytime Anti-β2-glycoprotein-I IgG/IgM (anti-β2GPI) APS — ELISA Generally valid anytime

docs.title: Antiphospholipid syndrome — 2023 ACR/EULAR classification criteria
docs.text:
These are research classification criteria, not diagnostic criteria — a patient can have APS clinically without meeting the score. Validation: specificity 99% vs 86% for the 2006 revised Sapporo criteria; sensitivity 84% vs 99%.

Entry criterion: at least 1 documented APS-associated clinical criterion and at least 1 positive aPL test (LA, or moderate/high aCL, or moderate/high anti-β2GPI, IgG or IgM), with the positive laboratory test occurring within 3 years of the clinical criterion.

Classification requires ≥3 clinical points AND ≥3 laboratory points — you cannot compensate for an inadequate clinical score with extra laboratory points, or vice versa. Within each domain, only the highest-weighted item counts. Do not score a manifestation if an equally or more likely alternative explanation exists.

Clinical domains:

Domain Criterion Points 1. Macrovascular VTE VTE with a high-risk VTE profile (e.g., major provoking factor) 1 VTE without a high-risk VTE profile 3 2. Macrovascular arterial thrombosis Arterial thrombosis with a high-risk cardiovascular profile 2 Arterial thrombosis without a high-risk cardiovascular profile 4 3. Microvascular Suspected: livedo racemosa, livedoid vasculopathy, aPL nephropathy, or pulmonary hemorrhage (exam/imaging) 2 Established: same findings confirmed by biopsy or definitive testing, plus myocardial disease or adrenal hemorrhage 5 4. Obstetric ≥3 consecutive pre-fetal losses <10 wk and/or early fetal deaths 10 wk–15 wk 6 d 1 Fetal death 16 wk–33 wk 6 d without severe preeclampsia or placental insufficiency 1 Severe preeclampsia or severe placental insufficiency <34 wk, ± fetal death 3 Severe preeclampsia and severe placental insufficiency <34 wk, ± fetal death 4 5. Cardiac valve Otherwise unexplained valve thickening 2 Otherwise unexplained valve vegetation 4 6. Hematologic Otherwise unexplained thrombocytopenia, lowest-ever platelet count 20–130 ×10⁹/L 2

Laboratory domains:

Laboratory finding Points Lupus anticoagulant positive once 1 Persistent lupus anticoagulant 5 Persistent moderate/high IgM aCL and/or anti-β2GPI 1 Persistent moderate IgG aCL and/or anti-β2GPI 4 Persistent high IgG aCL or anti-β2GPI 5 Persistent high IgG aCL and high IgG anti-β2GPI 7

Titer thresholds (standardized ELISA): moderate is 40–79 units; high is ≥80 units. The old ">99th percentile" cutoff is gone for classification. Low titers, IgA, and non-criteria antibodies (anti-phosphatidylserine/prothrombin, anti-domain-I β2GPI) do not score. IgG and IgM are not added together — a patient whose only positive test is IgM aCL/anti-β2GPI can reach at most 1 laboratory point and cannot be classified. Chemiluminescence and other automated assays have no validated moderate/high equivalents yet — do not transfer the ELISA cutoffs to them (2024/2025 ISTH laboratory guidance uses the assay-specific local cutoff, usually >99th percentile).

Persistence: two consecutive positive tests ≥12 weeks apart. If one serial result is moderate and the other high, score it moderate unless two consecutive high results are available. A single LA result can earn 1 point when repeat testing is not available.

Triple positivity = persistent positivity for LA + aCL + anti-β2GPI (studies applying the 2023 thresholds generally require IgG/IgM ≥40 units for both solid-phase tests). It is the strongest serologic predictor of thrombotic and obstetric events. Isotype matters: IgG-driven triple positivity carries much more risk than IgM-only — in one cohort, about half of IgM-only triple-positive patients had no clinical involvement. There is no separate "triple-positive = X points" row: persistent LA scores 5 points and high IgG on both solid-phase antibodies scores 7, in their respective domains.

What no longer scores: early pregnancy losses on their own, VTE in a patient with a high-risk VTE profile on its own, and isolated IgM. A "B-level" VTE combined with an obstetric item also does not reach the clinical threshold.

docs.title: Rapid approach
docs.text:
1. Treat the thrombotic event now. Anticoagulate VTE when indicated; acute arterial stroke needs the stroke pathway. Never choose immediate anticoagulation solely because APS is suspected.
  2. Ask the one question that decides whether to test at all: "Will a positive or negative result change something I am actually going to do?" If the answer is no, don't test.
  3. Send the anytime tests now (DNA + antibody immunoassays). Defer the functional tests (protein C, protein S, antithrombin, lupus anticoagulant) until the acute phase has passed and anticoagulation is off or bridged.
  4. Act on the result that matters most: APS. A positive inherited test after a first unprovoked VTE usually changes nothing; APS changes the drug.

docs.title: The prescriptive flow (what I want done, in order)
docs.text:
1. For VTE, anticoagulate for the event itself — primary treatment is generally 3–6 months; the duration decision comes after. Do not wait for any test result.
  2. Decide test vs no-test by scenario (table below). Default: do not test after a first unprovoked VTE or a surgery-provoked VTE. Test when the default is to stop anticoagulation and a positive result would extend it.
  3. Send Step 1 tests now (DNA + aCL/anti-β2GPI — valid anytime, even anticoagulated).
  4. Send Step 2 tests later (protein C, protein S, antithrombin, lupus anticoagulant) — ≥3 months into treatment, off interfering anticoagulants, with the washouts in the table below. Repeat any low result off confounders before labeling a hereditary deficiency.
  5. Interpret and act: APS (especially triple-positive) → warfarin, INR 2–3; avoid DOACs. Positive inherited thrombophilia after a first unprovoked VTE → usually no change (indefinite anticoagulation was already favored). Provoked VTE (nonsurgical major transient / pregnancy / postpartum / COC) with a positive test → continue indefinitely. Negative panel → do not use it as reassurance to stop after an otherwise unprovoked VTE.
  6. Family planning and relatives: test for a known familial high-risk defect (antithrombin, protein C, or protein S deficiency) when it would change contraception, HRT, or pregnancy prophylaxis. Do not screen the general population before COCs.
  7. Disposition and follow-up: driven by the thrombotic event, not the panel. Hematology referral for APS, triple positivity, unusual-site thrombosis, or a confirmed deficiency. Confirm APS persistence at ≥12 weeks.
Scenario Test to guide duration? ASH 2023 approach First unprovoked DVT/PE No Do not test to determine duration (Rec 1 — conditional, very-low-certainty) Surgery-provoked VTE No Do not test to determine duration VTE with a nonsurgical major transient risk factor (e.g., ≥3 days bed rest with acute illness) Yes Test; if thrombophilia found, continue indefinitely, else stop (Recs 3–5) Pregnancy- or postpartum-associated VTE Yes Test; same approach as above Combined-oral-contraceptive-associated VTE Yes Test; same approach as above CVT or splanchnic thrombosis, and you plan to stop anticoagulation Yes Test; if thrombophilia found, continue indefinitely (Recs 7, 9) CVT or splanchnic thrombosis, already planned for indefinite anticoagulation No Do not test solely for duration (Recs 8, 10) Known familial AT/PC/PS deficiency (patient or relative) Yes, selective Test for the known defect — can change prophylaxis / contraception / HRT decisions General population before starting COCs No Do not screen

docs.title: Workup
docs.text:
Step 1 — send now (valid anytime, even anticoagulated)

  • Factor V Leiden PCR — DNA test; unaffected by acute thrombosis, heparin, warfarin, or DOACs.
  • Prothrombin G20210A PCR — DNA test; same.
  • Anticardiolipin IgG and IgM — ELISA; generally valid anytime (transient positivity possible with acute illness — confirm persistence at ≥12 weeks).
  • Anti-β2-glycoprotein-I IgG and IgM — ELISA; same.
  • Lupus anticoagulant — defer if possible. LA is the most anticoagulant-sensitive test in the panel: UFH/LMWH, warfarin, and DOACs all distort dRVVT/aPTT assays (false positives and negatives). If it must be sent on anticoagulation, the result needs review/validation by an expert laboratory.
  • → If Step 1 is normal and the plan is to stop anticoagulation, confirm with the treating clinician that stopping is safe and indicated before any washout/testing. Two-stage approach: DNA + aCL/anti-β2GPI on anticoagulation, then LA + protein C/S + antithrombin off it.

Step 2 — send later (functional tests, off interfering anticoagulants)

  • Timing: protein C, protein S, and antithrombin no sooner than ≥3 months into anticoagulation for the acute thrombosis (BSH Grade 2B). An alternative is to test 2–4 weeks off anticoagulation, which fits the usual timing of a D-dimer for stop/continue decisions.
  • Protein C activity — chromogenic activity assays are less DOAC-susceptible than clot-based assays; clot-based PC can be falsely increased by DOACs (masking deficiency). Warfarin falsely lowers PC.
  • Protein S, free antigen preferred — C4b-binding protein rises acutely, lowering free protein S; warfarin falsely lowers PS; activity assays are DOAC-affected (anti-Xa drugs gave falsely high PS in one study).
  • Antithrombin activity — heparin lowers AT activity/antigen; acute thrombosis consumes AT; anti-Xa drugs gave falsely low AT in one study (assay-dependent), while factor Xa inhibitors can falsely increase AT in Xa-based assays and dabigatran can falsely increase AT in thrombin/IIa-based assays.
  • Lupus anticoagulant — repeat to confirm persistence (≥12 weeks apart). For LMWH, draw ≥12 h after the last dose, as close as possible to the next dose. Do not test on therapeutic UFH unless the lab has validated heparin-neutralizing methodology.
  • Washouts before testing (Anticoagulation Forum): warfarin ≥2 weeks (if PC/PS is needed while anticoagulation must continue, switch to heparin/LMWH for ≥2 weeks first); DOACs ≥48 hours, longer with renal impairment (Connors: ≥5 half-lives, usually 2–3 days or more); heparin/LMWH ≥24 hours; fondaparinux ≥48 hours, longer with renal impairment.
  • Confirm before labeling: repeat any low protein C, protein S, or antithrombin on a separate sample off confounders. Rule out acquired causes first — liver disease, DIC, sepsis, vitamin K deficiency. Do not interrupt clinically necessary anticoagulation solely to obtain a panel.

Step 3 — unusual-site thrombosis extras (when CVT or splanchnic thrombosis, or cytopenias/hemolysis)

  • JAK2 V617F — with unexplained erythrocytosis, thrombocytosis, or leukocytosis, or splanchnic thrombosis. The ASH thrombophilia panel does not cover JAK2-positive MPN — order it separately.
  • PNH flow cytometry — with cytopenias, hemolysis, or unusual-site thrombosis.
  • CBC, LDH, haptoglobin, reticulocytes — screen for the cytopenia/hemolysis pattern that points at PNH or an MPN.
  • → Hematology referral. BSH does not recommend heritable testing for unusual site alone — it does recommend aPL testing, JAK2 or an MPN panel, and PNH testing when cytopenias or hemolysis are present.

docs.title: How each anticoagulant distorts each test
docs.text:
Test Acute thrombosis Heparin / LMWH Warfarin DOACs FVL, prothrombin G20210A (PCR) Not affected Not affected Not affected Not affected aCL, anti-β2GPI (ELISA) Not affected Not affected Not affected Not affected Protein C activity Can be falsely low Usually not affected Falsely low Clot-based assays affected Protein S (free antigen preferred) Can be falsely low Usually not affected Falsely low Activity assays affected; anti-Xa drugs gave falsely high PS in one study Antithrombin activity Can be falsely low Falsely low Usually not affected Anti-Xa drugs gave falsely low AT in one study, assay-dependent APC resistance (clot-based) Can be affected Affected Affected Falsely low ratio, mimicking FVL Lupus anticoagulant Not recommended Affected (depends on assay and neutralizer) Affected False positives

Memory aid: DNA tests anytime; aCL/β2GPI usually anytime; protein C/S/antithrombin later and off interfering anticoagulants; lupus anticoagulant preferably later and off essentially all anticoagulants. If recurrence risk is too high to stop anticoagulation at all, the decision to continue has already been made, and testing rarely changes management.

docs.title: Do NOT order
docs.text: Test / panel Why not MTHFR C677T / A1298C Do not order. Not associated with VTE (ASH 2023); ACMG 2025 technical standard — routine MTHFR testing not recommended for thrombophilia, recurrent pregnancy loss, or reproductive carrier screening; ISTH-affiliated 2022 consensus — not risk factors for arterial or venous thrombosis, should be removed from panels; ACOG and BSH agree. Variants are present in up to 45% of people by ethnicity and predict neither first VTE nor recurrence. Heterozygosity, homozygosity, or compound heterozygosity should not be labeled a thrombophilia and should not alter anticoagulation. (Distinct from rare severe autosomal-recessive MTHFR deficiency — homocystinuria phenotype.) Routine fasting homocysteine is also insufficient. Factor VIII, IX, XI levels Low-value extras — not part of the recommended panel PAI-1 level; SERPINE1 / PAI-1 4G/5G polymorphism Low-value extras — omit Broad thrombophilia genetic / polygenic-risk panels Omit outside a defined indication Anti-phosphatidylserine/prothrombin (aPS/PT) or anti-domain-I β2GPI as routine first-line ISTH recommends against adding them as routine first-line APS assays; they do not score in the 2023 criteria Inherited panel (FVL, prothrombin, PC/PS/AT) for an arterial event Inherited thrombophilias are principally venous — order the complete APS panel instead. ACMG: routine FVL/prothrombin testing not generally recommended for personal/family history of arterial thrombotic disorders (CAD, ischemic stroke) Population-wide thrombophilia screening before COCs ASH strongly recommends against it

docs.title: Management
docs.text:
Step 1 — thrombotic APS, especially triple-positive: warfarin, not a DOAC

  • Warfarin (VKA) — target INR 2–3 for a first unprovoked venous thrombotic APS event. This is the conventional standard and the only drug target verified in this run's research.
  • Avoid DOACs in triple-positive APS. BSH recommends against starting DOACs in triple-positive APS (1B); patients already on a DOAC should generally be switched to a VKA after discussion of risks and benefits (continuing the DOAC beats no anticoagulation if the patient declines). EULAR specifically recommends against rivaroxaban in triple-positive APS (excess arterial events in the high-risk TRAPS population). The 2026 ACC statement likewise reserves VKA for high-risk APS: triple positivity, arterial or small-vessel thrombosis, organ involvement, or valve disease. Across RCTs, DOACs carried about 5-fold higher odds of arterial events, mainly stroke, than warfarin — and the meta-analysis found no clear interaction by triple-positive status, which suggests VKA is the better choice for most thrombotic APS.
  • Arterial APS is more individualized: VKA remains preferred, INR 2–3 versus 3–4, or in selected circumstances VKA plus low-dose aspirin, per recurrent-thrombosis and bleeding risk. Triple positivity alone is not an indication to automatically target INR 3–4.
  • Duration: long-term anticoagulation is suggested even after VTE with minor provoking factors in triple-positive patients (BSH 2C).
