  • Asymptomatic triple-positive carriers (no APS by criteria): thromboprophylaxis in high-risk situations such as surgery or immobility; hydroxychloroquine considered case by case; aggressive control of cardiovascular risk factors and counseling against estrogen; risk assessment for antenatal and/or postpartum prophylaxis in pregnancy. BSH does not routinely recommend low-dose aspirin for primary prevention (2B); EULAR 2019, by contrast, recommends low-dose aspirin for high-risk-profile carriers — the two disagree, so document the reasoning.
  • → For non-APS VTE, the DOAC is the usual agent (apixaban is the most commonly used in practice — see Cerebral venous thrombosis for the house DOAC discussion). DOAC doses are not restated here — see the VTE/CVT treatment pages.

Step 2 — inherited thrombophilia positive after a first unprovoked VTE: usually no change

  • Heterozygous FVL or prothrombin G20210A: usually does not change duration or drug choice. It may matter for counseling, pregnancy/hormonal exposures, and sometimes relatives — but the VTE itself, not the mutation, is usually driving the decision for extended therapy.
  • Protein C, protein S, or antithrombin deficiency: potentially more consequential for family counseling/testing, pregnancy, prophylaxis during transient high-risk situations, and assessment of unusual or recurrent thrombosis — but after a first conventional unprovoked proximal DVT/PE, the indication for extended anticoagulation usually already exists independent of the result.
  • Confirm the deficiency first: a reported deficiency must be biologically credible and appropriately confirmed (repeat off confounders), because acute thrombosis and anticoagulant therapy confound these assays.
  • The exception within the exception: if the patient has unprovoked VTE and high bleeding risk and is leaning toward stopping, a positive result — especially AT/PC/PS deficiency, which carries higher recurrence risk — may tip the decision toward extended therapy.

Step 3 — provoked VTE with a positive test, or a known familial defect: extend or prevent

  • Provoked VTE (nonsurgical major transient risk factor, pregnancy/postpartum, COC-associated) with thrombophilia found: continue anticoagulation indefinitely rather than stopping after primary treatment. Conditional recommendation, very-low-certainty evidence — largely modeling, not direct RCTs — and the most debated part of the 2023 guideline.
  • Family planning — hormonal contraception/HRT: for a woman with a family history of VTE and a known familial antithrombin, protein C, or protein S deficiency, test for the known familial defect; if positive, avoid combined oral contraceptives and use the result when considering HRT. Do not test solely for known heterozygous FVL or prothrombin mutation in the family to decide COCs/HRT.
  • Family planning — pregnancy: testing can change antepartum/postpartum prophylaxis when there is a known high-risk familial thrombophilia — ASH specifically supports selective testing in families with antithrombin deficiency, homozygous FVL, or combined FVL + prothrombin mutation (a positive result can lead to antepartum prophylaxis); postpartum testing/prophylaxis applies to a somewhat broader set including protein C/S deficiencies. For a woman who has already had VTE, her own history already calls for avoiding estrogen and giving antepartum/postpartum prophylaxis whatever the test shows — the main value of testing is for asymptomatic female relatives considering estrogen or pregnancy.
  • Unaffected relatives: testing is most useful when the family has a specific, known, high-risk defect. If a first-degree relative has confirmed antithrombin, protein C, or protein S deficiency, selective testing can influence thromboprophylaxis during otherwise minor transient risks (immobilization, illness). A family history of heterozygous FVL or prothrombin G20210A generally does not justify testing to decide prophylaxis around minor risk factors.

Avoid

  • Ordering MTHFR and acting on it — a positive MTHFR variant is not a thrombophilia and must not extend anticoagulation, trigger family screening, or change contraception decisions.
  • Using a negative panel as reassurance to stop anticoagulation after an otherwise unprovoked VTE — ASH explicitly modeled that strategy and rejected it.
  • Using a positive inherited test to extend anticoagulation after a first unprovoked VTE — the unprovoked event itself already usually justifies considering indefinite therapy.
  • Starting or continuing a DOAC in triple-positive APS — especially rivaroxaban, especially with arterial disease.
  • Testing functional assays during the acute event or on interfering anticoagulants and calling the result a hereditary deficiency — repeat off confounders first.
  • Ordering the inherited panel for arterial thrombosis — send the APS panel instead.

TRICARE — verified rules and the current form

Determine outpatient drug coverage separately from emergency stroke treatment. Anticoagulant, antiplatelet, lipid-drug, dose and quantity rules are product/indication specific; do not infer “no PA” from generic status. Reversal agents and inpatient reperfusion use the facility pathway. Medical authorization for procedures is distinct from pharmacy coverage.

Current PA/MN details, benefit routing and packet · Live Formulary Search. Check the exact product, beneficiary and venue on the prescribing date.

docs.title: Disposition
docs.text:
• Admit vs discharge is driven by the thrombotic event, not the panel — PE with hemodynamic compromise, extensive DVT, CVT with hemorrhage or depressed consciousness, and splanchnic thrombosis with bowel ischemia admit; a stable first DVT/PE with reliable follow-up can go home on anticoagulation.
  • Follow-up: repeat/confirmatory testing at ≥12 weeks for APS persistence (LA, aCL, anti-β2GPI) and at ≥3 months for protein C/S/antithrombin. Hematology referral for APS, triple positivity, unusual-site thrombosis, or a confirmed deficiency. Document the provoked/unprovoked classification — it, not the panel, drives the duration decision.
  • Counseling points: a positive inherited test after unprovoked VTE does not make the patient "more clot-prone" in a way that changes their own treatment — its value is mostly for family planning and relatives. A negative test does not make them low-risk.

Military medicine — duty, retention and deployment

  • Profile / function: Restrict hazardous duties while evaluating a new vascular event; document residual vision, strength, language, cognition, recurrence risk and bleeding risk.
  • Retention / MEB–MAR2: DoDI V2 5.26.b and Army 3-31f guide cerebrovascular retention assessment. Workup for a clotting disorder alone does not establish a permanent disability. Use the retention framework; permanent P3/4 does not by itself select DES versus MAR2.
  • Deployment / medications: Therapeutic anticoagulation is a major CENTCOM exclusion; nonaspirin antiplatelets create a separate waiver issue. Do not stop indicated treatment to make a member deployable. See the disease AND drug screen for the current CENTCOM rules and waiver packet.
  • Special duty: flight, diving and other special assignments have separate standards and waiver authorities; a general duty profile does not clear them.
  • LOD / EPTS: document onset, duty status, exposures and aggravation objectively. The designated authority determines LOD/EPTS; neither in-service diagnosis nor a genetic finding settles it automatically.

docs.title: 📚 Discover — evidence brief
docs.text:
Written from primary guidelines and trials; source articles are a reading list, not copied.

  • ASH 2023 is the anchor, and its logic is counterintuitive on purpose. The guideline recommends against testing after unprovoked VTE — not because the tests are useless, but because indefinite anticoagulation is already the plan, so the result cannot change it. Testing is suggested exactly where the default is to stop: nonsurgical major transient risk factors, pregnancy/postpartum, COC-associated VTE, and CVT/splanchnic thrombosis where stopping is planned. Test only when the result has a plausible management consequence.
  • MTHFR is out. ASH, ACMG (2025 technical standard), ISTH-affiliated consensus, ACOG, and BSH all agree: MTHFR C677T/A1298C is not associated with VTE, is present in up to 45% of people, and should be removed from panels. A positive result must not be labeled a thrombophilia or used to extend anticoagulation.
  • APS is the exception that changes the drug, not just the duration. The 2023 ACR/EULAR criteria are weighted (≥3 clinical + ≥3 laboratory points, entry criterion, 3-year window, persistence ≥12 weeks) and deliberately trade sensitivity (84%) for specificity (99%). Triple positivity — persistent LA + aCL + anti-β2GPI — is the highest-risk serologic profile, and it means warfarin (INR 2–3), not a DOAC: DOACs carried ~5-fold higher odds of arterial events, mainly stroke, than warfarin across RCTs. BSH (1B) and EULAR (against rivaroxaban) and the 2026 ACC statement all point the same way.
  • Timing is half the test. DNA tests and aCL/anti-β2GPI ELISAs can be sent anytime; protein C, protein S, antithrombin, and lupus anticoagulant cannot be trusted acutely or on anticoagulation. Warfarin falsely lowers protein C/S; heparin lowers antithrombin; DOACs cause false-positive lupus anticoagulants and can falsely raise clot-based protein C/S. The two-stage approach (DNA + antibodies now, functional tests later) is the practical fix.
  • The family-planning use is the clearest one. Testing a known familial high-risk defect (antithrombin, protein C, or protein S deficiency) changes contraception, HRT, and pregnancy prophylaxis — for the patient and for asymptomatic relatives. Heterozygous FVL/prothrombin alone does not justify testing for those decisions, and population screening before COCs is strongly discouraged.

Key sources: ASH 2023 thrombophilia testing guideline (Middeldorp et al.); 2023 ACR/EULAR APS classification criteria (Barbhaiya et al.); ACMG 2025 MTHFR technical standard; BSH APS guidance; ISTH SSC laboratory guidance.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Middeldorp S, Nieuwlaat R, Baumann Kreuziger L, et al. American Society of Hematology 2023 guidelines for management of venous thromboembolism: thrombophilia testing. Blood Advances. 2023;7(22):7101-7138. — The anchor: Recommendation 1 (do not test to guide duration after unprovoked VTE), Recs 3–5 (test for nonsurgical major transient / pregnancy / postpartum / COC-associated VTE), Recs 7–10 (CVT/splanchnic — test only if stopping is planned).
  2. Barbhaiya M, Zuily S, Naden R, et al. The 2023 ACR/EULAR Antiphospholipid Syndrome Classification Criteria. Arthritis & Rheumatology / Annals of the Rheumatic Diseases. 2023. — Weighted criteria: entry criterion, ≥3 clinical + ≥3 laboratory points, titer thresholds 40–79 / ≥80 units, persistence ≥12 weeks, 3-year window.
  3. Knight JS, Erkan D. Rethinking antiphospholipid syndrome to guide future management and research. Nature Reviews Rheumatology. 2024. — Triple positivity as the highest-risk serologic phenotype; IgG vs IgM isotype risk.
  4. American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics. MTHFR technical standard. 2025. — Routine MTHFR testing not recommended for thrombophilia, recurrent pregnancy loss, or reproductive carrier screening.
  5. British Society for Haematology. Guideline on antiphospholipid syndrome / thrombophilia testing. — Against starting DOACs in triple-positive APS (1B); aPL screening after unprovoked VTE (Grade 1B); long-term anticoagulation even after VTE with minor provoking factors in triple-positive patients (2C); no routine low-dose aspirin for primary prevention (2B).
  6. ISTH Scientific and Standardization Committee. Laboratory detection and interpretation of antiphospholipid antibodies (2024/2025 update). — Assay-specific local cutoffs (>99th percentile); LA per ISTH methodology; aPS/PT and anti-domain-I β2GPI not routine first-line assays.
  7. Connors JM. Thrombophilia testing and venous thrombosis. New England Journal of Medicine. 2017. — NEJM testing algorithm (Figure 1, September 21, 2017): who to test after a first VTE; washout intervals (warfarin ≥2 weeks; DOACs ≥5 half-lives).
  8. Official TRICARE sources, retrieved forms and access limits.

Evidence/policy audit: 21 November 2026. Material changes were checked against the linked primary sources; this is an AI-assisted review, not certification of every dose or claim. Review scope and source limits.

docs.title: IVIG / PLEX / Rituximab order sets
docs.text:
Last reviewed: November 2026

One-liner: the prescriptive order sets for the three workhorse immunotherapies in acute neuroimmunology — IVIG, plasma exchange (PLEX/TPE), and rituximab — across Guillain-Barré syndrome, CIDP, myasthenic crisis, NMOSD relapse, and autoimmune encephalitis: which rescue to start, the exact doses and rates, how to sequence them without washing one out with the next, and when rituximab belongs. For the neurologist or intensivist admitting an acute antibody-mediated attack, and for the clinician writing the orders at 2 a.m. Educational clinical decision-support, not medical advice — verify doses and eligibility against current labeling and guidelines before ordering.

🚩 Red flags — don't start immunotherapy before you check these

Pattern Worry Do now Respiratory or bulbar weakness (MG crisis, GBS) Ventilatory failure — the clock is the airway, not the antibody Admit to ICU/step-down, forced vital capacity + negative inspiratory force, secure the airway before debating IVIG vs PLEX Rapidly progressive weakness with autonomic instability (GBS) Dysautonomia, arrhythmia, labile blood pressure Continuous monitoring; IVIG is preferred over PLEX here — PLEX volume shifts worsen instability Fever, untreated infection, or sepsis before rituximab B-cell depletion during active infection; HBV reactivation Hold rituximab, treat the infection, screen HBsAg + anti-HBc first — see Step 3 IgA deficiency with prior anaphylaxis, CKD, or thrombotic history before IVIG Anaphylaxis, acute kidney injury, thrombosis — the IVIG boxed warnings For prior severe hypersensitivity/anaphylaxis, obtain specialist/pharmacy review of the exact product’s contraindications before any rechallenge. Low-IgA product selection alone does not make it safe. Address renal/thrombotic risks separately Severe NMOSD attack (optic neuritis, myelitis, brainstem) and the clock is running Every day of delay costs vision and cord — complete recovery ~40% if PLEX starts within 2 days vs 3.7% if ≥7 days Steroids + PLEX essentially simultaneously; do not finish a full steroid course first

docs.title: Diagnosis / classification — which syndromes this page covers
docs.text:
This page is therapeutics, not diagnosis. It assumes the syndrome is already named. The five presentations it covers, with the rescue logic for each:

Syndrome Rescue principle Durable control Myasthenic crisis (impending or manifest) PLEX or IVIG — equal efficacy in trials; expert consensus holds PLEX works faster Rituximab once stable — especially MuSK+ or refractory disease Guillain-Barré syndrome (unable to walk, GBS-DS ≥3, within 4 weeks of onset; or ambulatory but rapidly progressing / bulbar / respiratory risk) IVIG or PLEX — equal efficacy; never both routinely None — rituximab has no role in routine acute GBS; steroids alone are ineffective NMOSD relapse (AQP4+ or seronegative) High-dose steroids plus early PLEX — PLEX is primary therapy alongside steroids, not a salvage after steroid failure Rituximab (or an approved mAb) after the PLEX course ends; oral steroid taper 3–6 months Autoimmune encephalitis (esp. neuronal-surface antibody: NMDAR, LGI1, CASPR2) Steroids ± IVIG or PLEX, started early and empirically once infection is reasonably excluded Rituximab as preferred second line; refractory → tocilizumab or bortezomib within ~1 month CIDP (induction / maintenance) IVIG first line in most; PLEX an induction alternative (5–10 sessions alternate days) IVIG maintenance 1 g/kg q3wk, or rituximab for nodopathy / refractory disease — see CIDP & IVIG order set for the full CIDP workup

The one rule that governs the whole page: IVIG and PLEX are the rescue therapies; rituximab is not a rescue drug. B-cell depletion takes weeks and does not lower existing antibody, because plasma cells are CD20-negative. Rituximab cannot replace PLEX in an acute attack — it is the bridge into maintenance, and it goes in after the rescue course ends.

docs.title: Rapid approach
docs.text:
1. Secure the airway and the circulation first — respiratory/bulbar status, dysautonomia, hemodynamics, venous access. That triage decides IVIG vs PLEX as much as the diagnosis does.
  2. Name the syndrome and the tempo — fulminant/rapid (intubation, rising ventilation risk, NMOSD attack within 48 h, severe myelitis) favors PLEX for speed; autonomic instability, sepsis, poor access, or children favor IVIG.
  3. Order the rescue today, the durable control after — pick IVIG or PLEX from the table below, run its order set, and plan rituximab (when indicated) only after the PLEX course is finished.

docs.title: The prescriptive flow (what I want done, in order)
docs.text:
1. Confirm the syndrome and grade severity — respiratory/bulbar exam, GBS disability scale, NMOSD attack severity (optic nerve / cord / brainstem), AE severity (ICU, status epilepticus/NORSE, dysautonomia, depressed consciousness).
  2. Run the shared pre-immunotherapy workup (orderset below) — labs, serologies before IVIG (it causes false-positive antibody results for weeks), HBV screen before rituximab, infection screen, pregnancy test where applicable.
  3. Pick the rescue from the decision table — IVIG or PLEX, matched to syndrome and tempo. Start it the same day; do not wait for antibody results in a fulminant attack.
  4. If the rescue is inadequate, switch by the rules, not by reflex — GBS is the exception: routine IVIG→PLEX, PLEX→IVIG, or a second IVIG course for simple poor response is not recommended. MG crisis, NMOSD, and AE do allow sequential/escalating therapy — see the sequencing rules.
  5. Start durable control after rescue — rituximab (when indicated) after the final PLEX session, never before or between sessions. Cover NMOSD with an oral steroid taper for 3–6 months, because early relapses after the first rituximab dose are described.
  6. Monitor for the therapy-specific harms — IVIG: thrombosis and AKI (boxed warnings), hemolysis at 5–10 days; PLEX: hypotension, citrate toxicity, fibrinogen fall; rituximab: infusion reactions, infection, hypogammaglobulinemia, late-onset neutropenia. Disposition and follow-up below.

docs.title: Workup — shared pre-immunotherapy checklist
docs.text:
Order before any of the three — do this first

  • CBC with differential, CMP (creatinine, LFTs), Na/K, Mg, ionized Ca — baseline for IVIG (renal, hemolysis), PLEX (citrate, fibrinogen), and rituximab (neutropenia).
  • Coagulation: PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogen; blood type + antibody screen — before PLEX, and before IVIG if plasma support could be needed.
  • Draw clinically indicated antibody/infectious serologies before IVIG or PLEX when feasible. Select AChR/MuSK, ganglioside, nodal/paranodal, AQP4/MOG, or neuronal panels by phenotype; do not send every panel for every syndrome or delay emergency rescue for send-outs. IVIG causes false positives that persist for weeks.
  • Infection screen — active infection review, fever workup; HCV, HIV, IGRA for TB (rituximab); do not give rituximab during a severe active infection.
  • HBV screen before rituximab: HBsAg + anti-HBc in everyone (add anti-HBs to characterize immunity). If either is positive: HBV DNA + hepatology, antiviral prophylaxis (entecavir or tenofovir) — see Step 3.
  • Quantitative IgG / IgA / IgM before rituximab — baseline IgG <3 g/L predicts infection risk; IgA status matters before IVIG if there is a history of severe/selective IgA deficiency or prior anaphylaxis.
  • Pregnancy: β-hCG before rituximab in patients of reproductive potential; contraception during treatment and for 12 months after the last dose per current product labeling, with individualized specialist counseling.
  • Vaccines before rituximab — pneumococcal, influenza, COVID-19, recombinant zoster ≥2–4 weeks before the first dose; if not VZV-immune, live varicella vaccine >4 weeks before. No live vaccines during B-cell depletion.
  • Volume / cardiac / thrombotic risk assessment before IVIG — age, immobility, prior VTE or arterial events, CAD, estrogens, central lines, hyperviscosity (cryoglobulins, marked hypertriglyceridemia, monoclonal gammopathy); ensure DVT prophylaxis in immobilized inpatients and hydration.
  • Baseline brain MRI in MS (rituximab) and CD19+ B-cell count (baseline; useful later if B-cell-guided redosing is planned).

docs.title: Choosing the rescue — decision table
docs.text:
Syndrome First rescue Favor PLEX when Favor IVIG when Myasthenic crisis PLEX or IVIG + ICU/step-down monitoring Intubated, rapidly worsening, marked bulbar disease, need for fastest response — particularly MuSK-MG Difficult vascular access, hemodynamic instability, sepsis, logistical preference GBS IVIG or PLEX (not both) Either is effective; useful when IVIG unsuitable Autonomic instability, children, PLEX access limited — often the simplest practical default NMOSD relapse IVMP 1 g/day × 3–5 days + very early PLEX Severe optic neuritis, longitudinal/extensive myelitis, major motor deficit, brainstem attack, rapid tempo, prior steroid-refractory attacks — start PLEX concurrently, don't wait for steroid failure IVIG is not routine rescue in AQP4-NMOSD — the 2025 consensus recommends against it; use only if PLEX is contraindicated Autoimmune encephalitis IVMP ± IVIG or PLEX, started early Fulminant antibody-mediated phenotype, severe dysautonomia/status epilepticus, concomitant demyelination, high thrombotic risk Agitation/behavioral disease making line safety difficult, bleeding/coagulopathy concerns, easier logistics; IVIG has the best safety profile CIDP IVIG (see CIDP page) Induction alternative when IVIG is unsuitable or has failed; 5–10 sessions alternate days First line in most; maintenance 1 g/kg q3wk

Step 1 — IVIG order set (start here for most GBS / MG crisis / AE)

  • GBS: IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day × 5 days (total 2 g/kg), preferably begun within 2 weeks of weakness onset. MG crisis / exacerbation: total 2 g/kg over 2–5 days (1 g/kg/day × 2 days is acceptable in selected exacerbations; benefit begins in days to weeks, lasts 4–8 weeks). CIDP induction: 2 g/kg over 2–5 days, then maintenance 1 g/kg every 3 weeks (practical range 0.4–1 g/kg q2–6wk, individualized to the lowest effective dose and longest interval; use objective response and an adequate trial before declaring failure; the ICE trial’s maintained week-24 INCAT response was 54% vs 21% with placebo). Severe AE: total 2 g/kg over 2–5 days.
  • Dosing weight: dose on actual body weight in most patients; in obesity many centers use adjusted body weight to limit volume, viscosity, and thrombotic load.
  • Infusion rates are product-specific — follow that product's label, never transplant a rate table between products. 10% examples: Gammagard Liquid — start 0.5 mL/kg/h, increase gradually as tolerated to max 5.4 mL/kg/h; other 10% labels — start 0.5 mg/kg/min for 15 min, increase every 15 min to max 8 mg/kg/min (Gamunex-C starts 2 mg/kg/min → max 8 mg/kg/min; Privigen 0.5 → 8 mg/kg/min). Escalate stepwise ~every 15–30 min, checking vitals before each step. Use the slowest practicable rate for first-ever infusions, renal/thrombotic risk, IgA deficiency, or a product change.
  • Premedication is NOT routinely required — reserve acetaminophen + antihistamine (± hydrocortisone) for patients with prior infusion reactions.
  • Monitoring: vitals at baseline, each rate change, and end of infusion. BUN/creatinine before the first infusion and at intervals after. CBC/Hb, LDH, haptoglobin, DAT if symptomatic or high risk for hemolysis (~5–10 days post-infusion; non-O blood groups, high dose). Watch for aseptic meningitis (hours–2 days, worse with high dose or rapid rate), TRALI (within 6 h), and volume overload in heart failure.
  • Boxed warnings: thrombosis and acute kidney injury. Thrombosis ~1% per infusion in a neuropathy cohort (reported range 1–13%), mostly within 14 days — hydrate, use the minimum rate, split dosing, DVT prophylaxis. AKI risk is higher with CKD, diabetes, age >65, and sucrose-stabilized products — hydrate first and avoid sucrose products.
  • Mild reactions: slow or pause the infusion, restart at the last tolerated rate. Anaphylaxis: stop, give epinephrine; use a low-IgA product next time.
  • → No routine second course in GBS (SID-GBS: no benefit, more thrombosis). If no response, switch by the sequencing rules below — do not reflexively repeat IVIG. → Step 2 if PLEX is the pick instead, or Step 3 for durable control.

Step 2 — PLEX order set (when PLEX is the pick)

  • Default prescription: 1.0–1.5 total plasma volumes (TPV) per session, ~5 exchanges over 7–14 days (range 4–7; up to 10 in NMOSD). GBS: 4–5 exchanges, 12–15 L total, within 4 weeks of onset (best in the first week). MG crisis: 5 sessions over 7–10 days (no benefit to routinely extending beyond 5). NMOSD: ~5 exchanges, daily or every other day, up to 10 — start within 2 days when severe. AE: 5–7 exchanges every other day over ~10 days (5 exchanges qod is the Canadian consensus regimen for severe AE). CIDP induction: 5–10 sessions on alternate days.
  • Plasma volume: Kaplan formula — 0.07 × weight (kg) × (1 − hematocrit). Removal is exponential: 1.0 PV removes ~63%, 1.5 PV ~78%.
  • Replacement fluid: 5% (4.5–5%) albumin as standard. FFP only for bleeding, low fibrinogen, or an impending procedure. Check fibrinogen serially — it falls ~60–70% per 1 PV albumin exchange; for hemorrhagic risk, maintain fibrinogen >1.0 g/L (100 mg/dL) with partial FFP replacement or post-PLEX cryoprecipitate (BSH target).
  • Vascular access: peripheral first whenever technically adequate — a 16–17 G apheresis/dialysis needle is ideal (16–18 G cannulas at lower flows); centrifugal TPE runs ~50–120 mL/min. If central access is needed, use a short, rigid, large-bore dual-lumen apheresis/hemodialysis catheter (11.5–12 Fr, internal jugular preferred); ultrasound-guided, sterile placement, heparin or 4% citrate locks, tPA for occlusion, remove promptly after the course. Membrane TPE needs substantially higher flow and more often requires a dialysis-type catheter.
  • Pre-PLEX checks: CBC; Na/K/creatinine; ionized Ca, Mg; PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogen; blood type/antibody screen. Hold ACE inhibitors 24–48 h before PLEX (bradykinin-mediated hypotension). Monitor vitals, BP/HR, symptoms, fluid balance, and access function during each session; reassess fibrinogen and ionized Ca serially during intensive (daily) courses.
  • Hypotension (most common complication, ~12% of patients / 2.4% of sessions): slow or pause PLEX, supine/Trendelenburg, restore intravascular volume — BSH gives 250 mL 0.9% saline as the initial maneuver for vasovagal/hypovolemic events; assess for bleeding, anaphylaxis, arrhythmia. GBS with severe dysautonomia deserves especially conservative flow and volume management.
  • Citrate toxicity / hypocalcemia: progression is perioral/acral paresthesias → cramps/tetany → QT prolongation/arrhythmia. Slow citrate delivery, give oral or IV calcium by severity; prophylactic calcium is reasonable with prior citrate reactions, baseline hypoCa/hypoMg, liver/renal dysfunction, or high citrate exposure. Target ionized Ca >0.9 mmol/L. Plasma replacement adds substantial citrate — another reason albumin is preferred.
  • Other complications: catheter-related (pneumothorax, arterial puncture, bleeding, thrombosis, fibrin sheath, CLABSI — prevent with ultrasound guidance, proper locking, early removal); allergic reactions to albumin or FFP (~9.5%); infections between sessions (~12% in one cohort); removal of protein-bound drugs — give IV medications after the day's exchange.
  • Steroids can run concurrently — give after the session on PLEX days. IgG replacement if IgG falls below 150 mg/dL after repeated courses (German MG guideline), given after PLEX is finished.
  • → PLEX is the rescue, not the maintenance. Plan the durable control (Step 3) while the course runs. → Step 3.

Step 3 — rituximab order set (durable control — after rescue, never as the rescue)

  • Common adult schedule: rituximab 1,000 mg IV on days 1 and 15, then maintenance every ~6 months — fixed schedule, or redosed when CD19 B cells return (common trigger CD19 >1% of lymphocytes; CD27+ memory B cells are an alternative and may need fewer infusions). Disease-specific regimens:
    • Relapsing MS: 1,000 mg days 1 and 15 (HERMES — 91% fewer Gd+ lesions vs placebo), or 1,000 mg × 1 then 500 mg q6mo (RIFUND-MS — 3% relapses vs 16% on dimethyl fumarate over 24 months). OLYMPUS (primary progressive MS, 1,000 mg × 2 q24wk) missed its primary endpoint.
    • AQP4+ NMOSD: 1,000 mg days 1 and 15 (alternative 375 mg/m² weekly × 4); maintenance 1,000 mg × 2 (2 g/cycle) q6mo, or redose when CD19 >1%. Lower-dose regimens (500 mg q6mo; 100 mg-based) come from observational studies only. Hopkins cohort: 2 g q6mo in most patients. MENACTRIMS 2026: extending the interval by CD19 return worked as well as fixed q6mo dosing.
    • Generalized MG: new-onset AChR+ — 500 mg × 1 (RINOMAX — 71% vs 29% reached minimal manifestations at week 16). Refractory / MuSK+ — 375 mg/m² weekly × 4, or 1,000 mg × 2; redose at relapse or B-cell return (~6 months). BeatMG (375 mg/m² × 4, repeated at 6 months, established AChR+) showed no steroid-sparing benefit — best results are in MuSK+. In one MuSK cohort, 375 mg/m² weekly × 4 followed by 2 monthly doses had fewer relapses than 1 g × 2 (18% vs 80%).
    • Autoimmune encephalitis (second line: NMDAR, LGI1, CASPR2): 1,000 mg × 2, 2 weeks apart, or 375 mg/m² weekly × 4. Pediatric: 750 mg/m² × 2 (max 1 g/dose). Usually no maintenance; consider redosing at 6 months in selected relapsing NMDAR disease. Escalate after 2–4 weeks without response to first-line therapy — rituximab was the preferred second line of ~80% of experts.
  • Infusion rates (label): first infusion start 50 mg/h, increase by 50 mg/h every 30 min to a maximum of 400 mg/h. Later infusions start 100 mg/h, increase by 100 mg/h every 30 min to 400 mg/h. Dilute to 1–4 mg/mL. Do not import the accelerated 90-minute protocol as the default neurologic protocol — it is supported in selected lymphoma/chemotherapy circumstances only. SC rituximab (Rituxan Hycela) is not interchangeable, is not indicated for autoimmune disease, and must never be given IV.
  • Premedication, 30 min before every infusion: acetaminophen + an antihistamine (e.g. diphenhydramine 50 mg) + methylprednisolone 100 mg IV. Some centers add an H2 antagonist — institutional, not a universal evidence-based requirement.
  • Infusion reactions (most common adverse event, mostly the first dose, typically 30–120 min in): fever/chills, flushing, pruritus/urticaria, nausea, dyspnea, bronchospasm, hypoxia, angioedema, hypotension. Mild–moderate: stop the infusion, give antihistamine/acetaminophen ± steroid, then restart at ≥50% lower rate once symptoms resolve. Anaphylaxis, bronchospasm, or hypotension: epinephrine, fluids, bronchodilators, steroids, oxygen. Recurrent or severe reactions: desensitization is preferred, or switch to a humanized anti-CD20. Stop permanently after a life-threatening reaction.
  • HBV prophylaxis (if HBsAg+ or anti-HBc+): entecavir or tenofovir with hepatology involvement — duration is hepatology/guideline-directed, commonly at least 12 months after anti-CD20 therapy, with longer follow-up or prophylaxis in selected settings. The FDA label warns of reactivation up to 24 months; it does not set a universal prophylaxis duration.
  • Monitoring: CD19 count about every 6 months, or before each dose if redosing is CD19-guided. IgG/IgM/IgA every 6 months or before each course — IgG falls progressively with cumulative dose; if IgG stays <3–4 g/L with recurrent serious infections, consider extending the dosing interval and starting Ig replacement. CBC with differential every 6 months, plus whenever there is fever or infection, to catch late-onset neutropenia. Ask about infections at each visit. Consider PJP prophylaxis if steroids or other immunosuppressants are given at the same time. Watch for HBV reactivation in patients with past infection.
  • Risks to counsel on: serious infections in 12.7% of an MS/NMOSD cohort; in RINOMAX follow-up, 12.5–18.8% had a severe infection — risk higher with age >65 and low IgG; IgG <500 mg/dL was associated with nearly a 3-fold adjusted risk of serious infection vs IgG ≥700 mg/dL (aHR 2.98). Hypogammaglobulinemia rises with cumulative exposure — reported in up to 44% of children treated for autoimmune CNS disease, where it can be severe. Late-onset neutropenia: in 2,686 Swedish MS patients, 6.2% had any episode, grade 3–4 in 1.0%, often with infection, at a median of 360 days after starting. PML: very rare, but carries an FDA boxed warning — new subacute cognitive, visual, motor, or coordination symptoms or suspicious MRI lesions should trigger withholding therapy; note that the serum JCV antibody index is not validated for rituximab PML risk stratification, so serial index testing does not reproduce the natalizumab algorithm. Other: HBV reactivation (can be fatal), impaired vaccine response, colitis/IBD-like illness, serum sickness; PRES and cardiac events reported.

docs.title: Sequencing rules — the part that gets people in trouble
docs.text:
Sequence Verdict Why PLEX → IVIG Pharmacologically correct order PLEX removes IVIG — always give IVIG after the PLEX course. In GBS it adds no benefit and is not recommended; in MG/AE it is acceptable as a bridge once PLEX is finished IVIG → PLEX Avoid, especially within 2 weeks of IVIG PLEX washes out the infused immunoglobulin. If PLEX is truly needed (IVIG failure in crisis), accept the IVIG investment is lost — there is no required two-week waiting interval for necessary rescue. Exception: a life-threatening crisis deteriorating after IVIG — do not withhold necessary PLEX to preserve the IVIG dose PLEX → rituximab Correct — rituximab after the last PLEX session PLEX 24–72 h after rituximab removes ~47–54% of the dose and cuts AUC by 26%. If rituximab cannot wait until PLEX is finished: dose at least 4–6 h after a session and leave ≥48 h before the next exchange; consider a supplemental dose if exchanges follow closely. No universal "safe 24-hour interval" or supplemental dose is validated — coordinate with pharmacy/apheresis Rituximab → PLEX Avoid Same washout — hold biologics during PLEX: satralizumab, tocilizumab, inebilizumab, and natalizumab are large intravascular IgGs that PLEX removes efficiently; re-dose after the course IVIG + PLEX together (GBS) Do not combine routinely No benefit over either alone (Hughes 1997, n=383); EAN/PNS explicitly does not recommend PE immediately followed by IVIG Second IVIG course (GBS) Not routine SID-GBS: no benefit, more thrombosis. Lack of rapid improvement 5–10 days after IVIG in a ventilated GBS patient is not by itself an indication to wash out IVIG and try PLEX — axonal injury and delayed recovery explain persistent weakness Complement inhibitors + PLEX Supplemental dose required PLEX substantially removes C5 inhibitors: eculizumab — supplemental dose within 60 min after each session (300 mg if the last dose was 300 mg, 600 mg if ≥600 mg); ravulizumab — supplemental dose within 4 h. FcRn blockers (efgartigimod, rozanolixizumab, nipocalimab) are also removed by PLEX and speed clearance of IVIG and other IgG monoclonals — reconcile every biologic with apheresis before the first exchange

Switching, by syndrome:

  • MG crisis: no response to IVIG → PLEX helped in retrospective series (do not delay necessary rescue to preserve the prior IVIG dose). In a prolonged severe crisis with inadequate response, sequential rescue is reasonable — and when both are planned, PLEX followed by IVIG is the favored order. Start steroids/immunosuppression after PLEX/IVIG; delay steroids a few days because they can cause transient worsening.
  • GBS: treatment-related fluctuation (initial improvement/stabilization, then clear worsening) is different from poor response — retreatment with the same modality can be considered. ≥3 fluctuations or progression beyond ~8 weeks should trigger reconsideration of acute-onset CIDP or an autoimmune nodopathy rather than repeated empirical GBS treatment.
  • NMOSD: insufficient recovery → repeat the apheresis course and/or steroids; immunoadsorption is an alternative to PLEX. Breakthrough relapse on rituximab: check CD19/CD27 repopulation and anti-drug antibodies, and switch to a monoclonal with a different mechanism (e.g. complement inhibitor or satralizumab). Prior poor response to steroids, or a good response to PLEX, in past attacks → PLEX first line next time.
  • AE: unlike GBS, switching between first-line modalities is reasonable in refractory AE — if a steroid/IVIG strategy has clearly failed, PLEX can be added. First-line failure is defined as no improvement or worsening after 5–10 days in severe AE vs ~2–4 weeks in mild/moderate disease (Canadian consensus 2024) — deliberately earlier in severe disease so second-line rituximab is not delayed. Refractory disease → tocilizumab or bortezomib within ~1 month.

Avoid

  • Rituximab as acute rescue — it takes weeks to deplete B cells and does not touch existing antibody; it cannot rescue a respiratory, spinal-cord, optic-nerve, or encephalitic emergency.
  • Routine IVIG for acute AQP4-NMOSD attacks — the 2025 NMOSD consensus recommends against it; steroids + early PLEX is the rescue. (MOG-IgG-associated disease is different — the calculus changes.)
  • Sequential PLEX + IVIG in GBS, or a second IVIG course for simple poor response — no benefit, more harm.
  • Transplanting infusion rates between IVIG products — rates are product-specific; use the label for the product actually hanging.
  • The 90-minute accelerated rituximab protocol as a neurologic default — supported in selected lymphoma/chemotherapy settings, not as the neuroimmunology standard.
  • Serial JCV antibody-index monitoring to stratify rituximab PML risk — not validated; it does not reproduce the natalizumab algorithm.

TRICARE — verified rules and the current form

Confirm medical versus pharmacy benefit, exact product, indication, dose and site. IVIG brands do not share every approved indication; an infusion order does not establish insurance coverage. Current diagnosis-specific PA and continuation forms were not all obtainable in this review. Submit objective diagnostic evidence, prior therapy and safety/monitoring records rather than an invented universal failure threshold.

Current PA/MN details, benefit routing and packet · Live Formulary Search. Check the exact product, beneficiary and venue on the prescribing date.

docs.title: Disposition
docs.text:
• Admit every patient in this page's scope: MG crisis, GBS unable to walk or rapidly progressing, severe NMOSD relapse, severe AE — ICU or step-down with respiratory/bulbar monitoring, and apheresis + pharmacy coordinated before the first exchange.
  • Discharge only after the rescue course is complete, the patient is stable off respiratory support, the durable-control plan is written (rituximab date, HBV/IgG/CD19 baselines drawn, vaccine plan), and the PLEX/IVIG washout rules are documented in the handoff so the next team does not undo the rescue.
  • Follow-up: CIDP maintenance — INCAT / I-RODS / grip strength at each infusion to confirm response and guide tapering; try reducing dose every 6–12 months for the first 2–3 years. Rituximab — CD19 and IgG every ~6 months, CBC with any fever/infection, infection review at every visit. NMOSD — relapse-prevention therapy started before discharge; do not leave the patient on steroids alone.

Military medicine — duty, retention and deployment

  • Profile / function: Assess the underlying disease and treatment effects; record infection, infusion and monitoring risks in functional terms.
  • Retention / MEB–MAR2: Retention follows the underlying condition and Service standard. Receiving an infusion alone is not the same as a PEB finding. Use the retention framework; permanent P3/4 does not by itself select DES versus MAR2.
  • Deployment / medications: CENTCOM lists injectable and immunosuppressive/immune-modifying treatments. Self-injection does not bypass waiver review; describe vaccine, lab, cold-chain and missed-dose requirements. See the disease AND drug screen for the current CENTCOM rules and waiver packet.
  • Special duty: flight, diving and other special assignments have separate standards and waiver authorities; a general duty profile does not clear them.
  • LOD / EPTS: document onset, duty status, exposures and aggravation objectively. The designated authority determines LOD/EPTS; neither in-service diagnosis nor a genetic finding settles it automatically.

docs.title: 📚 Discover — evidence brief
docs.text:
Written from primary guidelines and trials; source articles are a reading list, not copied.

  • Rescue first, durable control second is the organizing principle: IVIG and PLEX work in days; rituximab works in weeks and cannot rescue an acute attack. Every sequencing error on this page — PLEX after IVIG, rituximab before PLEX — is a washout error.
  • GBS is the exception to "switch if it didn't work." IVIG and PLEX are equally effective, combining them adds nothing, a second IVIG course adds harm (SID-GBS), and persistent weakness 5–10 days after IVIG is usually axonal injury and slow recovery, not a failed drug. Treatment-related fluctuation is the one pattern where retreatment makes sense.
  • NMOSD is the opposite: move PLEX early. The 2025 NMOSD consensus and current NMOSD attack-management guidance put apheresis alongside high-dose steroids as primary therapy, with 5–7 alternate-day exchanges preferably within ~5 days of onset, and explicitly recommend against routine IVIG for acute AQP4-NMOSD attacks.
  • Rituximab's evidence is trial-anchored but off-label in all four conditions. RIFUND-MS (1 g → 500 mg q6mo), RINOMAX (single 500 mg in new-onset MG), and the Hopkins NMOSD cohort (2 g q6mo) give the dosing; the label still governs infusion rates, premedication, and HBV screening. The 2026 OVERLORD-MS data and the Swedish late-onset-neutropenia cohort (n=2,686) are the newest safety/efficacy signals.
  • What changed recently: NEMOS attack-management recommendations and subsequent NMOSD consensus reposition PLEX from salvage to primary therapy; the 2024 Canadian AE consensus formalizes earlier second-line escalation in severe disease (5–10 days, not 2–4 weeks).

Key sources: 2023 EAN/PNS GBS and 2021 EAN/PNS CIDP guidelines; AANEM IVIG consensus (Muscle & Nerve 2023, Tavee et al.); ASFA guidelines on therapeutic apheresis; ICE trial (CIDP); HERMES and RIFUND-MS (rituximab in MS); RINOMAX (rituximab in new-onset MG); NEMOS / 2025 NMOSD consensus; Canadian consensus on autoimmune encephalitis (2024); 2024 Nordic MG guidance.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Shahrizaila N et al. Guillain-Barré syndrome. Lancet. 2021 — GBS presentation, IVIG vs PLEX equivalence, treatment-related fluctuation.
  2. van Doorn PA, Van den Bergh PYK, Hadden RDM, et al. European Academy of Neurology/Peripheral Nerve Society guideline on diagnosis and treatment of Guillain-Barré syndrome. Eur J Neurol. 2023 — GBS: IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day × 5 days or PLEX 4–5 exchanges/12–15 L; do not combine; no routine second course.
  3. Van den Bergh PYK et al. European Academy of Neurology/Peripheral Nerve Society guideline on diagnosis and treatment of chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy. Eur J Neurol. 2021 — CIDP induction 2 g/kg, maintenance individualized from 1 g/kg q3wk; PLEX 5 exchanges over 2 weeks.
  4. Tavee J et al. Updated consensus statement on IVIG in neuromuscular disorders (AANEM). Muscle & Nerve. 2023 — IVIG dosing, pre-infusion screening, thrombotic/renal risk, product-specific rates.
  5. Narayanaswami P, Sanders DB, Wolfe G, et al. International Consensus Guidance for Management of Myasthenia Gravis: 2020 Update. Neurology. 2021. See also the 2016 consensus for IVIG/PLEX rescue principles.

  6. Kümpfel et al. NEMOS revised NMOSD recommendations, Part II — attack therapy and long-term management. Severe attacks may need early combined steroid/apheresis treatment; the claimed 2026 ASFA edition/category upgrade was not verified and is not relied upon here.

  7. Svenningsson A et al. Safety and efficacy of rituximab versus dimethyl fumarate in relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (RIFUND-MS). Lancet Neurol. 2022 — rituximab 1,000 mg × 1 then 500 mg q6mo; 3% vs 16% relapses.

  8. Hauser SL et al. B-cell depletion with rituximab in relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (HERMES). N Engl J Med. 2008 — rituximab 1,000 mg × 2; 91% fewer Gd+ lesions.
  9. Wu J et al. Rituximab in new-onset generalized myasthenia gravis: long-term follow-up of the RINOMAX clinical trial. Eur J Neurol. 2025 — long-term follow-up. The 71% vs 29% week-16 result comes from the 2022 RINOMAX randomized report.
  10. Hahn C, Budhram A, Alikhani K, et al. Canadian consensus guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of autoimmune encephalitis. 2024 — severe AE: steroids + IVIG or PLEX from the outset; first-line failure 5–10 days (severe) vs 2–4 weeks (mild/moderate); rituximab preferred second line.
  11. Rituxan (rituximab) US prescribing information (Genentech; DailyMed) — infusion rates (first 50 mg/h → max 400 mg/h; subsequent 100 mg/h → 400 mg/h), premedication (acetaminophen + antihistamine + methylprednisolone 100 mg IV), HBV boxed warning, PML boxed warning, contraception 12 months.
  12. Gammagard Liquid (immune globulin intravenous) US prescribing information (FDA label, updated 2025-12-10) — CIDP dosing and infusion-rate titration (start 0.5 mL/kg/h → max 5.4 mL/kg/h); thrombosis and AKI boxed warnings.
  13. Official TRICARE sources, retrieved forms and access limits.

Evidence/policy audit: 21 November 2026. Material changes were checked against the linked primary sources; this is an AI-assisted review, not certification of every dose or claim. Review scope and source limits.

docs.title: Radiculopathy & Plexopathy
docs.text:
Last reviewed: November 2026

One-liner: arm or leg pain, weakness, and sensory loss that follow a nerve root (radiculopathy) or a plexus element (plexopathy) — for the on-call neuro or PCP seeing a patient with radiating pain and a focal deficit, the job is to exclude the dangerous cause, localize to root vs plexus vs nerve, and treat in a time-limited, stepped way that gets most patients better without surgery.

🚩 Red flags — image now, refer urgently

Pattern Worry Do now Urinary retention / overflow incontinence, saddle anesthesia, fecal incontinence or reduced anal tone, bilateral or multiroot leg deficits Cauda equina / conus syndrome Emergent MRI + immediate spine/neurosurgical evaluation — do not trial conservative care Rapidly progressive or severe motor weakness Major nerve-root or cord compression Urgent MRI + spine referral — no conservative trial first Hyperreflexia, clonus, Babinski/Hoffmann, gait dysfunction, hand clumsiness, long-tract signs Cervical myelopathy / cord compression Urgent cervical MRI Fever, IV drug use, indwelling catheter (LR+ 15.7), immunosuppression, recent infection, severe focal spinal pain Discitis / osteomyelitis / epidural abscess Urgent MRI with contrast + labs (ESR/CRP, CBC, blood cultures) History of cancer (LR+ 27.9 when combined with clinical suspicion), unexplained weight loss, age >50, failure to improve within ~1 month Malignancy / metastasis MRI with contrast + cancer workup Trauma, osteoporosis, long-term steroid use Fracture Image the level (CT for bony detail)

docs.title: Diagnosis / classification
docs.text: Radiculopathy is pain, dysesthesia, weakness, sensory loss, and reflex loss in a dermatomal/myotomal pattern from a single root — most often a disc herniation (lumbar: usually L4–5 or L5–S1) or cervical spondylosis/foraminal stenosis. Plexopathy is the same kind of deficit spread across more than one peripheral nerve and more than one root level, but coherent within one plexus (brachial or lumbosacral). The two are distinguished clinically by the pattern, and electrodiagnostically by the SNAP/paraspinal rule below — not by imaging alone.

docs.title: The exam that localizes
docs.text:
Test / finding What it tells you Spurling's test (cervical) Highly specific for cervical radiculopathy (specificity 0.84–1.00) — a positive test supports the diagnosis; a negative test does not exclude it Upper-limb neurodynamic test cluster (cervical) A negative cluster helps rule radiculopathy out (sensitivity 0.97) Straight-leg raise / crossed SLR (lumbar) Crossed SLR is specific (0.90); a positive ipsilateral SLR supports a lumbar root lesion Reduced reflexes (especially triceps) and arm pain worse than neck pain (cervical) Raise the likelihood of cervical radiculopathy Myelopathy screen (cervical) Hyperreflexia, gait change, loss of hand dexterity — if present, this is no longer isolated radiculopathy; image the cord urgently Mimics to exclude Shoulder disease, carpal tunnel, ulnar entrapment, and "double crush" (root + entrapment together)

Think in trunks and cords, not just dermatomes, for plexopathy:

  • Upper trunk C5–6: deltoid, biceps, supraspinatus/infraspinatus, brachioradialis weakness; reduced biceps/brachioradialis reflex; lateral arm/forearm sensory loss.
  • Middle trunk C7: triceps, wrist and finger extensors; triceps reflex.
  • Lower trunk C8–T1: intrinsic hand muscles, finger flexors; medial forearm/hand sensory loss.
  • Posterior cord: deltoid + radial-innervated muscles. Medial/lateral cords: combinations of median/ulnar/musculocutaneous deficits.
  • Upper lumbar plexus L1–4: hip flexion/adduction and knee extension weakness; reduced patellar reflex; anterior/medial thigh and medial leg sensory loss.
  • Sacral plexus L4–S4: hip abduction/extension, hamstrings, ankle and toe muscles; Achilles reflex abnormalities; posterior thigh, leg and foot sensory loss.
  • A plexopathy becomes particularly likely when the pattern cannot be explained by one root or one terminal nerve — e.g., simultaneous suprascapular and musculocutaneous abnormalities.

docs.title: Rapid approach
docs.text:
1. Exclude the dangerous thing first (red-flag screen above). Any red flag → urgent MRI and spine referral; no conservative trial.
  2. Localize: root vs plexus vs nerve. Dermatomal/myotomal single-root pattern → radiculopathy. Multi-nerve, multi-root, plexus-coherent pattern → plexopathy. Discrete, stepwise deficits in individual named nerves, often in more than one limb → mononeuropathy multiplex (see the differential table).
  3. Route: uncomplicated radiculopathy → conservative care first (Step 1). Suspected plexopathy → EMG/NCS + dedicated plexus MRI and an etiologic workup (Step 1 for plexopathy).
  4. Reassess on a clock: radiculopathy not improving at 4–6 weeks → MRI and consider ESI or surgical referral; progressive deficit at any point → escalate immediately.

docs.title: The prescriptive flow (what I want done, in order)
docs.text:
1. Red-flag screen + neuro exam (motor, sensory, reflexes, gait, myelopathy signs, bladder/bowel, saddle sensation). Document the exact myotome/dermatome.
  2. If no red flags and the exam is stable: start conservative care now — activity + NSAID + early PT (Step 1). Do not image routinely.
  3. If the pattern is plexus-coherent (not one root): order EMG/NCS and dedicated plexus MRI, and start the etiologic workup — do not anchor on a spine MRI.
  4. Reassess at 2–6 weeks. Improving → continue and taper. Not improving or worsening → MRI (if not already done), ESI for severe concordant radicular pain, spine referral.
  5. Surgery only for the indications below — progressive deficit, emergent compression, or persistent disabling radicular pain with a concordant lesion after an adequate nonoperative trial (~6–12 weeks).
  6. Disposition + follow-up: almost always outpatient for uncomplicated radiculopathy; admit for red flags, myelopathy, or cauda equina.

docs.title: Workup
docs.text: Uncomplicated radiculopathy needs no routine imaging or labs. The ACR rates noncontrast MRI as may be appropriate for acute cervical radiculopathy without trauma/red flags; a stable uncomplicated presentation can often begin conservative care without immediate imaging — most cases resolve with conservative care, herniated discs shrink over time, and spondylotic changes are common in people without symptoms. Interpret any MRI only alongside the clinical findings, never on its own — false positives and false negatives are frequent.

docs.title: When to get MRI
docs.text: Situation Imaging Urgent / emergent — cauda equina, myelopathy/cord compression, suspected infection or cancer, severe or progressive deficit (including multi-level deficits) MRI now (with contrast if infection or malignancy is suspected — MRI without and with IV contrast is the appropriate first study for suspected infection) Elective — persistent symptoms after 4–6 weeks of failed conservative care, if the patient is a candidate for intervention or the diagnosis remains uncertain MRI without contrast (cervical: "may be appropriate" even for acute uncomplicated radiculopathy, "usually appropriate" for chronic radiculopathy per the 2024 ACR cervical criteria; lumbar: after ~6 weeks of optimal medical management in surgical/intervention candidates). ACOEM: MRI at 3–4 weeks is reasonable if an epidural is planned Not recommended Routine early MRI (does not improve outcomes, increases downstream procedures); repeat MRI without clinical change; radiographs alone (rarely change acute management without red flags) MRI contraindicated or obscured by hardware CT myelography is the alternative; CT also shows bony anatomy, foraminal osteophytes, and ossification for surgical planning

docs.title: Labs
docs.text: Order ESR/CRP and CBC only when infection or cancer is suspected. For suspected plexopathy, the lab panel is broader — see the plexopathy workup below.

docs.title: Electrodiagnostics (EMG/NCS)
docs.text:
Not needed when the diagnosis is clear. Use EMG/NCS when clinical and imaging levels don't match, when surgery is being considered, or to exclude peripheral neuropathy/entrapment. The AANEM recommends needle EMG plus at least one motor and one sensory nerve conduction study in the affected limb. Two timing points that matter:

  • EMG may be falsely unrevealing very early in an axonal radiculopathy — interpret with symptom duration in mind.
  • For plexopathy, study at about 3–4 weeks after onset (fibrillations take ~3 weeks to appear) and repeat at about 3–6 months to track reinnervation.

Workup — suspected plexopathy

  • EMG/NCS (extensive, compared with the other side): SNAP amplitude is the most useful marker of axon-loss plexopathy and maps the element involved; motor NCS are insensitive for screening — side-to-side CMAP amplitude estimates the percentage of motor axon loss, which matters for prognosis. Needle EMG is the most sensitive test for motor axon loss and shows the proximal extent; MUAPs show continuity and early reinnervation.
  • Dedicated plexus MRI / MR neurography with STIR and contrast — the main imaging study (ACR: preferred initial imaging for nontraumatic plexopathy once localization is made). Brachial plexus MRI: sensitivity 81%, specificity 91%, accuracy 88% vs surgery/follow-up; added information beyond exam and EDx in 45% of patients. Lumbosacral plexus MRI changed management in 71% of patients in one series; abnormal nerve signal correlates with active denervation on EMG. MR neurography evaluates nerve caliber/enlargement, T2/STIR hyperintensity, loss of normal fascicular architecture, enhancement, and muscle denervation edema/atrophy.
  • High-resolution ultrasound complements MRI for superficial segments, dynamic and traumatic lesions, and fascicular detail (operator-dependent). For trauma, CT myelography or MRI can show root avulsion.
  • Labs, tailored to the case: HbA1c, CBC, ESR/CRP; ANA, ANCA, SSA/SSB, RF/CCP, cryoglobulins, hepatitis B/C (vasculitis); SPEP/immunofixation + free light chains (amyloid); HIV, syphilis, Lyme; CSF (cells, protein, cytology/flow) if infiltrative or inflammatory disease is suspected. If malignancy is suspected: CT chest/abdomen/pelvis or PET.
  • Genetics when the pattern fits: PMP22 deletion for painless recurrent palsies (HNPP); SEPT9 for familial recurrent painful episodes (hereditary neuralgic amyotrophy).
  • Targeted fascicular nerve biopsy only for unexplained progressive plexopathy — e.g., to find perineurial tumor spread, lymphoma, or vasculitis.
  • → Localization confirmed → treat the cause (see Management, Step 3 for plexopathy).

docs.title: Radiculopathy — conservative care first
docs.text:
The natural history is favorable: 75–90% of patients with chronic radiculopathy improve with nonoperative care, and conservative care is appropriate for symptoms under about 6–8 weeks with mild-to-moderate deficits and no progressive neurologic loss. Cervical evidence is much thinner than lumbar — most cervical recommendations are extrapolated from lumbar data. The approach is multimodal and time-limited: education + staying active, PT/exercise, and short courses of NSAIDs. Medications are short-term symptom control, not disease-modifying treatment.

Step 1 — first-line: stay active + NSAID + early PT (start here for most)

  • Keep the patient active and educate about the generally favorable natural history. Bed rest does not help.
  • NSAID — ibuprofen 400–600 mg PO q6–8h (max 2,400 mg/day Rx; 1,200 mg/day OTC) or naproxen 500 mg PO BID (max 1,000–1,250 mg/day), for about 1–2 weeks, then reassess. Lowest effective dose, shortest time. Screen for GI, renal, and cardiovascular risk; add a PPI if GI risk is high. Avoid in CKD stage 4–5, with anticoagulants, or in uncontrolled heart failure.
  • Physical therapy / exercise — refer early: directional-preference exercises and activity in the acute phase; add strengthening and neurodynamic mobilization in the subacute phase. In the Fritz trial, early PT for sciatica of <90 days improved disability and pain more than usual care. Cervical PT components: cervical/scapular stabilization and strengthening, postural and ergonomic training, neural mobilization when tolerated, selective manual therapy, traction in appropriately selected patients, progressive home exercise.
  • → No reliable improvement across 2–6 weeks, or pain remains disabling → Step 2.

Step 2 — persistent disabling radicular pain: selective steroid or ESI

  • Oral corticosteroid — only selectively, and know the split: prednisone 60 mg × 5 days, then 40 mg × 5 days, then 20 mg × 5 days (Goldberg trial). Pain improves only ~0.56/10 at <2 weeks, with a small long-term function gain (7.4/100) and no change in surgery rates. VA/DoD 2022 recommends against systemic steroids; NICE recommends against oral corticosteroids for sciatica. Reserve for clear radicular findings (dermatomal pain/deficits, positive SLR) and counsel that the benefit is small and short-term and steroids do not reduce the need for surgery. Adverse effects: insomnia, nervousness, increased appetite; watch glucose in diabetes. Best dose is unknown — avoiding higher doses may reduce harm. Do not use a Medrol Dosepak or prednisone taper routinely for lumbar radiculopathy.
  • Cervical exception: the limited cervical RCT evidence is more favorable — prednisolone 50 mg/day × 5 days, tapered over the subsequent 5 days produced clinically important improvement in 75.8% vs 30% with placebo (better pain and Neck Disability Index scores) — but this was a single small trial of 59 patients, so a short course is a selective option for severe cervical radiculopathy, not a default.
  • Epidural steroid injection (ESI) — image-guided transforaminal or interlaminar, usually in the subacute phase after ~4–6 weeks of failed conservative care, or to bridge severe pain. Probably reduces short-term (~2–6 week) pain and disability (AAN 2025: probably effective short-term; NNT ~4 for pain and ~6 for disability over ≤3 months in cervical/lumbar radiculopathy; long-term pain benefit is uncertain). A 2026 systematic review found even lower doses — dexamethasone 4 mg, methylprednisolone 20 mg, triamcinolone 10 mg — sometimes produced outcomes statistically indistinguishable from higher doses. Do NOT prescribe a predetermined "series of three" — repeat only on meaningful response to the first procedure. Cervical transforaminal injections with particulate steroid carry rare but catastrophic neurovascular risk — nonparticulate dexamethasone is preferred.
  • → Still disabling after an adequate trial with a concordant lesion → Step 3 (surgical referral).

Step 3 — surgical referral

Do not require a completed conservative trial when there is: progressive or substantial motor weakness; cervical myelopathy; cauda equina/conus syndrome; spinal instability; epidural abscess; tumor causing neurologic compression; or another compressive lesion threatening permanent neurologic injury.

Elective referral (neurologically stable degenerative radiculopathy) becomes reasonable with persistent disabling radicular pain or neurologic dysfunction despite an adequate nonoperative trial (~6–12 weeks) and imaging demonstrating a concordant compressive lesion. Cervical: spine referral/interventional evaluation when symptoms fail to improve after roughly 4–8 weeks; NASS-derived recommendations describe a 6–12 week nonoperative period as reasonable in stable patients. Lumbar: ACR identifies patients with persistent or progressive symptoms after ~6 weeks of optimal medical management who are candidates for surgery/intervention.

Results are better when leg or arm pain predominates over axial pain. Fusion is not indicated for axial low back pain alone. Cervical caveat: most patients improve whatever the treatment — in RCTs of surgery vs standardized nonsurgical care, surgery gave only a small benefit for disc herniation and no significant benefit for spondylosis at 12 months.

Avoid

  • Routine gabapentinoids for lumbar sciatica — pregabalin (PRECISE trial, titrated up to 600 mg/day) was no better than placebo for acute or chronic sciatica, with more adverse effects and misuse potential. NICE recommends against them. Reconsider or avoid; use only for another compelling neuropathic indication.
  • Opioids for radicular pain — poor efficacy, dependence risk, and they blunt the response to specific treatment.
  • Bed rest — continued activity beats it.
  • A predetermined "series of three" ESIs — repeat only on meaningful response.
  • Particulate steroid for cervical transforaminal ESI — rare but catastrophic neurovascular risk; use nonparticulate dexamethasone.
  • Duloxetine for radiculopathy — evidence is indeterminate.

TRICARE — verified rules and the current form

Check the exact analgesic/formulation and requested service. A guideline recommendation for MRI, epidural injection or surgery does not automatically establish coverage. Document deficits, function and conservative treatment without allowing authorization delays to postpone emergency evaluation of progressive weakness or cauda equina syndrome.

Current PA/MN details, benefit routing and packet · Live Formulary Search. Check the exact product, beneficiary and venue on the prescribing date.

docs.title: Conservative-treatment evidence at a glance
docs.text: Treatment Typical adult regimen Evidence (lumbar) Evidence (cervical) Practical role NSAID Ibuprofen 400–600 mg PO q6–8h or naproxen 500 mg PO BID, ~1–2 weeks Small short-term benefit for pain/disability; low-quality evidence of slight global improvement in sciatica; all NSAIDs perform about the same; systematic reviews show little/no clear improvement in pain or disability vs placebo for true radicular leg pain Direct RCT evidence limited; commonly used for short-term nociceptive/inflammatory pain Reasonable first-line analgesic if no GI/renal/CV contraindication — symptomatic, not disease-modifying Gabapentin / pregabalin If used for another compelling neuropathic indication: gabapentin often starts 300 mg daily → BID → TID; pregabalin 75 mg BID PRECISE (NEJM 2017): no better than placebo for acute or chronic sciatica; more adverse effects Controlled evidence lacking; reviews still mention them for persistent radicular pain Do not start routinely, especially for lumbar sciatica Oral corticosteroid Prednisone 60 mg × 5 d → 40 mg × 5 d → 20 mg × 5 d (Goldberg) Pain ~0.56/10 better at <2 weeks; function +7.4/100; no change in surgery rates; VA/DoD and NICE recommend against Prednisolone 50 mg/day × 5 d, taper over 5 d: 75.8% vs 30% improved (single trial, n=59) Selective only, for clear radicular findings; counsel benefit is small and short-term Epidural steroid injection Image-guided transforaminal or interlaminar, subacute phase Probably reduces short-term (2–6 week) pain/disability; AAN 2025: probably effective short-term Cervical: more caution; nonparticulate dexamethasone preferred Bridge for severe disabling radicular pain — restores sleep, mobility, work, rehab participation; not definitive treatment of the compressive lesion PT / exercise Early referral; directional-preference exercise acutely; strengthening + neurodynamic mobilization subacutely Early PT beat usual care for disability (Fritz trial, sciatica <90 days) Stage-based expert consensus; technique superiority uncertain Centerpiece of conservative care; universally recommended first-line nonpharmacologic care

docs.title: Surgery — comparative outcomes
docs.text:
Cervical: ACDF vs posterior cervical foraminotomy (PCF) — for single-level cervical radiculopathy, PCF is noninferior to ACDF for arm-pain relief and success rate; the two differ mainly in complication profile and long-term revision risk.

Outcome ACDF PCF (open or minimally invasive) Success (Odom), FACET RCT 76% at 1 year; 74% at 2 years 88% at 1 year; 81% at 2 years (noninferior) Arm pain / NDI Comparable Comparable Neck pain Somewhat worse; new cervicalgia 34% Less neck pain (statistically better, small difference); 23% Serious surgery-related adverse events, 2 years (FACET) 9% (7 reoperations) 8% (9 reoperations) Reoperation at 2 years ~6% ~8% Approach-specific complications Dysphagia, dysphonia/RLN injury, esophageal/vascular injury, pseudarthrosis, implant failure, adjacent-segment disease Early posterior neck pain, wound infection (2.2% vs 0.2%), dehiscence, pulmonary embolism, recurrent foraminal herniation 5-year revision (national database, n≈32,000) 14.8% 19.0% Length of stay / cost Longer, higher ~1 day shorter; ~$9,100 less Motion preservation No (fusion) Yes Best anatomy Central/paracentral disc, significant anterior osteophyte/disc complex, disc-space collapse; useful when stabilization is desirable Unilateral lateral/foraminal disc or osteophyte, preserved alignment and stability; best fit is unilateral foraminal soft disc or foraminal stenosis at 1–2 levels with lordosis preserved, in patients who want to keep motion

Lumbar: microdiscectomy vs laminectomy — these treat different problems (disc herniation vs stenosis), so the procedure is chosen by pathology, not by head-to-head outcome. A small laminotomy/hemilaminectomy is often part of the exposure for a microdiscectomy, but a full decompressive laminectomy is generally unnecessary for an isolated posterolateral disc herniation.

Microdiscectomy (herniated disc with radiculopathy) Laminectomy (central/lateral-recess stenosis, neurogenic claudication) Effect Leg-pain relief good to excellent in most; good/excellent result in ~70–90% of appropriately selected patients. In chronic sciatica lasting 4–12 months, beat standardized nonoperative care at 1 year. SPORT (disc herniation, radiculopathy ≥6 weeks): faster and greater improvement in leg pain, function, and disability than continued nonoperative treatment in as-treated analyses; advantage persisted through 8 years (adjusted 8-year effects: SF-36 bodily pain +10.9, physical function +10.6, ODI −11.2). Even so, 30–70% report some ongoing pain Decompression improves pain over conservative care at 3–6 months; benefit lasts but fades by 2–4 years. Adding fusion gives no benefit over decompression alone for stenosis without instability Complications Overall ~10%: recurrent herniation ~7% (up to ~10% in other series; 4–6% in pooled series), reoperation ~4–8%, durotomy ~2–4%, deep infection <1%, wrong-level surgery 0.7%, nerve-root injury <1%. Open, micro, and endoscopic techniques give similar 2-year results; endoscopic shortens hospital stay but may carry more durotomy and reherniation SPORT lumbar stenosis: dural tear ~9%, wound infection 2%, reoperation 13% at 4 years, 18% at 8 years (recurrent stenosis or progressive spondylolisthesis ~half of reoperations). National registry: overall complication rate 16.8% (durotomy, urinary retention, wound infection common); risk rises with age, higher ASA class, multilevel surgery, longer operative time. Wider exposure → more blood loss, durotomy (higher in revision surgery and elderly), iatrogenic instability or late spondylolisthesis if facets are taken

Choose by pathology, not by preference:

Pathology Preferred operation Unilateral cervical foraminal soft disc/osteophyte, preserved alignment/stability PCF or ACDF — outcomes essentially equivalent Cervical central/anterior compression, disc collapse, instability, kyphotic segment Usually ACDF Single-level lumbar posterolateral disc herniation causing sciatica Microdiscectomy Lumbar central/lateral-recess stenosis with claudication ± multiroot radiculopathy Laminotomy/laminectomy decompression Disc herniation + stenosis Limited decompression plus discectomy, tailored to anatomy Instability/spondylolisthesis requiring stabilization Decompression ± fusion, depending on documented instability rather than radiculopathy alone

docs.title: Plexopathy — management by cause
docs.text:
Treat the cause; supportive care is the mainstay. Neuropathic pain drugs (gabapentin, pregabalin, duloxetine, TCAs) — gabapentin often starts 300 mg daily → BID → TID, pregabalin 75 mg BID — plus PT/OT, bracing, and glycemic control in diabetic LRPN.

Cause Management Traumatic avulsion / rupture Refer promptly after suspected avulsion/rupture; reconstruction is often time-sensitive within ~3–6 months, or when there is no clinical or EMG reinnervation. Options: nerve grafts, nerve transfers Tumor / neoplastic (Pancoast lung, breast, lymphoma — usually painful, lower plexus) Tumor-directed therapy (systemic therapy, radiotherapy and/or surgery) while treating neuropathic and cancer-related pain Radiation plexopathy (usually painless, upper plexus, with myokymia) No established disease-reversing therapy. Rehabilitation, orthoses/assistive devices, neuropathic-pain treatment; first exclude recurrent malignancy. Myokymic discharges are particularly suggestive of radiation injury and much more frequent in radiation-induced than neoplastic plexopathy, but neither their presence nor absence is absolutely diagnostic Neuralgic amyotrophy / Parsonage-Turner (abrupt severe shoulder/upper-arm pain → patchy weakness days later; often surprisingly multifocal) Pain control and targeted PT/OT are central. Early corticosteroids may shorten the acute painful phase in some patients, but high-quality randomized evidence is limited; chronic rehab emphasizes motor-control retraining and avoidance of excessive loading Diabetic / nondiabetic LRPN (acute/subacute severe hip or thigh pain → asymmetric proximal weakness/atrophy → spread to other territories, sometimes bilateral, often with weight loss) Optimize diabetes care, analgesia, gait/fall support, orthotics when needed, PT/OT. Microvasculitic inflammation is implicated; evidence for immunotherapy is limited. EDX is an axonal, multifocal radiculoplexus neuropathy — paraspinal denervation does not argue against the diagnosis. MRI is often used primarily to exclude malignancy, structural disease, infection, and other infiltrative causes Vasculitis / sarcoid / infection / abscess / hematoma Immunosuppression for vasculitis or sarcoid; abscess drainage; hematoma evacuation or stopping anticoagulation Compressive (thoracic outlet, mass, retroperitoneal hematoma, psoas/iliacus lesion) Relieve the compressive structure

Prognosis: recovery is often incomplete — counsel realistically. In a 2026 tertiary series of 124 lumbosacral plexopathy patients, the commonest causes were diabetic LRPN (n=43), perioperative injury (32), idiopathic/nondiabetic LRPN (18), and radiation (15), then autoimmune, neoplastic, traumatic, and infectious causes.

docs.title: Plexopathy vs radiculopathy vs mononeuropathy multiplex
docs.text:
Feature Radiculopathy Plexopathy Mononeuropathy multiplex Clinical pattern Dermatomal pain/sensory loss, myotomal weakness, usually one or a few adjacent roots Weakness and sensory loss across several nerves in one limb, proximal + distal, not fitting one root or one nerve Discrete, stepwise deficits in individual named nerves, often in more than one limb, distal-predominant Neck/back pain Often prominent Variable — Lesion site vs DRG Preganglionic Postganglionic Postganglionic SNAPs Normal, even in a numb dermatome Reduced/absent in the involved trunk/cord territory — which gives localizing value Reduced in affected nerves only, often patchy across limbs Paraspinal EMG Denervation present Normal (spared posterior primary rami) Normal Limb EMG Muscles sharing a root across different nerves Muscles sharing a plexus element (trunk/cord/division) across nerves and roots Muscles of each affected nerve, with sparing of other nerves from the same root Plexus MRI Usually normal May show nerve enlargement, T2 signal, enhancement, mass — Spine MRI May show concordant foraminal/root disease May be incidental — Typical causes Disc, spondylosis, zoster, diabetic, carcinomatous See causes table above Vasculitis, diabetes, HNPP, leprosy, Lyme, HIV, sarcoid, lymphoma

Pitfalls: radiculoplexus neuropathy (diabetic or nondiabetic LRPN) involves roots, plexus, and nerves together — paraspinal denervation does not exclude a plexus process. Bilateral or asymmetric multifocal disease means vasculitic mononeuritis multiplex, LRPN, and polyradiculopathy all need to be considered. The key conceptual distinction is anatomic coherence: plexopathy maps to a plexus; mononeuropathy multiplex maps to multiple separate nerves.

A useful EDX definition: abnormalities involving at least two peripheral nerves derived from more than one root distribution.

docs.title: Disposition
docs.text:
Uncomplicated radiculopathy is an outpatient diagnosis — treat, start PT, arrange follow-up, and give a written plan with the reassessment clock (2–6 weeks) and return precautions (new weakness, saddle numbness, bladder/bowel change, fever). Admit for red flags, myelopathy, cauda equina, or infection. Suspected plexopathy is outpatient unless the cause needs admission (tumor, abscess, hematoma) — but the workup (EMG/NCS + plexus MRI + etiologic labs) should not wait, and suspected traumatic avulsion needs prompt specialist referral; 3–6 months is a reconstruction window, not a referral target.

Military medicine — duty, retention and deployment

  • Profile / function: Document objective strength, sensation, dexterity, lifting/carrying and load-bearing limits; protect a weak limb from further injury.
  • Retention / MEB–MAR2: Apply the relevant spinal/peripheral-nerve standard and expected recovery. Persistent inability to perform the PMOS differs from failure of medical retention standards. Use the retention framework; permanent P3/4 does not by itself select DES versus MAR2.
  • Deployment / medications: Evaluate the diagnosis and each drug. Topiramate/gabapentin for an eligible non-BH condition is not automatically limiting; pregabalin, opioids and certain named anticonvulsants require separate review. See the disease AND drug screen for the current CENTCOM rules and waiver packet.
  • Special duty: flight, diving and other special assignments have separate standards and waiver authorities; a general duty profile does not clear them.
  • LOD / EPTS: document onset, duty status, exposures and aggravation objectively. The designated authority determines LOD/EPTS; neither in-service diagnosis nor a genetic finding settles it automatically.

docs.title: 📚 Discover — evidence brief
docs.text:
Written from primary guidelines and trials; source articles are a reading list, not copied.

  • The diagnosis is clinical; imaging is timed, not routine. Without red flags, a focused exam plus a trial of conservative care is the right first move — routine early MRI does not improve outcomes and increases downstream procedures. MRI earns its place at ~4–6 weeks if symptoms persist and the result will change management, or immediately for cauda equina, myelopathy, infection, or progressive deficit.
  • The exam still carries numbers. Spurling's is highly specific (0.84–1.00), a negative upper-limb neurodynamic cluster helps rule cervical radiculopathy out (sensitivity 0.97), and a crossed straight-leg raise is specific (0.90) — use them before ordering anything.
  • Conservative care is a time-limited trial, not a holding pattern. Activity + NSAID + early PT is the centerpiece; the two drugs clinicians reach for most — gabapentinoids and oral steroids — have the weakest support for lumbar sciatica (PRECISE: pregabalin no better than placebo; VA/DoD and NICE both recommend against systemic steroids). ESI is a bridge for severe disabling pain, not a cure for the compressive lesion, and never a predetermined "series of three."
  • Surgery is a pathology choice. PCF is noninferior to ACDF for single-level cervical radiculopathy (FACET: 2-year success 81% vs 74%), trading dysphagia and fusion for more wound infection and a higher 5-year revision rate (19.0% vs 14.8%). Lumbar microdiscectomy and laminectomy are not competitors — one treats herniation, the other stenosis — and SPORT still anchors the long-term picture (8-year ODI advantage −11.2 points for discectomy).
  • Plexopathy is a localization exercise, not a spine problem. Multi-nerve, multi-root, plexus-coherent deficits plus the SNAP/paraspinal rule (reduced SNAPs, normal paraspinals) separate it from radiculopathy; dedicated plexus MRI/MR neurography is the imaging test (ACR), and brachial plexus MRI runs 81% sensitive / 91% specific. The commonest lumbosacral cause in a 2026 tertiary series was diabetic LRPN — a radiculoplexus neuropathy, so paraspinal denervation does not exclude a plexus process.

Key sources: ACR Appropriateness Criteria Cervical Pain or Cervical Radiculopathy: 2024 Update (Eldaya et al., JACR 2025); ACR Appropriateness Criteria Plexopathy: 2021 Update (Boulter et al., JACR 2021); VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Low Back Pain (2022); NICE Low Back Pain and Sciatica (NG59); AAN 2025 epidural steroid injection review; FACET trial (ACDF vs PCF); SPORT (lumbar disc herniation and lumbar stenosis); PRECISE trial (NEJM 2017); Goldberg et al. oral prednisone trial; Fritz et al. early PT trial; AANEM electrodiagnostic guidance.
