docs.title: Trigeminal neuralgia
docs.text:
Last reviewed: July 2026

One-liner: paroxysmal, electric-shock facial pain in one or more trigeminal divisions (usually V2/V3), triggered by innocuous stimuli — light touch, chewing, talking, brushing teeth, cold air. Volleys of stabbing pain with pain-free intervals. Multiple sclerosis can present with trigeminal neuralgia — always keep it on the table.

🚩 Red flags for a secondary cause — image everyone

Features that point away from classical TN and toward a structural or demyelinating cause:

  • Sensory loss or other cranial-nerve deficit on exam
  • Bilateral symptoms
  • Age < 40 at onset
  • Poor response to sodium-channel-blocking drugs

Any of these — and honestly, all first presentations — warrant MRI to look for neurovascular compression, a tumor, or an MS plaque at the root entry zone.

docs.title: Diagnose & classify (ICHD-3)
docs.text:
• Phenotype: brief (a fraction of a second to 2 min), shock-like/stabbing, triggered, division-specific pain with normal sensation between attacks. A "concomitant continuous pain" variant (a background aching/burning between the shocks) exists, predicts a harder course, and needs different drugs (see the continuous-pain note in Step 2).
  • Classify: classical (proven neurovascular compression with morphological change — atrophy or displacement of the nerve), secondary (MS, tumor, AV malformation), or idiopathic (no cause found).

🚩 Screen for depression and suicidality — the "suicide disease" is not hyperbole

TN carries a doubled suicide/self-harm risk (standardized incidence ratio ~2.1, higher in women) and roughly a third of patients report suicidal ideation; anxiety, depression, and pain intensity all track with worse suicidality. (A large cohort also found increased stroke and MI risk.) Ask every TN patient about mood and suicidal ideation, treat the pain aggressively, and co-manage psychological burden — pain control is the intervention, and unrelieved TN is a safety issue, not just a comfort issue.

docs.title: Rapid approach
docs.text:
1. Confirm the phenotype (above) with a normal interictal exam.
  2. MRI brain — thin cuts through the pontine cistern / course of CN V for vascular compression, demyelination (MS), or tumor.
  3. Start a sodium-channel blocker (Step 1) — titrate to pain freedom.
  4. Refer for surgery early if pain isn't controlled or the drug isn't tolerated — don't grind through five drugs first.

docs.title: The prescriptive flow (what I want done, in order)
docs.text:
1. Confirm phenotype + MRI (exclude MS/tumor, characterize neurovascular compression).
  2. Start carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine, titrate to effect (Step 1). Screen HLA-B*15:02 before carbamazepine in at-risk ancestry.
  3. Inadequate or not tolerated? Add or switch to a second-line agent (Step 2) — lamotrigine, gabapentin/pregabalin, baclofen, or botulinum toxin A.
  4. Acute pain crisis (can't eat/drink/take pills): admit for IV fosphenytoin or lidocaine + rehydration (crisis order set).
  5. Refractory or poorly tolerated on adequate medical therapy: refer for surgery — microvascular decompression is first-line surgery for classical TN with neurovascular compression; ablative procedures for poor surgical candidates.
  6. MS plaque on MRI: pivot to the demyelinating work-up — the TN is a symptom of the larger diagnosis.

docs.title: Workup
docs.text: MRI is mandatory — it both excludes secondary causes (especially MS and posterior-fossa tumors) and characterizes neurovascular compression for surgical planning. Baseline CBC, sodium, LFTs before starting carbamazepine/oxcarbazepine; HLA-B*15:02 genotyping before carbamazepine in patients of Han Chinese, Thai, or other Southeast Asian ancestry (SJS/TEN risk).

docs.title: Management
docs.text:
Step 1 — first-line: a sodium-channel blocker (start here for everyone)

Both are first-line (EAN 2019). Start low, titrate to pain freedom, then hold the lowest effective dose.

  • Carbamazepine — start 100–200 mg BID, titrate by ~100–200 mg every few days; usual effective 600–800 mg/day (range 200–1200 mg/day), divided. Most effective agent; least well tolerated. Monitor CBC, sodium (hyponatremia), LFTs; it has an ECG effect and major CYP-inducing drug interactions. Screen HLA-B*15:02 first in at-risk ancestry.
  • Oxcarbazepine — start 300 mg BID, titrate to 600–1800 mg/day divided. Better tolerated with comparable efficacy and fewer interactions — a reasonable default — but hyponatremia is more common (check sodium).

→ Pain not controlled, or intolerable side effects → Step 2 (and start thinking about surgical referral in parallel).

Natural history — try a drug-free trial after sustained remission

TN remits and relapses: ~50% get a remission of up to 6 months. After sustained pain freedom, attempt a slow taper off the sodium-channel blocker — long-term CBZ/OXC carries cumulative toxicity (hyponatremia, marrow suppression, interactions). Warn the patient that attacks tend to get worse over time despite treatment, so relapse is likely and the drug can be restarted.

Step 2 — add-on / second-line (alone or added to Step 1)

Per EAN 2019, any of these may be used alone or as add-on when first-line fails or isn't tolerated:

  • Lamotrigine — titrate slowly (25 mg, up over weeks to ~200–400 mg/day) for rash/SJS risk; good add-on evidence.
  • Gabapentin / pregabalin — off-label alternatives or add-ons; consider particularly when continuous neuropathic pain coexists. Evidence in TN is limited. Use the oral dose table and the chosen product’s low-start titration/renal-dose instructions; monitor sedation, ataxia and respiratory risk with opioids.
  • Baclofen — 5–10 mg TID up to ~60–80 mg/day; classic add-on to carbamazepine (taper on discontinuation).
  • Botulinum toxin type A — a specialist-administered off-label adjunct. EAN’s recommendation is weak and based on very-low-quality evidence. Studies used 25–100 units, with variable products and injection methods; this range is not a transferable injection prescription, and different toxin products’ units are not interchangeable. Discuss an experienced injector’s product-specific protocol.
  • Increasingly used off-label: eslicarbazepine (once-daily, fewer interactions than CBZ — a reasonable dibenzazepine switch) and lacosamide (another Na-channel blocker). Phenytoin is a further option.
  • In trials: vixotrigine (Nav1.7-selective) and basimglurant (mGluR5 modulator) — novel mechanisms; not yet approved.

Concomitant continuous pain needs different drugs — and steer away from ablation

Carbamazepine/oxcarbazepine reliably help the paroxysmal shocks but are usually insufficient for the continuous aching/burning component. Add gabapentin/pregabalin or an antidepressant (e.g., a TCA/SNRI) for the continuous pain. Avoid ablative procedures when continuous pain is prominent — lesioning has a high rate of worsening neuropathic pain in this subgroup. (Percutaneous Meckel's-cave steroid/anesthetic injection is an emerging option for refractory continuous-pain cases.)

Acute TN crisis — can't eat, drink, or keep pills down (admit)

A severe exacerbation is a genuine emergency (dehydration, weight loss, unable to take oral meds).

  • Admit for rehydration and IV therapy.
  • IV fosphenytoin — rescue loading (commonly ~10–20 mg PE/kg) reduces pain within ~2 h; cardiac monitoring.
  • IV lidocaine — ~5 mg/kg over 1 h, monitored — relief up to ~24 h; buys time to up-titrate an oral agent or arrange surgery.
  • Up-titrate/optimize the oral sodium-channel blocker in parallel; involve neurology/neurosurgery.

Step 3 — refractory → procedural (refer early; don't over-medicate)

Offer surgery when pain is not sufficiently controlled medically, or medication is poorly tolerated — early referral beats stacking five drugs.

  • Microvascular decompression (MVD) — first-line surgery for classical TN with confirmed neurovascular compression; the most durable result (open posterior-fossa surgery; ~2/3 pain-free at 10 years). Vs Gamma Knife (meta-analysis): MVD gives more pain relief (RR ~1.9), less recurrence (RR ~0.3), and longer pain-free intervals (median ~94 vs ~53 months) — but higher overall surgical complications, though less post-procedure numbness. Counsel the trade-off: durability vs invasiveness.
  • Ablative / less-invasive (for poor surgical candidates or secondary TN): stereotactic radiosurgery (Gamma Knife), percutaneous rhizotomy (radiofrequency, glycerol, or balloon compression). Lower invasiveness, but higher recurrence and sensory-loss/anesthesia-dolorosa trade-offs — and avoid ablation when continuous pain is prominent (worsens neuropathic pain).

TRICARE — verified rules and the current form

Check the exact carbamazepine/oxcarbazepine, adjunct formulation and quantity in the current formulary. Off-label botulinum treatment for TN requires the regional coverage determination; the migraine PA is not its authorization. No universal no-PA claim for every generic was verified.

docs.title: Disposition
docs.text:
Outpatient, unless the patient is in a pain crisis (admit — see order set). Escalate to neurosurgery/ENT when medication fails or isn't tolerated. If the MRI shows an MS plaque, pivot to the demyelinating work-up — the TN is a symptom of the larger diagnosis.

Military medicine — duty, retention and deployment

  • Profile / function: Record incapacitating headache days, abortive success, preventive trials and drug effects. Grounding or hazardous-duty restrictions depend on attacks and treatment effects.
  • Retention / MEB–MAR2: Headache: DoDI V2 5.26.g and Army 3-31g; trigeminal neuralgia and other diagnoses need their applicable standard, rather than automatically borrowing the migraine threshold. Use the retention framework; permanent P3/4 does not by itself select DES versus MAR2.
  • Deployment / medications: CENTCOM disruptive migraine may require waiver; injectable CGRP therapy/Botox is separately relevant. Valproate, carbamazepine and lamotrigine are named medication exceptions even when used for pain/headache. See the disease AND drug screen for the current CENTCOM rules and waiver packet.
  • Special duty: flight, diving and other special assignments have separate standards and waiver authorities; a general duty profile does not clear them.
  • LOD / EPTS: document onset, duty status, exposures and aggravation objectively. The designated authority determines LOD/EPTS; neither in-service diagnosis nor a genetic finding settles it automatically.

docs.title: 📚 Discover — evidence brief
docs.text:
• Sodium-channel blockers (carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine) are first-line (EAN 2019: CBZ 200–1200 mg/day; OXC 300–1800 mg/day); oxcarbazepine is usually better tolerated with comparable efficacy but more hyponatremia.
  • Second-line/add-on: lamotrigine, gabapentin, pregabalin, baclofen, botulinum toxin A (evidence firmed up — ~OR 7.5 for ≥50% relief), phenytoin — alone or as add-on. Eslicarbazepine and lacosamide are increasingly used off-label; vixotrigine (Nav1.7) and basimglurant (mGluR5) are in trials.
  • The "suicide disease" is real — doubled suicide/self-harm risk (SIR ~2.1), ~1/3 with suicidal ideation; screen mood/SI and treat pain aggressively.
  • Concomitant continuous pain responds poorly to CBZ/OXC alone — add gabapentin/pregabalin or an antidepressant, and avoid ablative procedures (worsen neuropathic pain).
  • MRI for everyone — to catch MS and structural causes and to plan surgery.
  • Refer for surgery early. MVD gives the most durable relief (~2/3 pain-free at 10 y) and beats Gamma Knife on pain relief/recurrence/durability (median ~94 vs ~53 months), at the cost of higher surgical complications (but less numbness).
  • Natural history remits and relapses — try a drug-free taper after sustained remission (cumulative CBZ/OXC toxicity), but expect worsening over time.
  • Acute crisis = admit for rehydration and specialist-directed, monitored IV fosphenytoin or lidocaine.
  • Screen HLA-B*15:02 before carbamazepine in Southeast Asian ancestry (SJS/TEN).

Key sources: ICHD-3 (TN criteria); EAN 2019 & AAN/EFNS 2008 guidelines; MVD-vs-Gamma-Knife meta-analysis and Barker et al. (durability); botulinum-toxin meta-analyses; TN suicide-risk cohorts; emerging-drug (eslicarbazepine/lacosamide/vixotrigine/basimglurant) reviews.

docs.text:
1. Headache Classification Committee of the International Headache Society. ICHD-3.
  2. Bendtsen L, et al. European Academy of Neurology guideline on trigeminal neuralgia. Eur J Neurol. 2019;26(6):831–849.
  3. Cruccu G, et al. AAN-EFNS guidelines on trigeminal neuralgia management. 2008; Cruccu G, et al. Trigeminal Neuralgia. NEJM. 2020 (continuous-pain management).
  4. Psychological burden: Ehinger E, et al. TN and risk of cerebrovascular disease, MI, and suicide (J Headache Pain 2026, SIR ~2.1); Fishbein NS, et al. Suicidal ideation in TN (2024).
  5. Surgery / emerging drugs / BoNT-A: Fonseca PEO, et al. MVD vs Gamma Knife meta-analysis (Neurosurg Rev 2026); Barker FG, et al. Long-term MVD outcome (NEJM 1996); Stern JI, et al. Medical management of refractory TN (Curr Opin Neurol 2026 — eslicarbazepine/lacosamide/IV Mg); botulinum-toxin umbrella review (Drugs 2026) and meta-analyses.

Evidence/policy audit: 21 November 2026. Material changes were checked against the linked primary sources; this is an AI-assisted review, not certification of every dose or claim. Review scope and source limits.

docs.title: Military medicine — profiles, retention & deployability
docs.text:
Policy review: 21 November 2026

One-liner: write the functional restrictions today; separately decide retention, deployment, and special-duty clearance. A normal clinic examination does not answer all three questions, and a pharmacy approval answers none of them.

docs.title: The first five minutes
docs.text:
1. Protect the member and unit. Restrict driving, weapons, heights, water operations, flight, or remote duty according to the actual deficit, risk of sudden incapacity, and medication effects. Document a review date and who will reassess.
  2. Use retention standards for someone already serving. DoDI 6130.03 Volume 2 and the member’s Service regulation apply. Volume 1 is for accession; do not import its exclusions into an established Soldier’s retention decision.
  3. Identify an immediate retention trigger. Under current DoDI V2 5.26.k, diagnosed epilepsy prompts medical/personnel action on diagnosis; 5.26.d likewise addresses permanent/progressive dementia. Do not defer these actions solely to finish an arbitrary treatment clock. Provoked seizures are addressed separately in 5.26.j.
  4. For other conditions, assess the actual governing standard. The general DoD neurologic functional/treatment framework in 5.26.a does not cancel a more specific or stricter Army standard. Record diagnosis, adequate treatment, trajectory, and duty effects. Seek the profiling/MEB physician’s help when standards intersect.
  5. Check the destination and every medication. Use the deployment and medication guide. A condition may meet retention standards while still requiring a theater waiver.

docs.title: Army: choose the correct pathway
docs.text:
Finding Practical next step Temporary impairment with reasonable recovery expected Temporary profile with specific restrictions, linked extensions, treatment and reassessment plan Meets retention standards but permanent restrictions may prevent PMOS performance Consider MAR2, the administrative MOS-retention/reclassification process Fails retention standards at the medical retention determination point (MRDP), or another governing referral trigger applies Coordinate DES referral, using the appropriate permanent profile and approval-authority process Permanent PULHES 3/4 Requires the proper approval/review pathway; the number alone does not establish whether the member belongs in MAR2 or DES Guard/Reserve member Determine duty status, component-specific processing and any required LOD determination before promising the active-duty pathway or benefits

MRDP is a decision point, not a requirement to wait a year. It may be reached earlier when further functional improvement is not expected. Twelve months on temporary profile for the same condition is an administrative threshold requiring disposition review under Army procedures. Do not keep restarting an unlinked profile to hide the clock, and do not wait for every coexisting condition to stabilize once a qualifying referral is due.

The profiling provider describes the condition and restrictions; the designated approval authority reviews the permanent profile and referral. The MEB assesses whether retention standards are met; the PEB makes the formal fitness/disability determination. A treating clinician’s prediction is not a PEB finding. Use the installation’s current e-Profile/MEB process rather than telling a member that a particular signature guarantees separation.

docs.title: Common neurologic retention references
docs.text:
These are starting references, not a substitute for reading the whole applicable standard. Check current Army publication status and any intervening policy before signing.

Condition DoDI 6130.03 V2 Army reference / bedside implication Epilepsy 5.26.k AR 40-501 3-31i; coordinate action on diagnosis under current DoD policy. Do not cite 5.26.c for epilepsy Provoked seizures 5.26.j Distinguish an acute symptomatic event from epilepsy; document cause, recurrence, treatment and safety risk Migraine / other incapacitating headache 5.26.g 3-31g: ≥3 incapacitating days/month prompts neurologist evaluation; document preventive drug/dose/duration and response. Army provisions address a prophylaxis trial and direct referral when response is unlikely Stroke / recurrent TIA / vascular lesion 5.26.b 3-31f; residual function, mechanism, recurrence and treatment matter MS / chronic or recurrent demyelination 5.26.f 3-31e; use the specific Army standard rather than assuming good control cancels it TBI with residual impairment 5.26.h 3-31j; document cognition, balance, vision, headache and task performance after appropriate treatment Generalized myasthenia 5.26.l 3-31c; ocular-only disease is a specific exception in the standard, not blanket deployment clearance Permanent/progressive dementia 5.26.d 3-31k; initiate appropriate action on diagnosis. A potentially reversible encephalopathy requires diagnosis and functional reassessment Neuromuscular disease / neuropathy / paralysis 5.26.e / i, depending on diagnosis Apply the relevant disease and functional standard; do not force LEMS into a single exhaustive code Sleep disorders 5.27 3-32 and relevant 3-31h narcolepsy provisions; treatment response and daytime function matter Tremor / dystonia / syncope 5.26.m / n Frequency, function and sudden-incapacity risk drive restrictions; aviation has separate standards

docs.title: What to put in the note
docs.text:
• Diagnosis and diagnostic confidence; date of onset and objective findings.
  • Treatments tried: drug, dose, dates, adherence, benefit, adverse effects, and why stopped.
  • Function: actual lost duty days, observed task limits, attacks, recovery time, and safety risks. “Doing well” is not an operational assessment.
  • Current restrictions, expected duration, recovery trajectory, follow-up and referral plan.
  • For deployment: destination, mission, medical support, supply/monitoring needs, and the specialist’s assessment for the waiver authority.
  • For LOD/EPTS: record facts and records supporting onset/aggravation. Diagnosis during service does not itself establish LOD; a genetic diagnosis does not itself establish EPTS. The designated authority makes that determination.

docs.title: Sources and boundaries
docs.text:
• DoDI 6130.03 Volume 2, Change 2, 6 February 2026.
  • DoDI 6025.19 — Individual Medical Readiness, current 2026 change.
  • Army Publishing Directorate: AR 40-501 (27 June 2019), AR 40-502 (27 June 2019), DA Pam 40-502 (18 December 2023), and AR 635-40. Check the current controlled versions and local implementation; this review did not authenticate every internal MAR2 procedural step.
  • CENTCOM medical requirements and the official Army-hosted MOD 18 Tab A.

For the current review’s scope and remaining source limits, see Evidence and update policy.

docs.title: Deployment — check the disease AND the medication
docs.text:
Policy checked: 21 November 2026

One-liner: “stable on treatment” starts the discussion. It does not finish the deployment screen. The destination, job, resupply, monitoring and consequences of a missed dose all matter.

docs.title: Which decision are you making?
docs.text:
Decision Authority / action Retention in Service Current DoDI 6130.03 V2 + Service standards; profiles and DES/MAR2 guide Medical readiness category DoDI 6025.19 distinguishes deployable, deployable with limitations, temporarily nondeployable, and permanently nondeployable; use the formal criteria and readiness system A particular deployment Current combatant-command/component requirements, assignment and waiver authority Aviation / dive / other special duty Separate Service standards and waiver process, even if the member can deploy in another role

The table below is specifically CENTCOM MOD 18 Tab A. Do not export its time intervals or drug exclusions to every theater. The controlling theater/component publication at the time of screening takes precedence over this summary.

docs.title: Disease screen — CENTCOM
docs.text:
Condition What MOD 18 says / what to document Seizure disorder Seizure activity within the last year is not waiverable. A stable anticonvulsant regimen with one year seizure-free may be considered for waiver; current anticonvulsant use for prior seizures requires review. This theater rule does not replace retention action for diagnosed epilepsy Migraine Waiver when frequent/severe attacks disrupt duty. Include attack frequency, severity, functional impact, response with/without therapy, abortive success and previous/current regimens; neurologist endorsement is encouraged TBI Predeployment evaluation is required for any severity. MOD 18 lists release after 24 symptom-free hours after one mTBI, 7 symptom-free days after a second within 12 months, and neurologic and psychological evaluation after three TBIs of any severity. These are theater screening requirements, not replacements for TBICoE progressive return-to-activity or proof of recovery MS Waiver request must address stability, functional limitations, heat vulnerability and medication requirements. Apply Service retention standards independently Recurrent syncope / vertigo Document cause, control and incapacity risk; recurrent syncope requires waiver review. Vertiginous disorders need review unless controlled on medication available in theater History of heat stroke / rhabdomyolysis Waiver assessment includes recency, recurrence, organ damage/sequelae and ability to perform rigorous duty in similar heat. Do not clear from a normalized CK alone Stroke / TIA / CVST / dissection Assess deficits, recurrence, cause and monitoring; therapeutic anticoagulation or nonaspirin antiplatelet therapy creates a separate medication issue below. A healed image alone does not settle clearance MG / LEMS / CIDP / NMOSD / MOGAD / inflammatory myopathy No blanket clearance based on outpatient stability. Apply general condition criteria plus infusion/injection, immunosuppression, infection, lab, cold-chain and missed-dose risks. Explain rescue needs and whether the receiving location can actually provide them Progressive neurologic disease / dementia Duty and retention assessment comes first. Respiratory, bulbar, mobility or cognitive impairment and dependence on specialty care can preclude deployment even without a named theater paragraph OSA Mild (AHI and RDI <15/h) generally requires no waiver. Moderate (AHI 15–30/h) can proceed without waiver when asymptomatic, adherent, and Epworth <10. Severe (AHI >30/h) requires a waiver. AHI >60/h also needs a deployment recommendation from a pulmonologist, neurologist or sleep specialist. Symptomatic OSA is not waiverable. Complex/central apnea and ASV/AVAPS are nondeployable under this policy. Document PAP ≥4 hours on >70% of nights over 30 days for moderate/severe OSA, and bring rechargeable backup and supplies Acute encephalitis / meningitis / botulism / nerve-agent injury / new cord syndrome Stabilize, treat and evacuate as indicated. Return-to-duty/deployment decisions follow recovery, residual deficits, treatment and current theater requirements; discharge from hospital is not deployment clearance

MOD 18 general criteria include stability, low likelihood of deterioration/evacuation, feasible treatment, and no more than quarterly routine visits. A diagnosis absent from this table can still be disqualifying under those criteria.

docs.title: Medication screen — CENTCOM
docs.text:
Drug or class Practical rule under MOD 18 Tab A section I Therapeutic anticoagulants (warfarin, apixaban, rivaroxaban; also assess other agents) The policy calls the named therapeutic anticoagulants strictly disqualifying. Do not promise an available waiver. Obtain the component medical authority’s disposition; do not stop indicated anticoagulation to pass screening Nonaspirin antiplatelets (e.g., clopidogrel, ticagrelor, prasugrel) Listed as disqualifying medications requiring waiver review. Medically indicated aspirin use must be documented. The policy lists dabigatran in this section, but clinically it is an anticoagulant, not an antiplatelet Asundexian (Sunharbo) Newly approved after MOD 18 was issued. Apply the general anticoagulant, bleeding-risk and medication criteria through the component medical authority. Its absence from the named examples does not establish deployment clearance Antiseizure drugs for epilepsy or behavioral health Medication and underlying condition require review. CENTCOM’s one-year seizure rule applies separately Anticonvulsants for migraine/neuropathic pain Generally not intrinsically limiting when the condition meets theater criteria. Named exceptions: valproate/divalproex, carbamazepine, lamotrigine still require medication waiver review. A separate controlled-substance, adverse-effect or monitoring rule can still apply Topiramate / gabapentin for eligible non-BH conditions Not automatically disqualifying solely because they are anticonvulsants. Check cognition, balance, heat intolerance/oligohidrosis, stones, sedation and mission fit; topiramate is not a heat-exposure waiver Controlled substances, CSA I–V Waiver category includes benzodiazepines, opioids, sedative-hypnotics, stimulants and other controlled agents. Pregabalin, lacosamide, brivaracetam, cenobamate, modafinil/armodafinil and lasmiditan require assessment under this rule even when a different drug-class exception seems favorable. Confirm the current schedule of the exact drug CGRP antibodies; other SC/IM/IV therapies Injectable medication of any type requires waiver, except EpiPens. This includes home injections; self-administration does not erase the rule. Address storage, supply and injection/infusion support Botulinum toxin Current/recent use for severe pain is specifically listed; injections also trigger the general injectable rule. Include indication, response, interval, wear-off and consequences of delay Immunosuppressants / immune modifiers Chronic systemic steroids, relevant antineoplastics even for noncancer use, and biologic modifiers are listed. Describe infection risk, vaccines, CBC/LFT/Ig monitoring, and missed-dose/relapse consequences for anti-CD20, complement/FcRn therapies and other immune treatments Dopamine agonists (ropinirole, pramipexole, etc.) Specifically listed. Assess sudden sleep, hallucinations, impulse-control and orthostatic effects; levodopa is assessed on its own indication, effects and support needs Antipsychotics / lithium Specifically listed regardless of the nonpsychiatric reason for use; quetiapine for sleep is still quetiapine Any medicine needing titration, lab monitoring or special storage; any with dangerous missed-dose consequences General medication criteria can require waiver even if the drug is absent from the examples. Include the indication, dose, route, stability interval, adverse effects, monitoring and resupply plan Oral triptan / gepant / beta-blocker / antidepressant No universal drug-class clearance. Evaluate migraine or other diagnosis, adverse effects, monitoring and mission. Absence from a named list is not proof of deployability

Do not destabilize effective care to make a form easier. MOD 18 itself favors requesting a waiver over changing the route of a stable effective treatment. Explain the options to the member and coordinate with the waiver authority. Pharmacy coverage and deployment suitability remain separate decisions.

docs.title: A waiver packet that answers the question
docs.text:
1. Destination, dates, duty/MOS, austere exposure, medical support and evacuation access.
  2. Diagnosis, objective confirmation, event/relapse dates, stability interval, residual examination and functional limits.
  3. Drug list with indication, route, dose, last change, adverse effects, cold-chain limits, monitoring frequency and next scheduled treatment.
  4. Previous failures and why the current regimen is needed; consequences and rescue plan if medication or a visit is delayed.
  5. Supply plan through deployment and transit, storage/power needs, realistic local follow-up and contingency care.
  6. Specialist assessment of likely deterioration, incapacitation, mission impact and evacuation risk; current profile and relevant tests.
  7. Route through the Service component medical waiver channel. The theater/component surgeon or designated authority decides; the treating clinician recommends and supplies evidence.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
• CENTCOM current theater medical requirements.
  • MOD 18 Tab A — official Army-hosted public copy, sections 1, 7A and 7I. Source checked 21 November 2026; verify the theater’s latest version before screening.
  • DoDI 6025.19, current 2026 change.
  • DoDI 6130.03 Volume 2.

See Evidence and update policy for scope. This is a clinical interpretation of the cited policy, not an issued waiver or a guarantee of eligibility.

docs.title: TRICARE — getting the treatment to the patient
docs.text:
Coverage sources checked: 21 November 2026

One-liner: first identify the exact product, strength, indication and benefit. “FDA-approved,” “formulary,” “no PA” and “deployable” answer four different questions. The fax machine, regrettably, still has opinions.

docs.title: Start here
docs.text:
1. Open the TRICARE Formulary Search for the exact strength/form, beneficiary and pharmacy venue. Record the result and date; retrieve the linked current PA and medical-necessity forms.
  2. Separate pharmacy benefit (Express Scripts) from medical benefit (regional contractor/authorized treatment site). An infusion or clinician-administered drug may need a medical authorization even if absent from the pharmacy PA list. Home self-injection may use a different pathway from the vial.
  3. Distinguish PA (coverage criteria), nonformulary medical necessity (MN), quantity limits, referral and site-of-care approval. One approval does not automatically satisfy the others.
  4. For an active-duty Service member, nonformulary drugs require medical necessity under the current pharmacy rules. The retrieved PA forms direct the prescriber to submit to Express Scripts first even when approval appears unlikely. Subsequent reconsideration may be available through the appropriate MTF. For other beneficiaries, a nonformulary drug may be available at network/mail pharmacies at higher cost without MN, while PA still applies; MN matters for MTF access or reduced cost share. Confirm the specific plan and venue.
  5. Submit the current form/electronic PA with the needed records. Save the approval dates, quantity, route, indication and renewal requirements. Do not delay an emergency treatment while pursuing routine outpatient authorization.

docs.title: Headache — current forms actually retrieved
docs.text:
The following is a 21 November 2026 snapshot, not a promise of approval. Pharmacy history can satisfy some automated rules; a manually completed form may still be needed when that history is absent or incomplete.

Product / indication Verified access rule What the current manual form asks for Emgality 120 mg migraine formulation Uniform formulary; no PA displayed in the live lookup Exact migraine product matters. Do not apply the cluster formulation’s PA to the 120 mg pens. Check loading and dispensing quantities Emgality 100 mg ×3, episodic cluster Formulary with PA Adult; neurologist prescribing/consultation; not pregnant/trying; episodic cluster; failure/intolerance/contraindication to verapamil or topiramate or lithium; no concurrent preventive CGRP therapy. Initial 6 months, renewal documents ≥50% reduction in weekly attacks Ubrelvy 50/100 mg acute Formulary with PA/history-based rule Adult; neurologist/consultation; failure after 2 months each of two listed triptans (sumatriptan, rizatriptan, zolmitriptan, eletriptan), or documented intolerance/contraindication; no other gepant. Form shows no expiration after approval Qulipta, prevention Formulary with PA/history-based rule Adult; neurologist/consultation; chronic migraine, or qualifying episodic frequency/disability below; no other gepant; failure/intolerance/contraindication to one drug from two oral preventive classes AND one injectable CGRP preventive, with the form’s 2-month trials. Initial 6 months, response-based renewal Nurtec ODT, acute Nonformulary + PA; MN is a separate decision PA: adult, neurologist/consultation, no other gepant, two listed triptans plus Ubrelvy failed/intolerable/contraindicated. MN: Ubrelvy and three formulary triptans documented separately. Do not confuse the PA’s two-triptan requirement with the MN form’s three Nurtec ODT, episodic prevention Nonformulary + PA; MN separate Qualifying episodic migraine; two oral classes + one injectable CGRP preventive + Qulipta, each with required trial/contraindication/intolerance evidence. The current PA form has an exception to the Qulipta trial for patients already stable on Nurtec prevention. Initial 6 months, response-based renewal; MN asks for Qulipta + injectable preventive history Aimovig / Ajovy Official list has a 365-day prior-use/history PA rule; live Aimovig result directs users to preferred Emgality 120 mg Do not label them universally “no PA.” Current manual criteria were not successfully retrieved for this review; obtain the exact current form before telling the patient how many failures qualify Zavzpret Official October list: PA required; nonformulary See the dated DoD committee criteria below and obtain the current PA and MN forms

Episodic preventive thresholds: both forms accept 4–7 migraine days/month for 3 months plus MIDAS >11 or HIT-6 >50. The alternative on Qulipta is 8–14 days/month for 3 months. The May 2026 Nurtec form says at least 8 days/month for 3 months, within a confirmed episodic-migraine preventive indication. Qulipta separately has a chronic-migraine pathway.

Preventive renewal: the retrieved Qulipta/Nurtec forms accept ≥50% reduction in monthly headache days or specified functional improvement: MIDAS baseline 11–20 falls ≥5 points; baseline >20 falls ≥30%; HIT-6 falls ≥5; MPFID falls ≥5. Nurtec acute renewal asks for a positive clinical response. These are payer criteria, not the only ways a patient can benefit clinically.

Quantities are separate from treatment safety. The live 100 mg Ubrelvy result showed 16 tablets/30 days and 48/90 days at mail/MTF; Nurtec showed 8/30 days acute versus 16/30 days preventive. Individual authorization and dispensing edits may differ. A prescription quantity limit is not evidence that more frequent clinical exposure is safe.

docs.text:
Use the live search if these versioned links stop resolving. Dates below are the dates printed on forms returned by the live tool in this review, not invented revision dates.

docs.title: Botulinum toxin — medical benefit and regional criteria
docs.text:
TRICARE’s coverage policy distinguishes chronic migraine from episodic migraine, cluster, tension-type and other daily headaches. A PTH or NDPH phenotype does not automatically create a covered indication. Establish the actual diagnosis; do not relabel a patient to obtain payment.

Region / source Practical documentation West — policy revised 20 August 2025, retrieved November 2026 Adult; ≥15 headache days/month for >3 months, ≥8 with migraine features and ≥4-hour headache duration; at least one first-line oral preventive failed or prior botulinum treatment, and specialist involvement. Initial first treatment plus two subsequent treatments over six months; continuation requires documented improvement or maintained benefit East — public MP22-030E returned at review Adult; headache frequency ≥15 days/month for ≥3 months, qualifying migraine duration/features; preventive medication ineffective/not tolerated for ≥3 months. Confirm current requested product, units, procedure, follow-up authorization and continuation rules with the contractor

The regional policies are not identical. Use the current region’s authorization route rather than importing a pharmacy gepant PA or another insurer’s checklist.

  • TRICARE botulinum coverage.
  • West botulinum policy.
  • East botulinum policy MP22-030E.

docs.title: Other neurology drugs — what was and was not verified
docs.text:
These entries come from the official October 2026 PA/NF files (PA worksheet internally dated 7 October 2026, posted 29 October). A PA flag establishes a restriction, not the clinical criteria. Unless stated above, the drug-specific manual criteria were not independently obtained in this review; the packet below helps gather records, but is not a substitute for the form.

Drug / exact formulation Verified restriction or route What to obtain before prescribing through insurance Firdapse Pharmacy PA required Current LEMS diagnostic, prescriber and continuation criteria; diagnosis/objective testing and response records Ingrezza, Austedo Pharmacy PA required Current indication-specific TD/HD criteria and required prior treatment; baseline and follow-up movement/function scale Nuplazid Pharmacy PA + nonformulary Current Parkinson psychosis PA/MN, previous treatment and safety documentation Radicava ORS, Evrysdi Pharmacy PA required Current ALS/SMA diagnosis, functional/respiratory or genetic criteria, renewal measures and specialty-pharmacy route; do not invent a universal FVC cutoff Vyvgart Hytrulo 1,000 mg/5 mL prefilled syringe New-to-market pharmacy PA flag Exact CIDP versus gMG criteria and self-administration route. The 1,008 mg vial and IV Vyvgart are different products/benefit pathways HyQvia / Hizentra Prior-use lookback rule: PA when no prior use in 365 days Current indication, prior Ig response, dose conversion and continuation form. IVIG brand indications are not interchangeable Kesimpta, Mayzent, Zeposia, Mavenclad, Enspryng, Zilbrysq Pharmacy PA required Product-specific diagnosis/serostatus, label safety screening, prior therapies and renewal criteria Gilenya Prior-use lookback rule: 390 days Exact brand/generic and current form; do not apply its history rule to every S1P agent Vumerity Pharmacy PA; nonformulary in October file Exact current PA and MN criteria; do not assume brand restrictions equal generic dimethyl fumarate rules Lisraya 30 mg New-to-market pharmacy PA; nonformulary Current dermatomyositis PA/MN and safety monitoring requirements; FDA approval does not imply unrestricted access Leqembi IQLIK initiation pack / 360-mg maintenance device New-to-market pharmacy PA flags Verify the NDC and pack. The July FDA label supplies a 500-mg starting dose as two 250-mg injections and a separate 360-mg maintenance device. The October payer file describes the starting pack as 500 mg/2.5 mL. Confirm current benefit, pack and authorization with pharmacy Lecanemab IV / donanemab; ocrelizumab, alemtuzumab, rituximab, C5 therapies, inebilizumab, clinician-administered Ig; Spinraza, Qalsody, Itvisma Often medical-benefit/specialty-site review. West’s medical-drug list explicitly includes Leqembi and Kisunla Current regional drug + procedure/site authorization. Absence from the pharmacy list does not mean no PA. Obtain the current indication-specific checklist before promising access Livsayis (cemdisiran), Klygefa (gefurulimab), Sunharbo (asundexian) FDA approvals in November 2026, after the October pharmacy snapshot Confirm the current benefit, exact product, PA/MN and administration route directly. For complement therapies, also confirm REMS access. Current individual coverage was not established by this review Generic acute/maintenance drugs No blanket “generic = no PA” rule Search exact strength/form and benefit. Lacosamide/modafinil absence from this list alone does not prove unrestricted coverage. Quantity, age, diagnosis or other edits may apply

docs.title: Additional criteria from dated DoD committee records
docs.text:
The October 2026 files confirm the restrictions listed above. These older committee records give details useful for preparing documentation. Confirm them against the current form before using a specific restriction, trial length, or renewal threshold.

Drug What the dated official criteria requested Zavzpret Adult acute migraine, neurologist prescribing or consultation, no concurrent small-molecule CGRP drug, and failed/intolerable/contraindicated intranasal sumatriptan AND either Nurtec or Ubrelvy. Initial 6 months, then document clinical benefit. Confirm current PA and separate nonformulary MN. August 2023 DoD minutes Evrysdi Neurologist, documented SMN1 molecular diagnosis, ≥2 SMN2 copies in this version, SMA type, weight and dose, reproductive counseling when applicable, and restrictions on concurrent nusinersen and advanced ventilator dependence/paralysis. Initial 6 months, then documented improvement or stabilization for annual renewal. The 2023 age/dose table predates later label changes. Confirm the current form, especially for infants, tablet use or combination/sequential treatment. August 2023 DoD minutes Briviact tablet or oral solution October claims rule references prior brivaracetam or levetiracetam use within 180 days. The May 2024 manual criteria specified neurologist prescribing, focal-onset seizures, and insufficient response, intolerance or contraindication to levetiracetam. This version did not expire. Confirm the exact formulation and current rule. May 2024 DoD minutes Zilbrysq The 2024 criteria asked for adult AChR-positive gMG, neurologist prescribing, prior pyridostigmine, steroid-sparing treatment and FcRn antagonist history, vaccination documentation, and no concurrent FcRn/C5 therapy. Initial 6 months, with annual renewal based on documented benefit. Separate payer requirements from the current FDA vaccination and REMS requirements. May 2024 DoD minutes Nuplazid Adult hallucinations or delusions due to Parkinson disease psychosis, neurologist/psychiatrist/geriatric specialist involvement, attempted adjustment of PD medicines, QT/arrhythmia assessment, and no additional antipsychotic. The 2024 revision shows an MMSE item being edited. Confirm the current form before applying a cognitive cutoff. This version listed no PA expiration. November 2024 DoD minutes Firdapse The published records requested neurologist/oncologist prescribing and laboratory evidence of LEMS. Older records predate the pediatric label and include historical Ruzurgi language. Use the current form for age, step therapy and renewal. February 2019 DoD minutes

docs.title: Build a usable authorization packet
docs.text:
• Beneficiary/plan/region and prescriber details; exact generic + brand, strength, formulation, route, dose, quantity/day supply, indication and requested site.
  • Diagnostic evidence relevant to the requested drug: e.g., headache diary/MIDAS/HIT-6; seizure type; AChR/AQP4 results; electrodiagnostic CIDP evidence; amyloid confirmation and baseline MRI; genetic diagnosis. Include only what the form and clinical indication require.
  • A treatment table with drug, dose, start/stop dates, duration, adherence, response, adverse reaction, and specific reason a contraindicated option cannot be used. “Failed everything” is not documentation.
  • Label-required safety testing, vaccines/REMS where applicable, and a monitoring plan. These clinical requirements and payer step therapy are different things.
  • Continuation evidence using the same baseline measure and actual response; approval dates and impending renewal deadline.
  • If denied, read the reason: wrong benefit/site, missing data, nonformulary MN and lack of coverage are different problems. Use the plan’s reconsideration/appeal route with the relevant records and evidence.

docs.text:

Unresolved on this review: current specialty-drug clinical PA forms beyond those linked above, some current formulary tiers, Ajovy’s live service result, East botulinum continuation detail, US Family Health Plan-specific rules and individual benefit eligibility. They are deliberately not replaced with guessed failure counts or guaranteed approvals. Recheck the live tool and contractor when the prescription is written.

docs.title: Motor Neuron Disease
docs.text:
Last reviewed: October 2026

One-liner: the prescriptive approach to ALS and its motor-neuron-disease cousins — how to diagnose them fast, which disease-modifying drugs are actually on the table in 2026 (riluzole, edaravone, tofersen for SOD1), the Relyvrio rise-and-fall every patient will ask about, the SMA drug cabinet, and the respiratory/nutrition/symptom orderset that determines survival. For the on-call neurologist or PCP seeing progressive weakness in clinic, on admit, or in the ED.

🚩 Red flags — don't miss these

Pattern Worry Do now Bulbar-onset ALS (dysarthria, dysphagia, tongue fasciculations) with weight loss Aspiration, rapid nutritional collapse Same-visit swallow screen, dietitian, discuss PEG early — do not wait for the weight to fall off Respiratory symptoms (orthopnea, morning headache, daytime somnolence, weak cough) in known or suspected ALS Impending ventilatory failure ABG, overnight oximetry, pulmonary referral for NIV evaluation — NIV is the single biggest survival lever Weakness with sensory signs, sphincter involvement, or a sensory level This is not MND — myelopathy or something else MRI spine now; do not anchor on ALS until the spine is cleared Conduction block on NCS in an asymmetric pure-motor syndrome Multifocal motor neuropathy (anti-GM1) — IVIG-responsive, treatable EMG/NCS with conduction-block protocol; anti-GM1 antibodies; neurology — do not label this ALS Rapidly progressive weakness + ophthalmoplegia or fatigability Myasthenia gravis / LEMS, not MND AChR/MuSK (and VGCC) antibodies, RNS ± single-fiber EMG, neurology now; the ice-pack test is a useful bedside adjunct for ptosis — edrophonium is gone Bulbar weakness + perioral fasciculations, gynecomastia, hand tremor in a man Kennedy disease (SBMA) — CAG repeat in the androgen receptor Androgen-receptor CAG repeat testing; genetic counseling; it mimics ALS but the management and prognosis differ

docs.title: Diagnosis / classification
docs.text:
Use the Gold Coast criteria (Shefner et al., 2020) — they replaced the El Escorial "possible/probable/definite" ladder and are what trials now enroll on:

  1. Progressive motor impairment — documented by history or repeated examination.
  2. UMN + LMN signs in at least one body region, OR LMN signs in at least two body regions (bulbar, cervical, thoracic, lumbosacral).
  3. Investigations exclude other disease processes.

Body regions are bulbar, cervical, thoracic, lumbosacral. In practice: if you see tongue fasciculations (LMN bulbar) plus brisk jaw jerk (UMN bulbar), you are already most of the way there — the EMG then confirms LMN involvement in clinically silent regions (fibrillations, positive sharp waves, chronic reinnervation).

Variants that share the page but change the counseling:

Entity What differs Prognosis note Classic ALS (limb or bulbar onset) Mixed UMN/LMN Median 3–5 years from symptom onset Progressive muscular atrophy (PMA) Pure LMN Often evolves into ALS; treat as ALS for trial purposes Primary lateral sclerosis (PLS) Pure UMN, ≥4 years without LMN signs Much slower; diagnosis is retrospective Progressive bulbar palsy Bulbar-predominant Usually declares itself as ALS within 1–2 years Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) SMN1 loss, childhood/adult-onset Disease-modifying drugs exist — see SMA section below

docs.title: Rapid approach
docs.text:
1. Exclude the mimics that change everything — cervical spondylotic myelopathy (sensory level, sphincters), multifocal motor neuropathy (conduction block), Kennedy disease, myasthenia, inclusion body myositis. MND is a diagnosis of pattern + exclusion; the MRI cervical spine and the EMG/NCS are not optional.
  2. Confirm the motor-neuron pattern clinically — mixed UMN (spasticity, hyperreflexia, Babinski, pseudobulbar affect) and LMN (fasciculations, atrophy, weakness) signs across regions. Tongue fasciculations and split-hand wasting (thenar > hypothenar) are high-yield bedside findings.
  3. Send genetics on every ALS patient — C9orf72, SOD1, TARDBP, FUS at minimum. A SOD1 result unlocks tofersen; a C9orf72 result changes family counseling. Do not restrict testing to "familial" cases — ~10% of apparently sporadic ALS is genetic.
  4. Start riluzole once the clinical ALS diagnosis is established — the rest of the disease-modifying decisions (edaravone, tofersen) and all of the survival-determining care (NIV, nutrition, symptom control) run in parallel, not in series.

docs.title: The prescriptive flow (what I want done, in order)
docs.text:
1. Confirm pattern + exclude mimics — exam across all four regions, MRI brain and cervical spine (thoracic if indicated), EMG/NCS with a motor-neuron protocol.
  2. Baseline the patient — ALSFRS-R, FVC (sitting and supine), MIP/SNIP, weight, swallow screen, orthopnea/morning-headache review, depression and PBA screen.
  3. Start riluzole after clinical diagnosis (Step 1 below); do not wait for genetics.
  4. Send the ALS gene panel and route by result: SOD1-positive → tofersen pathway; all others → an edaravone discussion (modest, contested benefit — below).
  5. Set the survival infrastructure in parallel — pulmonary (NIV thresholds), GI (PEG timing), speech therapy, PT/OT, palliative care introduced early by name.
  6. Run the symptom orderset — sialorrhea, spasticity, cramps, PBA, pain, sleep, constipation. Symptoms are what the patient feels; function is what the scales measure.
  7. Disposition and follow-up — ALS clinic every 1–3 months; FVC and weight at every visit; advance-directive and goals-of-care conversations before a crisis.

docs.title: Workup
docs.text:
ALS workup — order as a set

  • MRI brain + cervical spine (contrast as indicated) — exclude myelopathy, mass, demyelination; thoracic spine if thoracic signs.
  • EMG/NCS — motor-neuron protocol: fibrillations/positive sharp waves + chronic reinnervation across regions; NCS to hunt conduction block (MMN), demyelination (CIDP), sensory involvement (not ALS).
  • Labs: CK (often mildly elevated), TSH, B12, SPEP/immunofixation, serum/urine protein electrophoresis; anti-GM1 if MMN suspected; Lyme/HTLV as indicated by exposure.
  • Genetics: ALS gene panel (C9orf72 repeat expansion, SOD1, TARDBP, FUS minimum) for every patient; androgen-receptor CAG repeats if Kennedy disease suspected; SMN1 testing if SMA in the differential.
  • Pulmonary baseline: FVC sitting and supine, MIP, SNIP, overnight oximetry; ABG if hypercapnia suspected.
  • Swallow/nutrition baseline: bedside swallow screen → videofluoroscopy if abnormal; weight, albumin/prealbumin trend.

Avoid

  • Do not diagnose ALS on weakness alone without the UMN/LMN pattern and the mimic workup. Cervical myelopathy with superimposed LMN signs from foraminal disease is the classic trap — the spine MRI comes before the label.
  • Do not delay riluzole for genetics. The panel takes weeks; the drug does not need it.
  • Do not prescribe Relyvrio to new patients — withdrawn from the US/Canadian market in April 2024 after PHOENIX failed. Patients will ask; have the saga straight (below).

docs.title: Management
docs.text:
Step 1 — riluzole (start here for every ALS patient)

  • Riluzole 50 mg PO BID, 1 hour before or 2 hours after meals — the only drug with a replicated survival signal (~2–3 months median). Cheap, generic, well tolerated.
  • Monitoring: LFTs at baseline, monthly ×3, then every 3 months — hold/stop if ALT >5× ULN or bilirubin rises; CBC if febrile (neutropenia is rare but real).
  • → Continue indefinitely; add Step 2 agents on top, not instead.

Step 2a — edaravone (discuss; benefit is modest and contested)

  • Evidence, stated plainly: the pivotal trial (MCI186-19) enrolled an enriched early population — disease ≤2 years, FVC ≥80%, every ALSFRS-R item ≥2 — and showed ALSFRS-R decline of −5.0 vs −7.5 over 24 weeks. A large German real-world cohort found no benefit. Offer it to patients who resemble the trial population, with that framing; it is reasonable to decline.
  • Radicava ORS (oral) 105 mg (5 mL) PO or via feeding tube once daily. Cycle 1: 14 days on, 14 days off. Subsequent cycles: 10 treatment days within a 14-day period, then 14 drug-free days. Take in the morning after fasting: 8 h after a high-fat meal, 4 h after a low-fat meal, or 2 h after a caloric supplement; no food for 1 h after the dose (water allowed).
  • Radicava IV 60 mg IV over 60 minutes if oral is not an option — Cycle 1: daily ×14 then 14-day drug-free period; then 10 of 14 days, then 14-day drug-free.
  • Oral is bioequivalent to IV and is the default; reserve IV for dysphagia without tube access. Warnings include hypersensitivity and sulfite allergic reactions (both IV and ORS formulations contain a sulfite).
  • → If started, continue with riluzole and reassess at each clinic visit.

Step 2b — tofersen (for SOD1-ALS only)

  • Indication: adults with SOD1-mutation ALS — requires a positive SOD1 genetic result (~2% of ALS). FDA accelerated approval April 2023 on the NfL biomarker.
  • Qalsody 100 mg/15 mL intrathecal bolus over 1–3 minutes. Loading doses on days 1, 15, and 29, then every 28 days indefinitely. Remove ~10 mL CSF before each injection; warm to room temperature before administration.
  • Why it matters: VALOR's 28-week ALSFRS-R missed significance, but plasma NfL fell 55% vs a 12% rise on placebo (p<0.0001) with 35% CSF SOD1 knockdown — and long-term open-label data show early starters declining meaningfully slower than delayed starters across function, strength, vital capacity, and death-or-ventilation risk.
  • Watch for: myelitis/radiculitis, increased intracranial pressure with papilledema, aseptic meningitis — labeled neurologic serious adverse events (~8–9% in trials); LP-related headache/back pain is common.
  • → Give with riluzole/edaravone as tolerated; this is an add-on, not a swap.

The Relyvrio saga — what to tell patients who ask

  • Relyvrio (sodium phenylbutyrate + taurursodiol, AMX0035) was FDA-approved in September 2022 on a single small phase 2 trial (CENTAUR, n=137) after an intense patient-advocacy campaign — an unusually thin evidence base for approval.
  • The confirmatory phase 3 PHOENIX trial (n=664, 48 weeks) failed: no significant ALSFRS-R difference vs placebo (P=.667), no secondary endpoints met.
  • Amylyx voluntarily withdrew Relyvrio from the US and Canadian markets in April 2024. It is not available to new patients; existing patients could transition to a free-drug program.
  • Counseling line: "It was approved on early data, the big trial showed it doesn't work, and it's off the market. The approved options today are riluzole, tofersen if you carry SOD1, and edaravone, which helps at most a selected group."

docs.title: Spinal muscular atrophy — the drug cabinet
docs.text:
SMA is the motor neuron disease with the most disease-modifying options, and adults with SMA — survivors of the treatment era — are now a growing adult-neurology population.

Agent Who Dosing Key cautions Nusinersen (Spinraza) — SMN2 splicing ASO All ages, all SMA types 12 mg/5 mL intrathecal; loading doses on days 0, 14, 28, the 4th 30 days after the 3rd, then every 4 months LP burden forever; thrombocytopenia/renal monitoring per label Risdiplam (Evrysdi) — SMN2 splicing modifier Pediatric and adult patients Daily PO: <2 months 0.15 mg/kg; 2 months–<2 years 0.2 mg/kg; ≥2 years and <20 kg 0.25 mg/kg; ≥2 years and ≥20 kg 5 mg With or without food, same time daily; formulation/feeding-tube instructions per current label Onasemnogene abeparvovec (Zolgensma) — one-time AAV9 gene therapy <2 years, biallelic SMN1 mutations 1.1×10¹⁴ vg/kg IV once Boxed warning: acute serious liver injury and liver failure. Screen AAV9 antibodies first; prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day starting the day before, ≥30 days then taper; monitor LFTs, platelets, troponin-I (hepatotoxicity, TMA, cardiac signals)

Nusinersen also has a 2026 high-dose option: **50 mg intrathecal, repeated 14 days later, then 28 mg beginning 4 months after the SECOND loading dose, repeated every 4 months, with label-specific transition rules for patients on the 12-mg regimen. These regimens are not interchangeable by vial substitution. Current FDA label.

An intrathecal onasemnogene formulation (Itvisma) for patients ≥2 years was approved in 24 November 2025 for patients with confirmed SMN1 mutation. It has its own intrathecal label and serious safety/monitoring requirements; do not substitute the Zolgensma IV dose. Itvisma FDA product information.

docs.title: The survival infrastructure — respiratory, nutrition, symptoms
docs.text:
These orders determine survival more than any disease-modifying drug. Build them in parallel with Steps 1–2, not after.

Respiratory — the NIV and cough plan

  • Start NIV when: orthopnea/dyspnea or morning headache/daytime somnolence, or FVC <50% predicted (consider at <80% with symptoms), or MIP <60 cmH₂O, or sniff nasal pressure <40 cmH₂O, or PaCO₂ ≥45 mm Hg, or nocturnal SpO₂ ≤88% for ≥5 consecutive minutes (the CMS coverage criteria — document the one you used).
  • Cough assist (mechanical insufflation-exsufflation) when peak cough flow <270 L/min; below 160 L/min the cough is ineffective — do not wait for pneumonia.
  • NIV is the single largest survival intervention in ALS. Refer to pulmonary before the crisis; the evaluation visit should happen while FVC is still >50%.

Nutrition — the PEG plan

  • Discuss gastrostomy early, before substantial weight loss or respiratory decline. Offer it for dysphagia, inadequate intake, weight loss, prolonged mealtimes, or aspiration events — place it before FVC falls below 50% if possible; FVC <50% is not an absolute prohibition. A specialist team can select technique and ventilatory support when the patient presents later.
  • Videofluoroscopy when the bedside screen is abnormal; dietitian at every ALS clinic visit; weigh the patient every visit without exception.

Symptom control — run all of these

  • Sialorrhea: glycopyrrolate 1–2 mg PO TID–QID (max 8 mg/day) → atropine 1% drops 1–2 drops SL q4–6h → scopolamine 1.5 mg patch q72h → botulinum toxin to salivary glands → low-dose radiotherapy as last resort.
  • Pseudobulbar affect: dextromethorphan/quinidine (Nuedexta) 20/10 mg — 1 capsule daily ×7 days, then 1 capsule q12h; QTc caution from quinidine. SSRIs are a second-line option for PBA.
  • Spasticity: baclofen titrated to effect; tizanidine if sedation is an issue; intrathecal baclofen pump for severe refractory spasticity.
  • Cramps: stretching and hydration first; mexiletine 150 mg PO BID (ECG/cardiac monitoring) or levetiracetam. Not quinine — FDA warning for serious hematologic toxicity when used for cramps.
  • Pain: NSAIDs/acetaminophen → gabapentinoids for neuropathic components → opioids when indicated; do not undertreat end-of-life pain.
  • Sleep/anxiety/depression: treat directly and early; screen at every visit. Constipation from immobility and anticholinergics needs a standing bowel regimen.

TRICARE — verified rules and the current form

Radicava ORS and Evrysdi require pharmacy PA in the official October file. Spinraza, Qalsody and gene therapy need benefit/specialty-site review; absence from the pharmacy list is not “no PA.” Current drug-specific functional/respiratory/genetic and renewal criteria were not obtained; retrieve them before promising access.

Current PA/MN details, benefit routing and packet · Live Formulary Search. Check the exact product, beneficiary and venue on the prescribing date.

docs.title: Disposition
docs.text:
• ALS clinic every 1–3 months — multidisciplinary (neurology, pulmonary, GI, speech, PT/OT, dietitian, social work, palliative care). FVC, weight, and ALSFRS-R at every visit.
  • Admit for: respiratory decompensation, aspiration pneumonia, dehydration from dysphagia, fall with injury, or caregiver crisis. Most ALS care is outpatient until it suddenly isn't — the threshold for admission is lower than it looks.
  • Goals-of-care conversations early and explicitly: NIV vs tracheostomy with invasive ventilation, PEG acceptance, code status, hospice triggers. Document while speech is intact.
  • PMA/PLS: same clinic structure; PLS patients need less respiratory urgency but equal spasticity and mobility management.

Military medicine — duty, retention and deployment

  • Profile / function: Document progressive weakness, respiratory/bulbar function and assistive requirements. Prioritize multidisciplinary ALS/SMA care and safe work restrictions.
  • Retention / MEB–MAR2: Army 3-31a/b and the applicable DoDI neuromuscular/paralytic standards guide early retention/referral assessment. Do not wait a year solely because progression is gradual. Use the retention framework; permanent P3/4 does not by itself select DES versus MAR2.
  • Deployment / medications: Progressive impairment and specialty/respiratory needs may preclude deployment. Oral therapy does not erase the diagnosis; injections, intrathecal therapy and monitoring need separate assessment. See the disease AND drug screen for the current CENTCOM rules and waiver packet.
  • Special duty: flight, diving and other special assignments have separate standards and waiver authorities; a general duty profile does not clear them.
  • LOD / EPTS: document onset, duty status, exposures and aggravation objectively. The designated authority determines LOD/EPTS; neither in-service diagnosis nor a genetic finding settles it automatically.

docs.title: 📚 Discover — evidence brief
docs.text:
Written from primary guidelines and trials; source articles are a reading list, not copied.

  • The ALS drug story of the last decade is tofersen and Relyvrio in opposite directions. Tofersen earned the first accelerated approval for a genetic cause of ALS on a biomarker (NfL) after missing its clinical primary — and the long-term open-label data now show early treatment meaningfully slowing decline, validating the biomarker-first bet. Relyvrio took the opposite path: approved on a thin phase 2 dataset under advocacy pressure, then killed by its own confirmatory trial and withdrawn in 2024. The lesson for the next ALS drug: confirmatory data before celebration.
  • Genetics is now therapeutic, not just prognostic. Every ALS patient gets a panel; SOD1 opens the tofersen door, and presymptomatic SOD1 carriers are in the ATLAS trial testing whether treatment before symptoms changes the disease course.
  • Edaravone is the drug to discuss, not default. Its approval rests on one trial in an enriched early population, and real-world cohorts have not reproduced the benefit.
  • The ALS pipeline has far more failures than successes. Counsel trial participation honestly: most ALS trials fail, and enrolling is still worth doing.
  • Survival is won in the symptom clinic, not the infusion suite: NIV timing, PEG before FVC <50%, sialorrhea control, and early palliative integration move the needle more than any current disease-modifying drug except possibly early tofersen.

Key sources: Shefner et al. Gold Coast criteria 2020; Miller et al. VALOR (NEJM 2022) and long-term tofersen OLE (JAMA Neurol 2025); MCI186-19 and the German edaravone cohort; CENTAUR and PHOENIX for the Relyvrio record; AAN/EFNS/EAN/NICE respiratory guidance for NIV thresholds.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Shefner JM, et al. A proposal for new diagnostic criteria for ALS. Clin Neurophysiol. 2020;131:1975–1978 — the Gold Coast criteria: progressive motor impairment + UMN/LMN spread + exclusion.
  2. Miller TM, et al. Trial of Antisense Oligonucleotide Tofersen for SOD1 ALS. N Engl J Med. 2022;387:1099–1110 (VALOR) — ALSFRS-R missed significance; NfL −55% vs +12% placebo; basis for accelerated approval.
  3. Miller TM, et al. Long-Term Tofersen in SOD1 Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis. JAMA Neurol. Published online December 22, 2025 — week-148 NfL reductions 67%/64%; early-start slower decline across function, strength, vital capacity, and death-equivalent risk; serious neuro AEs 8.7%.
  4. Qalsody (tofersen) FDA label — accelerated approval April 2023; intrathecal dosing and neurologic warnings. DailyMed
  5. Writing Group, Edaravone (MCI-186) ALS 19 Study Group. Safety and efficacy of edaravone in well defined patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Lancet Neurol. 2017;16:505–512 — the enriched-population pivotal trial.
  6. Witzel S, et al. Safety and effectiveness of long-term intravenous administration of edaravone for treatment of patients with ALS. JAMA Neurol. 2022;79:121–130 — German multicenter cohort; no benefit over best supportive care.
  7. Amylyx discontinues AMX0035 after PHOENIX failure, April 2024 — PHOENIX (n=664, 48 wks) missed ALSFRS-R (P=.667) and all secondaries; Relyvrio voluntarily withdrawn from US/Canada; free-drug program for existing patients.
  8. Spinraza (nusinersen), Evrysdi (risdiplam) and Zolgensma (onasemnogene abeparvovec) FDA labels — SMA dosing and boxed warning. DailyMed
  9. Official TRICARE sources, retrieved forms and access limits.
