docs.title: Movement Disorders
docs.text:
Last reviewed: October 2026

One-liner: the high-yield, prescriptive management of tardive dyskinesia (VMAT2 inhibitors), Parkinson disease motor fluctuations and adjuncts, neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, Parkinson disease psychosis, Huntington's chorea, and the atypical-parkinsonism (MSA/PSP/CBS) red flags that should make you reconsider a Parkinson diagnosis. For the on-call neurologist or PCP seeing these in clinic, on admit, or in the ED.

🚩 Red flags — don't miss these

Pattern Worry Do now Parkinsonism + early severe autonomic failure (nOH, urinary retention/incontinence, erectile dysfunction) within the first years MSA — not idiopathic PD Orthostatics + post-void residual; brain MRI (pons, MCP, putamen); neurology referral — do not anchor on PD Parkinsonism + early postural instability with unprovoked (often backward) falls within ~1 year, slowed vertical saccades / downgaze palsy PSP Test vertical saccade speed/range at bedside; MRI midbrain (hummingbird sign); neurology referral Markedly asymmetric rigidity/akinesia plus a cortical sign (limb apraxia, cortical sensory loss, alien-limb phenomenon) Corticobasal syndrome Document the cortical sign explicitly; MRI asymmetric frontoparietal atrophy; neurology referral Fever + rigidity + altered mentation after a dopamine blocker — or after a PD patient's levodopa was stopped or missed NMS / parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia ICU-level care; stop the blocker or restart levodopa now — emergencies Acute dystonic reaction, stridor, or dysphagia after starting/changing a dopamine blocker Drug-induced movement emergency Diphenhydramine 50 mg IV or benztropine 1–2 mg IV; airway assessment — emergencies Chorea + depression/suicidal ideation on a VMAT2 inhibitor Boxed-warning neuropsychiatric risk Urgent safety assessment — do not simply up-titrate; see Huntington's/TD sections

docs.title: Rapid approach
docs.text:
1. Is this an emergency? Fever and rigidity, stridor, or a PD patient who has missed levodopa doses go to Inpatient emergencies first.
  2. Is this drug-induced? Review antipsychotics, antiemetics (metoclopramide, prochlorperazine), and recent starts/stops. Drug-induced parkinsonism and tardive syndromes are common and reversible causes — don't label idiopathic PD until you've cleared the med list.
  3. Is it Parkinson disease or an atypical syndrome? Apply the red-flag screen above. Atypical features change prognosis, counseling, and management — and some (MSA autonomic failure) need same-visit workup.
  4. Match the problem to the treatment lane: TD → VMAT2 inhibitor; PD wearing-off → adjunct by phenotype; nOH → pressor strategy; PDP psychosis → pimavanserin/clozapine/quetiapine; Huntington's chorea → VMAT2 inhibitor with boxed-warning monitoring.
  5. Reassess atypical parkinsonism longitudinally — early on, all three atypical syndromes can closely mimic PD and each other; MRI signs are highly specific but insensitive early, so a normal scan does not exclude atypical parkinsonism.

docs.title: The prescriptive flow (what I want done, in order)
docs.text:
1. Confirm the phenomenology (tremor, bradykinesia/rigidity, chorea, dystonia, myoclonus, tics) and exclude drugs as the cause.
  2. Screen for atypical parkinsonism (red-flag box) before settling on PD — document falls chronology, urinary symptoms, orthostatics, vertical gaze, cortical signs, and levodopa response.
  3. Treat the dominant problem first using the tiered order sets below (TD → PD fluctuations → nOH → psychosis → chorea).
  4. If parkinsonism is atypical: work up the suspected syndrome (orthostatics + PVR for MSA; targeted MRI review; autonomic testing/MIBG where ambiguous), refer to neurology, and counsel on prognosis — disease-modifying therapy for MSA/PSP/CBD remains investigational (see Discover).
  5. Disposition + follow-up: most management is outpatient with structured follow-up (AIMS for TD, motor diaries for PD fluctuations, supine/upright BP logs for nOH). Admit for drug-induced emergencies, severe psychosis, or unsafe swallowing/falls.

docs.title: Diagnosis / classification
docs.text:
Parkinson disease (MDS clinical diagnostic criteria, Postuma et al. 2015): bradykinesia plus rest tremor and/or rigidity, with supportive criteria and absence of absolute exclusions. A sustained, substantial levodopa response supports PD — but an initial response does not exclude MSA or a PSP variant.

Tardive dyskinesia: involuntary choreoathetoid movements (classically orofacial) emerging during or after dopamine-receptor-blocking therapy. Document a baseline AIMS (items 1–7) and functional impact before treatment; a VMAT2 inhibitor can be used while antipsychotic treatment continues.

Atypical parkinsonism: MSA (α-synuclein, glial cytoplasmic inclusions), PSP and CBD (4R-tau). CBS names the clinical presentation; CBD names the pathology — CBS may result from CBD, PSP, Alzheimer disease, or another pathology, and CBD need not present as CBS. Across clinicopathologic series, 7–35% of clinically diagnosed cases are misdiagnosed; the hardest early distinction is MSA-P vs PSP-P.

docs.title: Inpatient emergencies — act now
docs.text:
The movement-disorder calls that come from the ward or the ED. Every one is treatable if it is recognized early, and two of them are caused by the hospital.

Picture Think Discriminator Fever, lead-pipe rigidity, altered mentation, autonomic instability, high CK — days after starting or raising a dopamine blocker Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) Bradyreflexia, rigidity; evolves over days The same picture in a PD patient whose levodopa was stopped, missed or cut (NPO, admission, surgery) Parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia syndrome Recent dopaminergic withdrawal — no blocker needed Agitation, inducible/ocular clonus, hyperreflexia, diaphoresis, diarrhea — hours after a serotonergic drug Serotonin syndrome (Hunter criteria) Clonus and hyperreflexia; evolves over hours Oculogyric crisis, torticollis, trismus or stridor within days of a dopamine blocker or antiemetic Acute dystonic reaction Recent metoclopramide, prochlorperazine or haloperidol; often young

NMS and parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia — ICU-level care

  • NMS: stop the dopamine blocker; ICU for rigidity, hyperthermia or autonomic instability; active cooling and IV fluids; trend CK and creatinine (rhabdomyolysis/AKI); DVT prophylaxis. Lorazepam 1–2 mg IV q4–6h for mild disease or catatonic features. Moderate–severe: bromocriptine 2.5 mg PO/NG q8h (titrate to a maximum of 40 mg/day) and/or dantrolene 1–2.5 mg/kg IV, repeated to a maximum of 10 mg/kg/day, for severe rigidity and hyperthermia — drug evidence is observational. No antipsychotic rechallenge for ≥2 weeks after resolution, and then a low-potency agent at a low dose.
  • Parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia: restart carbidopa-levodopa at the patient's usual dose now — by NG tube if needed (immediate-release tablets can be crushed). No enteral route → rotigotine transdermal patch (LEDD converters such as OPTIMAL count 1 mg rotigotine ≈ 30 mg levodopa) or apomorphine SC with specialist input. NMS-level cooling, fluids and monitoring in parallel.

Parkinson disease in hospital — the NPO patient

  • Give PD medications on time — within 30 minutes of the home schedule; mark the order time-critical. Missed doses cause rigidity, dysphagia, aspiration, falls and parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia.
  • NPO is not "nothing." Immediate-release carbidopa-levodopa can be crushed and given by NG tube; controlled-release/extended-release forms must not be crushed — convert to the IR equivalent. No enteral route → rotigotine patch (above).
  • Never give dopamine blockers: haloperidol, droperidol, metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, promethazine and the typical antipsychotics. Antiemetic: ondansetron 4 mg IV — but never with apomorphine (contraindicated: profound hypotension and loss of consciousness). Delirium: treat the cause; if a drug is unavoidable, quetiapine 12.5–25 mg PO (see psychosis).
  • On an MAO-B inhibitor (rasagiline, selegiline, safinamide): no meperidine, tramadol, methadone, dextromethorphan or linezolid — serotonin syndrome and hypertensive risk.

Serotonin syndrome and acute dystonia

  • Serotonin syndrome: stop every serotonergic drug; supportive care; lorazepam 1–2 mg IV for agitation; cyproheptadine 12 mg PO/NG, then 2 mg q2h while symptoms continue (maintenance 8 mg q6h). Temperature >41 °C → sedation, non-depolarizing paralysis and intubation — antipyretics do not work because the heat is muscular. Avoid physical restraints (isometric contraction drives hyperthermia).
  • Acute dystonic reaction: diphenhydramine 50 mg IV/IM or benztropine 1–2 mg IV/IM — response within minutes; then benztropine 1–2 mg PO BID (or diphenhydramine 25–50 mg PO q6h) for 2–3 days to prevent recurrence. Laryngeal dystonia (stridor) is an airway emergency — treat in a monitored setting with airway backup ready.

TRICARE — verified rules and the current form

Ingrezza/Austedo require PA; Nuplazid requires PA and is nonformulary in the October files. Their indications and formal contraindications differ. Do not invent a tetrabenazine-failure requirement without the current form. PD infusions/injections, botulinum treatment and other services need product/site-specific review.

Current PA/MN details, benefit routing and packet · Live Formulary Search. Check the exact product, beneficiary and venue on the prescribing date.

docs.title: Tardive dyskinesia — VMAT2 inhibitors
docs.text:
Both valbenazine (Ingrezza) and deutetrabenazine (Austedo/Austedo XR) are FDA-approved for TD with level-A evidence and similar AIMS efficacy (roughly 2–3 point placebo-adjusted reduction; responder rates ~33–50%). There is no head-to-head trial — choose on dosing, titration granularity, CYP2D6/hepatic considerations, QTc, renal function, and formulary, not on assumed efficacy differences. Both labels advise avoiding congenital long QT or relevant QT-associated arrhythmia; this is a warning, distinct from their formal contraindication lists.

Step 1 — start a VMAT2 inhibitor (pick one)

  • Valbenazine — 40 mg PO once daily × 1 week, then 80 mg PO once daily; 40 or 60 mg once daily may be used per response/tolerability. With or without food. CYP2D6 poor metabolizer or strong CYP2D6 inhibitor → 40 mg once daily. Strong CYP3A4 inhibitor → 40 mg once daily. Moderate/severe hepatic impairment → 40 mg once daily. Avoid MAOIs (including the 14-day washout); strong CYP3A4 inducers are not recommended. No renal dose adjustment is required, including severe renal impairment, under the current label. Formal contraindication: hypersensitivity.
  • Deutetrabenazine — Austedo XR 12 mg PO once daily (with or without food) or immediate-release 6 mg PO BID with food; increase by 6 mg/day at weekly intervals to lowest effective dose, max 48 mg/day. CYP2D6 poor metabolizer or strong CYP2D6 inhibitor → max 36 mg/day. Do not crush/chew/break. Contraindicated in hepatic impairment (any degree). Renal pharmacokinetics have not been studied; do not call it renal-neutral or automatically prefer it over valbenazine in CKD.
  • Baseline and serial AIMS (same examiner/method); assess eating, speaking, social interaction — not just the score. Expect response to build over weeks; symptoms recur toward baseline within ~4 weeks of stopping valbenazine.
  • QTc: valbenazine — assess QT before dose increases in at-risk patients (effect grows with exposure, e.g., CYP2D6 PM or interacting drugs). Deutetrabenazine — labeled QT effect not clinically significant within recommended dosing, but avoid with congenital long QT, history of arrhythmia, bradycardia, or uncorrected hypo-K/Mg. Review the antipsychotic and full med list — neither choice is QT-neutral.
  • → Inadequate response or intolerable adverse effect on one agent → consider switching to the other (no head-to-head data guides this; re-baseline AIMS).

docs.title: Starting treatment for Parkinson disease
docs.text:
For established early PD with motor symptoms that warrant medication, immediate-release levodopa is the preferred initial dopaminergic treatment (AAN 2021, Level B). Do not make a newly diagnosed patient navigate the adjunct table first.

  • A labeled starting regimen is carbidopa/levodopa IR 25/100 mg PO three times daily; individualize and titrate to the lowest effective dose. Frailty, orthostasis, nausea, and hallucinations may warrant a slower specialist-guided start.
  • Review swallowing, falls, cognition, BP, sleepiness, and impulse-control symptoms. Arrange exercise/physiotherapy and a movement-disorders follow-up plan.
  • 2026 label update: evaluate vitamin B6 before treatment and periodically; replace deficiency. Levodopa may begin/continue during supplementation. New seizures in a treated patient warrant assessment for deficiency among other causes.
  • Dopamine agonists are an option for selected younger patients, but avoid them in patients at high risk from hallucinations, daytime sleepiness, cognitive impairment, or impulse-control disorders. Sudden sleep attacks and orthostasis matter at the wheel and on duty.
  • In hospital, administer the patient’s established doses at their actual home times. NPO requires an urgent enteral/alternative plan, not an accidental drug holiday.

docs.title: Parkinson disease motor fluctuations — choosing the adjunct
docs.text:
All three are once-daily add-ons to carbidopa-levodopa that reduce OFF time. None is an antidyskinetic — safinamide's trial endpoint of ON time without troublesome dyskinesia does not mean it treats established dyskinesia. If dyskinesia itself is the dominant problem, reassess levodopa dose/timing and consider amantadine — immediate-release 100 mg PO BID (up to 100 mg TID), or extended-release Gocovri 137 mg PO at bedtime × 1 week, then 274 mg at bedtime; reduce for renal impairment; watch hallucinations, livedo reticularis, ankle edema. It is the only agent that reduces both dyskinesia and OFF time.

Phenotype Preferred adjunct Why Troublesome dyskinesia + OFF time Istradefylline or safinamide (paired with a plan to monitor/adjust levodopa) Non-dopaminergic (A2A) and MAO-B/glutamate mechanisms rank more favorably for low dyskinesia risk; opicapone carries the highest dyskinesia signal (↑ levodopa Cmax 43–44%, AUC 62–94%) — use with particular caution here Non-troublesome wearing-off (predictable end-of-dose) Opicapone reasonable first pick Largest OFF-time reduction (~1 hr vs placebo; ON time without troublesome dyskinesia ↑ ~1.1 hr), convenient once-daily; safinamide a reasonable alternative On a strong CYP3A4 inducer (carbamazepine, phenytoin, rifampin) Opicapone or safinamide — avoid istradefylline Rifampin ↓ istradefylline AUC 81%, abolishing efficacy; label advises against the combination. (St. John's wort also rules out safinamide — serotonergic contraindication — leaving opicapone.)

Step 1 — start the phenotype-matched adjunct

  • Istradefylline (Nourianz) — 20 mg PO once daily, may increase to 40 mg once daily. Max 20 mg/day with a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor or in moderate hepatic impairment; avoid in severe hepatic impairment and with strong CYP3A4 inducers. No labeled contraindications, but can worsen dyskinesia/hallucinations — caution in major psychotic disorder.
  • Opicapone (Ongentys) — 50 mg PO at bedtime, no food 1 hour before or after. 25 mg/day in moderate hepatic impairment; avoid in severe hepatic impairment and in end-stage renal disease. Contraindicated with nonselective MAOIs and with pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma/catecholamine-secreting tumors (selective MAO-B inhibitors permitted). Watch for worsened dyskinesia, hypotension/syncope, and interactions with COMT-metabolized drugs (catecholamine vasopressors).
  • Safinamide (Xadago) — 50 mg PO once daily, may increase to 100 mg once daily after 2 weeks. Max 50 mg/day in moderate hepatic impairment; contraindicated in severe hepatic impairment. Contraindicated with other MAOIs/linezolid, tramadol, methadone, meperidine, SNRIs, TCAs/tetracyclics, cyclobenzaprine, stimulants, methylphenidate/ amphetamines, St. John's wort, dextromethorphan (serotonin syndrome / hypertensive risk). Taper 100 → 50 mg × 1 week before stopping. Avoid very-high-tyramine (>150 mg) foods.
  • → OFF time persists → reassess levodopa dose/timing and adherence before stacking adjuncts; refer to neurology rather than combining multiple adjuncts empirically.

docs.title: Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension (nOH)
docs.text:
Goal: fewer symptomatic upright episodes — not normalizing every reading. Before drugs: medication review, volume/salt, abdominal binder/compression, avoid heat/large meals/prolonged standing. Then one pressor, chosen largely by supine-hypertension risk. All pressor choices require supine-BP assessment. Droxidopa may have a lower supine-HTN signal than midodrine but still carries a boxed warning; it is not automatically appropriate for severe supine hypertension. A specialist may consider off-label pyridostigmine in selected patients. Avoid indiscriminate fludrocortisone/midodrine when supine BP is excessive.

Step 1 — start one pressor (choose by supine-BP risk)

  • Droxidopa (Northera) — 100 mg PO TID (on arising, midday, late afternoon); increase by 100 mg/dose every 24–48 hours to symptoms/BP, max 600 mg TID (1,800 mg/day). Last dose ≥3 hours before bedtime. Take consistently with or without food. Boxed warning: supine hypertension — check supine BP before treatment and after increases; if supine HTN persists despite head-of-bed elevation, reduce or discontinue. Efficacy beyond 2 weeks not established — reassess continued benefit periodically. Carbidopa can blunt peripheral conversion to norepinephrine — assess individual response; higher doses may be needed with carbidopa/levodopa. Caution in CHF, arrhythmia, chronic renal failure; no dosing recommendation if GFR <30. Avoid with nonselective MAOIs/linezolid.
  • Midodrine — alternative first-line pressor: start 2.5 mg PO 2–3 times daily during waking hours, titrate to 10 mg TID; last dose ≥4 hours before bedtime (some guidance says 5 hours). Short half-life (3–4 h). Boxed warning: supine hypertension — indirect meta-analysis shows a greater supine-HTN signal than droxidopa. Contraindicated in persistent excessive supine HTN, urinary retention, acute renal disease, severe organic heart disease.
  • Fludrocortisone — off-label volume-expanding adjunct (no requirement to try first): 0.1 mg PO each morning; max 0.2 mg/day (>0.2 mg/day not recommended). Monitor potassium, edema, weight, supine BP. Contraindicated in heart failure; poor choice with supine HTN (effect not confined to upright hours). Adrenal suppression risk above 0.3 mg/day.
  • → Inadequate on one pressor → may switch agents or cautiously combine (combination ↑ HTN risk; limited comparative evidence) — involve neurology/autonomic specialist.

Step 2 — manage coexistent supine hypertension

Supine HTN coexists in a majority of autonomic-failure patients; balance orthostatic symptom/fall burden against long-term CV risk.

  • Non-pharmacologic first: avoid lying flat after daytime pressors; elevate head of bed ≥10°; last pressor dose well before bedtime (droxidopa ≥3 h; panel consensus ≥5 h); bedtime carbohydrate snack; home BP diary or ABPM to distinguish sustained nocturnal vs post-pressor HTN.
  • If nocturnal supine HTN remains severe (≥180 mmHg systolic or ≥110 diastolic) despite measures, a specialist may consider a short-acting bedtime antihypertensive (e.g., losartan or a nitroglycerin patch removed in the morning) — limited evidence; morning BP and nighttime fall risk must guide. Avoid reflex prescribing.

docs.title: Parkinson disease psychosis
docs.text:
First: distinguish persistent PDP from delirium (abrupt change, infection, new meds, sleep disruption). If hallucinations are mild with retained insight, drug treatment may not be needed — review and taper expendable contributors first (anticholinergics → amantadine → dopamine agonists → MAO-B inhibitors → COMT inhibitors → levodopa last), but reflex dopaminergic reduction that sacrifices motor control has little effect on psychosis and worsens function — the severity-stratified approach is increasingly favored.

Step 1 — mild-to-moderate, bothersome but not crisis psychosis: pimavanserin

  • Pimavanserin (Nuplazid) — 34 mg PO once daily, with or without food; no titration. Only FDA-approved treatment for hallucinations/delusions of PDP (selective 5-HT2A inverse agonist — no dopaminergic antagonism, so motor benefit is preserved). Steady state ~10–12 days; clinical effect may take 4–6 weeks; if no benefit by ~8 weeks, discontinuation is reasonable. With a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor → 10 mg once daily; avoid moderate/strong CYP3A4 inducers. Caution if CrCl <30.
  • QTc: prolongation is a Warnings/Precautions item (not boxed) — ~5–8 msec at 34 mg, concentration-dependent. Baseline ECG; correct hypo-K/Mg; avoid with known QT prolongation, congenital long QT, arrhythmia history, symptomatic bradycardia, or other QT-prolonging drugs.
  • Boxed warning (class effect): increased all-cause mortality in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis — this does not prohibit the PDP indication, including PDP with dementia. Monitor peripheral edema, confusional state, falls.
  • → Crisis-level, severe/refractory, or pimavanserin failure/intolerance → Step 2.

Step 2 — severe/refractory psychosis or need for rapid response

  • Low-dose clozapine — most robust efficacy (highest-ranked in network meta-analysis): 6.25–50 mg/day (do NOT use schizophrenia titration in a frail PD patient). Least motor side effects. Boxed warnings: severe neutropenia, orthostatic hypotension/bradycardia/ syncope, seizures, myocarditis/pericarditis/cardiomyopathy, dementia-related mortality. The clozapine REMS was removed in 2025 — ANC monitoring was not: weekly months 1–6, every 2 weeks months 7–12, then monthly with normal counts. Off-label for PDP in the US; requires close monitoring infrastructure.
  • Quetiapine — when clozapine monitoring is impractical and rapid/sedating effect is acceptable: start 12.5–25 mg PO qHS, titrate cautiously. Off-label; RCT evidence has not reliably established efficacy (possibly inferior to placebo in NMA). Reassess whether it is actually helping — don't continue solely because it's easy to prescribe. Sedation and orthostatic hypotension are especially problematic in PD.

docs.title: Huntington's disease chorea — VMAT2 inhibitors
docs.text:
Tetrabenazine, deutetrabenazine and valbenazine (since August 2023) are all FDA-approved for Huntington's chorea, and all carry a boxed warning for depression and suicidality in HD (prompted historically by a suicide in the tetrabenazine phase III program). Screen for depression/suicidal ideation before treatment and repeatedly during titration; involve caregivers. Tetrabenazine/deutetrabenazine are contraindicated in active suicidality or untreated/inadequately treated depression in HD. Valbenazine carries a boxed warning, requiring careful psychiatric assessment; it has a different formal contraindication list. None is disease-modifying. No blinded head-to-head trial establishes superior efficacy — choose on dosing/adherence, tolerability, CYP2D6 simplicity, hepatic function, and cost.

Step 1 — start chorea treatment (pick one VMAT2 inhibitor)

  • Deutetrabenazine (often the practical first pick — simpler CYP2D6 handling, BID or once-daily XR): Austedo XR 12 mg PO once daily (with or without food) or immediate-release 6 mg PO BID with food; +6 mg/day at weekly intervals; max 48 mg/day. CYP2D6 poor metabolizer or strong CYP2D6 inhibitor (fluoxetine, paroxetine, quinidine, bupropion) → flat cap 36 mg/day (~3-fold active-metabolite AUC rise). No routine genotyping required. Contraindicated in hepatic impairment. Do not combine with another VMAT2 inhibitor, an MAOI, or reserpine.
  • Tetrabenazine (reasonable when tolerated/working, or when cost/access favors the generic): 12.5 mg PO each morning × 1 week → 12.5 mg PO BID week 2 → +12.5 mg/day at weekly intervals; split BID, and TID once ≥37.5 mg/day. CYP2D6 genotyping required before exceeding 50 mg/day: EM/IM → max 100 mg/day, 37.5 mg single dose; PM or strong CYP2D6 inhibitor → max 50 mg/day, 25 mg single dose. Contraindicated in hepatic impairment. Do not combine with another VMAT2 inhibitor, an MAOI, or reserpine.
  • Valbenazine (once daily, no genotyping step; the same drug as the TD lane above): 40 mg PO once daily → +20 mg every 2 weeks → 80 mg once daily (40 or 60 mg where response/tolerability lands) — KINECT-HD. Dose reductions for CYP2D6 poor metabolizers, strong CYP2D6 or CYP3A4 inhibitors, and moderate–severe hepatic impairment per label; avoid MAOIs. Watch somnolence and parkinsonism.
  • Overnight conversion tetrabenazine → deutetrabenazine is supported (ARC-HD): start deutetrabenazine the day after stopping tetrabenazine using the conversion table; chorea control is preserved and improves with titration. No taper needed for either agent; re-titrate deutetrabenazine if interrupted >1 week.
  • Monitor: depression/suicidality, sedation, akathisia/restlessness, parkinsonism/rigidity, swallowing, falls — and whether reduced chorea actually improves function. Review QT risk and sedating/QT-prolonging co-meds.

docs.title: Atypical parkinsonism — MSA, PSP, CBS: the discriminator table
docs.text:
Use this at the bedside when parkinsonism doesn't behave like PD. Early severe autonomic failure, recurrent unprovoked falls, or cortical signs should prompt reassessment — and a sustained, substantial levodopa response supports PD, though an initial response doesn't exclude MSA or PSP-parkinsonism.

Feature MSA PSP CBS/CBD Earliest distinguishing pointer Early severe autonomic failure — nOH, erectile dysfunction, urinary urgency/retention (PVR >100 mL within first 5 years); up to ~50% lack it at onset Vertical supranuclear gaze palsy (especially downgaze) / slowed vertical saccades; early postural instability with backward falls Markedly asymmetric limb rigidity, dystonia, myoclonus plus a cortical sign — limb apraxia, cortical sensory loss, alien-limb phenomenon Levodopa response Poor (initial response in ~30%) Poor (PSP-parkinsonism may briefly resemble PD) Poor Autonomic involvement Prominent, rapidly progressive (preganglionic/central; MIBG usually normal/mildly reduced — up to 1/3 reduced, limiting specificity) Absent/mild — predominant early autonomic failure points away from PSP Absent/mild — not a defining feature Other bedside pointers Cerebellar signs, stridor, disproportionate antecollis, early marked dysarthria, jerky postural minipolymyoclonus, pyramidal signs Axial rigidity, "careless"/reckless gait, rocket sign, frontal-executive/verbal-fluency impairment; RBD argues against tauopathy (toward synucleinopathy) Limb dystonia + falls favor non-Alzheimer (CBD/PSP) pathology; asymmetry alone does not separate CBS from PD Characteristic MRI sign Hot cross bun (cruciform pontine T2), pontine/MCP/cerebellar atrophy; putaminal atrophy or iron-sensitive signal change (MSA-P) Hummingbird/penguin (sagittal midbrain atrophy, pontine sparing), morning-glory/Mickey-Mouse (axial), SCP atrophy; MRPI highly sensitive/specific for PSP-RS Asymmetric posterior frontal–parietal/perirolandic atrophy, contralateral to the more affected limb; perirolandic + temporal sparing distinguishes CBD from PSP (~91% accuracy) Pathology α-synuclein (glial cytoplasmic inclusions) 4R-tau 4R-tau (CBS = syndrome; CBD = pathology)

Early MSA-P discriminator (Mov Disord 2019): postural instability (H&Y ≥3) + orthostatic hypotension + overactive bladder + urinary retention at early disease — ≥2 of these 4 features yields high MSA-P probability (AUC 0.94).

Two diagnostic traps: (1) the hot-cross-bun sign is not specific to MSA (spinocerebellar ataxias and others produce it); (2) normal early MRI does not rule out an atypical syndrome — MRI signs are highly specific but insensitive early.

Workup when atypical parkinsonism is suspected: document chronology of falls, urinary symptoms, and levodopa response; examine vertical saccade speed/range, cerebellar function, limb praxis/cortical sensation; orthostatic vitals + post-void residual; MRI targeted to midbrain, pons, cerebellar peduncles, putamen, and asymmetric frontoparietal cortex; consider autonomic testing, cardiac MIBG, and planimetric MRI metrics (MRPI, pons:midbrain ratio) in ambiguous cases.

docs.title: Disposition
docs.text:
• Outpatient for TD, PD fluctuations, nOH titration, PDP, and Huntington's chorea — with structured follow-up (AIMS, motor diaries, BP logs, psychosis target-symptom tracking).
  • Admit or urgent referral for: drug-induced movement emergencies (dystonic reaction with airway concern), severe/crisis psychosis, active suicidality on a VMAT2 inhibitor, injurious falls or unsafe swallowing in atypical parkinsonism, or malignant supine hypertension.
  • Atypical parkinsonism: early neurology referral; counsel that disease-modifying therapy is investigational — see Discover for the ATH434 signal.

Military medicine — duty, retention and deployment

  • Profile / function: Document falls, freezing, bradykinesia, tremor, cognition, dyskinesia and orthostasis; assess driving and sudden sleep risk.
  • Retention / MEB–MAR2: Use the specific progressive-neurologic or functional standard rather than treating every tremor or drug-induced syndrome as permanent unfitness. Use the retention framework; permanent P3/4 does not by itself select DES versus MAR2.
  • Deployment / medications: CENTCOM specifically lists dopamine agonists, antipsychotics and injectable drugs. Levodopa and other treatments still require review of indication, stability, monitoring and incapacitating effects. See the disease AND drug screen for the current CENTCOM rules and waiver packet.
  • Special duty: flight, diving and other special assignments have separate standards and waiver authorities; a general duty profile does not clear them.
  • LOD / EPTS: document onset, duty status, exposures and aggravation objectively. The designated authority determines LOD/EPTS; neither in-service diagnosis nor a genetic finding settles it automatically.

docs.title: 📚 Discover — evidence brief
docs.text:
Written from primary guidelines and trials; source articles are a reading list, not copied.

  • The emergencies are the hospital's own making: NMS from a dopamine blocker, parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia from a missed levodopa dose, and serotonin syndrome from MAO-B inhibitor interactions. On-time PD medication and a "no dopamine blockers" order prevent most of them.
  • VMAT2 inhibitors are first-line for both TD and Huntington's chorea — valbenazine and deutetrabenazine for TD (KINECT 3, AIM-TD/ARM-TD; 2025 network meta-analysis: both first-line, valbenazine most consistent data); tetrabenazine, deutetrabenazine and — since 2023 — valbenazine for Huntington's chorea. No head-to-head trials exist in either indication; choice is driven by dosing, CYP2D6/hepatic handling, QTc, and formulary.
  • PD adjunct selection is phenotype-driven. Istradefylline and safinamide are the more dyskinesia-sparing options; opicapone gives the largest OFF-time reduction but the highest dyskinesia signal; istradefylline is unusable with strong CYP3A4 inducers. None treats established dyskinesia — that's amantadine's lane.
  • nOH management is supine-HTN management. Droxidopa and midodrine both carry boxed warnings for supine hypertension; the Bayesian meta-analysis (Chen 2018) shows the greater supine-HTN signal with midodrine. Fludrocortisone is capped at 0.2 mg/day and contraindicated in HF.
  • PDP: pimavanserin first-line when motor preservation matters (34 mg QD, no titration, 4–6 weeks to effect, QTc +5–8 msec, dementia-mortality boxed warning as a class effect); clozapine most efficacious for severe/refractory disease (6.25–50 mg/day; REMS removed in 2025, ANC monitoring continues); quetiapine convenient but unproven in RCTs.
  • Atypical parkinsonism is a clinical diagnosis supported by imaging, not made by it. The MDS criteria anchor each syndrome (MSA: Wenning 2022; PSP: Höglinger 2017; CBD: Armstrong 2013); the ≥2-of-4 early MSA-P rule (AUC 0.94) and PVR >100 mL are the most actionable bedside numbers.
  • MSA disease modification — ATH434 signal (early, unverified): additional analyses from the randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled ATH434-201 Phase 2 trial in MSA, presented as a poster at the 2026 MDS Congress (Seoul), were announced via company press release (Oct 5, 2026): ATH434 50 mg slowed functional decline by ~52% versus placebo on the 11-item UMSARS at Week 52, with baseline CSF neurofilament light chain as a covariate; baseline CSF NfL predicted the rate of decline. This is company-reported topline from a press release, not peer-reviewed data — verify against the poster/publication before citing the numbers, and treat the CEO's "clinically meaningful" framing as company characterization. A Phase 3 confirmatory trial is planned.

Key sources: MDS diagnostic criteria (Postuma 2015 PD; Wenning 2022 MSA; Höglinger 2017 PSP; Armstrong 2013 CBD); KINECT 3 / AIM-TD / ARM-TD (TD); FIRST-HD / ARC-HD (Huntington's); BIPARK / SETTLE / safinamide program (PD adjuncts); Gibbons 2017 nOH consensus; Cummings 2014 pimavanserin; Alterity Therapeutics ATH434-201 press release 2026-10-05 (unverified topline).

docs.title: Multiple sclerosis
docs.text:
Last reviewed: July 2026

One-liner: immune-mediated demyelinating disease of the CNS, defined by lesions disseminated in space and time — typically a young adult with relapsing neurologic events that recover incompletely, accumulating disability over decades.

Who this is for: the provider seeing a first demyelinating event, and the one managing an established MS patient's relapse, DMT, or board. In a military population MS matters disproportionately — it presents in the 20–40 window, which is the active-duty demographic, and it is a named referral condition under AR 40-501 3-31e.

🚩 Before you call it MS

MS is over-diagnosed. Misdiagnosis studies consistently find that a meaningful fraction of patients carrying an MS label never had it — most often because non-specific white-matter T2 hyperintensities (migraine, small-vessel disease) were read as demyelination, or because criteria were applied to a syndrome that was never a true demyelinating attack.

Do not diagnose MS on MRI alone. The 2024 McDonald criteria require a compatible clinical syndrome or a rigorously defined radiologically isolated syndrome — not "white spots."

Red flags that argue against MS and for a mimic:

  • Normal brain MRI in someone with suspected MS — reconsider hard.
  • Longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis (≥3 vertebral segments) → NMOSD or MOGAD, not MS.
  • Severe, bilateral, or steroid-dependent optic neuritis, or optic neuritis with a swollen disc → MOGAD/NMOSD.
  • Area postrema syndrome (intractable hiccups, nausea, vomiting) → NMOSD until disproven.
  • Meningeal signs, fever, encephalopathy, seizures → infection, ADEM, autoimmune encephalitis.
  • CSF pleocytosis >50 cells, neutrophils, or very high protein → not typical MS.
  • Absent oligoclonal bands with an otherwise "classic" picture — still possible, but lower your confidence and widen the differential.
  • Progressive myelopathy without relapses → B12/copper deficiency, HTLV-1, dural AV fistula, spondylotic compression, hereditary spastic paraplegia, adrenomyeloneuropathy.
  • Systemic features (rash, arthritis, sicca, oral/genital ulcers, uveitis) → sarcoid, lupus, Sjögren, Behçet.

Send AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG before you start a DMT

This is the single highest-consequence step on the page. NMOSD and MOGAD are not MS, and several MS drugs make NMOSD worse — interferon-beta, natalizumab, and fingolimod have all been associated with severe NMOSD attacks. Starting an MS DMT in an unrecognized NMOSD patient can precipitate blindness or a devastating myelitis.

Send serum cell-based AQP4-IgG/MOG-IgG when the syndrome raises concern for NMOSD or MOGAD, particularly severe/bilateral optic neuritis, LETM/conus disease, ADEM, or atypical brainstem/ cortical presentations. Broad low-pretest-probability screening can generate misleading low-positive MOG results; interpret through the published criteria before choosing a DMT. Cell-based assay, not ELISA. Draw before or well after steroids/PLEX where possible, since treatment lowers titers and produces false negatives.

docs.title: Rapid approach
docs.text:
1. Confirm it is a true demyelinating attack — objective, CNS-localizing, >24 h, no fever/infection.
  2. MRI brain and full spine with and without gadolinium, using an MS protocol.
  3. Test for AQP4-IgG/MOG-IgG when the clinical/MRI phenotype warrants it; use serum cell-based assays and interpret low positives cautiously. Do not delay urgent attack treatment.
  4. LP for oligoclonal bands and kappa free light chain index when the diagnosis isn't already secure, and always when the presentation is atypical.
  5. Apply the full 2024 McDonald decision framework with an MS specialist. DIT is not required in every qualifying pathway; the simplified lists below are an orientation, not the complete diagnostic matrix.
  6. Treat the relapse if disabling (steroids → PLEX for refractory).
  7. Start a DMT — early, and in most cases high-efficacy.
  8. Address symptoms and the military disposition — profile, and a DES referral under 3-31e.

docs.title: Diagnosis — the 2024 McDonald criteria
docs.text:
Which version you are using

The current framework is the 2024 revisions of the McDonald criteria, developed by the International Advisory Committee on Clinical Trials (ECTRIMS + National MS Society) and published in The Lancet Neurology in September 2025. The "2024" in the name refers to when the panel reported, not the publication date — expect to see both years cited.

They are new enough that published critique already exists in Lancet Neurology correspondence, largely concerning the risk of over-diagnosis as the criteria become more permissive. Apply them with the mimic list above in hand.

What changed that matters at the bedside:

Change What it means Optic nerve is now a fifth topography for DIS The four classic regions (periventricular, cortical/juxtacortical, infratentorial, spinal cord) are joined by the optic nerve — demonstrated by orbital MRI, OCT inter-eye asymmetry, or visual evoked potentials Kappa free light chain index Accepted as an alternative to oligoclonal bands for demonstrating dissemination in time. Automated, quantitative, and doesn't require electrophoresis Central vein sign (CVS) Supportive imaging biomarker; improves specificity by distinguishing demyelinating from vascular white-matter lesions Paramagnetic rim lesions (PRL) Supportive; marks chronic active lesions and increases diagnostic confidence Radiologically isolated syndrome can now become MS RIS may be diagnosed as MS when DIS is met plus one of: evidence of DIT, CSF positivity, or a threshold number of CVS-positive lesions (e.g. ≥6) Unified across the lifespan and course One framework for relapsing and progressive disease, paediatric through late-life presentations

Dissemination in space (DIS) — lesions in ≥2 of 5 CNS regions:

  1. Periventricular
  2. Cortical or juxtacortical
  3. Infratentorial
  4. Spinal cord
  5. Optic nerve (new in 2024)

Dissemination in time (DIT) — any one of:

  • A new lesion on follow-up MRI compared with a baseline scan
  • Simultaneous enhancing and non-enhancing lesions on a single scan
  • CSF-specific oligoclonal bands (substitutes for DIT)
  • Elevated kappa free light chain index (new in 2024; substitutes for DIT)
  • A second clinical attack

Practical: how the MRI should be ordered

Brain MRI with and without gadolinium, 3 mm slices, including 3D FLAIR, T2, T1 pre/post, and DWI. Full spine (cervical + thoracic) with and without contrast — cord lesions carry diagnostic and prognostic weight and are frequently missed when only the cervical spine is imaged. Add orbital MRI with fat suppression if optic nerve involvement is the question. Ask the radiologist explicitly for central vein sign and paramagnetic rim lesions if your centre has susceptibility-weighted sequences — they now carry diagnostic weight.

docs.title: Disease course — name it, because it drives the DMT
docs.text:
Phenotype Pattern Clinically isolated syndrome (CIS) First demyelinating attack, criteria not yet fully met Radiologically isolated syndrome (RIS) Incidental MS-typical MRI lesions, no clinical attack. Under 2024 criteria a subset now qualify as MS Relapsing–remitting (RRMS) ~85% at onset. Discrete attacks with variable recovery Secondary progressive (SPMS) Gradual accumulation after an initial relapsing course; classified as active/non-active and with/without progression Primary progressive (PPMS) ~10–15%. Progression from onset, no early relapses; older, more male, more often myelopathic

PIRA — progression independent of relapse activity — is the concept that reframed modern MS care: disability accrues even when relapses and new lesions stop. It is why "no relapses" is not the same as "well controlled," and why the field is chasing agents that touch smouldering inflammation.

docs.title: The prescriptive flow (what I want done, in order)
docs.text:
1. Is this a true relapse? New or worsening objective neurologic deficit lasting >24 hours, in the absence of fever or infection. Rule out pseudo-relapse — a UTI, any infection, heat, or metabolic stress unmasking prior deficits. Check temperature and urinalysis before you reach for steroids. Treating a pseudo-relapse with steroids does harm and no good.
  2. Treat the relapse if it is disabling. Mild sensory relapses often need nothing.
  3. Confirm the serology is back — AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG — before committing to an MS DMT.
  4. Start a DMT. Do not "watch and wait" on active relapsing disease. Time to first effective therapy is the variable that most predicts long-term disability.
  5. Match the DMT to the patient — disease activity, pregnancy plans, JCV status, comorbidity, monitoring burden, and, for a service member, deployability of the monitoring regimen.
  6. Treat symptoms explicitly — spasticity, fatigue, bladder, neuropathic pain, mood, gait. Symptom burden drives function far more than EDSS does.
  7. Baseline the disability — EDSS or timed 25-foot walk and 9-hole peg, documented. You will need it for the board and for judging DMT failure.
  8. Start the military disposition early. MS is a named DES referral condition.

docs.title: Acute relapse management
docs.text:
Step 1 — high-dose corticosteroids

  • Methylprednisolone 1000 mg IV daily × 3–5 days. No taper required for most relapses.
  • Oral is equivalent at bioequivalent dose — oral methylprednisolone 1000 mg daily × 3–5 days performs comparably to IV in randomised comparisons and is far easier logistically. Use it when IV access or infusion capacity is the constraint.
  • Add gastroprotection (PPI), monitor glucose (especially in diabetics), and warn about insomnia, mood lability, and metallic taste.
  • Do not treat a pseudo-relapse. Fever or infection first — treat that, reassess in days.

Step 2 — plasma exchange, for steroid-refractory relapse

Escalate if there is no meaningful improvement after the steroid course, particularly for a severe attack (dense myelitis, severe optic neuritis with poor acuity, brainstem syndrome).

  • PLEX — 5–7 exchanges over 10–14 days, typically every other day.
  • Start early. Benefit is greatest when initiated within days to a few weeks of onset; waiting months forfeits most of the effect.
  • Response rates in steroid-refractory demyelinating attacks are substantial, and PLEX is especially important in NMOSD, where it should be considered first-line alongside steroids rather than as rescue.

Step 3 — IVIG, when PLEX is unavailable or contraindicated

  • IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day × 5 days (total 2 g/kg).
  • Evidence in acute MS relapse is weaker than for PLEX — treat it as the fallback, not the equal. It is a reasonable choice when vascular access, haemodynamic instability, or availability rules out exchange, but is not automatically preferred in pregnancy. A disabling attack during pregnancy needs individualized neurology/obstetric planning; PLEX remains an option for severe steroid-refractory disease.

Do not

  • Do not give steroids for a pseudo-relapse.
  • Do not use chronic or pulsed steroids as a disease-modifying strategy — they do not alter the course.
  • Do not delay DMT initiation waiting for the relapse to fully resolve.

docs.title: Disease-modifying therapy
docs.text:
The central modern question is strategy, not just drug: start high-efficacy immediately, or escalate from a platform agent? The field has moved decisively toward early high-efficacy treatment, driven by observational data showing better long-term disability outcomes and by the recognition that damage accrued early is not recoverable.

The evidence status, stated honestly

The two randomised trials built to settle this — DELIVER-MS (36-month brain volume loss) and TREAT-MS (sustained EDSS-plus worsening) — are the definitive tests, and their outcome results are not posted in the trial registries as of 22 November 2026. DELIVER-MS’s registry estimates primary completion in July 2027; TREAT-MS records primary completion in July 2026. Completion dates are not outcome results. DELIVER-MS’s June 2026 treatment-decision report describes choices, not proof that one strategy improves disability. DELIVER-MS registry · TREAT-MS registry.

Meanwhile the position has firmed. The July 2026 NEJM review by Hauser states that long-term prospective trials and real-world experience indicate the most effective control of relapsing disease is achieved by initiating high-efficacy therapy at the earliest possible time. Counsel accordingly — but say plainly that randomised confirmation is still pending.

docs.title: The tiers
docs.text:
High-efficacyModerate — S1P modulatorsPlatform / lower-efficacyProgressive disease

Anti-CD20 monoclonals — the current workhorses of MS care.

  • Ocrelizumab (Ocrevus) — 300 mg IV × 2 doses two weeks apart, then 600 mg IV every 6 months. Also the only agent approved for PPMS (ORATORIO).
    • Ocrevus Zunovo is ocrelizumab coformulated with hyaluronidase (ocrelizumab/hyaluronidase-ocsq): 920 mg/23,000 units in 23 mL SC over about 10 minutes every 6 months, administered by a healthcare professional with label-directed premedication and observation. Approved for the same adult indications as IV. Do not substitute the IV dose or route. OCARINA II showed comparable pharmacokinetics and efficacy. Current label.
    • Paediatric approval, 8 May 2026 — for relapsing–remitting MS specifically, ages ≥10 years and ≥25 kg (55 lb). Note this is narrower than the adult label, which covers relapsing forms including CIS and active SPMS. Based on OPERETTA II vs fingolimod (non-inferior ARR; 48% fewer new/enlarging T2 and 87% fewer enhancing lesions).
  • Ofatumumab (Kesimpta) — 20 mg SC at weeks 0, 1, and 2; then 20 mg monthly starting at week 4, self-administered after instruction. The logistically simplest high-efficacy option and often the right answer for a mobile population.
  • Ublituximab (Briumvi) — 150 mg IV initially, 450 mg two weeks later, then 450 mg 24 weeks after the FIRST infusion and every 24 weeks thereafter. The first infusion takes about 4 hours; later infusions about 1 hour. Use label-directed premedication and monitoring. FDA label. Five-year ULTIMATE I/II open-label extension data (JAMA Neurology, February 2026) confirm sustained low annualised relapse rate and a favourable long-term safety profile.
  • Rituximab — off label. The OVERLORD-MS protocol used 1,000 mg IV initially, then 500 mg IV every 6 months with infusion precautions. Other neurology regimens differ; use a documented MS protocol and the shared safety order set. Trial protocol. No longer merely "widely used." OVERLORD-MS (NEJM, July 2026) is the first head-to-head randomised trial: in 216 newly diagnosed relapsing patients across 12 Norwegian and Swedish centres, rituximab was non-inferior to ocrelizumab for freedom from new or enlarging T2 lesions between months 6 and 24 (92.2% vs 94.8%; risk difference −2.6 percentage points, 95% CI −9.4 to 4.3, against a 10-point non-inferiority margin). Clinical activity was minimal in both arms.
    • The caveat is infection: 82% vs 69% of participants had an infection on rituximab versus ocrelizumab, though serious adverse events were similar (8% vs 7%).
    • Earlier observational data (JAMA Neurology, 2023) found higher relapse rates with rituximab in routine practice — likely reflecting dosing and interval heterogeneity rather than a true efficacy gap.
    • Practical read: rituximab is a defensible, far cheaper anti-CD20 choice with randomised support, provided the dosing is disciplined and you accept a higher infection burden. This matters a great deal for formulary-constrained care.

Extended-interval dosing

Extending the interval between anti-CD20 doses — rather than fixed 6-monthly infusions — is increasingly used to reduce infection risk, hypogammaglobulinaemia, and cost, typically guided by B-cell repopulation or immunoglobulin levels. It is a proposed general strategy rather than a labelled regimen, so document the rationale. Relevant to the TRICARE cost conversation and to any patient accumulating infections on standard dosing.

Others:

  • Natalizumab (Tysabri) — 300 mg IV every 4 weeks. Highly effective, but PML risk — stratify with JCV antibody index. High index plus prior immunosuppression plus long duration is the danger zone. A biosimilar (Tyruko) is available.
  • Alemtuzumab (Lemtrada) — 12 mg/day IV for 5 consecutive days, then 12 mg/day for 3 days 12 months later. Specialist/REMS treatment; the label generally reserves it for inadequate response to at least two MS drugs. Give label-directed steroid premedication and herpes prophylaxis. Secondary autoimmunity (thyroid, ITP, anti-GBM) requires monthly CBC/creatinine/urinalysis and thyroid tests every 3 months until 48 months after the last infusion. Prescribing information.
  • Cladribine (Mavenclad) — 3.5 mg/kg PO cumulative over two yearly courses (1.75 mg/kg per year), each split into two cycles. Prescribe from the weight-based cycle table, not a flat daily dose. Screen for pregnancy, malignancy, infection and lymphopenia; complete the label’s pretreatment and monitoring requirements. Generally used after inadequate response/intolerance to an alternative MS drug; not recommended for CIS. Current label.
  • Autologous haematopoietic stem cell transplantation (aHSCT) — off-label, but it appears to provide durable long-term benefit in relapsing MS, and in selected patients with aggressive, highly active disease failing conventional therapy it is a legitimate consideration rather than a fringe option. Requires an experienced transplant centre; treatment-related morbidity is real. A late-stage randomised trial (NCT04047628) is ongoing. Worth raising early in a young service member with aggressive disease, where the alternative is decades of accumulating disability.
  • Fingolimod, siponimod, ozanimod, ponesimod — oral.
  • First-dose bradycardia monitoring (agent-dependent), macular oedema screening, lymphopenia, and VZV serology + vaccination before starting.
  • Severe rebound disease on discontinuation is a real hazard — never stop an S1P agent abruptly without a bridging plan.
  • Siponimod is labelled for relapsing forms (CIS, RRMS, and active SPMS) — not restricted to SPMS — but EXPAND is why it is the usual pick in active SPMS. Requires CYP2C9 genotyping.
  • Interferon-beta (Avonex, Rebif, Plegridy, Betaseron) — flu-like reactions, LFTs. Best pregnancy safety record of the DMTs.
  • Glatiramer acetate (Copaxone, Glatopa; a further generic approved January 2026) — injection site reactions and immediate post-injection reactions. FDA boxed warning: serious/fatal anaphylaxis can occur with the first dose or after years of treatment. Symptoms may overlap a post-injection reaction; persistent/worsening breathing, throat, circulatory, or multisystem symptoms require emergency treatment. Discuss pregnancy use individually.
  • Teriflunomide — teratogenic, long half-life, requires cholestyramine accelerated elimination. Avoid in anyone who may become pregnant.
  • Fumarates — all three deliver the same active metabolite, monomethyl fumarate, and share flushing, GI upset, and lymphopenia (PML risk if prolonged and severe). Check absolute lymphocyte count before starting and periodically.
    • Dimethyl fumarate (Tecfidera) — the original; generic available. GI intolerance is the usual reason for discontinuation.
    • Diroximel fumarate (Vumerity) — second-generation, bioequivalent monomethyl fumarate exposure and therefore comparable efficacy, but substantially better GI tolerability — EVOLVE-MS-2 showed a 46% reduction in days with GI symptoms of at least moderate severity versus dimethyl fumarate. The right switch for a patient failing dimethyl fumarate on tolerability rather than efficacy.
    • Monomethyl fumarate (Bafiertam) — the active metabolite given directly; approved for relapsing forms in adults.
  • Ocrelizumab — currently the only DMT approved for PPMS. The effect is modest and concentrated in younger patients with inflammatory activity.
  • Siponimod (Mayzent) — approved for relapsing forms of MS in adults, which by label includes CIS, RRMS, and active SPMS — the same broad indication most relapsing-MS DMTs carry. It is not label-restricted to active SPMS, though EXPAND is the trial that makes it the natural choice there. Requires CYP2C9 genotyping.

BTK inhibitors — the actual state of play. This class targets B cells and CNS-resident microglia, and because these agents are brain-penetrant they are the leading attempt to reach the compartmentalised inflammation behind a closed blood–brain barrier that drives progression. Recent trials have sorted the class sharply.

  • Fenebrutinib — a highly selective, non-covalent BTK inhibitor, and as of mid-2026 the most convincing agent in the class. Three positive phase 3 trials:
    • FENtrepid (PPMS) — met its primary endpoint of non-inferiority to ocrelizumab for 12-week composite confirmed disability progression, with a 12% risk reduction (HR 0.88; 95% CI 0.75–1.03). Presented ACTRIMS, February 2026. Genentech/Roche describe it as the first investigational agent in over a decade to reduce disability progression in PPMS.
    • FENhance 1 and 2 (relapsing MS) — both met their primary endpoint versus teriflunomide, with ARR reductions of 51.1% and 58.5% (n≈1,497 combined, 96 weeks), plus reduced risk of disability worsening (26% and 20%). Presented AAN, 2026. Liver enzyme elevations >3× ULN were comparable to teriflunomide.
    • Not FDA-approved as of this audit. Roche announced FDA acceptance for priority review on 30 September 2026 for relapsing MS and PPMS. Sponsor regulatory announcement. If approved it would be the first high-efficacy oral covering both relapsing MS and PPMS.
  • Tolebrutinib — brain-penetrant but relatively non-selective, and its programme is mixed at best. Present it accurately:
    • HERCULES (non-relapsing SPMS) — positive: a 31% reduction in the risk of 6-month confirmed disability progression (HR 0.69; 95% CI 0.55–0.88; P=0.003). Note this is a hazard-ratio risk reduction, not a "delay" — the sponsor's press language differs from the NEJM primary analysis.
    • GEMINI 1 and 2 (relapsing MS) — failed. Not superior to teriflunomide on annualised relapse rate (0.13 vs 0.12 and 0.11 vs 0.11; n=1,873). A pooled 6-month confirmed-disability-worsening signal favoured tolebrutinib (29% risk reduction, nominal P=0.023) but could not be formally tested because the hierarchical testing plan had already failed.
    • PERSEUS (PPMS) — failed its primary endpoint (6-month composite confirmed disability progression); MRI measures improved only. Sanofi will not pursue PPMS registration.
    • Regulatory: FDA Complete Response Letter, December 2025 — not approved in the US. EU Cenrifki marketing authorisation was issued 19 June 2026 for adults with SPMS without relapses in the preceding two years, and the UAE approved it for non-relapsing SPMS in August 2025. Given the GEMINI and PERSEUS results, treat near-term US approval as genuinely uncertain rather than imminent.
  • Remibrutinib — in phase 3 (REMODEL-1 and REMODEL-2); no primary results yet.

Progressive MS needs phenotype- and jurisdiction-specific counseling. Ocrelizumab is FDA-approved for PPMS and siponimod for active SPMS. Fenebrutinib remains under FDA review. Tolebrutinib has positive HERCULES evidence and EU authorization for SPMS without recent relapses, while the US application received a CRL. Do not translate lack of a US approval into lack of any treatment evidence. Rehabilitation, exercise, symptom management and vascular-risk care remain essential. EMA Cenrifki indication.

docs.title: Choosing — the practical decision table
docs.text:
Situation Reasonable choice Newly diagnosed, active RRMS Anti-CD20 (ofatumumab if self-injection suits; ocrelizumab if infusion is easy) Highly active / aggressive at onset Anti-CD20, natalizumab (if JCV negative), or alemtuzumab/cladribine induction Wants pregnancy soon Glatiramer or interferon; or anti-CD20 timed so infusion precedes conception. Avoid teriflunomide entirely JCV antibody positive, high index Avoid natalizumab; anti-CD20 instead Needs oral, low monitoring S1P modulator or fumarate — accept lower efficacy Established PPMS Ocrelizumab if inflammatory activity; otherwise rehabilitation-led care Active SPMS Siponimod (EXPAND) or an anti-CD20 — "active" means relapses or new/enhancing lesions, and that activity is what predicts benefit. For non-relapsing SPMS there is no approved option in the US (tolebrutinib received a CRL) Cost or formulary constrained Rituximab — now supported by randomised non-inferiority data (OVERLORD-MS), accepting a higher infection rate Aggressive disease failing high-efficacy therapy Consider aHSCT referral to an experienced centre Breakthrough on a platform agent Escalate to high-efficacy — do not switch laterally

Before the first dose of any DMT

Screen: CBC with differential, CMP, hepatitis B (HBsAg + anti-HBc), hepatitis C, HIV, TB (quantiferon), VZV IgG, and pregnancy test. Vaccinate before starting — live vaccines are contraindicated once immunosuppressed, and anti-CD20 blunts vaccine response, follow the chosen product’s schedule: for anti-CD20 agents, generally ≥4 weeks for live vaccines and, when possible, ≥2 weeks for non-live vaccines before initiation. Do not delay urgent disease treatment without a specialist plan.

Hepatitis B reactivation with anti-CD20 is a named, preventable catastrophe. Check it every time. Monitor immunoglobulins on long-term anti-CD20 — hypogammaglobulinaemia accumulates over years and drives infection risk.

TRICARE — verified rules and the current form

The October pharmacy list flags Kesimpta, Mayzent, Zeposia and Mavenclad for PA. Vumerity is PA/nonformulary, and Gilenya has a prior-use rule. Confirm current forms and exact brand/generic requirements. Ocrelizumab, ublituximab, rituximab and other clinician-administered treatments need benefit/site-specific authorization. The live pharmacy restriction alone does not establish a medical-benefit criterion.

Current PA/MN details, benefit routing and packet · Live Formulary Search. Check the exact product, beneficiary and venue on the prescribing date.

docs.title: Symptomatic management
docs.text:
Symptom control determines function more than any DMT does. Ask about all of it — patients under-report.

Symptom First-line Spasticity Baclofen 5–10 mg TID titrated (max ~80 mg/day); tizanidine 2–4 mg TID (sedation, hypotension, LFTs); stretching and PT throughout. Intrathecal baclofen or botulinum toxin for focal/severe Fatigue Screen for sleep apnoea, depression, thyroid, anaemia, and deconditioning first — treat what you find. Exercise has the best evidence. Amantadine 100 mg BID, modafinil 100–200 mg daily Neurogenic bladder Post-void residual first — it determines the pathway. Retention → intermittent catheterisation. Storage/urgency → antimuscarinic or mirabegron (fewer cognitive effects); botulinum toxin for refractory detrusor overactivity. Treat UTIs promptly — they trigger pseudo-relapses Neuropathic pain / Lhermitte Gabapentin, pregabalin, duloxetine, amitriptyline Trigeminal neuralgia Common in MS and often bilateral — see trigeminal neuralgia. Carbamazepine/oxcarbazepine first Depression Prevalent and under-treated; suicide risk is elevated in MS. SSRI/SNRI plus psychotherapy. Screen at every visit Cognitive impairment Processing speed most affected. Formal neuropsych testing when duty or employment is in question Gait / walking speed Dalfampridine 10 mg BID (extended release) — improves walking in a responder subset. **Contraindicated with seizure history or CrCl ≤50 mL/min; even CrCl 51–80 requires a careful seizure-risk/benefit assessment. Check renal function before treatment and periodically** Heat intolerance (Uhthoff) Cooling strategies, activity timing, hydration. Operationally decisive — see the military box

Military medicine — duty, retention and deployment

  • Profile / function: Record relapse date, residual disability, visual/motor function, fatigue and heat sensitivity; protect against tasks that amplify those deficits.
  • Retention / MEB–MAR2: DoDI V2 5.26.f and Army 3-31e address demyelinating disease. Apply the specific Army standard; a monophasic syndrome and a chronic relapsing disorder are not interchangeable. Use the retention framework; permanent P3/4 does not by itself select DES versus MAR2.
  • Deployment / medications: CENTCOM MS requires stability/heat/medication assessment for waiver. SC self-injection still triggers the injectable rule; immunosuppression, infection risk and lab/infusion support require separate review. See the disease AND drug screen for the current CENTCOM rules and waiver packet.
  • Special duty: flight, diving and other special assignments have separate standards and waiver authorities; a general duty profile does not clear them.
  • LOD / EPTS: document onset, duty status, exposures and aggravation objectively. The designated authority determines LOD/EPTS; neither in-service diagnosis nor a genetic finding settles it automatically.

docs.title: 📚 Discover — evidence brief
docs.text:
What MS actually is. An adaptive-immune attack on CNS myelin with early and ongoing axonal loss. The relapsing phase is driven by peripheral lymphocyte trafficking across the blood–brain barrier — which is why drugs that deplete B cells or block trafficking work so well early. The progressive phase is dominated by compartmentalised inflammation behind a closed barrier: meningeal lymphoid aggregates, chronic active (rim) lesions, and microglial activation. That compartmentalisation is precisely why peripherally acting DMTs lose traction in progressive disease, and why brain-penetrant strategies like BTK inhibition were pursued.

Epstein–Barr virus is now regarded as a necessary, though not sufficient, cause — the 2022 Bjornevik cohort of over 10 million US military personnel showed a 32-fold increased risk of MS after EBV seroconversion, with no comparable signal for other viruses. The military relevance is direct: that landmark study was built on Department of Defense serum repository samples.

Why "early and effective" won the argument. Relapse-associated worsening and PIRA both contribute to disability, but the inflammatory window in which treatment demonstrably alters the trajectory is early. Axonal loss is not recoverable, brain volume loss proceeds silently, and patients who reach an EDSS milestone rarely come back. The observational literature consistently favours early high-efficacy therapy; DELIVER-MS and TREAT-MS are the randomised tests, and they had not reported primary results as of July 2026.

Where the field is heading. Two frontiers are worth knowing about even though neither is standard care. BTK inhibitors are the first serious attempt to modulate CNS-compartmentalised disease — the Lancet Neurology 2026 class review describes them as potential harbingers of treatments that reach processes behind an intact blood–brain barrier, and fenebrutinib's three positive phase 3 trials are the strongest evidence yet that the strategy works. CD19-directed therapy is the other: anti-CD20 agents spare CD20-negative plasmablasts and plasma cells, and CD19-targeted monoclonals or CAR T cells reach that compartment. Case series in autoimmune disease have reported dramatic benefit, and MS trials are beginning. Neither belongs in a counselling conversation yet, but both explain where the next decade of DMTs comes from.

Key trials and evidence:

  • OPERA I/II — ocrelizumab vs interferon beta-1a in RRMS; superior relapse and MRI outcomes. Established anti-CD20 as front-line therapy.
  • ORATORIO — ocrelizumab in PPMS; the first positive trial in primary progressive disease.
  • ASCLEPIOS I/II — ofatumumab vs teriflunomide; brought subcutaneous self-administered high-efficacy therapy into practice.
  • AFFIRM / SENTINEL — natalizumab efficacy, and the trials that surfaced PML.
  • CARE-MS I/II — alemtuzumab; durable effect, secondary autoimmunity.
  • EXPAND — siponimod in SPMS; benefit concentrated in active disease.
  • ULTIMATE I/II — ublituximab; 5-year extension data, JAMA Neurology 2026.
  • OVERLORD-MS — rituximab non-inferior to ocrelizumab in newly diagnosed relapsing MS (NEJM, July 2026); more infections with rituximab. The first anti-CD20 head-to-head.
  • HERCULES — tolebrutinib in non-relapsing SPMS; 31% reduction in risk of 6-month confirmed disability progression (HR 0.69). US outcome: Complete Response Letter, December 2025.
  • GEMINI 1/2 — tolebrutinib failed vs teriflunomide in relapsing MS.
  • PERSEUS — tolebrutinib failed in PPMS; PPMS registration abandoned.
  • FENtrepid — fenebrutinib non-inferior to ocrelizumab in PPMS (HR 0.88), ACTRIMS 2026.
  • FENhance 1/2 — fenebrutinib vs teriflunomide in relapsing MS; 51.1% and 58.5% ARR reductions, AAN 2026.
  • OPERETTA II — ocrelizumab vs fingolimod in paediatric RRMS; basis of the May 2026 approval.
  • EVOLVE-MS-2 — diroximel vs dimethyl fumarate; 46% fewer days with moderate-or-worse GI symptoms.
  • Bjornevik et al., Science 2022 — EBV and MS causality, from the DoD serum repository.
  • 2024 revisions of the McDonald criteria, Lancet Neurology, September 2025.
