docs.title: MOG antibody-associated disease (MOGAD)
docs.text:
Last reviewed: July 2026

One-liner: a distinct antibody-mediated demyelinating disease targeting myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein — neither MS nor NMOSD. It relapses less often, recovers far better, and is notoriously steroid-dependent, so the management problem is usually the taper rather than the attack.

Who this is for: anyone working up optic neuritis, myelitis, or ADEM — especially in children and young adults, where MOGAD is substantially more common than NMOSD.

🚩 The three-way fork

Optic neuritis and myelitis have three antibody-defined destinations, and they diverge in treatment and prognosis. Use serum cell-based antibody testing when the clinical/MRI phenotype fits; interpret low-positive MOG-IgG in context and avoid broad screening of nonspecific symptoms/MRI spots.

MS NMOSD (AQP4+) MOGAD Target Myelin (T-cell driven) Astrocyte AQP4 Oligodendrocyte MOG Optic neuritis Unilateral, retrobulbar, good recovery Severe, posterior/chiasmal, poor recovery Bilateral, anterior, marked disc swelling — but good recovery Myelitis Short segment, peripheral LETM, central LETM, often conus involvement ADEM No Rare Yes — the classic paediatric presentation Course Relapsing, then progressive Relapsing, no progressive phase Frequently monophasic (~30–50% of adults; higher in children); no progressive phase Recovery Variable Poor Good CSF OCB Positive ~85% Usually negative Usually negative Steroid response Good Good, but needs PLEX Excellent — but relapses on withdrawal

Regulatory update (21 November 2026): satralizumab is under FDA priority review for MOGAD, with an announced decision date of 10 January 2027. Priority review is not approval; its NMOSD indication does not establish a MOGAD label or insurance coverage.

docs.title: Diagnosis — 2023 international MOGAD panel criteria
docs.text:
The 2023 international MOGAD panel criteria (Banwell et al., Lancet Neurology) require all three of:

  1. A core clinical demyelinating event — one of six:
    • Optic neuritis
    • Myelitis
    • ADEM
    • Cerebral cortical encephalitis (often with seizures — a MOGAD-specific presentation)
    • Brainstem or cerebellar deficit
    • Cerebral monofocal or polyfocal deficit
  2. Positive MOG-IgG by cell-based assay
  3. Exclusion of alternative diagnoses

Titre matters — this is where the criteria bite

The criteria weight the result by titre, because low-positive MOG-IgG is common in people without MOGAD and is the main source of misdiagnosis.

  • Clear positive (high titre) + a core event + exclusion → MOGAD.
  • Low positive, borderline, or serum-only-positive-without-titre → requires additional supporting clinical or MRI features before the diagnosis can be made.
  • Never diagnose MOGAD on a low-positive antibody alone in an atypical syndrome.

Validation studies report high performance in patients with a high pre-test probability, but modest specificity and positive predictive value when applied broadly — which is exactly the over-testing trap. Send the assay when the syndrome fits, and interpret the titre, not just the sign.

Cell-based assay only. And note that MOG-IgG can be transiently positive after an ADEM-like illness and then disappear — repeat testing at 6–12 months helps distinguish monophasic from relapsing disease.

docs.title: Features that suggest MOGAD
docs.text:
• Bilateral simultaneous optic neuritis with prominent disc oedema and perineural enhancement on orbital MRI — but with good visual recovery, which is what separates it from NMOSD.
  • ADEM — particularly in children; MOGAD accounts for a large share of paediatric ADEM.
  • Cerebral cortical encephalitis with seizures — FLAIR-hyperintense cortical swelling, often unilateral. Frequently misdiagnosed as encephalitis or a first unprovoked seizure.
  • Myelitis with conus medullaris involvement.
  • Fluffy, poorly demarcated brain lesions that resolve substantially on follow-up imaging — quite unlike the persistent, sharply defined lesions of MS.
  • Steroid dependence — improvement on steroids, relapse as they are withdrawn. This pattern is strongly suggestive.

docs.title: The prescriptive flow (what I want done, in order)
docs.text:
1. Send cell-based MOG-IgG and AQP4-IgG on every optic neuritis, myelitis, ADEM, or cortical encephalitis.
  2. Interpret the titre, not just positive/negative.
  3. Treat the attack — steroids, with PLEX for severe or refractory presentations.
  4. Taper slowly. This is the single most important management point in MOGAD.
  5. Decide whether it is monophasic or relapsing — repeat serology at 6–12 months; persistent positivity predicts relapse.
  6. Individualize maintenance after the first attack using severity, recovery, relapse/taper history and specialist review. Observation can be reasonable after a fully recovered single attack; early maintenance can also be reasonable in a high-risk presentation (see below).
  7. Military disposition — profile, and referral under 3-31e.

docs.title: Acute attack treatment
docs.text:
Step 1 — steroids, then taper slowly

  • Methylprednisolone 1000 mg IV daily × 3–5 days.
  • Then an oral taper over weeks to months — not days.

This is the defining management point. MOGAD is exquisitely steroid-responsive and equally prone to rebound relapse on rapid withdrawal. A three-day pulse with no taper, which is perfectly reasonable in MS, frequently produces a relapse within weeks in MOGAD.

A prolonged taper, often around 3 months, is used after a significant attack based largely on observational evidence. Individualize dose/duration for severity, relapse during taper, infection/metabolic risk and the maintenance plan; this is not a mandatory minimum for every patient or a substitute for steroid-sparing treatment.

Step 2 — severe or refractory attack

  • PLEX 5–7 exchanges — for severe optic neuritis or dense myelitis, or steroid failure.
  • IVIG 2 g/kg — an effective alternative, and often preferred in children and in pregnancy.

docs.title: Maintenance therapy
docs.text:
The landscape just changed — and it is not yet FDA-approved

METEOROID, the phase 3 trial of satralizumab (anti-IL-6 receptor) in MOGAD, met its primary endpoint: a 68% reduction in relapse risk versus placebo, with 87% of treated patients relapse-free at 48 weeks versus 67% on placebo, a 66% reduction in annualised relapse rate, and onset of response as early as 8 weeks. Results were presented at the 2026 AAN Annual Meeting.

This is the first successful phase 3 trial in MOGAD. Satralizumab is FDA-approved for AQP4-seropositive NMOSD but is not yet approved for MOGAD — verify current regulatory status before counseling. CosMOG, evaluating rozanolixizumab (FcRn inhibitor), is also underway.

Until an agent is approved, maintenance is off-label and evidence is observational:

Options below are not a proven head-to-head ranking. On-treatment annualised relapse rates across observational cohorts run roughly: IL-6 blockade ~0.09, IVIG ~0.13–0.22, MMF ~0.3, rituximab ~0.5.

Option Dosing Notes IL-6 receptor blockade — tocilizumab 8 mg/kg IV every 4 weeks (satralizumab SC is the alternative) The largest comparative evidence base in MOGAD. Vilaseca et al. (JAMA Neurol, 2026; international multicentre, n=116, 90% tocilizumab): ARR fell from 0.64 to 0.09 (IRR 0.08; 95% CI 0.04–0.16 — a 92% reduction). Superior to low-dose IVIG (HR 4.5) but not significantly different from IVIG ≥1 g/kg q4wk (HR 2.0; 95% CI 0.8–4.5). Adverse events in 50% (mostly mild infections), 9% severe infections. Available as a biosimilar — substantially cheaper than satralizumab. Treat this as a first-line option, not a last resort IVIG ≥1 g/kg every 4 weeks — see the dosing warning below The best-established maintenance therapy, especially in children. Performs comparably to IL-6 blockade when properly dosed SCIG (subcutaneous immunoglobulin) Weekly or biweekly, self-administered Steadier immunoglobulin levels without peak-and-trough, self-administered at home. Data are limited but it is increasingly used — and it is the a way to reduce infusion-center visits, not a deployment clearance, which matters for a service member Mycophenolate mofetil Oral Reasonable oral maintenance; on-treatment ARR ~0.3 Methotrexate Oral/SC weekly Used in practice; limited MOGAD-specific evidence Azathioprine Oral Slow onset; requires steroid bridging for months. Phase 3 MOGwAI trial ongoing Chronic low-dose steroid — Sometimes the pragmatic bridge, with all the expected long-term costs Rituximab 1000 mg × 2, or 375 mg/m² weekly × 4 The weakest of the commonly used agents in MOGAD — do not carry NMOSD-level expectations across. Only ~55% remain relapse-free in meta-analysis; one long-term study found 61% of MOGAD patients relapsed (vs 28% of NMOSD; HR 2.8), and 79% of those relapses occurred despite CD19+ B cells suppressed below 1% — B-cell depletion simply does not prevent MOGAD attacks in many patients. Highest on-treatment ARR of the group (~0.5)

IVIG dose is the commonest reason IVIG 'fails'

Maintenance IVIG must be dosed at ≥1 g/kg every 4 weeks (commonly 1–2 g/kg q4wk).

In the 2026 comparative study, IL-6 blockade was significantly better than IVIG dosed below 1 g/kg q4wk (HR 4.5) but statistically indistinguishable from IVIG at ≥1 g/kg q4wk. The difference between an effective and an ineffective regimen is the dose, not the drug.

Before calling IVIG a failure and switching, check the dose and interval. Under-dosing is common and eminently fixable.

Who actually needs maintenance — this has shifted

The older teaching was to wait for a second attack, on the reasoning that a large share of MOGAD is monophasic and indefinite immunosuppression over-treats them. That default no longer holds unqualified.

MOGADOR2 (Neurology, 2024; French nationwide incident cohort, Class III evidence) found that relapse risk is highest early, and that initiating maintenance from the first attack substantially reduced it — a reported ~74% relative reduction (OR 0.26), with 2-year relapse risk of roughly 11% with early treatment versus 41% without. Separate work found that both corticosteroids continued ≥12 weeks and steroid-sparing maintenance independently lower relapse risk.

A defensible current approach:

  • Risk-stratify after the first attack rather than reflexively observing or reflexively treating.
  • Favour early maintenance when high-risk features are present: persistent MOG-IgG seropositivity, polyphasic first attack (HR ~2.4), elevated CSF protein (HR ~2.06), severe attack, myelitis at onset, or relapse during a steroid taper.
  • Observation remains reasonable for a single, fully recovered, monophasic-appearing attack in a patient who seroreverts to negative — but recheck serology at 6–12 months rather than assuming.
  • Early relapses predict more relapses: a relapse within 12 months carries HR ~2.11 for long-term relapsing disease, and within 90 days HR ~2.70 in adults. Treat an early relapse as a strong signal to commit to maintenance.

When can maintenance stop? — two 2026 datasets

One of the commonest questions in MOGAD, and until recently unanswerable. Note the two studies give different-looking numbers because they ask different questions — read both.

  • Boudot de la Motte et al. (JAMA Neurol, 2026; n=705 adults): the 1-year cumulative relapse risk after discontinuation was 8.7% (95% CI 1.0–15.9), with no rebound phenomenon. Lower risk was associated with treatment duration >1 year and >2 years since the last relapse.
  • Yeh et al. (Brain, 2026; Oxford NMO service, 190 patients, 236 discontinuation intervals): relapse followed 39% of discontinuations, at a median of 5.4 months. Estimated optimal durations were 10–18 months after a first attack and 20–30 months for relapsing patients, and persistent MOG-IgG positivity at the time of stopping predicted relapse (HR ~1.95 in relapsing disease).

Practical synthesis: de-escalation is genuinely feasible in MOGAD — unlike NMOSD, where stopping a complement inhibitor risks rebound. Aim for at least a year of treatment and two years relapse-free, recheck MOG-IgG before stopping (persistent positivity argues for continuing), and watch closely for the first 6 months, which is when relapses cluster.

For a service member this is the difference between indefinite infusion dependence and a realistic path back to full duty — see the military box.

Do not use MS disease-modifying therapies in MOGAD

Conventional MS DMTs do not prevent MOGAD relapses. Interferon-beta and glatiramer acetate show no relapse-prevention benefit, and there is no reason to expect the S1P modulators to help either.

The evidence for outright harm is strongest in NMOSD rather than MOGAD, so the argument here is futility rather than danger — but the practical consequence is the same: a patient left on an MS drug is an unprotected patient. If someone carrying an "MS" label turns out to be MOG-IgG positive, switch them to a MOGAD-appropriate regimen, do not continue the DMT.

How many patients relapse — the honest range

Reported relapse proportions vary widely, and the driver is follow-up duration and age, not disagreement about the disease. Roughly 30–50% of adults are monophasic, meaning 50–70% relapse with adequate follow-up. Children — particularly with an ADEM phenotype and seroreversion — are considerably more often monophasic (~74–83% in prospective incident paediatric cohorts).

Quote a range with its follow-up window, not a single number, and remember that a patient called monophasic at one year may be reclassified at five.

TRICARE — verified rules and the current form

Maintenance immunotherapies are off label for MOGAD as of 22 November 2026. Satralizumab remains under FDA review for this indication. The NMOSD Enspryng PA does not itself authorize MOGAD. Check the exact benefit and off-label medical-necessity requirements for IVIG/SCIg, rituximab or other selected treatment.

Current PA/MN details, benefit routing and packet · Live Formulary Search. Check the exact product, beneficiary and venue on the prescribing date.

Military medicine — duty, retention and deployment

  • Profile / function: Record relapse date, residual disability, visual/motor function, fatigue and heat sensitivity; protect against tasks that amplify those deficits.
  • Retention / MEB–MAR2: DoDI V2 5.26.f and Army 3-31e address demyelinating disease. Apply the specific Army standard; a monophasic syndrome and a chronic relapsing disorder are not interchangeable. Use the retention framework; permanent P3/4 does not by itself select DES versus MAR2.
  • Deployment / medications: CENTCOM MS requires stability/heat/medication assessment for waiver. SC self-injection still triggers the injectable rule; immunosuppression, infection risk and lab/infusion support require separate review. See the disease AND drug screen for the current CENTCOM rules and waiver packet.
  • Special duty: flight, diving and other special assignments have separate standards and waiver authorities; a general duty profile does not clear them.
  • LOD / EPTS: document onset, duty status, exposures and aggravation objectively. The designated authority determines LOD/EPTS; neither in-service diagnosis nor a genetic finding settles it automatically.

docs.title: 📚 Discover — evidence brief
docs.text:
Why MOGAD recovers when NMOSD does not. MOG sits on the outermost surface of the myelin sheath and the oligodendrocyte membrane, making it accessible to circulating antibody — but the target is myelin itself, and the oligodendrocyte largely survives. Demyelination is followed by genuine remyelination, which is why the fluffy MRI lesions of MOGAD often substantially resolve and why vision recovers even after dramatic bilateral disc swelling. NMOSD, by contrast, destroys astrocytes — a structural, complement-mediated necrosis that cavitates the cord and does not repair. Two antibody-mediated demyelinating diseases, opposite prognoses, largely because of what the antibody binds.

A precision worth keeping. It is tempting to say MOGAD is "not complement-mediated" — that overstates it. MOG-IgG damages myelin through several mechanisms: complement-dependent cytotoxicity, antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity, enhanced T-cell infiltration into the CNS, and direct disruption of the oligodendrocyte cytoskeleton. Complement is involved, but it is not the dominant, structurally destructive mechanism it is in AQP4 disease. That is the more accurate reason to expect complement inhibition to be less transformative here than in NMOSD — and it is also why IL-6 blockade, which acts further upstream on the antibody-producing and inflammatory axis, has performed well.

The nosological story. MOGAD spent years as "seronegative NMOSD" or "atypical MS," and patients were treated accordingly — often with agents that neither helped nor were needed. Its recognition as a distinct entity, formalised by the 2023 panel criteria, is one of the clearer recent wins in neuroimmunology. The 2026 METEOROID result marks its transition from a disease managed on observational habit to one with randomised evidence.

Key evidence:

  • Banwell B, et al., Lancet Neurology 2023 — international MOGAD panel proposed criteria.
  • METEOROID (2026) — satralizumab; 68% relapse-risk reduction, the first positive phase 3 in MOGAD.
  • Vilaseca et al., JAMA Neurology 2026 — IL-6 receptor blockade, n=116; ARR 0.64 → 0.09. The largest comparative maintenance dataset in MOGAD.
  • MOGADOR2 (Neurology, 2024) — early maintenance after the first attack cuts relapse risk.
  • Boudot de la Motte et al. (JAMA Neurol, 2026) and Yeh et al. (Brain, 2026) — treatment discontinuation.
  • Chen JJ et al. (JAMA Neurol, 2022) — maintenance IVIG, and the dose–response that makes ≥1 g/kg q4wk the target.
  • Validation cohorts of the 2023 criteria — strong performance at high pre-test probability, modest specificity when applied broadly.

The trial pipeline. MOGAD has gone from no trials to a genuine programme:

Trial Agent Status METEOROID Satralizumab (anti-IL-6R) Positive — first successful phase 3; not yet approved CosMOG Rozanolixizumab (FcRn antagonist) Ongoing TOMATO Tocilizumab (anti-IL-6R) Phase 2/3, ongoing MOGwAI Azathioprine Phase 3, ongoing Rituximab Anti-CD20 Phase 3, ongoing

docs.title: Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD)
docs.text:
Last reviewed: July 2026

One-liner: an antibody-mediated astrocytopathy — not a variant of MS — in which AQP4-IgG attacks aquaporin-4 water channels on astrocytes, producing severe optic neuritis and longitudinally extensive myelitis with poor recovery and high relapse-related disability.

Who this is for: anyone evaluating optic neuritis or myelitis. The entire reason this page exists is that treating NMOSD as MS can blind or paralyse the patient.

🚩 Why this distinction is urgent

Disability in NMOSD is relapse-driven. Unlike MS, there is no meaningful progressive phase — patients accumulate disability in discrete, devastating attacks. A single untreated myelitis can end ambulation; a single severe optic neuritis can end vision. Preventing the next attack is the whole game.

Several MS drugs make NMOSD worse. Interferon-beta, natalizumab, and fingolimod have all been associated with severe NMOSD exacerbations. Starting one in a misdiagnosed patient is an iatrogenic catastrophe.

Therefore: send cell-based serum AQP4-IgG in every optic neuritis and every myelitis, and do not start an MS DMT until it is back.

docs.title: When to suspect it over MS
docs.text:
Feature Points to NMOSD Myelitis Longitudinally extensive — ≥3 contiguous vertebral segments. Central cord, often with swelling and enhancement Optic neuritis Severe, bilateral or rapidly sequential, posterior/chiasmal, poor visual recovery, steroid-dependent Area postrema syndrome Intractable hiccups, nausea, or vomiting lasting days — a highly specific NMOSD presentation and often the first attack. Frequently misread as GI disease Brain MRI Often normal early, or lesions in AQP4-rich regions — periependymal around third/fourth ventricles, hypothalamus, dorsal brainstem, area postrema CSF Pleocytosis can be marked (>50 cells, sometimes neutrophilic); oligoclonal bands usually absent (~15–30%) Demographics Female predominance is strong (~9:1), median onset older than MS, over-represented in Black and Asian populations Coexisting autoimmunity Lupus, Sjögren, thyroid disease, myasthenia gravis Recovery Poor — incomplete recovery from attacks is the norm

Seronegative NMOSD

Roughly 10–25% of clinically definite NMOSD is AQP4-IgG negative. A negative test does not exclude the diagnosis.

In seronegative patients, send MOG-IgG — a substantial share prove to be MOGAD, which is a different disease with a different prognosis and treatment. That is the key point about the 10–25% figure: much of it is not seronegative NMOSD at all, it is unrecognised MOGAD.

True double-negative NMOSD (negative for both AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG) is a diagnosis of careful exclusion requiring the stricter 2015 clinical criteria — and it looks biologically different. A 2026 systematic review found it highly relapsing (73.6% relapsed) with a female-to-male ratio of only about 1.5:1, against roughly 9:1 in AQP4-positive disease. Do not assume it behaves like seropositive NMOSD; treat it aggressively (see below), but recognise the evidence base is thin.

Test with a cell-based assay, not ELISA. ELISA generates false positives at low titre that have caused real harm. And draw before steroids/PLEX where feasible — treatment suppresses titres and produces false negatives.

docs.title: Diagnosis (2015 international consensus criteria)
docs.text:
With AQP4-IgG positive: ≥1 core clinical characteristic + positive cell-based assay + exclusion of alternatives.

Without AQP4-IgG (or unknown status): stricter — ≥2 core characteristics from ≥1 attack, with at least one being optic neuritis, longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis, or area postrema syndrome, plus dissemination in space, plus supporting MRI findings, plus exclusion of alternatives.

The six core clinical characteristics:

  1. Optic neuritis
  2. Acute myelitis
  3. Area postrema syndrome — otherwise unexplained hiccups, nausea, vomiting
  4. Acute brainstem syndrome
  5. Symptomatic narcolepsy or acute diencephalic syndrome with NMOSD-typical MRI lesions
  6. Symptomatic cerebral syndrome with NMOSD-typical brain lesions

docs.title: The prescriptive flow (what I want done, in order)
docs.text:
1. Recognise the pattern — LETM, severe/bilateral optic neuritis, or area postrema syndrome.
  2. Send cell-based AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG immediately, before steroids where possible.
  3. Treat the attack hard and early — steroids and PLEX. Do not wait to see if steroids work in a severe attack.
  4. Start maintenance therapy without waiting for a second attack. In AQP4-positive NMOSD, the first attack is sufficient indication.
  5. Choose an FDA-approved agent over off-label rituximab where access permits.
  6. Screen for meningococcal disease risk before any complement inhibitor.
  7. Screen for coexisting autoimmunity.
  8. Start the military disposition — this is a DES referral condition.

docs.title: Acute attack treatment
docs.text:
Step 1 — steroids AND plasma exchange, together

  • Methylprednisolone 1000 mg IV daily × 5 days.
  • PLEX 5–7 exchanges over 10–14 days, typically every other day.

The key difference from MS: in NMOSD, PLEX is not rescue therapy — it is first-line alongside steroids for any severe attack. Do not run a full steroid course, wait, reassess, and only then consider exchange. Earlier PLEX predicts better visual and motor outcomes, and the therapeutic window is measured in days.

For a severe attack — poor acuity, dense myelitis — start both in parallel.

Step 2 — if refractory

  • IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day × 5 days where PLEX is unavailable or contraindicated.
  • Escalate maintenance therapy immediately; a breakthrough attack means the current regimen has failed.
  • Consider prolonged oral steroid taper as a bridge while maintenance therapy takes effect — unlike in MS, bridging matters here because the relapse risk is immediate and high.

docs.title: Maintenance therapy — prevent the next attack
docs.text:
Four monoclonal antibodies are FDA-approved for AQP4-IgG-seropositive NMOSD. In a disease where disability is entirely relapse-driven, this is the intervention that changes the patient's life.

Agent Target Dosing Notes Eculizumab (Soliris) C5 complement 900 mg IV weekly ×4; 1,200 mg at week 5, then q2wk PREVENT trial. Meningococcal vaccination mandatory Ravulizumab (Ultomiris) C5 complement Weight-based IV loading; first maintenance 2 weeks later, then q8wk (use current adult weight table) Approved 2024 (CHAMPION-NMOSD). Same target as eculizumab, engineered for a longer half-life — q8wk instead of q2wk Inebilizumab (Uplizna) CD19 B cells 300 mg IV on days 1 and 15; then 300 mg q6mo from first infusion N-MOmentum. Broader B-cell depletion than anti-CD20 (includes plasmablasts) Satralizumab (Enspryng) IL-6 receptor 120 mg SC at weeks 0, 2, 4, then q4wk SAkuraSky/SAkuraStar. Self-administered after loading; refrigeration, immunosuppression, monitoring and theater clearance still apply

Eculizumab biosimilar indications have expanded — check the current product label

The original approvals were restricted, but the current 2026 FDA labels for Bkemv and Epysqli include adult AQP4-IgG-positive NMOSD and adult AChR-positive gMG, in addition to PNH/aHUS. Do not use an old approval announcement to deny the newer indication. Verify the exact product, indication, interchangeability, REMS requirements, and benefit authorization with pharmacy; biosimilar status alone does not guarantee payer substitution or approval.

Off-label but genuinely useful options:

Agent Target Notes Tocilizumab IL-6 receptor (same as satralizumab) TANGO (Lancet Neurol 2020, phase 2, open-label, n=118): superior to azathioprine in highly relapsing NMOSD — median time to first relapse 78.9 vs 56.7 weeks, P=0.0026. Real-world data show ARR falling from ~1.9 to ~0.1. Included in the 2026 MENACTRIMS guidelines alongside the approved agents, and a substantially cheaper route to IL-6 blockade when satralizumab PA is denied Rituximab CD20 375 mg/m² weekly × 4, or 1000 mg × 2 doses two weeks apart; re-dose every 6 months or guided by CD19/CD20 B-cell reconstitution. See the caveats below Mycophenolate mofetil Antiproliferative Widely used globally; 5-year relapse-free survival ~51% Azathioprine Antiproliferative Slow onset — requires steroid bridging for months; 5-year relapse-free survival ~35%

How good are the approved agents really — read the comparative data carefully

The often-quoted figure is 5-year relapse-free survival of 100% for the C5 inhibitors, inebilizumab, and satralizumab versus 69.7% for rituximab (with MMF 51.1% and azathioprine 35.3%). That comes from Bilodeau et al., 2026 — a single-centre retrospective cohort at Mass General Brigham (176 patients, 2000–2024, median 9 years' follow-up), not head-to-head randomised data.

The nuance matters, and it cuts against a simple "approved beats rituximab" reading. When the same study combined efficacy with safety and tolerability into a composite relapse/serious-infection/treatment-limiting-event-free endpoint:

  • C5 inhibitors 91% vs rituximab 55% at 5 years — the C5 inhibitors clearly separate.
  • Inebilizumab 38% and satralizumab 79% (3-year data), and neither was statistically superior to rituximab on the composite: inebilizumab HR 1.23 (95% CI 0.24–3.12), satralizumab HR 1.01 (95% CI 0.16–2.68).

So: the C5 inhibitors have the strongest comparative case. For inebilizumab and satralizumab, the advantage over rituximab is a relapse-prevention signal that does not survive into a composite including harms — in a small single-centre cohort with wide confidence intervals. Do not overstate it to a patient or a formulary reviewer.

Rituximab's own cost is concrete: in that cohort 28% of rituximab treatment periods involved a serious infection, 34% a mild infection, and 13% hypogammaglobulinaemia. Long-term anti-CD20 exposure can produce hypogammaglobulinaemia requiring indefinite IVIG replacement — monitor immunoglobulins on every patient, indefinitely.

Indirect ranking — the network meta-analysis

A Bayesian network meta-analysis (J Neurol, 2025; 8 RCTs, 851 patients, 84% seropositive) ranked ravulizumab first for time to relapse — HR 0.00 (95% CrI 0.00–0.03), SUCRA 0.99, a 98% probability of being the superior agent — followed by eculizumab (0.76), tocilizumab (0.49), rituximab (0.47), and inebilizumab (0.45).

These are indirect comparisons across trials with different populations and endpoints, not head-to-head data, and the ravulizumab point estimate of exactly 0.00 reflects zero adjudicated relapses in CHAMPION-NMOSD rather than infinite efficacy. Treat the ranking as directional support for complement inhibition, not as a league table.

Stopping or switching a complement inhibitor — rebound risk

A provider who successfully stabilises a patient on eculizumab needs to know this before any future switch, including one forced by formulary change or deployment.

Disease reactivation clusters in the first ~3 months after eculizumab is stopped, including in patients relapse-free for years. Severe attacks have been reported around five half-lives after the last dose — eculizumab's half-life is only about 11 days, so protection is gone within weeks. One published case describes a severe attack 11 weeks after the final infusion during a switch to satralizumab.

Other series report uneventful switches, so this is a real risk rather than an inevitability — but it must be planned for:

  • Never stop a complement inhibitor without an overlapping bridge to the next agent.
  • Account for onset lag — anti-CD20 and IL-6 agents take weeks to months to protect.
  • Consider steroid cover through the transition.
  • Ravulizumab's half-life is roughly 5× longer than eculizumab's (~64 vs ~11 days), which gives a considerably wider and more forgiving window if a switch away from complement inhibition becomes necessary.

Seronegative NMOSD — no approved options

All four FDA-approved agents are indicated only for AQP4-IgG-positive disease. For seronegative patients the mainstays remain rituximab, mycophenolate mofetil, and azathioprine — this is a genuine unmet need, not a preference.

Treat aggressively anyway. A 2025 multicentre study found high-efficacy immunosuppression reduced relapse risk comparably in both groups — HR 0.27 in AQP4-positive and HR 0.21 in seronegative disease. Seronegativity is not a reason to under-treat.

Before any complement inhibitor — meningococcal risk

Eculizumab and ravulizumab block terminal complement and produce a profound, lasting susceptibility to Neisseria meningitidis. Both carry a boxed warning.

  • Vaccinate against meningococcus (ACWY and B) at least 2 weeks before the first dose.
  • If treatment cannot wait 2 weeks, vaccinate and give antibiotic prophylaxis to cover the interval.
  • Give the patient a wallet card and explicit instructions: any fever is an emergency.
  • Vaccination and antibiotics do not eliminate the risk. Evaluate possible meningitis/ meningococcemia urgently even with mild initial symptoms, a completed vaccine series, or prophylaxis. CDC advises MenACWY boosters every 5 years and MenB booster 1 year after the primary series, then every 2–3 years while risk persists. Consider ongoing antibiotic prophylaxis with the treating specialist.

Do not use in NMOSD

Interferon-beta, natalizumab, and fingolimod are associated with worsening NMOSD and are contraindicated. If a patient labelled "MS" deteriorates unexpectedly after starting one of these, send AQP4-IgG immediately — you may be watching a misdiagnosis declare itself.

Extend the caution to the whole S1P class — siponimod, ozanimod, ponesimod. The published case-series evidence is largely for fingolimod, but the mechanism of concern (lymphocyte sequestration rather than depletion) is shared across the class. There is no reason to take the risk when effective alternatives exist.

TRICARE — verified rules and the current form

Enspryng has a pharmacy PA flag. C5-antibody infusions and inebilizumab need product/indication-specific medical-benefit review. Obtain AQP4 serostatus, previous treatment, required safety screening and the current regional continuation criteria. Use the actual formulation and biosimilar label; a pharmacy list does not establish authorization for an infusion.

Current PA/MN details, benefit routing and packet · Live Formulary Search. Check the exact product, beneficiary and venue on the prescribing date.

docs.title: Monitoring and long-term care
docs.text:
• Immunoglobulins — check at baseline and periodically on any B-cell-depleting agent. Hypogammaglobulinaemia accumulates over years and can require indefinite IVIG replacement.
  • Meningococcal vaccination status — track and revaccinate on schedule for the whole duration of complement inhibition.
  • Relapse surveillance — clinical, with MRI as indicated. Attacks are stepwise, so document visual acuity, fields, and objective motor/sensory findings at each visit; you cannot reconstruct increments retrospectively.
  • Screen for coexisting autoimmunity — lupus, Sjögren, thyroid disease, myasthenia gravis.

GFAP — an emerging relapse biomarker

Serum/plasma glial fibrillary acidic protein, released from damaged astrocytes, is under study for confirming and predicting relapse — which is mechanistically apt, since NMOSD is an astrocytopathy. In a real-world IL-6-blockade cohort, baseline plasma GFAP >220 pg/mL was associated with substantially higher subsequent relapse risk (reported OR ~20).

Not yet standard of care and not a substitute for clinical judgement, but worth knowing about as it moves toward the clinic.

Pregnancy — plan it deliberately

With a female-to-male ratio near 9:1, most NMOSD patients are women of childbearing age, and this conversation should happen early rather than at the positive test.

  • The 2026 MENACTRIMS guidelines recommend planning conception after ≥12 months of disease stability, and resuming treatment early postpartum — the postpartum period carries elevated relapse risk.
  • Safety data across agents are limited; several appear relatively safe in pregnancy but none is well characterised. Coordinate with maternal-fetal medicine.
  • Do not simply stop therapy on a positive pregnancy test — an unplanned withdrawal, especially of a complement inhibitor, carries the rebound risk described above. Plan the transition.

Inebilizumab now carries indications beyond NMOSD

Inebilizumab (Uplizna) has since been approved for IgG4-related disease and for generalised myasthenia gravis (AChR- or MuSK-positive adults). Not directly relevant to NMOSD management, but it can change formulary positioning and the PA pathway — worth knowing when arguing an authorisation.

Military medicine — duty, retention and deployment

  • Profile / function: Record relapse date, residual disability, visual/motor function, fatigue and heat sensitivity; protect against tasks that amplify those deficits.
  • Retention / MEB–MAR2: DoDI V2 5.26.f and Army 3-31e address demyelinating disease. Apply the specific Army standard; a monophasic syndrome and a chronic relapsing disorder are not interchangeable. Use the retention framework; permanent P3/4 does not by itself select DES versus MAR2.
  • Deployment / medications: CENTCOM MS requires stability/heat/medication assessment for waiver. SC self-injection still triggers the injectable rule; immunosuppression, infection risk and lab/infusion support require separate review. See the disease AND drug screen for the current CENTCOM rules and waiver packet.
  • Special duty: flight, diving and other special assignments have separate standards and waiver authorities; a general duty profile does not clear them.
  • LOD / EPTS: document onset, duty status, exposures and aggravation objectively. The designated authority determines LOD/EPTS; neither in-service diagnosis nor a genetic finding settles it automatically.

docs.title: 📚 Discover — evidence brief
docs.text:
The mechanism explains the phenotype. AQP4 is the dominant water channel on astrocyte end-feet, and it is most densely expressed exactly where NMOSD strikes: the optic nerves, the central grey matter of the spinal cord, and the circumventricular organs — including the area postrema, which lacks a blood–brain barrier and is therefore directly exposed to circulating antibody. That anatomical fact is why intractable hiccups and vomiting are a neurologic presenting syndrome, and why the attack is an astrocytopathy with secondary demyelination rather than a primary attack on myelin. Complement activation following AQP4-IgG binding drives the necrotic, cavitating lesions that account for the poor recovery — and is precisely why C5 inhibition works so well.

The therapeutic era changed the disease. Before 2019, NMOSD was managed with off-label immunosuppression and carried a grim trajectory. Four approved biologics later, relapse-free survival at five years approaches 100% in trial and comparative cohorts. Few neurologic diseases have been transformed so completely in so short a span — which is exactly why the misdiagnosis question matters so much. The cost of calling NMOSD "MS" is no longer a mislabelled chart; it is a forfeited, highly effective treatment.

Key trials:

  • PREVENT — eculizumab; dramatic relapse reduction in AQP4-positive NMOSD.
  • CHAMPION-NMOSD — ravulizumab; extended q8-week dosing, FDA approval 2024.
  • N-MOmentum — inebilizumab (anti-CD19).
  • SAkuraSky / SAkuraStar — satralizumab (anti-IL-6R), with and without background therapy.
  • Wingerchuk et al., 2015 — international consensus diagnostic criteria.

docs.title: Myopathy
docs.text:
Last reviewed: October 2026

One-liner: the prescriptive approach to inflammatory myopathy in 2026 — which antibody changes the plan, the IMNM induction regimens that actually get used (anti-HMGCR vs anti-SRP), the dermatomyositis/polymyositis treatment ladder with the August 2026 brepocitinib (Lisraya) approval, myositis-associated ILD from chronic to rapidly progressive, and inclusion body myositis under the new 2024 ENMC framework. For the neurologist or rheumatologist seeing progressive weakness, a hot CK, or a myositis antibody panel that just resulted — and for the trainee with exertional rhabdomyolysis, the ICU patient who will not wean, and the young man with episodic paralysis.

🚩 Red flags — don't miss these

Pattern Worry Do now Rapidly progressive ILD, especially anti-MDA5 DM — rising O₂ needs over days to weeks Death from respiratory failure; this moves in days, not months Inpatient, multidisciplinary, upfront combination immunosuppression — do not wait for the complete antibody panel Dysphagia with aspiration risk (coughing on swallows, prolonged mealtimes, weight loss) in any myopathy Aspiration pneumonia — the killer in IBM and severe IMNM/DM Same-visit swallow screen → videofluoroscopy; dietitian; consider early IVIG in inflammatory disease CK >5,000 IU/L with myoglobinuria (tea-colored urine) — classically a trainee after PT Rhabdomyolysis → acute kidney injury, hyperkalemia, compartment syndrome Assess volume/renal/electrolyte risk; isotonic fluids when indicated, monitor, and decide admission by risk — exertional rhabdomyolysis Statin-exposed patient with severe proximal weakness and CK in the thousands Anti-HMGCR IMNM — stopping the statin alone does not treat it Anti-HMGCR antibody, muscle biopsy, start immunosuppression (early IVIG for moderate–severe) Inflammatory muscle biopsy labeled "polymyositis" in a patient over 45 with finger-flexor/quadriceps weakness IBM misdiagnosed as polymyositis — immunosuppression will not help and may harm Reconcile biopsy with the clinical pattern (2024 ENMC framework); only 43% of IBM biopsies show all three classic findings Systemic-sclerosis overlap about to get high-dose steroids for myositis Scleroderma renal crisis precipitated by steroids Rethink the steroid dose; involve rheumatology — the routine high-dose myositis approach does not apply

docs.title: Diagnosis / classification
docs.text:
Weakness is a pattern-recognition problem. Proximal symmetric weakness + elevated CK + myopathic EMG + muscle edema on MRI + inflammatory biopsy is the inflammatory myopathy pattern — but the antibody result re-sorts the patient into diseases with different organs at risk and different first moves.

The entities on this page:

Entity Pattern clue Organ risks that change management Dermatomyositis (DM) Heliotrope rash, Gottron papules/sign, shawl/V-sign; proximal weakness ILD (esp. MDA5), malignancy (esp. TIF1-γ, NXP2), dysphagia Antisynthetase syndrome Myositis + ILD + arthritis + Raynaud + mechanic's hands + fever Chronic or rapidly progressive ILD Immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy (IMNM) Severe proximal weakness, CK often >10× ULN, pauci-inflammatory necrotizing biopsy Anti-HMGCR (statin-associated), anti-SRP (severe, bulbar/respiratory) Polymyositis (PM) A diagnosis of exclusion Before escalating "refractory PM," reconsider antisynthetase syndrome, IMNM, IBM, and noninflammatory mimics Inclusion body myositis (IBM) Age ≥45, ≥12 months of slowly progressive finger-flexor + quadriceps weakness, dysphagia No effective immunotherapy — exercise and supportive care are the treatment

docs.title: The myositis antibody panel — what changes the plan
docs.text:
Order an expanded myositis-specific/myositis-associated antibody panel, but confirm anti-HMGCR is included or order it separately — some panels omit it. Include Ro52, PM/Scl, Ku, and U1-RNP for overlap disease.

Antibody Phenotype Risk that changes management Anti-MDA5 Amyopathic/hypomyopathic DM Rapidly progressive ILD — highest-risk serology; pulmonary assessment in parallel, not after send-outs return Anti-TIF1-γ DM Malignancy — strongest cancer association; full 2023 IMACS clinical-serologic cancer screening Anti-NXP2 DM Malignancy — strong cancer association Antisynthetase (Jo-1, PL-7, PL-12, EJ, KS) Myositis ± ILD, arthritis, Raynaud High ILD burden, including lung-dominant non–Jo-1 phenotypes Anti-OJ Antisynthetase Notable line-blot blind spot — reference-lab immunoprecipitation may be needed Anti-HMGCR IMNM, often statin-exposed Early IVIG for moderate–severe disease Anti-SRP IMNM, often severe Early rituximab; IVIG bridging for bulbar/respiratory disease Anti-Mi-2 Classic DM More treatment-responsive phenotype Anti-SAE DM Prominent dysphagia/skin disease Anti-cN1A (NT5c1A) IBM Supportive only — ~30–76% sensitive, >90–95% specific vs muscle disease, but positive in Sjögren (~36%), SLE (~20%), DM, IMNM; negative does not exclude IBM

Assay cautions: do not rely on a commercial line blot alone when the phenotype and the result disagree. For high-risk serologies (MDA5, TIF1-γ), pulmonary and cancer assessment proceed in parallel with send-out testing.

docs.title: Rapid approach
docs.text:
1. Sort emergent from routine on the first contact — respiratory symptoms, dysphagia with aspiration, or myoglobinuria are admit-now problems; a slowly progressive proximal weakness with a CK of 800 is a workup-in-clinic problem. Rapidly progressive ILD gets combination immunosuppression in days (below), not a months-long ladder.
  2. Establish the inflammatory-myopathy pattern — CK, aldolase, myopathic EMG (fibrillations, small polyphasic units), muscle MRI (edema vs fatty replacement), and muscle biopsy with immunostaining. Biopsy distinguishes DM (perifascicular atrophy), IMNM (necrosis, sparse inflammation), and IBM (rimmed vacuoles, protein aggregates — but see the 2024 ENMC update below).
  3. Send the antibody panel and risk-stratify by result — MDA5 → lungs now; TIF1-γ/NXP2 → cancer screening now; HMGCR/SRP → IMNM induction now; cN1A → supports IBM but never decides it.
  4. Treat the phenotype, not the CK — CK improvement alone is not remission; persistent weakness may be damage, steroid myopathy, or deconditioning. Reassess the diagnosis (MRI, repeat biopsy review) before escalating immunosuppression for a CK that will not normalize.

docs.title: The prescriptive flow (what I want done, in order)
docs.text:
1. Confirm pattern + exclude mimics — exam, CK, EMG/NCS, muscle MRI, biopsy; TSH, statin/drug review, and (once) the expanded antibody panel.
  2. Phenotype by antibody and organ involvement — lung (PFTs + HRCT for MDA5, antisynthetase, or any dyspnea), cancer screen (TIF1-γ/NXP2 per IMACS), swallow screen (dysphagia in any myopathy).
  3. Start the disease-specific induction below — IMNM gets early combination; DM/PM gets steroids + an early steroid-sparing agent; IBM gets exercise and supportive care, not immunosuppression.
  4. Reassess on a clock, not on hope — no convincing improvement by ~4–6 weeks on adequate therapy means reconsider the diagnosis and optimize combination treatment, not more months of the same.
  5. Run the monitoring and prophylaxis ordersets in parallel — PJP prophylaxis, HBV screening before rituximab, vaccine review, bone health, and rehab from day one.

docs.title: Workup
docs.text:
Myopathy workup — order as a set

  • CK, aldolase, AST/ALT (muscle source — check GGT when assessing liver), creatinine, TSH, ESR/CRP.
  • Expanded myositis antibody panel — confirm anti-HMGCR included; add Ro52, PM/Scl, Ku, U1-RNP. If phenotype–result mismatch, send reference-lab immunoprecipitation (OJ and other line-blot blind spots).
  • EMG/NCS — myopathic pattern; in IBM expect mixed short-duration and large long-duration units (can mimic neurogenic disease — do not mislabel).
  • Muscle MRI — edema (active inflammation) vs fatty replacement (damage); in IBM, distal quadriceps "melted" appearance, anterior > posterior thigh; guides biopsy site.
  • Muscle biopsy with immunostaining — DM: perifascicular atrophy, MAC deposition; IMNM: necrosis with sparse inflammation, MAC on non-necrotic fibers; IBM: endomysial CD8⁺ invasion, rimmed vacuoles, p62/TDP-43 aggregates (but only 43% show all three classic findings — see 2024 ENMC).
  • Lung: PFTs + HRCT chest for anti-MDA5, antisynthetase antibodies, or any dyspnea/cough — do not wait for the antibody panel if RP-ILD is suspected.
  • Cancer screening for adult DM (TIF1-γ/NXP2 highest risk) per the 2023 IMACS clinical-serologic framework — age- and symptom-appropriate screening at minimum.
  • Swallow screen in every myopathy patient with bulbar symptoms → videofluoroscopy/FEES if abnormal.

Avoid

  • Do not label an inflammatory biopsy "polymyositis" without reconciling it with the clinical pattern. The classic IBM trap — immunosuppression will not help and steroids may worsen weakness.
  • Do not chase the CK. Escalating immunosuppression for a persistently elevated CK without active weakness risks toxicity without benefit — distinguish active myonecrosis from fatty replacement, steroid myopathy, and deconditioning first.
  • Do not use methotrexate as an ILD treatment. With active ILD, mycophenolate, tacrolimus, or rituximab is the choice; methotrexate treats muscle/skin, not lung.

docs.title: Immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy (IMNM)
docs.text:
IMNM is the myopathy where early combination therapy beats prolonged steroid monotherapy. Anti-HMGCR (often statin-exposed — stopping the statin does not treat the disease) and anti-SRP (often severe, bulbar/respiratory involvement) drive different first moves.

Step 1 — IMNM induction (start here)

  • Prednisone 1 mg/kg/day PO (or methylprednisolone 500–1,000 mg IV daily ×3 days for severe/rapidly progressive weakness, significant dysphagia, or respiratory-muscle involvement, then ~1 mg/kg/day PO).
  • Do not linger on steroid monotherapy — the second agent starts with induction, not after steroids fail. Reassess every 2–4 weeks; no convincing improvement by ~4–6 weeks means reconsider the diagnosis and optimize combination treatment.

Step 2a — anti-HMGCR IMNM (moderate–severe: IVIG early)

  • IVIG 2 g/kg per cycle, divided over 2–5 days (e.g. 1 g/kg/day ×2 days or 0.4 g/kg/day ×5 days), every 4 weeks — prioritize early for moderate–severe disease, alongside steroids.
  • Add a conventional agent for maintenance: methotrexate 15 mg PO/SC weekly (titrate to 20–25 mg weekly) + folic acid 1 mg PO daily, or mycophenolate mofetil 500 mg PO BID (titrate to 1,000–1,500 mg BID), or azathioprine 50 mg PO daily (titrate toward 2–3 mg/kg/day; check TPMT/NUDT15 before full dose).
  • After ~2–3 monthly IVIG cycles plus a conventional agent with still-active disease, consider rituximab 1,000 mg IV ×2, two weeks apart (or 375 mg/m² weekly ×4).

Step 2b — anti-SRP IMNM (severe: rituximab early)

  • Rituximab 1,000 mg IV ×2, two weeks apart (or 375 mg/m² weekly ×4) — favored early in severe anti-SRP disease.
  • IVIG 2 g/kg per cycle (as above) for rapid bridging when bulbar or respiratory disease cannot wait for rituximab's 8–12-week onset.
  • Steroid backbone as in Step 1; assess emerging rituximab response around 8–12 weeks while bridging.

IMNM monitoring and prophylaxis

  • PJP prophylaxis when prednisone ≥20 mg/day is expected for ≥4 weeks, especially with a second immunosuppressant: TMP-SMX 80/400 mg PO daily or 160/800 mg PO three times weekly (renal adjustment; avoid casually combining with methotrexate — marrow toxicity) or atovaquone 1,500 mg PO daily with food.
  • HBV screening (HBsAg, anti-HBc) before rituximab; prophylaxis/specialist management if indicated; baseline immunoglobulins, CBC.
  • Conventional-agent labs: CBC with differential, AST/ALT, creatinine at baseline and ~every 2–4 weeks during titration, then every 8–12 weeks when stable.
  • IVIG: renal function, volume tolerance, thrombotic and hemolysis risk each cycle.

docs.title: Dermatomyositis / polymyositis — the treatment ladder
docs.text:
Glucocorticoids plus an early steroid-sparing agent, with IVIG introduced early for severe muscle or bulbar disease — not after multiple drug failures. Most sequencing recommendations remain low-certainty evidence and expert consensus. "Polymyositis" is a diagnosis of exclusion (see above).

2026 update — brepocitinib (Lisraya) for adult DM

FDA prescribing information, August 2026: adult DM, 30 mg orally daily, with pretreatment infection/laboratory/pregnancy/vaccine review.

Brepocitinib (Lisraya) was FDA-approved on August 27, 2026, for adult dermatomyositis at 30 mg PO once daily — the first new oral DM therapy in this space. Phase 3 (n=241): mean week-52 Total Improvement Score 46.5 vs 31.2 placebo; skin, functional, and steroid-sparing outcomes favored 30 mg; serious infections ~10% vs 1%. Do not combine with another JAK/TYK2 inhibitor or a biologic DMARD such as rituximab (label recommends against). The 15-mg dose is not an approved maintenance dose. Boxed warning: serious infection, malignancy, major cardiovascular events, thrombosis, mortality. Do not initiate (or interrupt) with ANC <1,000/mm³, ALC <500/mm³, or hemoglobin <8 g/dL; not recommended with eGFR <30 or Child-Pugh C; include GGT (AST/ALT may be muscle); lipids ~12 weeks after initiation. Its place relative to methotrexate, mycophenolate, IVIG, and rituximab is not yet established by head-to-head trials — and the indication does not extend to polymyositis or rapidly progressive ILD. Verify at the TRICARE Formulary Search before prescribing — new approvals lag formulary updates.

Step 1 — DM/PM induction (muscle-dominant disease)

  • Prednisone 0.5–1 mg/kg PO daily (usually 40–60 mg/day; higher end for substantial weakness or systemic disease). Maintain the initial dose until a clear response (~4–6 weeks), then taper. Severe/rapid disease: methylprednisolone 500–1,000 mg IV daily ×3 days → ~1 mg/kg/day PO.
  • Plus one steroid-sparing agent from day one:
    • Methotrexate 10–15 mg PO/SC once weekly → +2.5–5 mg every 2–4 weeks toward 20–25 mg weekly + folic acid 1 mg PO daily (good for muscle and skin; weekly — not daily; not an ILD treatment), or
    • Azathioprine 50 mg PO daily → toward 2–3 mg/kg/day (TPMT/NUDT15 first; slower onset), or
    • Mycophenolate mofetil 500 mg PO BID → 1,000–1,500 mg BID over 2–4 weeks (target 2–3 g/day; preferred with cutaneous disease or any ILD).
  • Measure: MMT-8, reproducible functional tasks, CDASI for skin, CK — CK alone is not remission, and persistent weakness may be damage.

Step 2 — when to add IVIG (escalate on a clock)

  • Escalate at presentation with aspiration-risk dysphagia, respiratory-muscle weakness, rapidly declining ambulation, or organ-threatening disease: hospital-level assessment, IV glucocorticoids, and early IVIG alongside the longer-acting strategy — do not require several oral-agent failures first.
  • ~4–6 weeks: no objective improvement or continued deterioration despite adequate glucocorticoids → confirm active disease, adherence, and diagnosis; add IVIG rather than waiting months for a slow oral agent.
  • ~8–12 weeks of an optimized conventional agent with persistent activity → optimize/switch the conventional agent or add IVIG/rituximab; in DM, consider brepocitinib (above).
  • IVIG regimen: 2 g/kg per cycle over 2–5 days (1 g/kg/day ×2 days or 0.4 g/kg/day ×5 days), every 4 weeks — 2 g/kg total per cycle, not per day. Assess over ~3–4 cycles (12–16 weeks) in stable disease; do not wait that long if deteriorating. Octagam 10% carries the US adult-DM indication (labeled max rate 0.04 mL/kg/min — do not generalize to other products); PM use is off-label with weaker evidence. ProDERM: 79% IVIG vs 44% placebo achieved ≥minimal improvement at week 16.

Step 3 — refractory disease (by phenotype, not a mandatory sequence)

  • Rituximab 1,000 mg IV on days 1 and 15 — guideline-supported refractory option; response more likely with anti-Jo-1, anti-Mi-2, anti-SRP or antisynthetase syndrome. Caveat: the RIM trial did not meet its randomized primary endpoint — do not present it as placebo-controlled proof of efficacy.
  • Tacrolimus ~0.075 mg/kg/day PO divided BID, trough 5–10 ng/mL (ACR/CHEST framework) — useful with ILD; monitor trough, creatinine, K⁺/Mg²⁺, BP (1–2× weekly the first month).
  • Cyclophosphamide 500–750 mg/m² IV every 4 weeks — for severe/refractory disease; CBC, creatinine, urinalysis before; CBC ~10–14 days post-dose; fertility, bladder toxicity, cumulative exposure counseling.
  • Tofacitinib 5 mg PO BID (off-label) — specialist option, particularly with ILD; TB/hepatitis screening, lipids, CV/VTE/malignancy assessment.
  • Abatacept 125 mg SC weekly — the 2025 phase 3 failed its primary (56.0% vs 42.5%, P=0.083); selective use only, not ahead of IVIG/rituximab.
  • Skin-predominant DM: photoprotection + topical corticosteroids/calcineurin inhibitors; hydroxychloroquine 200–400 mg/day (retinal screening) for cutaneous disease — it is not a treatment for muscle inflammation or ILD. Refractory skin disease: methotrexate/mycophenolate, IVIG, or brepocitinib.

Steroid taper and maintenance (practice-based)

  • Begin tapering once strength/function and organ activity are clearly improving (~4–6 weeks): >20 mg/day: −5–10 mg every 1–2 weeks; 20→10 mg/day: −2.5 mg every 2–4 weeks; <10 mg/day: −1 mg every 2–4 weeks. Pause for documented relapse; distinguish relapse from withdrawal or adrenal insufficiency.
  • Continue the conventional agent dose that achieved control; consider cautious reduction only after ~12–24 months of sustained inactive disease, ideally off steroids. After control on IVIG: 1 g/kg every 4 weeks or lengthen toward 6–8 weeks — one change at a time. Rituximab: repeat ~every 24 weeks when needed, individualized. Post-cyclophosphamide: transition to mycophenolate or azathioprine.

docs.title: Myositis-associated interstitial lung disease
docs.text:
ILD is a separate treatment pathway, titrated to lung severity — not a footnote to the muscle ladder. The two avoidable errors: treating irreversible weakness as persistent inflammation, and applying a months-long muscle schedule to rapidly worsening ILD. The 2023 ACR/CHEST SARD-ILD guideline and the 2026 ERS/EULAR CTD-ILD guideline both support immunosuppression and combination treatment including glucocorticoids for IIM-ILD (very-low-certainty evidence for much of it).

Myositis-ILD, clinically active but not rapidly progressive

  • Prednisone ~0.5–1 mg/kg/day PO as a short-term bridge plus mycophenolate mofetil 1–1.5 g PO BID — generally the preferred first-line ILD immunosuppressant in ACR/CHEST guidance.
  • Alternatives by phenotype/tolerability: azathioprine 2–3 mg/kg/day, tacrolimus ~0.075 mg/kg/day divided BID (trough 5–10 ng/mL), rituximab 1,000 mg IV days 1 and 15, or cyclophosphamide 500–750 mg/m² IV q4w.
  • Systemic-sclerosis overlap: high-dose steroids may precipitate renal crisis — do not apply the routine high-dose myositis approach.
  • Escalate on confirmed progression at any time: new/rising O₂ requirement, worsening dyspnea or exertional desaturation, increasing ILD on HRCT, or reproducible PFT decline. First exclude infection, aspiration, PE, heart failure, pulmonary hypertension, anemia, and respiratory-muscle weakness. Progressive pulmonary fibrosis criteria: 2 of 3 domains worsening within a year without another explanation.
  • If ILD progresses on adequately dosed mycophenolate: add or switch to rituximab, cyclophosphamide, or tacrolimus (more aggressive disease); tofacitinib 5 mg PO BID is a specialist option. IVIG 2 g/kg over 2–5 days may be added when severe muscle/bulbar disease coexists or infection concerns limit further immunosuppression. Prolonged high-dose glucocorticoids are not the strategy for ongoing progression.
  • RECITAL (severe/progressive CTD-ILD including myositis): rituximab 1 g at weeks 0 and 2 vs cyclophosphamide 600 mg/m² q4w ×6 — both improved FVC; rituximab not superior, but supported as an alternative.
  • Progressive fibrotic ILD despite management: nintedanib 150 mg PO BID with food (reduce to 100 mg BID for intolerance) — slows fibrotic progression; it does not replace immunosuppression for active disease and is not treatment for acute RP-ILD. LFTs monthly ×3, then ~every 3 months; watch diarrhea, weight loss, bleeding risk.
  • Monitor: PFTs every 3–6 months early, every 6–12 months when stable; repeat HRCT at ~3–6 months in IIM-ILD (2026 ERS/EULAR), earlier if progression is suspected.

Rapidly progressive ILD — especially anti-MDA5 (inpatient emergency)

  • This is a multidisciplinary inpatient emergency. Progression from baseline O₂ to high-flow or ventilation over days to weeks triggers urgent treatment and transplant-center consideration — do not wait for the complete antibody panel when the phenotype suggests myositis-associated RP-ILD.
  • Methylprednisolone 500–1,000 mg IV daily ×3 days, then prednisone ~1 mg/kg/day PO, individualized to response and complications.
  • Add two additional agents for confirmed or suspected anti-MDA5 RP-ILD (one or two for other RP-ILD phenotypes) — "triple therapy" means glucocorticoid plus two agents:
    • Rituximab 1,000 mg IV days 1 and 15, and/or
    • Tacrolimus ~0.075 mg/kg/day divided BID (trough 5–10 ng/mL), and/or
    • Cyclophosphamide 500–750 mg/m² IV q4w (intensified anti-MDA5 schedules need specialist protocols), and/or
    • IVIG 2 g/kg over 2–5 days (severe muscle/bulbar disease or infection concerns).
  • Reasonable expert-center combinations: steroid + rituximab + tacrolimus, or classical steroid + tacrolimus + cyclophosphamide. ACR/CHEST conditionally favored rituximab over cyclophosphamide for anti-MDA5 RP-ILD — but no single combination is established as universally superior, and a multicenter cohort (Clin Exp Rheumatol 2024) did not reproduce the historical Japanese triple-therapy survival benefit (higher mortality in the triple group). Treat true RP-ILD with early combination and individualized selection — not automatic cyclophosphamide triple for every MDA5-positive patient.
  • JAK inhibitors: tofacitinib 5 mg BID is a legitimate specialist option (a 515-patient 2025 cohort linked it to better 1-year transplant-free survival than CNIs, clearest in less severe/non-RP disease) — not established standalone rescue for fulminant RP-ILD. A 2026 matched JAKi-plus-CNI study showed no overall survival advantage; do not stack immunosuppressants indiscriminately.
  • Reassess same-day for rising O₂/ventilator needs or worsening imaging: disease activity vs infection, drug exposure, and whether to change the combination. Plasma exchange is salvage for refractory disease, not routine first-line — schedule it around rituximab/IVIG (it removes them). ECMO is an individualized bridge, usually tied to transplant planning.

docs.title: Inclusion body myositis (IBM)
docs.text:
As of October 2026, IBM remains a clinical–pathological diagnosis without an approved, established disease-modifying drug. The major diagnostic update is the 2024 ENMC framework, which formally incorporates muscle imaging and anti-cN1A antibodies. Treatment is rehabilitation, independence, and swallowing/respiratory management — not the immunosuppressive ladder used above.

IBM diagnosis — the 2024 ENMC framework

  • Common presentation: onset ≥45 years, progressive weakness for ≥12 months, CK ≤15× ULN, and deep finger-flexor and/or knee-extensor weakness. Uncommon presentations (younger, shorter duration, higher CK, atypical distribution) need stronger corroboration, not automatic exclusion.
  • Mandatory investigation: muscle biopsy showing necrotic fibers with endomysial lymphocytes surrounding non-necrotic fibers, with or without invasion. Rimmed vacuoles are not universally required — vacuoles and protein aggregates are one supportive category, not two.
  • Four supportive findings: (1) anti-cN1A; (2) rimmed vacuoles and/or cytoplasmic protein aggregates (p62/TDP-43); (3) mitochondrial abnormalities exceeding age expectations; (4) typical MRI and/or muscle-ultrasound pattern. Common presentation with both characteristic groups → biopsy finding alone; one group → biopsy + ≥1 supportive; uncommon → biopsy + ≥2 supportive. Imaging and antibodies do not replace biopsy.
  • Practical traps: a nondiagnostic biopsy does not settle it — sampling fatty-replaced muscle is uninformative; reconsider muscle selection, get expert review, repeat if it changes management or trial eligibility. EMG can mimic neurogenic disease. Atypical or rapid course → reconsider mimics (other IIM, muscular dystrophies, myofibrillar/multisystem proteinopathies, neurogenic disease).
  • Anti-cN1A use: supportive, not a verdict — negative does not exclude, positive does not establish. Most useful when an additional supportive finding resolves an incomplete picture. Confirm the panel actually includes cN1A; assay performance varies (ELISA ~30–50% sensitive). Do not use serial titers to monitor — follow function, swallowing, nutrition, and respiratory performance.

IBM — what not to do

  • Do not treat IBM with chronic immunosuppression. Steroids, methotrexate (failed to preserve strength/function in an RCT despite lowering CK), azathioprine, and other conventional agents have no convincing sustained benefit — and steroids may worsen weakness. Do not escalate merely because CK stays up or the biopsy is inflammatory.
  • Do not promise IVIG for limb weakness. No established disease-modifying effect; small studies suggest possible short-term swallowing benefit in selected patients — insufficient for routine treatment or aspiration-prevention claims. A carefully defined, time-limited trial for substantial objectively documented dysphagia may be considered by an IBM specialist (specify the functional outcome that justifies continuing; subjective improvement alone is not a reason for indefinite IVIG).
  • Failed/investigational agents to know by name: bimagrumab (RESILIENT, 251 patients, failed 6-minute walk), arimoclomol (failed IBMFRS over 20 months), ulviprubart/ABC008 (272-patient MUSCLE phase 2/3 failed IBMFRS at week 76 — investigational), sirolimus (44-patient trial missed primary knee-extension endpoint; secondary signals only), pioglitazone (2026 single-arm, no clinical improvement). Refer to a neuromuscular center for trial eligibility — not for unproven off-label combinations.

IBM — exercise and rehabilitation (the actual treatment)

  • Individualized exercise is generally safe and the only intervention consistently showing benefit — it improves conditioning and preserves selected muscle performance, but has not been proven to arrest IBM or change its natural history.
  • Starting framework (adapt with a neuromuscular physical therapist): aerobic ~3 days/week — start 10–15 minutes, build toward 20–30 minutes, recumbent cycling, conversational moderate effort; resistance ~2 nonconsecutive days/week — light-to-moderate, individualized repetitions, focus on residual strength, avoid failure, assisted/gravity-reduced for very weak muscles; range of motion + safe transfer practice, task adaptation, balance training. Increase one variable at a time; back off for prolonged pain, excessive fatigue, or worse next-day function. A transient post-exercise CK rise without strength loss does not require stopping.
  • Target what limits independence: knee buckling, unsafe chair/toilet transfers, foot drop, grip weakness, fatigue — walking aids/orthoses, raised seating, bathroom adaptations, assistive utensils, powered mobility. Hand weakness affects walker/wheelchair selection; assess functionally.
  • Blood-flow-restriction training is not routine care — limited evidence, trained supervision and vascular assessment only.

IBM — swallowing, respiratory, and follow-up

  • Swallowing: screen actively every visit (food/pills sticking, repeated swallows, coughing during meals, prolonged mealtimes, texture avoidance, weight loss) — low threshold for speech-language pathology; videofluoroscopy for bolus transit/upper-esophageal-sphincter dysfunction, FEES complementary. Manage by physiology: compensatory strategies, texture/posture/bolus adjustments, dietitian; cricopharyngeal dilation or myotomy for selected obstructive components; enteral nutrition when oral intake is unsafe or insufficient — before an emergency (a tube does not eliminate aspiration of secretions/reflux, and no IBM-specific survival benefit is established).
  • Respiratory: underrecognized and does not track limb weakness. Ask orthopnea, morning headache, unrefreshing sleep, daytime somnolence, weak cough, recurrent infections. Seated vital capacity + supine VC, inspiratory/expiratory pressures or SNIP, peak cough flow ~every 6 months individualized; overnight testing when hypoventilation is suspected (normal daytime O₂ does not establish adequate ventilation); NIV for documented nocturnal hypoventilation or chronic failure plus an airway-clearance plan.
  • Follow-up: neuromuscular every 3–6 months — IBMFRS (0–40), bilateral finger-flexor/knee-extensor strength (quantitative when available), falls/mobility/aid suitability, weight and nutrition. Do not use serial CK or anti-cN1A titers as treatment targets; repeat EMG/MRI/biopsy only for a new diagnostic question, an unexpected course, or research.
  • Prognosis counseling: years-to-decades course; wheelchair commonly necessary ~10–15 years after onset (wide range — not an individual deadline); aspiration-related respiratory disease, respiratory-muscle weakness, malnutrition, and disability complications are the major preventable threats. No enhanced malignancy screening — no clear excess cancer risk; continue age-appropriate screening.
  • Red-flag return: new inability to maintain nutrition/hydration, recurrent aspiration, orthopnea or resting dyspnea, ineffective cough during infection, unexpectedly rapid weakness — sudden deterioration warrants a search for a superimposed problem, not automatic attribution to IBM.

TRICARE — verified rules and the current form

Lisraya 30 mg is flagged for pharmacy PA and nonformulary status in the October files. IVIG, biologics, gene/enzyme therapy and home infusions need exact product/indication/benefit review. Current manual specialty criteria were not obtained; record diagnostic evidence, prior treatment and safety testing, and obtain the current form.

Current PA/MN details, benefit routing and packet · Live Formulary Search. Check the exact product, beneficiary and venue on the prescribing date.

docs.title: Rhabdomyolysis, toxic, critical-illness and metabolic myopathy
docs.text:
The non-inflammatory myopathies that most often reach a military neurologist — and the first one is an occupational disease of initial-entry training.

Exertional rhabdomyolysis — the trainee with dark urine

  • Recognize it: muscle pain, swelling and weakness out of proportion to the workout, often after unaccustomed eccentric exercise, heat, dehydration or a new PT program; tea-colored urine with a heme-positive dipstick but few RBCs on microscopy.
  • Labs now: CK, BMP (potassium, creatinine), calcium, phosphate, uric acid, LFTs, urinalysis with microscopy; ECG if potassium is high. Check core temperature and sickle cell trait status — exertional heat illness changes the disposition.
  • Fluids: isotonic crystalloid titrated to a urine output of roughly 200–300 mL/h until CK is clearly falling and the urine clears; watch for volume overload once AKI is established. Bicarbonate and mannitol have no proven benefit.
  • Admit for AKI, hyperkalemia, CK rising on fluids, inability to take oral fluids, heat illness, or compartment syndrome (pain on passive stretch, tense compartment — surgical consult for pressures and fasciotomy).
  • CHAMP/USU 2025 high-risk screen: CK ≥20,000 IU/L, possible compartment syndrome, McMahon score ≥6, AKI, dark urine/myoglobinuria, metabolic abnormalities, sickle cell trait, or unreliable follow-up prompt a higher level of care/inpatient consideration. Low-risk patients who can hydrate and reliably return may be managed with restricted activity and repeat assessment/labs in 24–72 hours. Diagnostic CK ≥5,000 alone is not an automatic admission threshold.
  • No NSAIDs until renal function is known to be normal; no further exertion until cleared.
  • Return to duty: follow the DoD CHAMP/USU clinical practice guideline for exertional rhabdomyolysis, which stratifies low vs high risk and sets a phased return. High-risk features include AKI, delayed recovery, a recurrent episode, rhabdomyolysis after minimal exertion, exertional heat illness, sickle cell trait, or a personal or family history of rhabdomyolysis or malignant hyperthermia → look for an underlying myopathy (below) before full duty.

Recurrent or unexplained rhabdomyolysis — find the metabolic myopathy

  • Triggers for workup: recurrent episodes, rhabdomyolysis after trivial exertion, fasting or fever, exercise intolerance with cramps or a second wind, CK persistently raised between episodes, or a family history.
  • Order: acylcarnitine profile, free and total carnitine, urine organic acids, and a metabolic myopathy / rhabdomyolysis gene panel that includes PYGM (McArdle), CPT2, RYR1 and the fatty-acid-oxidation genes. Biopsy and forearm exercise testing are now second-line to genetics.
  • The usual answers: CPT2 deficiency (episodes with prolonged exercise, fasting or fever; normal CK between) and McArdle disease (cramps and contractures in the first minutes of exercise; second-wind phenomenon). RYR1 variants link exertional rhabdomyolysis, exertional heat illness and malignant hyperthermia susceptibility — flag the anesthesia record.

Statin, steroid, critical-illness and periodic paralysis

  • Statin myopathy: myalgia with normal or mildly raised CK resolves within weeks of stopping the statin. Persistent/progressive weakness or marked CK elevation after stopping warrants evaluation for anti-HMGCR IMNM and other causes — see IMNM.
  • Steroid myopathy: proximal, hip-flexor-first weakness with a normal CK after weeks of glucocorticoids. The trap is reading it as a myositis relapse and raising the dose — normal CK with rising steroid exposure supports this possibility, but does not exclude active inflammatory disease. Reassess strength, imaging, and the clinical pattern before adjusting immunotherapy; taper glucocorticoids safely.
  • Critical illness myopathy: flaccid, often proximal weakness and failure to wean after sepsis, high-dose steroids or neuromuscular blockade; CK normal or mildly raised; sensation spared (unlike critical illness polyneuropathy). NCS show low CMAP amplitude with prolonged CMAP duration; direct muscle stimulation separates myopathy from neuropathy. Treat sepsis, control glucose, minimize steroids and NMBAs, mobilize early; recovery over weeks to months is usual.
  • Hypokalemic / thyrotoxic periodic paralysis: episodic flaccid weakness in a young man, often after a carbohydrate load or rest after exercise, with low K⁺ during the attack. Replete cautiously — oral when possible, IV no faster than 10 mEq/h, on a cardiac monitor — rebound hyperkalemia is common as potassium shifts back. Check TSH and free T4: thyrotoxic periodic paralysis also responds to propranolol while the thyrotoxicosis is treated.

docs.title: Disposition
docs.text:
• Inflammatory myopathy (DM/PM/IMNM/antisynthetase): rheumatology–neurology co-management; visits every 2–4 weeks during induction, spacing as disease stabilizes. PFTs every 3–6 months early when ILD is present. Admit for rapidly progressive ILD, aspiration-risk dysphagia, rhabdomyolysis with AKI risk, or respiratory-muscle weakness.
  • IBM: neuromuscular clinic every 3–6 months with PT/OT, speech-language pathology, dietitian, and pulmonary as indicated. Most care is outpatient and supportive — the interventions that matter are swallowing surveillance, NIV timing, falls prevention, and equipment.
  • Goals-of-care: in IBM, advance directives and feeding-tube preferences before a crisis; in severe inflammatory disease with ILD, transplant candidacy and ceilings of care discussed early.

Military medicine — duty, retention and deployment

  • Profile / function: Record objective strength, exertional tolerance, CK trajectory, organ injury and recovery. After exertional rhabdomyolysis use a graded return plan and recurrence/heat-risk assessment.
  • Retention / MEB–MAR2: Apply the diagnosed inflammatory, dystrophic, metabolic or exertional condition’s standard; a high CK alone does not decide permanent retention. Use the retention framework; permanent P3/4 does not by itself select DES versus MAR2.
  • Deployment / medications: CENTCOM history of heat stroke/rhabdomyolysis requires specific waiver review. Immunosuppression, injectables and monitoring are separate issues from the muscle diagnosis. See the disease AND drug screen for the current CENTCOM rules and waiver packet.
  • Special duty: flight, diving and other special assignments have separate standards and waiver authorities; a general duty profile does not clear them.
  • LOD / EPTS: document onset, duty status, exposures and aggravation objectively. The designated authority determines LOD/EPTS; neither in-service diagnosis nor a genetic finding settles it automatically.

docs.title: 📚 Discover — evidence brief
docs.text:
Written from primary guidelines and trials; source articles are a reading list, not copied.

  • Brepocitinib is the first genuinely new thing in the DM cabinet in years. Approved August 27, 2026, for adult dermatomyositis on a 241-patient phase 3 (week-52 Total Improvement Score 46.5 vs 31.2 placebo), it is a TYK2/JAK1 inhibitor dosed 30 mg daily — but the serious-infection signal (~10% vs 1%) and the boxed warning mean it is a selected-refractory option, not a first-line swap, and its place versus IVIG and rituximab awaits head-to-head data.
  • The 2024 ENMC IBM framework ends the rimmed-vacuole absolutism. Vacuoles and protein aggregates are now one supportive category among four, imaging and anti-cN1A are formally incorporated, and the criteria acknowledge what clinicians knew: only 43% of IBM biopsies in a 335-patient cohort showed all three classic findings. Biopsy is still mandatory — antibodies and MRI support, they do not replace.
  • The IBM drug pipeline keeps failing, and that is the point of the page. Bimagrumab (RESILIENT, n=251), arimoclomol, and now ulviprubart/ABC008 (MUSCLE, n=272, failed IBMFRS at week 76) all missed their primaries. Exercise remains the only active therapy with consistent benefit — which is why the IBM section is a rehab prescription, not a drug ladder.
  • RP-ILD rewards speed and punishes ritual. The 2023 ACR/CHEST guideline conditionally favors rituximab over cyclophosphamide for anti-MDA5 RP-ILD, but a multicenter cohort (Clin Exp Rheumatol 2024) failed to reproduce the historical Japanese triple-therapy survival benefit — the lesson is early individualized combination, not automatic cyclophosphamide triple for every MDA5-positive patient.
  • "Polymyositis" is now a diagnosis of exclusion on this page — before escalating apparently refractory PM, the framework forces reconsideration of antisynthetase syndrome, IMNM, IBM, and mimics. Several "refractory PM" cases in the literature were IBM all along.

Key sources: Allenbach & Benveniste, Inflammatory Myopathies (NEJM 2026); 2023 ACR/CHEST SARD-ILD guideline (Johnson et al., Arthritis Care Res 2024); 2026 ERS/EULAR CTD-ILD guideline (Antoniou et al., Eur Respir J 2026); BSR IIM guideline (Oldroyd et al., Rheumatology 2022); ProDERM (Aggarwal et al., NEJM 2022); RIM rituximab trial (Oddis et al., Arthritis Rheum 2012); RECITAL (Maher et al., Lancet Respir Med 2022); brepocitinib phase 3 (NEJM 2026) and DailyMed Lisraya label (Aug 2026); 272nd ENMC IBM workshop 2024; RESILIENT bimagrumab (Hanna et al., Lancet Neurol 2019); MUSCLE ulviprubart (Abcuro 2026); sirolimus (Benvéniste et al., Lancet Rheumatol 2020); MTX-vs-placebo in IBM (Badrising, Ann Neurol 2002); tofacitinib vs CNI in MDA5-ILD (Wu et al., Eur Respir J 2025).

docs.text:

  2. Oldroyd AGS, et al. British Society for Rheumatology guideline on management of paediatric, adolescent and adult patients with idiopathic inflammatory myopathy. Rheumatology (Oxford). 2022 — guideline-supported first-line and sequencing for DM/PM.
