docs.title: Coma — approach, workup & management
docs.text:
Last reviewed: November 2026

One-liner: an adult who cannot be roused — unresponsive to voice and to noxious stimulation, eyes closed, no purposeful movement. For the on-call neuro / ED / ICU provider: coma is a neurologic emergency, and the first hour decides the outcome — stabilize, reverse what is reversible, localize with the exam, and image before the cause declares itself.

🚩 Red flags — treat now, image as you go

Pattern Worry Do now Blown (unilateral fixed dilated) pupil, extensor posturing, Cushing response (hypertension + bradycardia + irregular breathing), rostral–caudal decline Uncal / transtentorial herniation, raised ICP Brain code: HOB 30–45°, neck midline, hyperosmolar therapy, brief hyperventilation as bridge, neurosurgery — see Step 2 Abrupt coma + abnormal ocular motility, quadriparesis, or extensor posturing with a relatively unrevealing CT Basilar artery occlusion CTA head/neck immediately — time-critical, potentially reversible; do not wait for MRI Fever + meningismus / seizure / immunocompromise / petechiae Bacterial meningitis or HSV encephalitis Blood cultures, then empiric antibiotics + dexamethasone (+ acyclovir if encephalitis possible) before CT or LP Subtle twitching (face/eyelids/limbs), gaze deviation, nystagmus, fluctuating exam, or coma that persists after a convulsion stops Nonconvulsive status epilepticus (NCSE) Urgent EEG / continuous EEG — NCSE occurs in 8–30% of unexplained altered mental status Ataxic (Biot) breathing, loss of cough/gag, progressive loss of brainstem reflexes Medullary failure / impending apnea Airway now; ICU; do not leave the bedside

docs.title: Diagnosis / classification
docs.text:
Coma is unarousable unresponsiveness: no eye opening, no command following, no purposeful movement, no intelligible speech. It localizes to either bilateral cerebral hemispheric dysfunction or dysfunction of the ascending reticular activating system (ARAS) in the diencephalon / upper brainstem. That single fact drives the whole exam: a focal or asymmetric finding points to a structural lesion; a symmetric exam with preserved brainstem reflexes points to a toxic-metabolic cause — with the exceptions listed in the pitfalls below.

The single most useful bedside rule: reactive pupils alongside otherwise absent brainstem reflexes strongly favor a toxic-metabolic cause. Structural brainstem damage usually takes out the pupillary reflex early.

docs.title: Score it — GCS and FOUR
docs.text:
Scale Components Range Use it for GCS Eyes 1–4, Verbal 1–5, Motor 1–6 3–15 Standard serial assessment, especially trauma. Limitations: does not test pupils, brainstem reflexes, eye movements, or respiratory drive; the verbal score is unusable once intubated. GCS 3–8 is the severe-impairment range that usually prompts airway and critical-care consideration. FOUR score Eye, Motor, Brainstem, Respiration — 0–4 each 0–16 Preferred in intubated and deeply comatose ICU patients and for brainstem evaluation; detects locked-in syndrome, which GCS misses. In ICU cohorts FOUR predicted mortality better than GCS; most patients with GCS 3 scored 1–8 on FOUR because brainstem function was preserved.

FOUR score in full (document it — or the GCS subscores plus brainstem reflexes — for every GCS 3T or deeply comatose patient):

Domain 4 3 2 1 0 Eye Eyelids open, tracking or blinking to command Eyelids open but not tracking Eyelids closed, open to loud voice Eyelids closed, open to pain Eyelids remain closed with pain Motor (upper limbs) Thumbs-up, fist, or peace sign Localizing to pain Flexion response to pain Extension response to pain No response, or generalized myoclonus status Brainstem Pupil and corneal reflexes present One pupil wide and fixed Pupil or corneal reflex absent Pupil and corneal reflex absent Absent pupil, corneal, and cough reflexes Respiration Not intubated, regular breathing Not intubated, Cheyne–Stokes Not intubated, irregular breathing Breathes above ventilator rate Breathes at ventilator rate, or apnea

docs.title: Rapid approach
docs.text:
1. ABCs before GCS — hypoxia and hypotension lower the score. Assess airway patency, respiratory pattern, SpO₂, ventilation, secretions, cough/gag. GCS ≤8 triggers an immediate airway assessment but is not by itself an absolute indication for intubation — intubate for inadequate oxygenation/ventilation, apnea or severe hypoventilation, loss of protective reflexes, inability to handle secretions, or progressive deterioration. A rapidly reversible cause (hypoglycemia, opioids) may make intubation avoidable. Document the neuro exam — especially pupils, eye position/movements, corneals, motor response and laterality — before paralytics or sedatives when feasible.
  2. Reverse the reversible, in parallel — finger-stick glucose, then dextrose if low; thiamine if at risk; naloxone if opioid respiratory depression. Do not give the old universal "coma cocktail" to everyone — use each intervention per bedside findings and risk factors.
  3. Localize with the P-E-M-B exam — Pupils → Eyes → Motor → Breathing/Brainstem (below). Pupils and eye movements carry the strongest localizing information; GCS quantifies severity, not anatomy.
  4. Image emergently — noncontrast head CT (± CTA) once stable for transport.
  5. Work the four immediately treatable categories in parallel — structural brain injury, nonconvulsive seizures/status, CNS infection/inflammation, toxic-metabolic causes — then escalate to EEG, MRI, and LP by the clock in the Workup section.

docs.title: The prescriptive flow (what I want done, in order)
docs.text:
1. Minutes 0–15: stabilize + reverse. ABCs, monitor, two IVs, core temperature, finger-stick glucose → dextrose if <~70 mg/dL (Step 1). Brief neuro exam before sedation/paralysis. Collateral history immediately (EMS, family, witnesses, records): last known well, onset/course, preceding headache/seizure/trauma, meds (anticoagulants, insulin, sedatives), substance exposures, epilepsy, diabetes, renal/hepatic disease, malignancy.
  2. Minutes 15–60: CT + first labs + treat the threat. Noncontrast head CT emergently; add CTA if basilar/large-vessel occlusion is plausible. Core labs and toxicology (below). Empiric antimicrobials immediately if infection is plausible — do not wait for CT or LP. Herniation signs → brain-code measures now.
  3. Hours 1–6: localize, then LP and EEG. Re-examine (P-E-M-B) and trend the FOUR score. LP once CT excludes mass effect and coagulopathy is corrected, if CNS infection/inflammation is suspected. Start EEG/cEEG if the cause is still unclear or there are subtle seizure signs.
  4. Hours 24–48: MRI + second-line labs + re-examine. MRI if still unexplained (sooner for suspected brainstem ischemia, encephalitis, PRES, diffuse axonal injury, or hypoxic injury). Do not label a persistently comatose patient "metabolic" or "postictal" without EEG + targeted MRI ± CSF.
  5. Day 3 and beyond: prognosticate multimodally, never from one exam. After cardiac arrest, formal prognostic assessment at ≥72 h, off sedation, normothermic. Consider brain-death evaluation only when the prerequisites in Step 3 are met.

docs.title: The clock
docs.text: Window Do 0–1 hour Core labs + toxicology; noncontrast CT (± CTA, ± C-spine imaging); empiric antimicrobials if infection possible 1–6 hours LP once CT excludes mass effect and coagulopathy is corrected; start EEG if cause still unclear or subtle seizure signs 24–48 hours MRI if still unexplained; second-line labs; re-examine. If CT is nondiagnostic, work a checklist: poisoning, infection, NCSE, endocrinopathy, and the rest of the toxic-metabolic panel

docs.title: Imaging — CT vs MRI vs CTA
docs.text:
Imaging — what, when, and why

  • Noncontrast head CT — obtain emergently. First-line in unexplained coma after stabilization. Rapidly identifies hemorrhage, mass effect/herniation, hydrocephalus, large infarction/edema, and most traumatic lesions. The 2024 ACR Appropriateness Criteria rate it "Usually Appropriate" as initial imaging when intracranial pathology or a focal deficit is suspected. Also: chest X-ray, especially after intubation.
  • CTA head/neck — add immediately when basilar or other large-vessel occlusion is plausible (abrupt coma, abnormal ocular motility, quadriparesis, extensor posturing with a relatively unrevealing CT), or when arterial occlusion, aneurysmal SAH, dissection, or cerebral venous sinus thrombosis is suspected. Basilar occlusion is time-critical and potentially reversible — do not wait for MRI. Consider CTV for venous thrombosis.
  • MRI brain — the key second-line test, when CT does not explain the exam or the suspected lesion is in the posterior fossa/brainstem. In one ICU cohort, adding MRI changed management in 76% of patients with acute disorders of consciousness, including a revised diagnosis in 20%. Get it within 24–48 hours for suspected stroke or encephalitis, as soon as the patient is stable; add gadolinium if infection, tumor, or inflammation is suspected. MRI first is reasonable in a stable patient with known malignancy, HIV, or endocarditis, or with suspected CNS infection/inflammation. After cardiac arrest, MRI is best on days 3–5 — DWI can be normal in the first 1–2 days. MRI finds what CT misses: encephalitis (e.g., HSV temporal-lobe involvement), PRES, hypoxic- ischemic injury, diffuse axonal injury and microbleeds, Wernicke encephalopathy, osmotic demyelination, and subtle SAH.
  • Do not delay treatment for imaging. In suspected meningitis/encephalitis, draw blood cultures and give empiric therapy before CT.

docs.title: EEG — for nonconvulsive status epilepticus
docs.text:
EEG — indications, duration, interpretation

  • Obtain urgent EEG / continuous EEG when: coma is unexplained after initial CT and labs; consciousness stays impaired after a clinical seizure or convulsive status; subtle repetitive phenomena (eyelid/facial twitching, nystagmus, gaze deviation, rhythmic limb movements, episodic posturing, fluctuating consciousness); acute cortical injury associated with seizures (ICH, SAH, ischemic stroke, TBI, encephalitis, cardiac arrest); unexplained episodic autonomic events; or treatment with anesthetic infusions for refractory status. ACNS recommends continuous EEG for suspected NCSE, started as soon as feasible.
  • Duration: at least 24 hours of monitoring is typical in comatose patients; consider ≥48 hours when the patient remains comatose, is sedated, or has periodic/epileptiform discharges. About 80–95% of patients ultimately found to have nonconvulsive seizures are detected in the first 24–48 hours, though seizures may appear later in comatose or sedated patients. If seizures are detected, continue cEEG until they have been controlled electrographically for at least 24 hours. The 2HELPS2B score from the first hour can shorten monitoring when early risk is low.
  • After cardiac arrest: AHA / Neurocritical Care Society recommend starting EEG as early as possible and continuing 72–120 hours if the patient does not wake. If continuous EEG is unavailable, do daily intermittent EEGs or transfer.
  • Interpretation: sedatives and antiseizure drugs affect the reading. EEG also aids diagnosis — triphasic waves suggest a metabolic cause; lateralized periodic discharges suggest a focal lesion. A 20–60-minute routine EEG can identify obvious NCSE, diffuse slowing, and triphasic morphology, but a negative routine EEG does not exclude NCSE.

docs.title: Lumbar puncture
docs.text:
LP — indications and safety

  • Indications: suspected meningitis or encephalitis (fever, meningismus, immunosuppression, or no other explanation); suspected SAH with a negative CT (>6 hours from onset); autoimmune or paraneoplastic encephalitis; carcinomatous meningitis; unexplained coma with MRI or EEG suggestive of encephalitis. In immunosuppressed patients, lower the threshold and broaden the testing.
  • Image before LP: a comatose patient meets criteria for CT first. Triggers include altered consciousness (ESCMID: GCS <10; UK: GCS ≤12), focal deficits, new seizure, papilledema, or abnormal posturing. Contraindications: brain shift or mass effect on CT, coagulopathy/thrombocytopenia (correct first), anticoagulation, skin infection at the puncture site.
  • Do not delay treatment for imaging: draw blood cultures, then give empiric antibiotics plus dexamethasone — and acyclovir if encephalitis is possible — before CT. Waiting for imaging is linked to worse outcomes.
  • CSF, at minimum: opening pressure, WBC with differential, RBC, protein, CSF glucose with simultaneous serum glucose, Gram stain, bacterial culture. Then phenotype-directed: HSV-1/2 PCR, VZV PCR, enterovirus PCR, cryptococcal antigen, fungal/mycobacterial studies, meningitis/encephalitis multiplex PCR where appropriate, oligoclonal bands / IgG index, autoimmune encephalitis antibodies, cytology / flow cytometry, xanthochromia. Save extra fluid frozen for later testing. A very early negative HSV PCR does not completely exclude HSV encephalitis — if clinical/MRI suspicion remains high, repeat CSF testing.

docs.title: Laboratory testing — tiered
docs.text: Tier Tests Timing / trigger Immediate (all patients) Point-of-care glucose; ABG/VBG with lactate; co-oximetry (CO, methemoglobin); CBC; CMP (Na, Ca, Mg, phosphate, BUN/Cr, LFTs); coagulation studies; ECG; troponin; pregnancy test On arrival Toxicology Serum ethanol, acetaminophen, salicylate, measured osmolality with osmolar gap, urine drug screen; levels of home medications (lithium, antiseizure drugs, baclofen) On arrival. Urine drug screens miss synthetic opioids and many benzodiazepines, and give false results — do not rely on a negative screen alone Hepatic / endocrine Ammonia, TSH ± free T4, cortisol Initial panel when the cause is unclear Infection Blood cultures, urinalysis + culture, chest X-ray; HIV, syphilis serology Before antibiotics if possible Second-line Thiamine level (draw before treatment, but never delay treatment), B12, CK, autoimmune/paraneoplastic antibodies in serum and CSF, heavy metals, expanded toxicology (LC-MS) When the first round of tests is unrevealing

docs.title: Pupils
docs.text:
Finding Suggests Small, reactive Metabolic cause (common); or bilateral pontine lesion Pinpoint (1–2 mm), reactive Pontine lesion, or opioid effect Midposition, fixed Midbrain lesion (or severe midbrain dysfunction) Dilated, fixed, unilateral Transtentorial (uncal) herniation or CN III lesion Dilated, fixed, bilateral Severe midbrain dysfunction or catastrophic anoxic injury Dilated, reactive Sympathetic response / mydriatic drug effect Symmetric, reactive pupils in deep coma Diffuse hemispheric dysfunction or toxic-metabolic cause Asymmetry or early loss of pupillary reactivity Structural (focal/brainstem) lesion Unequal, with ptosis and eye turned "down and out" CN III lesion — consider uncal herniation if acute Horner syndrome (miosis + ptosis + anhidrosis) Ipsilateral sympathetic interruption (hypothalamus → brainstem → cord) Light–near dissociation (reacts to near but not light) Dorsal midbrain (Parinaud) lesion Fixed midposition pupils with loss of all other brainstem reflexes Severe brainstem dysfunction or a toxic/metabolic mimic — urgent structural and toxicological evaluation; no favorable prognosis can be inferred from this finding alone

Pupil rule: reactive pupils + otherwise absent brainstem reflexes strongly favor a toxic-metabolic cause; asymmetric or early loss of pupillary reactivity favors structural disease. A single-point exam is not enough — trend the pupils with the FOUR score.

docs.title: Eye movements
docs.text: Finding Suggests Roving eye movements (slow, wandering, conjugate) Hemispheres impaired, brainstem intact — good sign in coma Ping-pong gaze (rapid horizontal oscillation) Bilateral hemispheric disease with intact brainstem Ocular bobbing (rapid downward, slow upward) Pontine lesion Ocular dipping (slow downward, rapid upward) Anoxic encephalopathy / diffuse cortical dysfunction Conjugate gaze toward the lesion side (eyes look toward the lesion) Acute frontal lobe lesion ("looks toward the lesion"); overcome by doll's-eyes (oculocephalic) maneuver Conjugate gaze away from the lesion Pontine lesion ("looks away"); cannot be overcome by doll's-eyes "Wrong-way" eyes (conjugate deviation toward the hemiparetic side, away from the hemispheric lesion) Thalamic hemorrhage Oculocephalic reflex (doll's eyes) intact Brainstem and vestibular pathways intact — a good prognostic sign Skew deviation (vertical misalignment) Brainstem lesion (commonly pontine) or cerebellar disease Internuclear ophthalmoplegia (adduction failure) MLF lesion (brainstem) Oculovestibular reflex (cold caloric) absent Vestibular nerve/brainstem pathway or midbrain/pons dysfunction Ocular movements absent Brainstem dysfunction — a marker for brain-death evaluation

docs.title: Motor responses
docs.text: Finding Suggests Symmetric withdrawal / localizing Intact motor pathways — a diffuse/toxic-metabolic cause Decorticate posturing (flexion) Lesion above the midbrain Decerebrate posturing (extension) Midbrain / upper pontine lesion — worse Asymmetric motor response (one side localizes, the other postures or is flaccid) Focal structural lesion — a hemispheric mass or unilateral injury Flaccid, no motor response Severe bilateral hemispheric, brainstem, or spinal cord injury; or the expected effect of sedatives/paralytics Extensor posturing that changes with stimulation Uncal herniation or acute structural shift Acute flaccid quadriparesis + coma Brainstem lesion; high cervical injury explains quadriparesis but does not itself explain coma Unilateral flaccid limb Focal lesion or peripheral process Generalized myoclonus (especially post-arrest) Consider status myoclonus, or myoclonic status epilepticus

docs.title: Breathing patterns
docs.text: Pattern Suggests Cheyne–Stokes (crescendo–decrescendo) Bilateral hemispheric / diencephalic dysfunction, or congestive heart failure Central neurogenic hyperventilation (>40/min sustained) Midbrain / upper pontine lesion Apneustic breathing (prolonged inspiration) Pontine lesion Cluster breathing Lower pontine / upper medullary lesion Ataxic (Biot) breathing (irregular, gasping) Medullary lesion — ominous, impending apnea Kussmaul breathing (deep, rapid) Metabolic acidosis (DKA, uremia, sepsis) Slow, shallow breathing Opioid / sedative effect, or medullary failure

docs.title: Herniation — rostral-to-caudal progression
docs.text: In transtentorial herniation the sequence is: unilateral pupil dilation → loss of consciousness and eye movements → extensor posturing → midposition fixed pupils with loss of oculocephalic reflex → irregular breathing. In downward herniation, the pupil changes first (third nerve compression); in central herniation the respiratory pattern deteriorates first. Central herniation: early confusion → pinpoint pupils → apneusis → ataxic breathing. Tonsillar herniation: bradycardia and respiratory arrest can occur with relatively preserved pupils.

docs.title: Management
docs.text:
Step 1 — First minutes: stabilize and reverse (every patient, immediately)

  • Airway / breathing: assess and secure the airway (intubate if indicated above). Document the neuro exam before paralytics or sedatives when feasible. If trauma is possible, use rapid-sequence induction with in-line cervical-spine stabilization. Target normocapnia (PaCO₂ 35–45 mmHg) unless herniation is suspected — then briefly hyperventilate to PaCO₂ 30–35 mmHg as a bridge.
  • Circulation: establish two IV lines. Assess for hemorrhage, shock, or sepsis. Maintain perfusion; correct hypotension promptly (avoid both hypo- and hyperperfusion).
  • Glucose (check immediately, in every comatose patient): point-of-care glucose. If <~70 mg/dL or symptomatic: D50 25 g IV (50 mL) or D10 in 100 mL boluses; repeat until the patient wakes or glucose normalizes. Recheck within 15 minutes. If no IV access: glucagon 1 mg IM. For sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycemia: dextrose infusion + octreotide 50–100 mcg SC/IV q6–8h, observe ≥24 hours (prolonged hypoglycemia risk). Do not delay dextrose to wait for thiamine.
  • Thiamine (if at risk — malnutrition, alcohol use, possible Wernicke): For suspected Wernicke, give 500 mg IV over 30 min every 8 h initially, or the institution’s evidence-based treatment regimen; see AMS. A one-off 100 mg dose is not the treatment regimen. Give promptly alongside dextrose without delaying glucose.
  • Naloxone (if opioid toxicity with respiratory depression): naloxone 0.04–0.4 mg IV titrated to adequate breathing, up to 2 mg; repeat doses as needed. Goal is breathing, not arousal. Fentanyl analogues may need larger doses. Xylazine does not respond. Naloxone wears off before long-acting opioids — monitor for recurrent respiratory depression and consider an infusion at ~two-thirds of the effective reversal dose per hour.
  • Seizure (if convulsing): lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg IV (max 4 mg/dose, may repeat once) or midazolam 10 mg IM (>40 kg) or diazepam 0.15–0.2 mg/kg IV (max 10 mg). Correct hypoglycemia or severe symptomatic hyponatremia in parallel; do not delay the benzodiazepine for ongoing convulsive status while awaiting laboratory confirmation.
  • What NOT to do in Step 1: do not give flumazenil empirically (seizure risk in chronic benzodiazepine users and co-ingestants); do not give the universal "coma cocktail" to every patient; do not assume ethanol explains the coma until structural injury and other toxic-metabolic causes are excluded; do not delay CT for a full laboratory panel.

Step 2 — Cause-directed management (the four categories, in parallel)

  • Herniation / acute intracranial hypertension (brain code): head of bed 30–45°, head/neck midline, adequate analgesia/sedation, ventilator synchrony. Hyperosmolar therapy: mannitol 0.5–1 g/kg IV or hypertonic saline 23.4% 30 mL central / 3% 250–500 mL (hypertonic saline preferred first — see the ICP page). Monitor sodium, chloride, osmolality/osmolar gap, renal function, and perfusion. These are toxicity/safety checks, not targets to exceed; see the ICP page for qualified limits. Target CPP 60–70 mmHg. Treat hyperthermia; maintain euvolemia. Dexamethasone only for vasogenic edema from tumor; abscess steroids only for severe edema/impending herniation under a specialist plan — harmful in TBI. Evacuate mass lesions; EVD for obstructive hydrocephalus. For refractory ICP: barbiturate coma to burst suppression, mild hypothermia 35–36 °C, or decompressive craniectomy.
  • Status epilepticus: first-line benzodiazepine (above). Second-line at ~20 min — ESETT showed equivalence, so choose by patient factors: levetiracetam 60 mg/kg IV max 4,500 mg; fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg IV max 1,500 mg PE at ≤150 mg PE/min; valproate 40 mg/kg IV max 3,000 mg (avoid in liver disease, POLG, pregnancy, hyperammonemia). Refractory = intubate + midazolam, propofol, or ketamine infusion (pentobarbital if those fail) to seizure or burst suppression. Super-refractory ≥24 h → consider immunotherapy if autoimmune etiology is suspected. When convulsions stop but consciousness doesn't return as expected, obtain urgent cEEG — NCSE may be continuing.
  • Hypoglycemia (severe, recurrent, or drug-induced): dextrose as in Step 1; identify the cause (sulfonylurea, insulin, sepsis, liver failure, endogenous hyperinsulinism). Sulfonylurea: dextrose infusion + octreotide (above), observe ≥24 h. Rapid correction of a reversible toxic-metabolic cause is one of the strongest predictors of a good outcome.
  • Toxic / metabolic: supportive ICU care first, specific antidote when indicated, early Poison Center / medical toxicology involvement for serious or uncertain poisoning. TCA with wide QRS: sodium bicarbonate 1–2 mEq/kg IV boluses. CO poisoning: 100% oxygen ± hyperbaric oxygen; obtain co-oximetry (standard pulse oximetry may appear normal). Toxic alcohols: fomepizole ± hemodialysis. Lithium, salicylate, valproate, selected barbiturates: consult toxicology/nephrology for EXTRIP-based dialysis indications, rather than dialyzing every exposure. Acetaminophen: N-acetylcysteine. Organophosphates: atropine
  • pralidoxime. Adrenal crisis: hydrocortisone 100 mg IV. Myxedema: IV levothyroxine + hydrocortisone first. DKA/HHS: fluids + insulin, slow osmolality correction. Uremia: dialysis. Hypercapnia: ventilation. Hypothermia: rewarming. Sepsis: source control + early antibiotics. Hepatic encephalopathy: treat precipitants + hyperammonemia; acute liver failure with cerebral edema is a distinct neurocritical emergency. Hypernatremia/hyperosmolar states: restore circulating volume and correct the water deficit at a controlled rate while treating the underlying cause.
  • Infection (meningitis/encephalitis): blood cultures, then empiric antibiotics plus dexamethasone — and acyclovir if encephalitis is possible — before CT or LP (see the neuroinfection regimens and local protocol). Never delay antimicrobials for imaging or LP.
  • Structural (hemorrhage, mass, hydrocephalus): correct coagulopathy, reverse anticoagulants, neurosurgery consultation early. Suspected basilar occlusion → CTA immediately, stroke team, thrombectomy consideration — see the stroke page.

Step 3 — Escalate: ICU, cEEG, MRI, LP, and prognostication

  • ICU admission for coma that persists after initial stabilization, for herniation/ICP management, refractory seizures, or any patient requiring airway support or frequent neuro checks.
  • Continuous EEG if the cause is unclear after initial workup, after convulsive status, or with subtle seizure signs (above). Continue until seizures are controlled electrographically for ≥24 h.
  • MRI if CT is unrevealing or the cause is still unclear at 24–48 h (above).
  • LP once CT excludes mass effect and coagulopathy is corrected (above).
  • Prognosis — multimodal, never from a single exam: etiology is the strongest determinant. Toxic/metabolic causes (including early-treated hypoglycemia) carry a good prognosis even in deep coma with absent brainstem reflexes. Avoid the self-fulfilling prophecy. After cardiac arrest, defer formal prognostication until ≥72 h after ROSC, or ≥72 h after rewarming if hypothermia was used, with sedation and other confounders excluded. Use an explicit multimodal guideline algorithm, not a tally of loosely timed findings. Absent early corneals, myoclonus without EEG, or an isolated NSE value must not determine withdrawal. Persistent coma at 72 h is not itself a poor-outcome prediction; indeterminate cases may require longer observation.

Features favoring recovery: rapid correction of a reversible cause; preserved pupillary, corneal, oculocephalic/vestibular and cough reflexes; improving motor responses and spontaneous eye opening; reactive/continuous EEG background. - Brain-death evaluation (BD/DNC): consider only with coma + absent brainstem reflexes + no respiratory drive and prerequisites met per the 2023 AAN/AAP/CNS/SCCM guideline: known catastrophic permanent mechanism with consistent imaging; observation ≥24 h after hypoxic-ischemic injury (≥24 h after rewarming to ≥36 °C if hypothermia ≤35.5 °C); core temp ≥36 °C; SBP ≥100 mmHg and MAP ≥75 mmHg; no severe metabolic/endocrine derangement; sedatives cleared (~5 half-lives or levels); neuromuscular blockade reversed (train-of-four). Do not evaluate if there is any consciousness, preserved brainstem reflex, brain-mediated movement, or spontaneous breathing. Ancillary blood-flow studies (nuclear perfusion, catheter angiography, transcranial Doppler) only when the exam/apnea test cannot be completed or another accepted indication applies; ancillary testing cannot bypass hypothermia or high sedative levels. Full exam and apnea-test details: see the brain death page.

Avoid

  • Do not intubate reflexively for GCS ≤8 without assessing oxygenation, ventilation, and protective reflexes — but do not delay when the airway is failing.
  • Do not give flumazenil empirically, and do not use the universal coma cocktail as a reflex.
  • Do not label a comatose patient "metabolic" or "postictal" without EEG and targeted MRI ± CSF.
  • Do not delay empiric antimicrobials for CT or LP in suspected CNS infection.
  • Do not evaluate for brain death before the prerequisites are met, and do not use a single early exam, a single biomarker, or a low GCS alone to prognosticate — especially after cardiac arrest.
  • Do not attribute coma to ethanol (or to any single cause) until structural injury and other toxic-metabolic causes are excluded.
  • Do not wait for MRI to treat suspected basilar occlusion or herniation.

TRICARE — verified rules and the current form

Emergency stabilization and inpatient treatment must proceed through the clinical/facility pathway. Outpatient drugs, prolonged home infusions and follow-up services may need separate benefit authorization. The official list flags Xifaxan 550 mg for PA; exact indication and quantity rules matter. Do not extrapolate this to every rifaximin strength or to all ICU drugs.

Current PA/MN details, benefit routing and packet · Live Formulary Search. Check the exact product, beneficiary and venue on the prescribing date.

docs.title: Disposition
docs.text:
• ICU admission for persistent coma, herniation/ICP management, refractory seizures, or airway support. Continuous EEG, frequent neuro checks (FOUR score trending), ICP management as needed.
  • Step-down / ward only for rapidly reversing causes (hypoglycemia, opioid toxicity) with return to baseline, normal imaging, and a clear plan for the underlying cause.
  • Goals-of-care discussion early when the cause is catastrophic, the patient is elderly or has advanced directives, or prognostication is poor — but never prognosticate from a single early exam, and never withdraw support based on a single finding.
  • Follow-up: after discharge, address the underlying cause — epilepsy management, substance-use treatment, metabolic workup, driving restrictions after seizures, and rehabilitation for any residual deficits.

Military medicine — duty, retention and deployment

  • Profile / function: Resuscitate and transfer to appropriate neurologic/critical care capability. Do not postpone treatment for an administrative readiness decision.
  • Retention / MEB–MAR2: A temporary acute restriction does not establish permanent unfitness. After recovery, use the diagnosed cause and residual function to determine profile, retention and rehabilitation needs. Use the retention framework; permanent P3/4 does not by itself select DES versus MAR2.
  • Deployment / medications: Active coma, delirium or intracranial hypertension is incompatible with routine operational duty. Reassess only after stabilization; document the underlying disease and all continuing drugs. See the disease AND drug screen for the current CENTCOM rules and waiver packet.
  • Special duty: flight, diving and other special assignments have separate standards and waiver authorities; a general duty profile does not clear them.
  • LOD / EPTS: document onset, duty status, exposures and aggravation objectively. The designated authority determines LOD/EPTS; neither in-service diagnosis nor a genetic finding settles it automatically.

docs.title: 📚 Discover — evidence brief
docs.text:
What this page covers: the first-hour approach to an adult in coma — stabilize, reverse the reversible, localize with the P-E-M-B exam, image emergently, then work the four immediately treatable categories (structural, seizures, infection, toxic-metabolic) with EEG, MRI, and LP by the clock.

What the evidence says:

  • The 2024 ACR Appropriateness Criteria (Soares et al., JACR 2024) rate noncontrast head CT as "Usually Appropriate" as the first imaging test in unexplained coma, with CTA added for suspected basilar or large-vessel occlusion — a finding mirrored in the NCS ENLS coma pathway.
  • EEG is not optional in unexplained coma. NCSE occurs in 8–30% of unclear altered mental status; about 80–95% of nonconvulsive seizures are detected within the first 24–48 hours of continuous EEG. Both sources in this run agreed that a persistently comatose patient should not be labeled "metabolic" or "postictal" without EEG.
  • Status epilepticus dosing is settled. The ESETT trial showed levetiracetam, fosphenytoin, and valproate are equivalent as second-line agents — choice should be by comorbidity, not by a false efficacy hierarchy. First-line benzodiazepine dosing (lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg, midazolam 10 mg IM, diazepam 0.15–0.2 mg/kg) is consistent across the ACEP and AES guidelines.
  • Herniation management is a bundle, not a single drug: HOB 30–45°, midline neck, CPP 60–70 mmHg, hyperosmolar therapy (mannitol 0.5–1 g/kg or hypertonic saline), normocapnia (PaCO₂ 30–35 only as a brief bridge), and dexamethasone for tumor-related vasogenic edema or selected severe abscess-associated edema/herniation, not routine abscess treatment. See the ICP page for the full tiered approach.
  • Prognostication after cardiac arrest is multimodal and time-gated. The ERC-ESICM 2021 algorithm and NCS 2023 guidance differ in predictor details. Use a complete current protocol, including ≥72 h after ROSC/rewarming and absence of confounding, rather than ≥2 of six predictors (absent pupillary + corneal reflexes at ≥72 h, absent N20 SSEP, highly malignant EEG after 24 h, status myoclonus within 72 h, NSE >60 µg/L, diffuse anoxic injury on imaging) before a poor outcome is considered likely — and 0–1 predictors means indeterminate, not good.
  • Brain death requires the complete 2023 AAN/AAP/CNS/SCCM prerequisites and examination. In adults, maintain SBP ≥100 AND MAP ≥75 mmHg; clear confounding drugs with adequate time for the actual exposure, renal/hepatic function and temperature. Follow the specified observation, apnea-testing and ancillary-test requirements. Use the brain-death page and the facility policy rather than a shortened checklist.

Limits: a coma syndrome does not supply a single retention paragraph. Diagnose and treat the cause, and reassess residual function after recovery. Empiric antimicrobial regimens are detailed on the neuroinfection page; adjust to local resistance, organ function and the individual patient.
