docs.title: Increased intracranial pressure (ICP)
docs.text:
Last reviewed: November 2026

One-liner: raised ICP and — more dangerous — brain herniation, in the acutely brain-injured adult (TBI, ICH, SAH, large stroke, mass lesion, hydrocephalus). For the on-call provider: treat the exam, not just the number — a patient can herniate with a "normal" ICP reading, and a complete Cushing triad is a late finding you must never wait for. Management is tiered: general measures for everyone, osmotherapy early (hypertonic saline first for most), and escalation only while ICP stays above threshold.

🚩 Red flags — impending or established herniation (treat now, image as you go)

Pattern Worry Do now New unilateral dilated, sluggish, or nonreactive pupil + declining consciousness Uncal herniation (CN III compression) Hyperosmolar rescue now (below), HOB 30–45°, brief hyperventilation as a bridge, emergent neurosurgery + CT when transport is safe GCS drop ≥2 points, new/worsening posturing, progressive bilateral pupil changes or loss of brainstem responses Central/downward herniation Same rescue pathway; do not wait for the ICP number to "confirm" it Cushing response — hypertension with wide pulse pressure + bradycardia + irregular breathing Late brainstem compression (seen in only ~⅓ of tonsillar herniations) Treat as herniation until proven otherwise Pinpoint pupils + sudden cardiorespiratory instability Upward/tonsillar herniation (posterior fossa) Urgent neurosurgery; if an EVD is in, drain slowly (overdrainage worsens upward herniation) Coma with hydrocephalus on CT (ICH/IVH, SAH) Obstructive hydrocephalus driving the pressure EVD — this is a therapeutic indication, not just monitoring

docs.title: Rapid approach
docs.text:
1. Recognize herniation clinically and treat it immediately — deterioration in consciousness, a new pupil abnormality, posturing, or evolving brainstem dysfunction. Do not wait for a complete Cushing triad or invasive confirmation.
  2. Stabilize and position: ABCs, prevent hypotension and hypoxia, head of bed 30–45°, neck midline, loosen collar/ETT ties.
  3. Urgent noncontrast head CT — in active herniation, stabilization and rescue treatment precede transport. MRI later; it must not delay emergency management.
  4. Start Tier 0 measures on everyone and give osmotherapy early (Step 1) — hypertonic saline is the default agent for most patients (see the comparison table).
  5. Call neurosurgery early — referral triggers are listed below; the benefit of surgery is timing-dependent, so refer before you are sure it is needed.
  6. Escalate by tier only while ICP stays above ~22 mmHg or herniation signs persist (Steps 2–3).

docs.title: Recognition — signs, herniation syndromes, imaging
docs.text:
Intracranial hypertension (a pressure) is not the same as herniation (tissue displacement). They often coexist, but local pressure gradients can displace tissue dangerously without a markedly elevated reading from a distant monitor.

Clinical signs of raised ICP — none is sensitive, and several are unavailable in the intubated, aphasic, or obtunded patient:

Finding Interpretation Headache (worse in the morning, lying flat, or with Valsalva), nausea, repeated vomiting Compatible but nonspecific Declining arousal — increasing somnolence, confusion, loss of command-following, progression toward coma The most concerning bedside sign when new or progressive Papilledema Supports intracranial hypertension when present — but may be delayed or absent in acute intracranial hypertension, even when pressure is severely elevated Diplopia from a sixth-nerve palsy False-localizing; does not identify the lesion side Pupil dilation, sluggish reactivity, or asymmetry >1 mm Automated pupillometry is more objective than the bedside exam; pupillary dilation alone has only ~28% sensitivity for elevated ICP GCS <9 and motor GCS <4 Severity markers that predict intracranial hypertension

The absence of headache or papilledema is not reassuring in an acutely deteriorating patient. Document the exam trajectory and its confounders: sedative/paralytic exposure, seizures, hypoxemia, hypercapnia, metabolic abnormalities, and pre-existing ocular abnormalities. An unexplained change prompts evaluation — not automatic attribution to sedation.

Herniation syndromes:

Syndrome Signature findings Uncal (lateral transtentorial) Fixed, dilated pupil ipsilateral to the lesion (CN III compression) with contralateral weakness. Compression of the opposite peduncle against the tentorium causes ipsilateral weakness — the Kernohan false-localizing sign, so weakness alone does not lateralize the lesion Central (downward transtentorial) Agitation → obtundation; small or mid-position fixed pupils bilaterally; decorticate then decerebrate posturing; Cushing triad Subfalcine Abulia; ACA compression → leg weakness, urinary retention Upward (cerebellar) / tonsillar Pinpoint pupils, sudden cardiorespiratory instability, Cheyne–Stokes breathing, sudden death

Imaging signs (CT):

Finding What it means Basal cisterns absent or compressed The CT sign most strongly linked to measured raised ICP (diagnostic OR ~9.6); crowding around the brainstem, concerning for transtentorial displacement Midline shift >5 mm significant, >15 mm poor prognosis (measure at the septum pellucidum, level of the foramen of Monro) Asymmetric mass effect — magnitude does not translate directly into a particular ICP Sulcal effacement or obliteration Loss of normal CSF spaces from swelling or mass effect Compression of the lateral or third ventricles Swelling/mass effect — but small ventricles are not required for raised ICP Mass lesion >25 cm³, hydrocephalus, loss of grey–white differentiation Mechanism and urgency drivers Posterior fossa crowding / fourth-ventricle compression Brainstem compression and obstructive hydrocephalus — may occur without substantial supratentorial shift Visible tissue displacement (subfalcine, uncal, downward, tonsillar, upward) Direct evidence of dangerous compartmental displacement

CT cannot supply an exact pressure, and no single examination or CT finding reliably excludes intracranial hypertension — absence of midline shift does not exclude diffuse intracranial hypertension. Optic nerve sheath ultrasound, transcranial Doppler, and pupillometry are adjuncts, not substitutes for indicated invasive measurement (ONSD cutoffs vary; TCD pulsatility index alone performs poorly).

Do not tap for an opening pressure

No lumbar puncture to obtain an opening pressure when there is a mass lesion with mass effect, a posterior fossa mass, obstructed CSF pathways, or suspected herniation — lowering spinal CSF pressure can worsen a dangerous pressure gradient.

docs.title: ICP monitoring — who, with what, and to what targets
docs.text:
The practical question is: will continuous ICP and CPP information change treatment in a patient at meaningful risk of intracranial hypertension? Monitoring is most useful when the examination is unreliable or insensitive — coma, sedation, or neuromuscular blockade. Device selection and indications follow the underlying disease, not coma alone.

Severe TBI — the familiar Brain Trauma Foundation selection criteria (third-edition criteria restated in the fourth edition; they do not meet the fourth edition's evidentiary standards for formal selection recommendations — BTF nonetheless recommends ICP-informed management of severe TBI, Level IIB):

  • Post-resuscitation GCS 3–8 plus an abnormal CT (hematoma, contusion, swelling, herniation, or compressed basal cisterns), or
  • Severe TBI with a normal CT plus at least two admission features: age >40 years, unilateral/bilateral motor posturing, or SBP <90 mmHg.

Contemporary ACS guidance (2024) supports monitoring with GCS ≤8 and structural CT injury, with consideration at higher GCS when lesions may progress, the neurological status deteriorates, or the examination will be limited — and favors serial examination/imaging when CT shows neither structural injury nor pressure signs. Use the post-resuscitation examination: a pharmacologically suppressed GCS is not equivalent to an unconfounded severe-TBI examination.

Beyond TBI (AHA/ASA classes):

Clinical setting Indication and limitations Spontaneous ICH/IVH with hydrocephalus contributing to depressed consciousness Ventricular drainage should be performed to reduce mortality (Class 1, B-NR) — a therapeutic EVD indication, not merely pressure observation Moderate/severe ICH or IVH with reduced consciousness ICP monitoring and treatment may be considered (Class 2b, B-NR); routine monitoring of every ICH patient is not established Aneurysmal SAH with acute symptomatic hydrocephalus Urgent CSF diversion is recommended (Class 1, B-NR); EVD is commonly appropriate, lumbar drainage only in selected CSF-flow patterns aSAH without hydrocephalus Monitoring may be considered when intracranial hypertension is suspected, particularly when the examination is limited Cerebellar infarction with obstructive hydrocephalus AHA/ASA recommends ventriculostomy; concomitant/subsequent decompression depends on neurological condition, brainstem compression, infarct size, and response — deterioration from brainstem compression needs urgent surgical assessment, and a supratentorial pressure reading must not delay it

Two exceptions to a broad "coma means monitor" approach:

  • Large hemispheric infarction: routine ICP monitoring has not been shown to improve outcomes and is discouraged by ESO consensus. Clinical herniation can precede a frontal ICP rise because of compartmental gradients — decompression decisions follow clinical and imaging evolution, without waiting for a pressure threshold.
  • Acute liver failure: SCCM (2023) suggests against invasive ICP monitoring even with advanced encephalopathy (conditional recommendation, very-low-certainty evidence).

Devices:

Device Main advantage Main limitation External ventricular drain (EVD) Gold standard — measures ventricular pressure and drains CSF therapeutically; preferred when hydrocephalus is present Hemorrhage, infection, obstruction, and overdrainage risks; accurate measurement requires leveling/care (below) Intraparenchymal monitor Continuous local pressure without needing ventricular access Cannot drain CSF; most devices cannot be re-zeroed after placement; a regional reading may not represent another compartment

Targets (BTF fourth edition, severe TBI):

Parameter Recommendation Level ICP Treat >22 mmHg IIB CPP Target 60–70 mmHg (CPP = MAP − ICP) IIB CPP augmentation Avoid aggressively forcing CPP >70 mmHg with fluids/pressors (respiratory failure risk) III Treatment decisions Integrate ICP, examination, and CT III SBP ≥100 mmHg at ages 50–69; ≥110 mmHg at ages 15–49 or >70 III PbtO₂ (if monitored) Keep ≥15 mmHg — (ACS)

Working notes on the numbers:

  • Normal resting adult ICP is ~7–15 mmHg — do not confuse the upper end of the normal reference range with a treatment threshold.
  • BTF sets no mandatory delay at 22 mmHg. ACS operational guidance uses 20–25 mmHg sustained for >5 minutes as the treatment trigger, and that range is reasonable when weighing higher-risk escalation such as decompressive craniectomy. Interpret magnitude, duration, recurrence, and CPP together — a transient cough-related spike and a sustained elevation are different problems. Clinical herniation requires immediate action at any number.
  • CPP is a gradient estimate, not a measurement of blood flow or oxygen delivery. MAP 85 with ICP 20 gives CPP 65 (in target); MAP 70 with ICP 20 gives CPP 50 — low despite an ICP below the treatment threshold; MAP 95 with ICP 30 also gives CPP 65 — in range, but the intracranial hypertension remains a separate problem. Neither "ICP acceptable" nor "CPP acceptable" is sufficient alone.
  • Where in 60–70? It depends partly on autoregulation. With preserved autoregulation, raising MAP may cause arteriolar constriction, reduce cerebral blood volume, and sometimes lower ICP; with impaired autoregulation it can do the opposite. A supervised MAP challenge or multimodal monitoring can individualize the target (SIBICC treats CPP manipulation as a monitored physiological intervention). If CPP is low, identify the dominant mechanism — low MAP, high ICP, or both — and treat that.
  • Outside TBI, ENLS uses CPP 60–70 in its general emergency algorithm, making it a reasonable initial working range in many monitored acute brain injuries — but the evidence for a universal ICP/CPP pair is substantially weaker outside TBI. Adapt to the disease, examination, imaging, hydrocephalus, and autoregulatory response.

Measurement details that change management: level the EVD transducer at the external auditory meatus/tragus (≈ foramen of Monro) and relevel after position changes; an ordinary fluid-coupled EVD does not give an accurate static ICP while simultaneously draining (briefly close per protocol, or use a separate sensor); an EVD drainage height ordered in cm H₂O is not the same number as an ICP displayed in mmHg; document whether MAP is referenced at the heart or the head — with head elevation, heart-level MAP overestimates cerebral-level perfusion pressure. These errors bite during transport, repositioning, and head-elevation changes. A functioning monitor adds information; it never replaces serial neurological assessment.

docs.title: The prescriptive flow (what I want done, in order)
docs.text:
1. Recognize and stabilize: herniation signs → rescue treatment now; ABCs, HOB 30–45°, prevent hypotension/hypoxia; urgent CT in parallel, neurosurgery called early.
  2. Tier 0 on everyone (Step 1, first box): positioning, analgesia/sedation, normocapnia, CPP support, normothermia, seizure treatment.
  3. Osmotherapy early (Step 1, second box): hypertonic saline first for most patients; mannitol when saline is unsuitable. Drain CSF if an EVD is in place; deepen sedation.
  4. Still >22 mmHg (or herniating)? → Step 2: mild hyperventilation as a bridge only, MAP challenge, neuromuscular blockade trial, continuous 3% saline.
  5. Refractory? → Step 3: barbiturate coma, decompressive craniectomy, ± mild hypothermia — with the family conversation about the mortality/disability trade-off.
  6. Disposition: neurocritical care unit; treat the cause (evacuate the lesion, drain the hydrocephalus, secure the aneurysm) — the tiers buy time, they are not the treatment.

docs.title: Workup
docs.text:
• Urgent noncontrast head CT (hemorrhage, swelling, hydrocephalus, surgical mass lesion); repeat with any unexplained change. MRI after the immediate crisis is controlled.
  • Labs: BMP with sodium and chloride, measured serum osmolality + osmolar gap (osmotherapy monitoring — see the table), CBC, coagulation studies, glucose; ABG for PaCO₂ confirmation (EtCO₂ underestimates PaCO₂).
  • Continuous EEG when seizures are suspected, with neuromuscular blockade (paralysis hides seizures), or in barbiturate coma (burst-suppression endpoint).
  • No LP for opening pressure in this population (see the warning above).

docs.title: Management
docs.text:
Step 1 — Tier 0: general measures (every patient, immediately)

  • Head of bed 30–45°, neck midline, loose cervical collar and ETT ties — protect venous outflow.
  • Analgesia + sedation: fentanyl infusion with propofol or midazolam — lowers ICP, cuts metabolic demand, prevents ventilator dyssynchrony. (Propofol dosing and cautions: Step 2 box.)
  • Normocapnia: PaCO₂ 35–40 mmHg. Keep SpO₂ >94%; avoid hypoxia.
  • CPP 60–70 mmHg, MAP >70, euvolemia, avoid hypotonic fluids.
  • Normothermia (<38 °C), glucose control, treat seizures; consider EEG — subclinical seizures raise ICP.

Step 1 — Tier 1: osmotherapy + CSF drainage + deeper sedation

Give osmotherapy for ICP >22 mmHg sustained, or immediately for herniation signs. Default agent: hypertonic saline (choice rationale and full comparison in the table below).

  • Hypertonic saline 3% — 250 mL IV over 15–30 min (≈2–5 mL/kg), peripheral access acceptable; or 23.4% — 30 mL over 10–20 min, central line only. Titrate doses to ICP.
  • Mannitol 20% — 0.5–1 g/kg IV over 15–30 min for a crisis (in-line filter); maintenance 0.25–0.5 g/kg every 4–6 h.
  • CSF drainage if an EVD is in place (EVD details: Step 2 box). If the monitor is intraparenchymal only, consider placing a ventriculostomy.
  • Deepen sedation and analgesia.

→ ICP controlled → hold the tier, monitor, wean deliberately. Still >22 mmHg → Step 2.

Step 2 — Tier 2: bridge and augment

  • Mild hyperventilation to PaCO₂ 32–35 mmHg — bridge only (see the warning box: rescue rules, 24-hour TBI caution, slow wean).
  • MAP challenge to test autoregulation and individualize the CPP target within 60–70.
  • Neuromuscular blockade — trial dose first: cisatracurium 0.1–0.2 mg/kg IV bolus; continue as an infusion (1–3 mcg/kg/min) only if the trial lowers ICP, and stop as soon as feasible. (Rocuronium ~0.6–1 mg/kg is the alternative bolus.) Mandatory deep sedation + analgesia, ideally processed-EEG verified; train-of-four target 1–2 twitches; cEEG (paralysis hides seizures); pupils become the motor exam. Its most consistent benefit is blunting ICP surges from coughing, suctioning, dyssynchrony, or posturing.
  • Continuous 3% saline infusion — ~0.5–1 mL/kg/h, titrated to a goal sodium (commonly 145–155) — the CREVICE approach. Note: the NCS endorses bolus therapy and accepts goal-sodium infusion, but does not endorse a standard adult infusion regimen; the rate above is published adult practice, not a guideline dose. Continuous hyperosmolar therapy also has no proven outcome benefit — the COBI trial of continuous 20% saline in moderate-to-severe TBI found no improvement in 6-month neurologic outcome (adjusted common OR 1.02, 95% CI 0.71–1.47) — so an infusion is a bridge for ICP control, not a therapy in itself. Wean gradually (below).
  • EVD drainage strategy: a closed system with intermittent drainage (drain only when ICP exceeds threshold — typically 22 mmHg; SIBICC uses 18–22) preserves continuous ICP measurement; continuous drainage controls ICP more effectively, but then measure ICP intermittently by clamping or with a separate parenchymal monitor. Level the transducer at the tragus; drain height usually 10–20 cm H₂O above it. Removing even small CSF volumes lowers ICP sharply (steep pressure–volume curve). Complications: tract hemorrhage in ~15%, malposition, ventriculitis — intermittent drainage and early weaning mean fewer complications.

→ Still refractory → Step 3. Any herniation sign at any point → rescue (osmotherapy ± brief PaCO₂ <30) while definitive treatment is arranged.

Step 3 — Tier 3: refractory ICP (salvage tier — time-limited, goals-of-care aware)

  • Barbiturate coma (pentobarbital) — only for ICP refractory despite maximal medical and surgical treatment, and only in a hemodynamically stable patient. Never prophylactically to induce burst suppression; SIBICC starts based on response to a test dose. Load 10 mg/kg IV over 30 min, then 5 mg/kg/h for 3 h, then 1–4 mg/kg/h. Endpoint is ICP control, not a serum level or the EEG — run continuous EEG and stop escalating once burst suppression appears (ICP will not fall further; toxicity will). Arterial line + cardiac output monitoring; strictly avoid hypotension.
  • Decompressive craniectomy — see the evidence section below; if done for TBI, a large frontotemporoparietal flap (≥12 × 15 cm).
  • Mild hypothermia 35–36 °C — an option in the refractory tier at some centers; not a substitute for the two measures above.
  • Propofol (from Step 1 sedation, deepened): target RASS −3 to −5. Start 5–20 mcg/kg/min, titrate to 50 mcg/kg/min, up to 75–80 mcg/kg/min (≈4.5–5 mg/kg/h); small boluses (0.5 mg/kg) can blunt an acute spike — only with hypotension anticipated and covered by a vasopressor. Propofol lowers ICP but has not been shown to improve mortality or 6-month outcome, and high doses cause significant harm.

docs.title: Hypertonic saline vs mannitol — the choice (nudge: saline first)
docs.text:
The Neurocritical Care Society 2020 cerebral edema guideline prefers hypertonic saline over mannitol for raised ICP in TBI and ICH (weak/conditional recommendation, low- to very-low-quality evidence — in SAH it specifically favors symptom-triggered HTS boluses over sodium-target regimens); in ischemic stroke either agent is acceptable. SIBICC, by contrast, endorses neither over the other and applies the same sodium/osmolality limits to both. Two honest caveats: no trial has shown a mortality or functional-outcome difference between the agents, and laboratory safety limits are not treatment goals — the ICP and examination response guides therapy, and routinely driving sodium to a preset high value has not been shown to improve neurologic outcomes.

Parameter Hypertonic saline Mannitol (20%) Bolus 23.4%: 30 mL over 10–20 min, central line only. 3%: 250 mL, or ~2–5 mL/kg over 15–30 min, peripheral acceptable. (7.5%/5% also used.) Doses titrated to ICP 0.5–1 g/kg IV over 15–30 min for a crisis; maintenance 0.25–0.5 g/kg q4–6h (FDA label: 0.25 g/kg over ≥30 min q6–8h). In-line filter Continuous infusion 3% at ~0.5–1 mL/kg/h, titrated to goal sodium (commonly 145–155); NCS accepts goal-sodium infusion or symptom-based boluses, but endorses no standard adult infusion regimen Not recommended — accumulates in injured brain, may cause rebound edema Mechanism Raises osmolality directly and expands intravascular volume Osmotic diuresis + rheologic effect; onset 10–15 min, peak 20–60 min, lasts 1–5 h Sodium target Na 145–155 mEq/L; little added benefit above 160 Not a direct target (diuresis can raise sodium) Usual limits SIBICC (both agents): Na <155, osmolality <320. Higher Na tolerated in crises; keep sustained Na <160 (DVT risk) and <170 (thrombocytopenia, anemia) Osmolar gap ≥20 is the usual hold point (accumulation, renal risk) — the gap is the NCS-preferred marker, but the NCS validates no specific cutoff; osmolality 320 is a traditional ceiling Monitoring Na every 4–6 h, osmolality, chloride (hyperchloremic acidosis), volume status, cardiopulmonary status (pulmonary edema), creatinine Osmolality + osmolar gap (draw ≥20 min after a dose, or the gap is falsely high), BMP, creatinine, urine output, volume status; replace losses to prevent hypovolemia Main risks Volume overload, CHF/pulmonary edema, hyperchloremia, osmotic demyelination if baseline Na is low, rebound edema if sodium is dropped quickly Hypovolemia and hypotension (lowers CPP), AKI, electrolyte loss, rebound ICP

Why saline wins for most patients: (1) larger and faster ICP reduction — meta-analyses show HTS lowers ICP more than equiosmolar mannitol, and it can work after mannitol has failed; (2) it keeps volume and CPP up instead of diuresing — decisive in TBI with hypotension and in SAH. Mannitol remains reasonable when saline is unsuitable (e.g., volume overload, hypernatremia already at limit) — and a hypotensive patient is precisely the one mannitol can hurt.

Osmotherapy cautions that apply to both: the Na/osmolality limits are not absolute — extra doses can still lower ICP, so weigh herniation risk against toxicity rather than withholding rescue at a number. Wean HTS gradually — let sodium fall no faster than ~8–10 mEq/L per 24 h to avoid rebound edema.

Avoid

  • Prolonged or prophylactic hyperventilation — vasoconstriction reduces CBF and risks ischemia (worst where autoregulation is impaired); avoid hyperventilation in the first 24 h after TBI, when CBF is lowest. Mild hypocapnia (32–35) is a Tier-2 bridge (one review suggests a maximum of ~2 h; others advise reversing promptly once ICP stabilizes); PaCO₂ <30 is rescue-only — refractory ICP or impending herniation (e.g., a dilated unreactive pupil), as a bridge to osmotherapy or surgery, for as short a time as possible. Confirm with an ABG; ideally guide with PbtO₂ or SjvO₂. Wean over hours — abrupt normalization causes rebound ICP (CSF bicarbonate adaptation).
  • Prophylactic mannitol in ICH — not shown to help; may promote hematoma expansion.
  • Corticosteroids for TBI, ICH, or stroke edema — no role. (Steroids may be used for tumor vasogenic edema; in brain abscess, reserve them for severe edema/impending herniation under specialist guidance, rather than routine use.)
  • Hypotonic fluids and any avoidable hypotension or hypoxia — each is a secondary-insult multiplier.
  • Propofol infusion syndrome (PRIS): risk rises at >4 mg/kg/h for >48 h, with catecholamine or corticosteroid co-therapy, young age, and low carbohydrate intake. Features: unexplained metabolic (lactic) acidosis, rhabdomyolysis (rising CK), hyperkalemia, hypertriglyceridemia, AKI, Brugada-like ECG changes or arrhythmias, refractory cardiac failure. Check lactate, CK, triglycerides, K⁺, creatinine at baseline and every 24–48 h (more often at high dose); watch for pancreatitis; count the lipid calories. If PRIS is suspected: stop propofol immediately, supportive care, consider ECMO or RRT.
  • Barbiturate coma pitfalls: hypotension and myocardial depression (expect pressors/ inotropes), immunosuppression (pneumonia, sepsis), ileus, hypokalemia during infusion with rebound hyperkalemia on withdrawal, hepatic dysfunction, hypothermia — and the loss of the neurological exam for days (very long context-sensitive half-life; pupils may become small or fixed; brain death cannot be assessed until levels clear). Taper; do not stop abruptly.
  • Continuous paralysis beyond need: longer ICU stays and more pneumonia, with no neurologic benefit; plus ICU-acquired weakness (worse with steroids), VTE, pressure injury, and corneal injury.

TRICARE — verified rules and the current form

Emergency stabilization and inpatient treatment must proceed through the clinical/facility pathway. Outpatient drugs, prolonged home infusions and follow-up services may need separate benefit authorization. The official list flags Xifaxan 550 mg for PA; exact indication and quantity rules matter. Do not extrapolate this to every rifaximin strength or to all ICU drugs.

Current PA/MN details, benefit routing and packet · Live Formulary Search. Check the exact product, beneficiary and venue on the prescribing date.

docs.title: Decompressive craniectomy — the evidence, honestly stated
docs.text:
Decompression reliably lowers ICP and saves lives across conditions; whether it improves function depends on the disease, the timing, and the patient's age. Every trial shows the same trade: death is traded for survival with dependency — so the patient's pre-injury function and likely values drive consent.

DECRA (2011) — early RESCUEicp (2016) — late, last-tier Population Diffuse TBI, no mass lesion, within 72 h TBI aged 10–65, within 10 days; mostly diffuse injury ICP trigger >20 mmHg for >15 min within 1 h despite Tier-1 therapy (early, modest elevation) >25 mmHg for 1–12 h despite 2 tiers of therapy (late, refractory) Operation Bifrontal Bifrontal (most) or unilateral Mortality No difference 6 mo: 26.9% vs 48.9%; 24 mo: 33.5% vs 54.0% (DC vs medical) Function Worse GOS-E at 6 mo; still favored medical care at 12 mo, but no longer significant More vegetative state and severe disability. Favorable outcome (upper severe disability or better): 42.8% vs 34.6% at 6 mo (NS); 45.4% vs 32.4% at 12 mo (P=.01) ICP/ICU Lower ICP, shorter ICU stay Same

The RESCUEicp trade-off, per 100 patients treated surgically: 21 more alive at 24 months — of these, 4 vegetative, 9 with severe disability, 8 with moderate disability. Good recovery was the same in both arms (~11%). Many survivors kept improving between 6 and 24 months (30% vs 14% improved by at least one GOS-E grade) — judge the outcome late, not at discharge. Note that "favorable outcome" in RESCUEicp included upper severe disability (independent at home for part of the day).

Guideline position (BTF 2020 severe-TBI update): secondary DC is recommended for late refractory ICP elevation (the RESCUEicp scenario) and advised against for early refractory elevation (the DECRA scenario) when the goal is improved outcome. These recommendations do not apply to primary DC (flap left off while evacuating a mass lesion); for acute subdural hematoma, RESCUE-ASDH found no functional difference between primary DC and craniotomy, with different complication profiles.

Malignant MCA infarction: in the pooled DECIMAL, DESTINY, and HAMLET trials, early hemicraniectomy reduced death (OR 0.19) and death or mRS >4 at 12 months (OR 0.26); a Cochrane analysis of 9 RCTs found death or severe disability with an OR of 0.22. Timing is the lever: surgery ideally within 48 h of onset and before herniation gives the largest benefit. Age splits the outcome: benefit for both survival and function is established under 60; over 60 (DESTINY II), mortality still falls, but a larger share of survivors are severely disabled (mRS 4–5).

Intracerebral hemorrhage: AHA/ASA (2022) — decompressive hemicraniectomy, with or without clot evacuation, may be considered to reduce mortality in supratentorial ICH when the patient is comatose, has a large hematoma with midline shift, or has ICP refractory to medical therapy; functional benefit is uncertain. The SWITCH trial (DC without evacuation for deep ICH 30–100 mL, ages 18–75, within 72 h) stopped early; its primary outcome trended toward benefit but was not significant (RR 0.77, 95% CI 0.59–1.01); the remaining evidence is small RCTs and retrospective series. Cerebellar ICH is different: urgent suboccipital evacuation if the patient is deteriorating, the brainstem is compressed, or there is hydrocephalus — an EVD alone is not adequate.

Other space-occupying lesions (standard practice): traumatic EDH/SDH — evacuate if the clot is large or there is significant shift, the GCS is falling, or a pupil becomes abnormal (common thresholds: EDH >30 mL, SDH >10 mm thick). Space-occupying cerebellar infarction — suboccipital decompression is well established. Tumors, abscesses, and hydrocephalus — treat the cause (resection, drainage, EVD or shunt); steroids for tumor vasogenic edema.

docs.title: When to refer to neurosurgery — early, before you are sure
docs.text:
Benefit in stroke and mass lesions depends on timing, so refer immediately or within the first hours for:

  • Any TBI with GCS ≤8, an operable mass lesion, or CT showing midline shift or effaced cisterns — for ICP-monitoring or evacuation consideration.
  • Clinical herniation: new fixed or dilated pupil, GCS drop ≥2 points, Cushing response.
  • ICP sustained above 20–22 mmHg despite Tier-1 therapy — so Tier-2 options and RESCUEicp-type decompression are considered before the patient becomes futile.
  • Large MCA infarct at diagnosis (>50% of the MCA territory on CT, or DWI volume >~145 mL), not after deterioration — especially under age 60; and any cerebellar infarct or hemorrhage with mass effect or hydrocephalus.
  • Supratentorial ICH with coma, shift, falling GCS, or hydrocephalus (for EVD); any cerebellar ICH ≥15 mL, or smaller with deterioration/compression/hydrocephalus.

docs.title: Disposition
docs.text:
• Admit: neurocritical care ICU for any monitored patient, any patient on osmotherapy or a Step 2–3 therapy, and any patient with herniation signs — with neurosurgery engaged. If the facility cannot provide monitoring/decompression, transfer early; monitor placement should accompany the treatment pathway, never become a prerequisite for rescue treatment.
  • Escalation conversations: the Step-3 tier trades death for survival with disability — document pre-injury function and the patient's values before decompression or barbiturate coma whenever time allows.
  • Weaning: ICP controlled ≥24 h → wean in reverse order of escalation, one step at a time; HTS sodium falls ≤8–10 mEq/L per 24 h; hyperventilation normalizes over hours; barbiturates taper.

Military medicine — duty, retention and deployment

  • Profile / function: Resuscitate and transfer to appropriate neurologic/critical care capability. Do not postpone treatment for an administrative readiness decision.
  • Retention / MEB–MAR2: A temporary acute restriction does not establish permanent unfitness. After recovery, use the diagnosed cause and residual function to determine profile, retention and rehabilitation needs. Use the retention framework; permanent P3/4 does not by itself select DES versus MAR2.
  • Deployment / medications: Active coma, delirium or intracranial hypertension is incompatible with routine operational duty. Reassess only after stabilization; document the underlying disease and all continuing drugs. See the disease AND drug screen for the current CENTCOM rules and waiver packet.
  • Special duty: flight, diving and other special assignments have separate standards and waiver authorities; a general duty profile does not clear them.
  • LOD / EPTS: document onset, duty status, exposures and aggravation objectively. The designated authority determines LOD/EPTS; neither in-service diagnosis nor a genetic finding settles it automatically.

docs.title: 📚 Discover — evidence brief
docs.text:
Written from primary guidelines and trials; source articles are a reading list, not copied.

  • Hypertonic saline is the default osmotic agent now — by guideline, not just habit. The NCS 2020 cerebral edema guideline prefers HTS over mannitol in TBI and ICH (weak recommendation, low-quality evidence); SIBICC stays neutral between the agents but standardizes the tiers and the shared Na <155 / osmolality <320 limits. No trial shows an outcome difference between the agents — the preference rests on ICP-lowering efficacy and on saline's volume/CPP profile. Treat the ICP and the exam, not the sodium number.
  • The 22 / 60–70 pair is BTF-anchored and operationalized by ACS 2024: treat ICP >22 mmHg (Level IIB), CPP 60–70 (IIB), never force CPP >70 (III), with age-banded SBP floors (≥100 at 50–69 y; ≥110 at 15–49 or >70 y, III). ACS frames 20–25 mmHg sustained >5 min as the practical trigger and ≥60 as the CPP floor adjusted for autoregulation.
  • Herniation is a clinical diagnosis that outruns the monitor. Pupillary dilation is only ~28% sensitive for elevated ICP, papilledema may be absent acutely, and compartmental displacement can precede any rise at a frontal monitor — the exam and the CT cisterns (OR ~9.6 when effaced) carry the early signal.
  • Decompression is two different operations in the evidence. Early bifrontal DC for modest ICP elevation (DECRA) worsened function; late last-tier DC for refractory hypertension (RESCUEicp) cut 24-month mortality from 54.0% to 33.5% at the price of more survivors with severe disability — with continued improvement out to 24 months. In malignant MCA stroke the calculus is better (pooled OR 0.19 for death) but only early (<48 h) and mainly under 60.
  • Monitoring has boundaries: routine ICP monitoring is not supported in large hemispheric infarction (ESO) or acute liver failure (SCCM 2023), while EVD drainage for hydrocephalus in ICH/IVH and SAH is a Class 1 treatment, not a monitoring choice.

Key sources: Brain Trauma Foundation severe TBI guidelines, 4th edition, and the 2020 BTF decompressive-craniectomy update; ACS Best Practices in the Management of Traumatic Brain Injury (2024); NCS Guidelines for the Acute Treatment of Cerebral Edema (2020); SIBICC consensus (2019–2020); ENLS intracranial hypertension protocol; the COBI trial of continuous hypertonic saline in TBI (JAMA 2021); AHA/ASA ICH (2022) and SAH guidelines; DECRA (NEJM 2011); RESCUEicp (NEJM 2016; JAMA Neurol 2022 24-month analysis); DECIMAL/DESTINY/HAMLET pooled analysis and DESTINY II; SWITCH (2024).

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Carney N, et al. Guidelines for the Management of Severe Traumatic Brain Injury, Fourth Edition. Neurosurgery. 2017 — ICP >22 mmHg treatment threshold (IIB), CPP 60–70 (IIB), avoid forcing CPP >70 (III), age-banded SBP floors (III), ICP-informed management (IIB).
  2. Hawryluk GWJ, et al. Guidelines for the Management of Severe Traumatic Brain Injury: 2020 Updates of the Decompressive Craniectomy Recommendations. Neurosurgery. 2020 — secondary DC for late (not early) refractory ICP elevation; large frontotemporoparietal flap ≥12 × 15 cm.
  3. Manley G, et al. Best Practices in the Management of Traumatic Brain Injury. American College of Surgeons. 2024 — GCS ≤8 + structural CT injury monitoring; ICP 20–25 mmHg sustained >5 min trigger; CPP ≥60 adjusted for autoregulation; PbtO₂ ≥15 mmHg.
  4. Cook AM, et al. Guidelines for the Acute Treatment of Cerebral Edema in Neurocritical Care Patients. Neurocrit Care. 2020 — NCS: hypertonic saline suggested over mannitol in TBI and ICH; bolus or goal-sodium strategies.
  5. Chesnut R, et al. [A Consensus-Based Interpretation of the Seattle International Severe Traumatic Brain Injury Consensus Conference (SIBICC) Algorithms. / SIBICC tiered algorithm. Intensive Care Med. 2019–2020] — Tier 0–3 escalation; shared Na/osmolality limits; EVD drainage threshold 18–22 mmHg; MAP challenge.
  6. Emergency Neurological Life Support (ENLS): Intracranial Hypertension and Herniation protocol (Neurocritical Care Society) — CPP 60–70 as the general emergency working range; herniation rescue sequence.
  7. Greenberg SM, et al. 2022 Guideline for the Management of Patients With Spontaneous Intracerebral Hemorrhage. Stroke. 2022 — ventricular drainage for ICH/IVH with hydrocephalus (Class 1); ICP monitoring may be considered (2b); decompressive hemicraniectomy may be considered to reduce mortality.
  8. Cooper DJ, et al. Decompressive Craniectomy in Diffuse Traumatic Brain Injury (DECRA). N Engl J Med. 2011 — early bifrontal DC for ICP >20: no mortality difference, worse functional outcome at 6 months.
  9. Hutchinson PJ, et al. Trial of Decompressive Craniectomy for Traumatic Intracranial Hypertension (RESCUEicp). N Engl J Med. 2016; and 24-month secondary analysis, JAMA Neurol. 2022 — last-tier DC for ICP >25: mortality 26.9% vs 48.9% at 6 mo and 33.5% vs 54.0% at 24 mo; per-100 trade-off (4 vegetative, 9 severe disability, 8 moderate disability among 21 additional survivors).
  10. Vahedi K, et al. Early decompressive surgery in malignant infarction of the middle cerebral artery: a pooled analysis of three randomised controlled trials (DECIMAL, DESTINY, HAMLET). Lancet Neurol. 2007 — death OR 0.19; death or mRS >4 at 12 mo OR 0.26; benefit concentrated under 60 and within 48 h. See also DESTINY II (age >60: mortality benefit, more severe disability) and the 2022 Cochrane review of surgical decompression for malignant cerebral edema (death or severe disability OR 0.22).
  11. Beck J, et al. SWITCH trial — decompressive craniectomy plus best medical treatment versus best medical treatment alone for spontaneous severe deep supratentorial ICH. 2024 — stopped early; primary outcome RR 0.77 (95% CI 0.59–1.01), not significant.
  12. Official TRICARE sources, retrieved forms and access limits.

Evidence/policy audit: 21 November 2026. Material changes were checked against the linked primary sources; this is an AI-assisted review, not certification of every dose or claim. Review scope and source limits.

docs.title: Neuroinfections
docs.text:
Last reviewed: October 2026

One-liner: fever plus a neurologic syndrome is a CNS infection until proven otherwise — obtain blood/CSF specimens promptly when safe, but never delay indicated antimicrobials for LP or imaging, and when the picture is subacute encephalopathy, run the infectious and autoimmune workups in parallel.

🚩 Red flags — treat first, prove later

Pattern Worry Do now Fever + neck stiffness + altered mentation Acute bacterial meningitis Blood cultures, dexamethasone + antibiotics with the first dose — never delay for LP or CT Trainee or barracks resident + fever + petechial/purpuric rash or meningism Meningococcal disease Ceftriaxone 2 g IV now, droplet precautions, call preventive medicine for contact prophylaxis — below Fever + encephalopathy or seizures after deployment or travel to a malaria zone Cerebral malaria Smears/rapid antigen now; IV artesunate — below Febrile encephalopathy + aphasia / focal deficit / seizures (temporal lobe) HSV encephalitis IV acyclovir immediately — do not wait for LP, MRI, or PCR Headache + fever + focal deficit or seizure Brain abscess Blood cultures, empiric abx, urgent neurosurgical + ID assessment HIV + subacute headache, often with raised ICP Cryptococcal meningitis LP with opening pressure; induction antifungals + serial therapeutic LPs Subacute meningitis + cranial neuropathies / hydrocephalus / low CSF glucose TB meningitis Treatment emergency — empiric HRZE after specimens; add dexamethasone Subacute memory loss / psychiatric change + seizures or movement disorder Autoimmune encephalitis MRI/EEG/LP + paired serum/CSF antibody panels; start immunotherapy at the probable stage — do not wait for antibodies

docs.title: Rapid approach
docs.text:
1. Resuscitate and draw blood cultures ×2 — then start empiric antimicrobials immediately. If LP is immediately safe and causes no clinically significant delay, obtain it first; otherwise give treatment now and sample as soon as safe.
  2. Classify the syndrome: acute meningitic (hours–days) → bacterial; febrile encephalopathy → HSV; focal lesion with fever → abscess; HIV + raised ICP → cryptococcal; subacute/chronic meningitis → TB/fungal; subacute encephalopathy → autoimmune.
  3. Image when indicated, then LP when safe — and measure the opening pressure at every LP.
  4. Route to the syndrome orderset below; tailor once CSF, serology, and cultures return.
  5. Treat the complications in parallel: raised ICP, seizures, hydrocephalus, hyponatremia.

docs.title: The prescriptive flow (what I want done, in order)
docs.text:
1. Blood cultures → empiric antimicrobials + adjunctive steroids (where indicated) — now.
  2. CT head first only if indicated (immunocompromise, focal deficit, papilledema, seizure, depressed consciousness); otherwise straight to LP. Measure opening pressure.
  3. Send the syndrome-specific tests (CSF profile, PCR, cryptococcal antigen, Xpert Ultra, VDRL, antibody panels) — but do not wait for results to treat.
  4. Control pressure and seizures while antimicrobials work; get neurosurgery involved early for abscess, hydrocephalus, or uncontrolled ICP.
  5. Narrow and set the duration once the organism (or antibody) is known; arrange follow-up imaging, repeat LPs, and secondary prophylaxis where indicated.

docs.title: Acute bacterial meningitis (adults)
docs.text:
Community-acquired. Dexamethasone and antibiotics ride in on the first dose together — steroids given later lose their benefit.

Step 1 — empiric antibiotics + dexamethasone (before the LP if needed)

  • Blood cultures ×2 — draw first, but never delay antibiotics for them.
  • Dexamethasone 10 mg IV q6h — give before or with the first antibiotic dose, up to 4 days; stop it if CSF is not consistent with bacterial meningitis (NICE: if delayed <12 h after antibiotics began, give promptly; if longer, seek ID advice). NICE continues dexamethasone for pneumococcus/Hib and stops it for other identified organisms.
  • Vancomycin 15–20 mg/kg IV q8–12h (IDSA: 30–45 mg/kg/day in divided doses; a 20–35 mg/kg loading dose is common in the critically ill) — actual body weight, adjust for renal function, trough 15–20 µg/mL or AUC-guided per pharmacy — + ceftriaxone 2 g IV q12h — adults 18–50.
  • Add ampicillin 2 g IV q4h (Listeria cover) if age >50, pregnant, or immunocompromised.
  • Alternative cephalosporin: cefotaxime 2 g IV q4–6h.
  • Any encephalitic feature (confusion out of proportion, focal signs, seizures) → add acyclovir 10 mg/kg IV q8h until HSV PCR returns — see HSV encephalitis.
  • CT head first if immunocompromised, focal deficit, papilledema, seizure, or depressed consciousness — then LP. Never delay antibiotics for CT or LP.
Age / risk Empiric regimen 18–50, immunocompetent Vancomycin + ceftriaxone 2 g IV q12h >50, pregnant, or immunocompromised Above + ampicillin 2 g IV q4h Healthcare-associated / post-neurosurgical Per IDSA 2017 — vancomycin + antipseudomonal β-lactam; tailor fast CSF Bacterial Viral Cells Neutrophilic pleocytosis Lymphocytic pleocytosis Glucose Low Normal Protein High Mildly elevated Opening pressure Often elevated Usually normal

TRICARE — verified rules and the current form

Treat CNS infection promptly; do not await a routine outpatient authorization. Prolonged antimicrobial therapy, home infusion, immune rescue and follow-up services need their own benefit/site arrangements. Record organism, indication, duration and monitoring. Public-health access pathways for antitoxin or uncommon drugs may differ from the pharmacy benefit.

Current PA/MN details, benefit routing and packet · Live Formulary Search. Check the exact product, beneficiary and venue on the prescribing date.

Step 2 — narrow by organism; set the duration

  • Narrow to organism-directed therapy once cultures/susceptibilities return; keep source control (devices, sinuses, ears) moving in parallel.
  • Duration is pathogen- and course-specific. NICE examples in uncomplicated recovered patients: meningococcus 5 days; pneumococcus 10 days; Hib 7 days (extend to 10 if not recovered); group B streptococcus 14 days; Listeria or Enterobacterales 21 days. The 10-day NICE vs 7-day conditional WHO comparison concerns selected cases without an identified pathogen, not all bacterial meningitis. Get ID advice for complications.
  • Healthcare-associated ventriculitis/meningitis (IDSA 2017): coagulase-negative staphylococci or S. aureus 10–14 days; gram-negative bacilli 10–14 days (some experts treat 21 days); repeatedly positive CSF cultures → 10–14 days after the last positive culture.

docs.title: HSV encephalitis (adults)
docs.text:
Febrile encephalopathy with confusion, personality/behavioral change, impaired consciousness, aphasia or another focal deficit, or new seizures — start acyclovir on suspicion. A normal early CSF cell count does not exclude it.

Step 1 — empiric IV acyclovir (do not wait for LP, MRI, or PCR)

  • Acyclovir 10 mg/kg IV q8h — start immediately; infuse each dose over ≥1 hour (never rapid/bolus push); maintain hydration; monitor renal function; adjust for renal impairment; dose by ideal body weight in obesity.
  • Duration 14–21 days: 14 days for an immunocompetent adult with a good response; 21 days if immunocompromised. (The U.S. label still lists 10 days — contemporary encephalitis guidance is 14–21.)
  • Response or complications may warrant specialist-guided extension.

Step 2 — tailor by PCR; know when to re-tap

  • HSV PCR negative but suspicion high: continue acyclovir and repeat CSF HSV PCR in 3–7 days — an early negative (first days of illness) does not rule out HSV encephalitis.
  • HSV PCR positive and improving: consider repeat CSF PCR near end of therapy only if the response is inadequate or the course is complicated; if PCR stays positive, continue IV treatment and reassess with infectious diseases.
  • Routine end-of-treatment LP is not required (U.S. IDSA approach; UK guidance differs and favors an end-of-course LP with continued treatment while PCR stays positive).
  • Two negative PCRs with persistent suspicion: reassess CSF timing/quality, MRI, and EEG — then broaden to alternative infectious and autoimmune diagnoses with specialists.

docs.title: Brain abscess (adults)
docs.text:
Urgent neurosurgical + ID assessment; blood cultures; abscess material for aerobic/anaerobic culture when feasible. For common community-acquired bacterial abscesses, ceftriaxone + metronidazole is a backbone; vancomycin and cefepime are scenario-specific additions.

Step 1 — empiric antibiotics by presumed source

  • Sinusitis source: ceftriaxone 2 g IV q12h + metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h. Add vancomycin if S. aureus/MRSA is plausible; assess the sinus focus for source control.
  • Otitis/mastoiditis source: ceftriaxone + metronidazole as above. If Pseudomonas is a credible concern (especially extension from otitis externa): cefepime 2 g IV q8h in place of ceftriaxone, retaining metronidazole; adjust for renal function.
  • Hematogenous source: ceftriaxone + metronidazole until the distant source is established; add vancomycin with bacteremia, endocarditis, or another staphylococcal source. Seek and treat the source — confirmed endocarditis gets organism-directed therapy, not automatic continuation of the full empiric regimen.
  • Metronidazole's role: anaerobic coverage with good abscess penetration; it does not replace the cephalosporin's aerobic coverage. Vancomycin is an addition for suspected staphylococcal infection, not a metronidazole substitute.
  • Do not delay treatment for sepsis, neurologic deterioration, impending herniation, or imminent rupture. (In a stable patient, ESCMID conditionally allows withholding antibiotics only if aspiration/excision happens promptly, preferably within 24 h, to improve diagnostic yield.)

Step 2 — duration, aspiration, excision

  • Duration: aspirated or medically managed bacterial abscess — 6–8 weeks of IV therapy, individualized to pathogen, drainage, course, and interval imaging. After complete excision, ~4 weeks; shorter courses are expert opinion only, not a rule.
  • Aspiration is preferred for most presumed bacterial abscesses: diagnostic pus, reduces the collection, reaches deep lesions with less tissue disruption (repeat aspiration may be needed). Get neurosurgical source control as soon as feasible.
  • Excision is considered for: superficial lesion in non-eloquent tissue, selected posterior-fossa lesions, difficult organisms (Nocardia, fungi), or a lesion not controlled by aspiration. No single size cutoff decides — mass effect, location, accessibility, diagnostic uncertainty, and response guide the choice.
  • Evidence is insufficient to recommend routine early oral step-down.

docs.title: Cryptococcal meningitis (HIV-positive adults)
docs.text:
Three-phase therapy — induction, consolidation, maintenance — plus active pressure management with serial therapeutic LPs. Acetazolamide, mannitol, and routine steroids are not substitutes for CSF drainage.

Step 1 — induction antifungals

  • Resource-rich setting (close inpatient monitoring): liposomal amphotericin B 3–4 mg/kg IV daily + flucytosine 25 mg/kg PO four times daily — for 2 weeks. Monitor renal function, blood counts, drug levels when available.
  • Resource-limited setting (AMBITION regimen): liposomal amphotericin B 10 mg/kg IV once on day 1 + flucytosine 25 mg/kg PO four times daily + fluconazole 1,200 mg PO daily for 14 days. The single amphotericin dose is not stand-alone — it depends on both oral drugs.
  • Adding flucytosine to amphotericin B gives faster fungal clearance and improves survival. Liposomal amphotericin B is preferred where resources allow (less nephrotoxicity); amphotericin B deoxycholate 0.7–1.0 mg/kg/day remains the mainstay where cost is limiting.
  • If the patient stays unstable or CSF culture stays positive, continue induction/intensified treatment rather than stepping down.

Step 2 — manage the pressure with serial therapeutic LPs

  • Measure opening pressure at the diagnostic LP and at every subsequent LP. An opening pressure ≥25 cm H₂O is associated with more complications — but do not use 25 cm H₂O as a reason to withhold drainage from a symptomatic patient.
  • Treat headache or neurologic signs of raised pressure promptly: drain enough CSF to reduce pressure by at least half or to <20 cm H₂O.
  • Repeat therapeutic LPs at least daily while symptoms or raised pressure persist; consider an early repeat LP even after a lower initial reading — pressure can rise later.
  • When daily LPs fail or cannot be tolerated: a temporary lumbar drain or ventriculostomy; a ventriculoperitoneal shunt only when pressure stays raised despite appropriate antifungal therapy and serial drainage (IDSA 2010). Involve neurosurgery early.

Step 3 — consolidation, maintenance, and ART timing

  • Consolidation: fluconazole 800 mg PO daily for at least 8 weeks; in a stable patient, NIH allows 400 mg daily once CSF cultures are sterile and ART has begun. Get a repeat LP with CSF fungal culture during/at the end of induction — a persistently positive cryptococcal antigen alone does not prove treatment failure.
  • Maintenance: fluconazole 200 mg PO daily for at least 1 year from the start of antifungal therapy. Stop only when the patient is asymptomatic + CD4 ≥100 cells/mm³ + suppressed HIV RNA on effective ART; restart if CD4 falls below 100.
  • ART timing — defer, don't rush: for a patient not already on ART, do not initiate immediately; NIH recommends deferring ART until 4–6 weeks after antifungals begin, individualized to clinical improvement, pressure control, and preferably CSF culture sterility. Early ART increased mortality (COAT trial) — the opposite of most OIs.

docs.title: TB meningitis (adults)
docs.text:
A treatment emergency: start antituberculous therapy promptly after specimens are drawn — do not wait for smear, molecular, or culture confirmation.

Finding Typical TBM pattern CSF Lymphocytic pleocytosis, high protein, low glucose Opening pressure Measure it; no validated TBM-specific cutoff — follow exam and imaging, not pressure alone Direct tests Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra is the preferred rapid initial test; send AFB smear (usually insensitive), mycobacterial culture (confirms + susceptibility) Yield tip ≥6 mL of CSF for TB testing improves yield; if CSF is scarce, prioritize the molecular test Negative tests Negative smear, Ultra/Xpert, or culture does NOT rule out TBM

Step 1 — empiric anti-TB therapy + dexamethasone (a treatment emergency)

  • Drug-susceptible TBM: isoniazid + rifampin + pyrazinamide + ethambutol (HRZE) daily for 2 months, then isoniazid + rifampin (HR) for 7–10 months. Total 9–12 months; many experts use 12 months (2HRZE/10HR). Do not substitute shorter pulmonary-TB regimens.
  • Daily adult doses (ATS/CDC/IDSA 2016): isoniazid 5 mg/kg (max 300 mg); rifampin 10 mg/kg (max 600 mg); pyrazinamide 1,000 / 1,500 / 2,000 mg and ethambutol 800 / 1,200 / 1,600 mg for 40–55 / 56–75 / 76–90 kg. Add pyridoxine 25–50 mg PO daily with isoniazid. The HARVEST trial (2025) did not show a survival benefit from its high-dose rifampin regimen; do not substitute it for standard therapy by default. Involve ID and the local TB program at diagnosis.
  • Adjunctive dexamethasone — start with TB treatment (Thwaites 2004; MRC grade I = GCS 15 without focal deficit; II = GCS 11–14, or 15 with a focal deficit; III = GCS ≤10):
    • Grade II–III — 8 weeks: IV 0.4 mg/kg/day week 1 → 0.3 week 2 → 0.2 week 3 → 0.1 mg/kg/day week 4; then oral 4 mg/day, falling by 1 mg/day each week over weeks 5–8.
    • Grade I — 6 weeks: IV 0.3 mg/kg/day week 1 → 0.2 mg/kg/day week 2; oral 0.1 mg/kg/day week 3; then oral 3 mg/day, falling by 1 mg/day each week over weeks 4–6.
  • The survival benefit is clearest in people without HIV; in HIV-positive adults the benefit was not established, so steroid use there is an individualized discussion.
  • Seek respiratory/extraneural specimens; repeat LP only if safe when suspicion stays high — and never withhold empiric treatment while searching.

Step 2 — pressure, hydrocephalus, and escalation

  • Do not perform serial LPs reflexively — there is no validated TBM-specific opening-pressure cutoff or mandatory serial-LP protocol. Follow the neuro exam and imaging.
  • If raised pressure is symptomatic and LP is safe, repeat therapeutic LPs may be considered with specialist input.
  • Urgent neurosurgical/neurocritical-care assessment for obstructive hydrocephalus, mass lesion, or herniation risk. Image for hydrocephalus, declining consciousness, or refractory intracranial hypertension — options include temporary ventricular drainage and, when needed, definitive CSF diversion.

docs.title: Neurosyphilis (adults)
docs.text:
A clinical and laboratory diagnosis — never a serum titer or a single CSF result alone. In an adult with compatible neurologic findings (meningitis, cranial neuropathy, stroke, cognitive change): serum serology and LP.

Test What it tells you Serum RPR or VDRL (quantitative) Baseline titer for follow-up Serum treponemal test (TP-PA or immunoassay) Confirms syphilis exposure; may stay reactive after treated disease — does not by itself establish active CNS disease CSF-VDRL Reactive = diagnostic (without substantial blood contamination) in a patient with neuro signs; highly specific but insensitive — a negative does NOT exclude neurosyphilis CSF-RPR Not an interchangeable, FDA-cleared substitute for CSF-VDRL CSF FTA-ABS / TP-PA Positive is less specific than CSF-VDRL; a negative makes neurosyphilis highly unlikely, especially with nonspecific symptoms CSF pleocytosis >5 WBC/mm³ is nonspecific; in HIV, >20 WBC/mm³ may improve specificity — not a stand-alone diagnostic rule

Step 1 — high-dose IV penicillin for symptomatic neurosyphilis

  • Aqueous crystalline penicillin G 18–24 million units/day IV — as 3–4 million units every 4 hours or by continuous infusion — for 10–14 days. IM benzathine penicillin G alone does not replace this regimen.
  • Ocular and otic syphilis get the same regimen even when CSF is normal; confirmed isolated ocular or auditory disease with an otherwise normal neuro exam does not change the treatment. Arrange prompt ophthalmology or otolaryngology assessment respectively before treatment when possible.
  • Adjunctive corticosteroids: sometimes used for ocular/otic syphilis, but benefit has not been proven — not a routine substitute for, and never a reason to delay, penicillin. Any use for a specific inflammatory complication is individualized with the relevant specialist.

docs.title: Neurocysticercosis (adults)
docs.text:
Diagnose and treat by lesion location, number, stage, and inflammation/obstruction. Seizures are the most common parenchymal presentation; late-onset epilepsy is a hallmark.

Step 1 — classify with imaging + serology

  • MRI + noncontrast CT: CT detects small calcifications best; MRI (with 3D volumetric sequences) delineates viable cysts, scolex, edema, ventricular/subarachnoid disease.
  • Absolute criteria: a visible scolex within a cyst on CT/MRI; histologic parasite identification; direct visualization of a subretinal cysticercus.
  • Serum T. solium EITB/immunoblot is the preferred confirmatory assay (more sensitive in serum for parenchymal disease, in CSF for extraparenchymal). Negative does NOT exclude a single lesion or calcified-only disease; antibody positivity does not prove parasites are viable. Antigen assays (serum/CSF, specialized lab) support viable cysticerci and help monitor subarachnoid disease.
  • Funduscopic exam before anthelminthics to exclude intraocular cysticerci.

Step 2 — anthelminthics + steroids (guideline regimens, not a patient-specific prescription)

  • 1–2 viable parenchymal cysts, no elevated ICP: albendazole 15 mg/kg/day PO in two divided doses with food, max 1,200 mg/day, for 10–14 days.
  • >2 viable parenchymal cysts (no elevated ICP): albendazole 15 mg/kg/day + praziquantel 50 mg/kg/day PO (praziquantel generally in three daily doses) for 10–14 days — dual therapy beats monotherapy for cyst resolution. Praziquantel monotherapy is less effective and not preferred.
  • Single enhancing lesion: albendazole 15 mg/kg/day with meals for 1–2 weeks is suggested (weaker evidence).
  • Subarachnoid disease: anthelminthics plus high-dose anti-inflammatory therapy, often far longer than parenchymal courses (can exceed a year) — specialist individualization.
  • Steroids start BEFORE the cysticidal drugs whenever antiparasitic therapy is planned. No universal dose: published parenchymal trial regimens include dexamethasone 0.1 mg/kg/day and 0.2 mg/kg/day; subarachnoid disease often needs prolonged, response-guided anti-inflammatory treatment and a slow taper; a generic 10-day course is not an adequate default. Screen for Strongyloides and latent TB when prolonged steroids are likely; monitor CBC and liver enzymes on albendazole courses >14 days.
  • Killing cysticerci can transiently worsen inflammation and neurologic symptoms — control seizures, edema, ICP, and hydrocephalus first.

Step 3 — when to avoid or defer anthelminthics

  • Diffuse cerebral edema / cysticercal encephalitis: do NOT start cysticidal therapy — it can precipitate fatal herniation. Steroids + ICP control instead.
  • Untreated hydrocephalus: contraindication — CSF diversion or surgery first.
  • Intraocular cysticerci: avoid anthelminthics — surgical removal, not antiparasitic drugs; treatment-induced inflammation can threaten vision.
  • Calcified-only lesions: no viable parasite — do NOT give anthelminthics; treat symptoms (including seizures).
  • Removable intraventricular cysts: favor neurosurgical removal; avoid preoperative anthelminthics (can inflame/disrupt the cyst).
  • Spinal NCC is not a blanket contraindication — medical or surgical per cord dysfunction, cyst location, arachnoiditis, and operative feasibility; evaluate cord compromise before starting anthelminthics.
  • Antiparasitic treatment is never an emergency — seizures and ICP come first.

docs.title: Autoimmune encephalitis — workup and treatment (adults)
docs.text:
Suspect AE with subacute (<3 months) working-memory loss, altered behavior/psychiatric symptoms, new seizures, movement disorder, speech dysfunction, catatonia, dysautonomia, or central hypoventilation. Faciobrachial dystonic seizures point toward LGI1. Normal MRI does not exclude AE. Status epilepticus, hypoventilation, or severe dysautonomia warrants monitored inpatient care and early neuroimmunology involvement.

Phenotype often points to the antibody:

Phenotype clue Think Days-onset viral-type prodrome → early psychiatric features → seizures, movement disorders (orofacial dyskinesias, chorea/dystonia), dysautonomia/hypoventilation NMDA-R >40 y, weeks-onset faciobrachial dystonic seizures + amnesia, disorientation, hyponatremia LGI1 (the commonest autoimmune limbic encephalitis in older adults; NMDA-R is commoner overall) Males >60 y, limbic features, neuromyotonia, Morvan syndrome CASPR2 Limbic encephalitis with prominent early seizures (strong SCLC association) GABA-B-R Refractory seizures/status with multifocal MRI lesions GABA-A-R Limbic encephalitis AMPA-R Insidious, often paraneoplastic, poorer immunotherapy response Intracellular/onconeural: Hu, Yo, Ri, Ma2, CV2/CRMP5, amphiphysin, GAD65

docs.title: Diagnostic criteria (Graus 2016 — syndrome-specific, not one universal scale)
docs.text:
Classification Key requirements Possible AE <3 months of working-memory deficit, altered mental status, or psychiatric symptoms; ≥1 of: new focal CNS finding, otherwise-unexplained seizure, CSF pleocytosis (>5 WBC/mm³), or MRI suggestive of encephalitis; reasonable exclusion of alternatives Probable antibody-negative AE Same subacute core; no better-defined AE syndrome; no well-characterized antibodies in serum and CSF; ≥2 of: suggestive MRI, inflammatory CSF (pleocytosis, CSF-specific oligoclonal bands, elevated IgG index), or inflammatory brain biopsy; exclusion of alternatives Probable anti-NMDAR encephalitis Rapid onset of ≥4 of 6 groups — behavior/cognition, speech, seizures, movement, consciousness, autonomic dysfunction/hypoventilation — plus abnormal EEG or inflammatory CSF; exclusion of alternatives (3 groups with a systemic teratoma can also qualify) Definite AE Syndrome-specific: definite anti-NMDAR requires a compatible symptom group + IgG anti-GluN1 in CSF with alternatives excluded; definite autoimmune limbic encephalitis can be diagnosed without an antibody — subacute limbic symptoms + bilateral medial-temporal T2/FLAIR changes + temporal EEG abnormality or CSF pleocytosis + exclusion of alternatives

A negative panel alone does not establish "probable seronegative AE"; conversely, absence of an antibody does not exclude clinically well-supported disease.

docs.title: Antibody panels — paired serum AND CSF
docs.text:
• Cell-surface/synaptic: NMDA-R (GluN1), LGI1, CASPR2, AMPA-R, GABA-A-R, GABA-B-R, DPPX, mGluR5, GlyR, dopamine-2 receptor.
  • Astrocytic/demyelinating: AQP4-IgG, MOG-IgG, GFAP-IgG — phenotype-directed (optic neuritis, myelitis, ADEM-like, cortical/brainstem lesions), not routine AE-panel substitutes.
  • Intracellular/onconeural (paraneoplastic): GAD65, Hu (ANNA-1), Yo (PCA-1), Ri (ANNA-2), Ma2, CV2/CRMP5, amphiphysin, SOX1, Tr, KLHL11.
  • CSF is more sensitive/specific for NMDA-R; LGI1 sensitivity is often higher in serum — test both. Commercial kits carry a high false-positive rate, especially serum-only (~1% of control sera); confirm with a second method in a reference lab when the picture is unclear.
  • Support with CSF analysis (oligoclonal bands, IgG index, antibody-specific indices) and routine infectious exclusion (HSV, VZV, enterovirus PCR).

Step 1 — first-line immunotherapy (start at the probable stage — do not wait for antibodies)

  • IV methylprednisolone 1 g IV daily for 3–5 days — a first-line option after appropriate infectious evaluation; often followed by an oral taper with PJP and osteoporosis prophylaxis.
  • IVIG 2 g/kg total IV over 2–5 days (commonly 0.4 g/kg/day × 5) — combine with steroids in severe disease; preferred when steroids are poorly tolerated.
  • Plasma exchange (PLEX): 5 exchanges on alternate days over ~10 days (up to 5–10 in published protocols) — alternative to IVIG alongside steroids in severe disease; do it before monoclonal B-cell therapies (PLEX depletes them).
  • For severe AE, combination first-line therapy (steroids + IVIG or PLEX) is recommended in the Canadian adult consensus.

Step 2 — second-line immunotherapy (earlier reassessment in severe disease)

  • Rituximab — preferred second-line (chosen by ~80% of experts; favored for neuronal cell-surface antibody disease): 1,000 mg IV × 2 doses 14 days apart, OR 375 mg/m² IV weekly for 4 weeks.
  • Cyclophosphamide — favored for suspected T-cell–mediated/classical paraneoplastic disease, with specialist/oncology input; the optimal regimen is not established. Published regimens: 600–1,000 mg/m² IV monthly for 3–6 months, or 15 mg/kg IV every 3 weeks for 4–6 months. Fertility concerns apply; monitor toxicity.
  • Reassess objective response and the diagnosis before escalation. In severe AE, no improvement/worsening after about 5–10 days of optimized first-line therapy may justify second-line treatment under the Canadian 2024 consensus. Other guidance generally uses 2–4 weeks. Reassess the diagnosis and trajectory with neuroimmunology, and individualize escalation in fulminant disease. Canadian consensus.
  • Refractory/third-line options (plasma-cell or cytokine directed): bortezomib, tocilizumab, daratumumab; emerging agents (inebilizumab, ofatumumab, efgartigimod, CAR-T).

Step 3 — tumor screening (at the initial evaluation — do not wait for antibody results)

  • NMDA-R: an underlying tumor in ~38% overall — almost always an ovarian teratoma, usually mature (benign), most often in women aged 12–45 — pelvic ultrasound/MRI, with follow-up imaging; tumor removal accelerates recovery.
  • Modality approach: CT chest/abdomen/pelvis; if negative, whole-body FDG-PET; mammography ± breast MRI; testicular ultrasound in men (especially Ma2); PET does not replace dedicated pelvic imaging for a possible teratoma.
  • High-risk antibody (Hu, CV2/CRMP5, Ma2, amphiphysin, GABA-B-R/SCLC) or high-risk phenotype with a negative first screen: repeat every 4–6 months for 2 years (2021 PNS-Care criteria — the interval the LEMS page uses); intensify with older age, smoking, or cancer history.

docs.title: Military and regional exposures
docs.text:
The exposures this population actually has — recruits in open-bay barracks, field training in tick country, and Soldiers back from deployment. Each one changes the empiric plan.

Meningococcal disease in trainees — treat, isolate, report

  • Fever + headache/meningism or a petechial/purpuric rash in a trainee → ceftriaxone 2 g IV now (do not wait for LP), droplet precautions for the first 24 hours of effective therapy, and call preventive medicine immediately — it is reportable, and contact tracing starts the same day.
  • Close-contact chemoprophylaxis (public-health-defined household/room contacts or direct oral-secretion exposures in the relevant pre-onset period — ideally within 24 h; not automatically an entire unit): ciprofloxacin 500 mg PO once, or rifampin 600 mg PO q12h × 2 days, or ceftriaxone 250 mg IM once (the choice in pregnancy). Check current CDC/local advisories for ciprofloxacin-resistant strains before relying on it.
  • MenACWY at accession lowers but does not abolish the risk — a vaccinated trainee with this picture is meningococcal until proven otherwise.

Tick-borne and arboviral — Missouri and the Ozarks

  • Fever + headache ± confusion after field time, April–September: start doxycycline 100 mg PO/IV q12h empirically for Rocky Mountain spotted fever and ehrlichiosis (Missouri is a high-incidence state for both); continue ≥3 days after defervescence, minimum 5–7 days. Do not wait for serology — thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, hyponatremia and transaminitis support it.
  • Heartland and Bourbon virus (Lone Star tick): fever, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, occasionally meningoencephalitis — no specific therapy; supportive care, testing through the state health department/CDC. "Ehrlichiosis" that does not respond to doxycycline is the clue.
  • Lyme neuroborreliosis (uncommon in Missouri — ask about prior postings and leave): facial palsy, radiculoneuritis, or lymphocytic meningitis → ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily or doxycycline 100 mg PO BID (or 200 mg once daily) for 14–21 days (IDSA/AAN/ACR 2020); parenchymal brain or spinal cord disease → IV.
  • West Nile neuroinvasive disease (late summer): meningitis, encephalitis, or acute flaccid paralysis — CSF WNV IgM; supportive care only.

Back from deployment or overseas travel

  • Fever + encephalopathy, seizures or coma after a malaria zone = cerebral malaria until proven otherwise — prophylaxis adherence does not exclude it. Thick/thin smears (repeat q12–24h × 3) or rapid antigen now; do not wait for confirmation in a sick patient. IV artesunate 2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12 and 24 h; reassess smears. Continue daily if needed under CDC guidance until parasitemia ≤1% and oral treatment is tolerated, then give a complete oral follow-on course. CDC’s August 2026 update recommends 5 days/10 doses of artemether-lumefantrine when used as follow-on for P. falciparum. Monitor for delayed hemolytic anemia weekly through 4 weeks after treatment begins.
  • Animal bite or bat exposure, abroad or at home — rabies post-exposure prophylaxis if never vaccinated: wound washing, human rabies immune globulin 20 IU/kg infiltrated into and around the wound, and rabies vaccine 1 mL IM (deltoid) on days 0, 3, 7 and 14 (add day 28 if immunocompromised). Previously vaccinated: vaccine on days 0 and 3, no HRIG. Clinical rabies is almost uniformly fatal — prevention is the whole game.
  • Also by region: Japanese encephalitis (Asia), tick-borne encephalitis (Europe), neurocysticercosis and TB meningitis (above).

docs.title: Disposition
docs.text:
• Admit: altered mentation, seizures, focal deficit, elevated opening pressure, respiratory compromise, suspected HSV/TBM, or any patient needing IV antimicrobials, serial LPs, or immunotherapy — this is overwhelmingly an inpatient disease family.
  • ICU: status epilepticus, refractory ICP, hydrocephalus, severe dysautonomia or hypoventilation (AE), posterior-fossa abscess, or TBM with declining consciousness.
  • Follow-up: repeat LPs (cryptococcal pressure/culture, TBM safety), interval imaging (abscess, NCC), serologic follow-up (neurosyphilis titers, cryptococcal consolidation), tumor surveillance (AE/paraneoplastic), and seizure/rehab planning.

Military medicine — duty, retention and deployment

  • Profile / function: Treat and evacuate acute CNS infection or encephalitis as indicated; coordinate public-health/preventive-medicine reporting and targeted exposure management.
  • Retention / MEB–MAR2: After recovery, assess residual cognition, seizures, motor function and the underlying disease. Infection diagnosis alone does not establish lifelong disability. Use the retention framework; permanent P3/4 does not by itself select DES versus MAR2.
  • Deployment / medications: Active infection, isolation needs, prolonged treatment, recurrent seizures and immunosuppression may prevent deployment; reassess diagnosis and every continuing drug before clearance. See the disease AND drug screen for the current CENTCOM rules and waiver packet.
  • Special duty: flight, diving and other special assignments have separate standards and waiver authorities; a general duty profile does not clear them.
  • LOD / EPTS: document onset, duty status, exposures and aggravation objectively. The designated authority determines LOD/EPTS; neither in-service diagnosis nor a genetic finding settles it automatically.

docs.title: 📚 Discover — evidence brief
docs.text:
Written from primary guidelines and trials; source articles are a reading list, not copied.

  • Steroids ride with the first antibiotic dose in bacterial meningitis (de Gans/van de Beek) — and stop when CSF says "not bacterial." NICE and WHO durations differ (10 vs 7 days); they are not interchangeable.
  • Treat HSV encephalitis for 14–21 days, not the 10-day label, and re-tap in 3–7 days when PCR is negative but suspicion stays high.
  • Brain abscess: ceftriaxone + metronidazole is a common community-acquired backbone; the source picks the third agent (cefepime for credible Pseudomonas, vancomycin for staph). Six to eight weeks IV; aspiration over excision for most.
  • Cryptococcal meningitis: the AMBITION single–high-dose liposomal amphotericin B regimen changed resource-limited induction; pressure is managed with serial therapeutic LPs, not acetazolamide; and ART is deferred 4–6 weeks — the opposite of most OIs.
  • TB meningitis is a treatment emergency — Xpert Ultra plus empiric HRZE, with a 6–8 week dexamethasone taper whose survival benefit is clearest without HIV.
  • Neurocysticercosis: albendazole + praziquantel beats monotherapy for >2 viable cysts; steroids start before the cysticidal drugs; never treat through uncontrolled ICP or hydrocephalus.
  • Train for the exposures this force has: meningococcal disease in barracks (treat, isolate, report, prophylax contacts), rickettsial infection after field time in Missouri (doxycycline before serology), and cerebral malaria in anyone back from a malaria zone (IV artesunate now).
  • Autoimmune encephalitis: start immunotherapy at the probable stage on paired serum+CSF panels; a negative panel neither proves seronegative AE nor excludes well-supported disease; screen for tumor at presentation, not after the antibodies return.

Key sources: WHO 2025 meningitis guidelines; NICE NG240 (2024); IDSA bacterial meningitis (2004), healthcare-associated ventriculitis/meningitis (2017), and encephalitis (2008) guidelines; ESCMID brain abscess guideline (Bodilsen 2024); NIH cryptococcosis OI guidelines (2024); WHO cryptococcal guidelines (2022); AMBITION (Jarvis, NEJM 2022) and COAT (Boulware, NEJM 2014); British Infection Society CNS TB guidelines; ATS/CDC/IDSA TB treatment (2016); Lancet Infectious Diseases TBM guideline (2025); Thwaites dexamethasone TBM trial (NEJM 2004); CDC syphilis STI and lab guidelines (2021/2024); IDSA/ASTMH neurocysticercosis guidelines (2018) and Del Brutto revised criteria (2017); Graus AE criteria (2016), Abboud best-practice recommendations (2021), Canadian AE consensus (2024), and paraneoplastic criteria update (2021).

docs.title: Immunocompromised patient — two additional night-shift traps
docs.text:
• HIV-associated cerebral toxoplasmosis: contrast MRI, CD4 count, Toxoplasma IgG and urgent ID involvement. Typical ring-enhancing lesions may justify an empiric treatment trial while lymphoma and other diagnoses remain in the differential. One NIH-preferred regimen is TMP 5 mg/kg + SMX 25 mg/kg IV/PO twice daily, adjusted for organ function, for at least 6 weeks, then maintenance until immune-reconstitution criteria are met. Obtain a tissue diagnosis earlier for atypical findings, deterioration during the first week, or absent clinical improvement by 10–14 days. Do not start steroids merely because lesions enhance; reserve them for clinically significant mass effect/edema.
  • PML: progressive focal deficits in an immunocompromised patient need MRI and CSF JCV PCR; a negative result does not always exclude it. Restore immune function with specialist input (including effective ART in HIV); acyclovir does not treat JCV. Reassess for IRIS if deterioration follows immune recovery.

2026 infectious encephalitis guideline: start IV acyclovir promptly when encephalitis is suspected. A negative multiplex panel does not replace pathogen-specific CSF testing when suspicion persists. The EAN–ESCMID guideline makes no recommendation for or against adjunct steroids in proven HSV encephalitis because evidence remains insufficient. Repeat HSV PCR/LP according to timing and clinical suspicion; do not stop treatment from a single prematurely negative sample.

docs.text:
1. World Health Organization. WHO guidelines on meningitis diagnosis, treatment and care. Geneva: WHO; 2025 — empiric regimens, dexamethasone timing, CSF interpretation tables.
