docs.title: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS)
docs.text:
Last reviewed: August 2026

One-liner: an antibody attack on presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels that throttles acetylcholine release — proximal weakness, autonomic dysfunction, and hyporeflexia. Half the time it is the first sign of a small-cell lung cancer.

Who this is for: anyone working up proximal weakness that looks like myasthenia but isn't behaving — and the reason the page exists is that finding LEMS means starting a cancer hunt.

🚩 LEMS is a paraneoplastic red flag until proven otherwise

~50–60% of LEMS is paraneoplastic, and the tumor is almost always small-cell lung cancer (SCLC). The neurologic syndrome frequently precedes the cancer diagnosis by months to years — so a new LEMS diagnosis is a mandate to search, and to keep searching if the first scan is clean.

  • Begin with high-quality chest CT; add FDG-PET/CT when initial imaging is negative or equivocal and suspicion remains, or under the specialist’s high-risk screening plan. Do not infer that every patient needs simultaneous CT and PET from a small sensitivity series. A chest radiograph is inadequate to exclude SCLC.

  • Repeat imaging every 4–6 months for 2 years if the initial search is negative (2021 PNS-Care criteria for high-risk phenotypes) — the tumor may not yet be radiologically visible.

  • Two years is a common initial surveillance framework, not a guarantee of no future cancer: 91–92% of SCLCs are found within 3 months of the LEMS diagnosis and 96% within 1 year. Detections beyond 2 years occurred almost entirely in patients who had been screened inadequately.
  • The strongest single risk factor is smoking. A smoker with LEMS has SCLC until proven otherwise.

docs.title: The triad that separates it from MG
docs.text:
Feature LEMS Myasthenia gravis Weakness pattern Proximal, legs > arms; gait first Ocular/bulbar first; fatigable On brief exercise Transiently improves (post-exercise facilitation) Worsens Reflexes Reduced or absent — and may return after exercise Normal Autonomic features Prominent — dry mouth, erectile dysfunction, constipation, orthostasis Absent Ocular involvement Mild or late Common, early Antibody P/Q-type VGCC (~90%; near 100% in SCLC-associated disease) AChR / MuSK Cancer link SCLC in ~50–60% Thymoma in 10–15%

The counterintuitive sign: strength and reflexes that improve after a few seconds of exercise (facilitation) point to LEMS, not MG. Dry mouth is the most consistent autonomic clue and is easy to ask about.

docs.title: Diagnosis
docs.text:
• Serology — P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channel (VGCC) antibody, positive in ~90% (range 85–95%; approaching 100% in SCLC-associated disease, ~91% in non-cancer LEMS).
    • Do not order N-type VGCC antibody — it lacks diagnostic value in LEMS.
    • P/Q-type positivity does not distinguish paraneoplastic from non-paraneoplastic disease and has no role in cancer risk stratification. SOX1 antibody does — 95% specific but only 65% sensitive for SCLC-LEMS, so a positive result is informative and a negative one is not.
  • Electrodiagnostics are characteristic and confirmatory:
    • Low baseline CMAP amplitude.
    • Decrement on low-frequency (2–5 Hz, usually 3 Hz) RNS, ≥10% — like MG, present in 94–98% but not specific.
    • But marked facilitation — CMAP amplitude increase ≥60% after 10 seconds of maximal exercise or after 20 Hz stimulation. Use ≥60% as the operating threshold (97% sensitive, 99% specific); the older ≥100% cut-off is more specific but misses 4–16%. This post-exercise facilitation is the signature and distinguishes it from MG.
    • High-frequency (20–50 Hz) stimulation works but is very painful — avoid it when post-exercise testing is feasible.
    • A subtler discriminator: on low-frequency RNS the decrement nadir falls at the 7th–10th stimulus in LEMS vs the 4th–5th in MG (cut-off 6.5, AUC 0.90).

  • The DELTA-P score stratifies SCLC risk and guides how aggressively to hunt — 1 point each, maximum 6, assessed at onset or within 3 months:

    Component Age at onset ≥50 years 1 Smoking at diagnosis 1 Weight loss ≥5% 1 Bulbar involvement 1 Erectile dysfunction (males) 1 Karnofsky performance status <70 1

    0–1 → 0–2.6% probability of SCLC; 4–6 → 83.9–100%. Prospective validation AUC 82.5% (the 94% figure comes from the derivation cohort and overstates real-world performance). The score shortens the surveillance interval — it never cancels the search. Every LEMS patient is screened regardless of score.

docs.title: The prescriptive flow (what I want done, in order)
docs.text:
1. Recognize the triad — proximal weakness + autonomic features + hyporeflexia, with facilitation.
  2. Confirm — VGCC antibody + EDx showing post-exercise facilitation.
  3. Hunt for cancer — this is the priority. CT chest, PET/CT when indicated → risk-adapted repeat imaging, often every 4–6 months for 2 years in high-risk patients. Score DELTA-P to set the interval, not to decide whether to look.
  4. Treat symptoms — amifampridine, divided 3–5× daily, titrated toward 50–80 mg/day.
  5. Treat the cause — the tumor (paraneoplastic) or immunotherapy (autoimmune/non-tumor).
  6. Military disposition — and note that a paraneoplastic LEMS is a cancer diagnosis first.

docs.title: Treatment
docs.text:
Step 1 — symptomatic: amifampridine

Amifampridine (3,4-diaminopyridine; Firdapse) — the FDA-approved first-line symptomatic therapy (2018; label covers adults and children ≥6 years). A potassium-channel blocker that prolongs the presynaptic action potential, increasing calcium influx and ACh release.

Adults / ≥45 kg Children <45 kg Start 15–30 mg/day 5–15 mg/day Titrate +5 mg/day every 3–4 days +2.5 mg/day every 3–4 days Max single dose 20 mg 10 mg Max daily 100 mg (US label) 50 mg
  • Divided dosing is mandatory, not stylistic — 3–5 times daily. The half-life is 1.8–2.5 hours (Tmax 20 min–1 h), so twice-daily dosing produces symptomatic troughs. Patients feel each dose within the hour.
  • The ceiling you should actually work to is 80 mg/day. The US label maximum is 100 mg/day, but 80 mg/day is both the EMA ceiling and the widely adopted expert cap on seizure-risk grounds — these are two different numbers, not a range. Real-world dosing sits well below either: mean 50.5 mg/day in the pivotal run-in and 66 mg/day long-term. Target 50–80 mg/day divided 3–4×.
  • Lower the starting dose in renal impairment (CLcr 15–90), any hepatic impairment, age ≥65, and — most importantly — NAT2 poor metabolizers. No dosing recommendation exists for ESRD or dialysis; it has not been studied.
  • NAT2 status matters more than renal function, and it is not a rare edge case. Poor acetylators have 3.5–4.5× the Cmax and 5.6–9× the AUC of rapid acetylators. Prevalence is 40–60% in White and African American populations, 10–30% in Japanese, Chinese and Korean populations. Start low.
  • Seizures occur in ~2% of patients without prior history and are dose-dependent; a prior seizure is an absolute contraindication, as is aminopyridine hypersensitivity. The reported seizures clustered at 100 mg/day, in a patient with brain metastases, and in one on high-dose theophylline — concomitant threshold-lowering drugs matter more than the absolute dose. A dedicated QTc study found no clinically relevant prolongation, so routine ECG monitoring is not required.
  • Expect paresthesia — it is the commonest adverse effect at 62%. Perioral and digital, starting within minutes of a ≥10 mg dose and lasting 5–10 minutes. Warn the patient in advance; most come to treat it as a marker that the dose has landed rather than a reason to stop. Also >10%: URI 33%; abdominal pain, nausea, diarrhea, headache, elevated LFTs and back pain ~14% each.
  • In children, watch weight — clinically significant weight loss occurred at doses ≥60 mg/day.

Pyridostigmine — not a substitute, but worth a trial as an add-on

The page used to say it "adds little," which is stronger than the evidence supports. The only randomized trial was intravenous, single-dose, and enrolled 9 patients (pyridostigmine alone was no better than placebo, and adding it to IV 3,4-DAP conferred no extra benefit). Chronic oral co-administration has never been randomized, and the observational signal runs the other way: 68% of a long-term cohort used it and 67% reported subjective benefit, and 13 of 25 patients in an open-label extension improved further when it was added.

Reasonable position: amifampridine first and always; a trial of oral pyridostigmine is justified in incomplete responders, where the risk is low and the potential benefit real.

Step 2 — treat the underlying driver

Paraneoplastic LEMS: treat the SCLC. Cancer treatment improves the neurologic syndrome — 7 of 11 patients surviving >2 months after tumor therapy improved substantially, one to complete remission at 7 years, though in 3 the improvement was transient. A pretreatment CMAP amplitude >3.0 mV predicts a better neurologic outcome. Expect 6–12 months, not weeks.

Non-tumor (autoimmune) LEMS: immunotherapy. Be honest with yourself about the evidence — no randomized trial exists for any oral immunosuppressant, or for plasma exchange, in LEMS.

  • Prednisone + azathioprine — first-line immunosuppression, open-label evidence only. Needed in 70% of non-tumor LEMS vs 44% of SCLC-LEMS. The regimen behind the best-reported results is prednisolone 60–100 mg on alternate days plus azathioprine 2.5 mg/kg/day (near-complete remission in 3 of 6 non-cancer patients within 6–12 months). Check TPMT and NUDT15 before azathioprine, and monitor CBC — see the MG page for the full monitoring schedule and the allopurinol interaction. Mycophenolate mofetil 1,000 mg PO BID is a reasonable substitute if azathioprine is not tolerated, but has no LEMS-specific data at all — and carries a boxed warning for embryofetal toxicity.
  • IVIG 2 g/kg over 2 days — the one crossover RCT (n=9) showed significant limb, bulbar and respiratory gains with a fall in VGCC titre; peak at 2–4 weeks, declining by 8. An acute or bridging option; selected refractory patients may receive individualized maintenance, with limited supporting evidence.
  • Plasma exchange — open-label only; 8 of 9 responded, peak at 10–15 days. For acute severe or rapidly progressive weakness.
  • Rituximab — fourth-line, for refractory disease, on case-level evidence only. No LEMS-specific protocol exists; the borrowed MG regimens are 375 mg/m² IV weekly × 4 or 1 g IV × 2 doses two weeks apart. Off-label. Screen HBsAg and anti-HBc before the first dose — boxed warning.
  • Give it time. Treatment effect on functional scales is generally reached at 6–12 months; escalating before then is usually premature. Treatment is typically indefinite, but sustained remission does occur — 5 of 63 patients stopped everything at a median of 4 years and stayed in remission for a median of 12 — so a cautious withdrawal trial is reasonable in durable remission.

Do not extrapolate the myasthenia biologics to LEMS

None of the agents that reorganized MG care has been trialed in LEMS. For complement inhibitors (eculizumab, ravulizumab, zilucoplan) this is a mechanistic mismatch, not merely a gap in the evidence — LEMS neuromuscular junctions do not show complement deposits, LEMS IgG works just as well in C5-deficient mice, and complement-incapable F(ab')₂ fragments transfer the phenotype. The mechanism is cross-linking and depletion of calcium channels, not membrane attack complex. Complement inhibition should not be expected to work here.

FcRn inhibitors have a better theoretical rationale, since LEMS is IgG-mediated — but remain untested in LEMS. Anti-CD19 CAR T has two case reports in MG/LEMS overlap: striking (wheelchair to full mobility in 2 months) and investigational, n=2.

Two exposures that catch LEMS patients out

  • Anesthesia and neuromuscular blockade. LEMS patients are markedly sensitive to neuromuscular blocking drugs. In a series of 37 patients across 60 operations, 4 (11%) had respiratory complications — and 3 of those were undiagnosed or untreated at the time. The risk concentrates in the patient nobody knew had LEMS. Tell anesthesia before any procedure, especially before thoracic surgery in a paraneoplastic case.
  • Immune checkpoint inhibitors can worsen pre-existing LEMS and have been reported to trigger de novo LEMS in neurologically asymptomatic SCLC patients. The causal evidence is graded low and rests largely on case reports — treat it as grounds for vigilance, not an established causal link. It matters increasingly, because checkpoint inhibitors are standard in exactly this population.

Same NMJ-drug cautions as MG

LEMS shares MG's sensitivity to neuromuscular-blocking drugs — aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, IV magnesium, and neuromuscular blockers can all worsen it. If a paraneoplastic patient is heading for thoracic surgery or chemotherapy, flag the NMJ sensitivity to the anesthesia and oncology teams. See the MG precipitant list.

Military medicine — duty, retention and deployment

  • Profile / function: Bulbar or respiratory weakness is an evacuation/airway problem before it is a profile problem. After stabilization document fatigability, strength, swallowing, autonomic effects and task endurance.
  • Retention / MEB–MAR2: Generalized MG: DoDI V2 5.26.l, Army 3-31c; ocular-only disease has a specific exception. LEMS, botulism and toxic paralysis require the applicable neuromuscular/functional standard, trajectory and recovery assessment. Use the retention framework; permanent P3/4 does not by itself select DES versus MAR2.
  • Deployment / medications: Assess crisis risk, treatment interruption, infection, monitoring, immunosuppression and injection/infusion support. Acute botulism/nerve-agent injury needs treatment/evacuation and exposure reporting, followed by cause-specific clearance. See the disease AND drug screen for the current CENTCOM rules and waiver packet.
  • Special duty: flight, diving and other special assignments have separate standards and waiver authorities; a general duty profile does not clear them.
  • LOD / EPTS: document onset, duty status, exposures and aggravation objectively. The designated authority determines LOD/EPTS; neither in-service diagnosis nor a genetic finding settles it automatically.

TRICARE — verified rules and the current form

Firdapse requires pharmacy PA in the official October 2026 list. The current manual diagnostic/prior-treatment/renewal form was not obtained; document the confirmed LEMS diagnosis and response, then obtain the form before promising approval. IVIG/immune therapy may need medical-benefit and site authorization.

Current PA/MN details, benefit routing and packet · Live Formulary Search. Check the exact product, beneficiary and venue on the prescribing date.

docs.title: 📚 Discover — evidence brief
docs.text:
Presynaptic, not postsynaptic — and that is the whole story. In LEMS, antibodies against P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels on the motor nerve terminal reduce the calcium influx that triggers acetylcholine vesicle release. Fewer quanta are released per impulse, so the first contraction is weak — but a burst of activity transiently loads the terminal with calcium, briefly increasing release and producing the facilitation that defines the syndrome on exam and on EMG. The same channels sit on autonomic terminals, which is why dry mouth and orthostasis travel with the weakness. It is the mirror image of myasthenia gravis, where the defect is postsynaptic receptor loss and repeated activity only worsens transmission.

The tumor connection is mechanistic. Small-cell lung cancer expresses functional voltage-gated calcium channels, and the anti-tumor immune response cross-reacts with the identical channels at the neuromuscular junction. LEMS is, in a real sense, the immune system finding the cancer before the radiologist does — which is exactly why the neurologic diagnosis obligates the search.

And that immune response appears to help. SCLC with LEMS carries substantially better survival than SCLC alone — median 17 vs 7 months in the Dutch registry and 18 vs 9.5 in a prospective UK cohort, with 5-year survival 21% vs 4.4%. The advantage persists in extensive disease and survives adjustment for stage, age, sex, performance status and sodium, so it is not simply lead-time bias from earlier detection. Tellingly, SCLC patients with low-titre VGCC antibodies but no clinical LEMS get no survival benefit — it appears to be the functionally pathogenic antibody response that matters. NCCN states plainly that the presence of LEMS does not imply metastatic or incurable disease. Counsel the patient accordingly; a paraneoplastic diagnosis here is not the worst version of an SCLC diagnosis.

But do not use the LEMS as a tumor monitor. This is the counterintuitive correction to a tempting assumption. Of 9 patients followed through tumor recurrence, only 2 had simultaneous worsening of their LEMS, and in both the link was questionable. The syndrome frequently does not flare when the cancer comes back. Oncologic surveillance runs on its own schedule; neurologic stability is not reassurance.

Key evidence:

  • Firdapse (amifampridine) FDA approval, 2018, expanded to children ≥6 years — the only amifampridine product now marketed in the US.
  • P/Q-type VGCC antibody — the confirmatory serology (~90%); SOX1 for cancer risk.
  • DELTA-P score — stratifies SCLC risk at diagnosis (prospective AUC 82.5%).
  • 2021 PNS-Care criteria — 4–6 monthly surveillance for 2 years in high-risk phenotypes.
  • Wirtz 2009 — the only randomized pyridostigmine trial (IV, n=9), and the reason the oral-add-on question is still open.
  • Amifampridine failed in myasthenia gravis (2026) — a negative randomized crossover trial of amifampridine added to pyridostigmine in AChR-positive MG. The presynaptic drug does not transfer to the postsynaptic disease, which is a neat confirmation of the mechanism.

docs.title: Nerve agent & organophosphate poisoning
docs.text:
Last reviewed: July 2026

One-liner: poisoning of the synaptic enzyme — acetylcholinesterase inhibition floods every cholinergic synapse with acetylcholine, producing a cholinergic crisis: muscarinic secretions, nicotinic paralysis, and CNS seizures. Death is by respiratory failure. The antidotes are atropine and pralidoxime, and decontamination protects everyone else.

Who this is for: the provider facing a cholinergic-crisis patient — nerve agent (sarin, VX, Novichok) in a CBRN or terrorism setting, or the far commoner organophosphate/carbamate pesticide poisoning. Recognize the shared cholinergic toxidrome, but oxime benefit differs by agent; known isolated carbamate poisoning needs toxicology advice rather than automatic OP extrapolation.

🚩 Recognize the cholinergic toxidrome — and protect yourself first

Two mnemonics, both worth knowing:

  • Muscarinic — DUMBELS: Defecation, Urination, Miosis, Bronchorrhea/Bronchospasm, Emesis, Lacrimation, Salivation. Bronchorrhea and bronchospasm are what kill — the patient drowns in secretions.
  • Nicotinic — "days of the week" MTWtHF: Mydriasis (can occur), Tachycardia, Weakness, Twitching/fasciculations, Hypertension, Fasciculations. Progresses to flaccid paralysis, including the diaphragm.
  • CNS: agitation, seizures, coma.

The classic bedside signal is pinpoint pupils + copious secretions + fasciculations in a collapsing patient.

Protect responders; decontamination and lifesaving treatment run together

Nerve agents and OPs are absorbed through skin and off-gas from clothing and vomit. A provider who treats an undecontaminated patient becomes the next casualty.

  • Don appropriate PPE. Remove all clothing (removes the majority of contaminant). Decontaminate skin (copious water; the RSDL kit for military nerve-agent decon).
  • This is a mass-casualty pattern — one index case with a cholinergic toxidrome and no trauma should raise a release/exposure event and trigger the CBRN chain.

docs.title: Mechanism in one line
docs.text: Acetylcholinesterase normally clears acetylcholine from the synapse. Inhibit it, and ACh piles up everywhere — at muscarinic (parasympathetic), nicotinic (neuromuscular junction and autonomic ganglia), and central synapses. This is the mechanistic opposite of myasthenia gravis (too little cholinergic transmission) — and, tellingly, an overdose of pyridostigmine or other cholinesterase inhibitors produces the same crisis.

docs.title: The prescriptive flow (what I want done, in order)
docs.text:
1. Protect responders — scene safety and appropriate PPE. Begin decontamination while protected personnel give lifesaving antidotes, suction, oxygen, and ventilation; do not wait for the end of decontamination in a crashing casualty.
  2. Airway and oxygen — suction the secretions; prepare for intubation.
  3. Atropine, immediately and aggressively — titrate to drying of secretions, not pupils or heart rate.
  4. Pralidoxime (an oxime) — reactivate the enzyme, before it "ages."
  5. Benzodiazepine — for seizures, and empirically in severe exposure.
  6. Escalate and support — mechanical ventilation, ICU, repeat/continuous atropine.
  7. Report — CBRN, public health, and (for occupational/pesticide) the appropriate authority.

docs.title: Treatment
docs.text:
Step 1 — atropine, titrated to secretions

  • Atropine 1–3 mg IV (2–6 mg in severe cases), doubling every 3–5 minutes until bronchial secretions dry and ventilation eases.
  • The endpoint is drying of secretions and improved oxygenation — NOT pupil size or heart rate. Miosis and bradycardia can persist despite adequate atropinization; chasing them leads to under- or over-dosing.
  • Severe poisoning can require tens to hundreds of milligrams over the resuscitation, then a continuous infusion. Do not under-dose out of caution about "normal" doses.
  • Atropine blocks the muscarinic effects; it does nothing for nicotinic weakness/paralysis — which is why the oxime matters.

Step 2 — pralidoxime (oxime), before the enzyme ages

  • Pralidoxime (2-PAM) 1–2 g IV over ~15–30 min (avoid bolus-induced hypertension), then a continuous infusion for severe poisoning.
  • Reactivates acetylcholinesterase before aging — an antidote addressing the nicotinic (neuromuscular) weakness.
  • "Aging" is the clock: the agent–enzyme bond becomes irreversible over time and the oxime no longer works. Aging is fast for some agents (soman in ~2 minutes), slower for most OP pesticides (hours). Give the oxime as early as possible — do not withhold it waiting for atropine to work; they are complementary.

Step 3 — benzodiazepine for seizures / severe exposure

  • Adult seizure rescue: midazolam 10 mg IM if >40 kg when IV access is unavailable; with IV access, diazepam 0.15–0.2 mg/kg IV (maximum 10 mg) is an alternative. Support ventilation and follow the status-epilepticus escalation protocol for persistent seizures.
  • Severe nerve-agent exposure: give the authorized field benzodiazepine per the CBRN protocol even before overt seizures when indicated. Do not replace the antidote/ventilation plan with a sedative alone.

Military autoinjectors — the field antidote

Warfighter self-aid/buddy-aid for nerve-agent exposure delivers the same three drugs:

  • ATNAA / DuoDote — a single autoinjector combining atropine (2.1 mg) + pralidoxime (600 mg) (ATNAA is the military designation; DuoDote the civilian EMS equivalent; the older Mark I kit was two separate injectors).
  • CANA (Convulsant Antidote, Nerve Agent) — diazepam 10 mg autoinjector for seizures.
  • Doctrine: repeat atropine/2-PAM autoinjectors per symptoms and training, then evacuate to definitive care and continuous therapy.

What not to do

  • Do not give succinylcholine — it is metabolized by the same cholinesterase the agent has inhibited, so its paralytic effect is massively prolonged. Use a non-depolarizing agent if paralysis is needed for intubation.
  • Do not delay the oxime waiting to see the atropine response — aging is irreversible.
  • Do not treat before decontamination unless you are in PPE — you will become a casualty.

TRICARE — emergency treatment and follow-up

Use emergency antidote stocks and the authorized clinical/logistics pathway for atropine, pralidoxime and seizure treatment. Routine outpatient PA is not a prerequisite for treating poisoning. For residual symptoms and follow-up prescriptions, verify the exact product and service benefit.

Coverage and benefit routing.

Military medicine — duty, retention and deployment

  • Profile / function: Bulbar or respiratory weakness is an evacuation/airway problem before it is a profile problem. After stabilization document fatigability, strength, swallowing, autonomic effects and task endurance.
  • Retention / MEB–MAR2: Generalized MG: DoDI V2 5.26.l, Army 3-31c; ocular-only disease has a specific exception. LEMS, botulism and toxic paralysis require the applicable neuromuscular/functional standard, trajectory and recovery assessment. Use the retention framework; permanent P3/4 does not by itself select DES versus MAR2.
  • Deployment / medications: Assess crisis risk, treatment interruption, infection, monitoring, immunosuppression and injection/infusion support. Acute botulism/nerve-agent injury needs treatment/evacuation and exposure reporting, followed by cause-specific clearance. See the disease AND drug screen for the current CENTCOM rules and waiver packet.
  • Special duty: flight, diving and other special assignments have separate standards and waiver authorities; a general duty profile does not clear them.
  • LOD / EPTS: document onset, duty status, exposures and aggravation objectively. The designated authority determines LOD/EPTS; neither in-service diagnosis nor a genetic finding settles it automatically.

docs.title: 📚 Discover — evidence brief
docs.text:
One enzyme, every cholinergic synapse. Acetylcholinesterase terminates cholinergic signaling by hydrolyzing acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft. Organophosphates and nerve agents phosphorylate the enzyme's active site, and while it is inhibited, acetylcholine accumulates at muscarinic, nicotinic, and central synapses simultaneously — which is why the toxidrome is so florid and multi-system. Atropine competitively blocks the muscarinic receptors (drying the lethal secretions), while pralidoxime attacks the problem upstream, prising the phosphoryl group off the enzyme to restore acetylcholinesterase itself — the only way to fix the nicotinic weakness that atropine can't touch.

"Aging" is why minutes matter. The phosphorylated enzyme undergoes a spontaneous chemical change — loss of an alkyl group — that makes the bond permanent. After aging, pralidoxime is useless and recovery depends on synthesizing new enzyme over days to weeks. Aging half-times vary enormously: soman ages in about two minutes, making oxime therapy nearly futile once symptoms are established, whereas many pesticide OPs age over many hours, leaving a real reactivation window. This single kinetic fact drives the doctrine of giving the oxime as early as possible and the military interest in pretreatment to shield a fraction of enzyme before exposure.

The MG connection, both directions. Nerve-agent poisoning is mechanistically an acetylcholinesterase-inhibitor overdose — the same drug class (pyridostigmine) used to treat myasthenia gravis. Push a cholinesterase inhibitor too far and you convert therapy into a cholinergic crisis; that is exactly the "cholinergic crisis vs myasthenic crisis" distinction at the MG bedside, and it is the reason pyridostigmine pretreatment against nerve agents is dosed and monitored so carefully.

Key references:

  • CHEMM (HHS) — Medical Countermeasures: atropine, pralidoxime for nerve-agent/OP exposure.
  • Organophosphorus nerve-agent poisoning — managing the poisoned patient (Br J Anaesth 2020).
  • Nerve agents — StatPearls.

docs.title: Acute weakness and Guillain–Barré syndrome
docs.text:
Last reviewed: November 2026

One-liner: Check breathing and swallowing while you localize. A patient can still be talking while their respiratory reserve is shrinking.

Get help now

Weak cough, difficulty handling secretions, bulbar weakness, respiratory distress, rapid progression, or marked blood pressure or heart-rate swings need early ICU and airway involvement. A reassuring oxygen saturation alone cannot exclude neuromuscular hypoventilation. Sudden asymmetric weakness goes to the stroke pathway. A sensory level, new retention or saddle symptoms warrants urgent spinal evaluation.

docs.title: What to do in order
docs.text:
Step 1 — Stabilize and localize

  1. Assess airway protection, voice, cough and breathing effort. Check vitals and bedside glucose. Monitor ECG and blood pressure if GBS is suspected. Keep oral intake on hold if swallowing is unsafe.
  2. Obtain baseline and serial forced vital capacity (FVC) and inspiratory/expiratory pressures where available. Record the trend, patient position, effort and quality of the mouth seal. If respiratory testing is unavailable, follow speech, cough, effort and secretion handling while arranging transfer as indicated.
  3. Measure limb and neck strength and reflexes. Map sensory loss and check for ocular symptoms, a sensory level or sphincter dysfunction. Review the time course, recent infection, medication changes and exposures. Use targeted electrolytes, including potassium, magnesium and phosphate, and CK when the pattern suggests metabolic weakness or myopathy.
Pattern Working route Progressive, relatively symmetric limb weakness with reduced reflexes, paresthesias or neuropathic pain GBS. Check facial, bulbar and autonomic findings. The classic pattern progresses over days and usually reaches nadir within four weeks. Variants can break the pattern. Fluctuating ptosis, diplopia or bulbar fatigue with preserved sensation Myasthenia. Look for impending crisis. Bilateral weakness with a level, back pain, or new bowel/bladder dysfunction Cord/conus/cauda equina. Early cord syndromes can have depressed reflexes. Prominent proximal weakness or myalgia, or weakness after a metabolic trigger Myopathy or electrolyte disorder. Treat a dangerous reversible cause in parallel.

Step 2 — Confirm the pattern while watching the airway

  • In suspected GBS, obtain CSF and EMG/NCS with neurology when feasible. Elevated CSF protein with few cells supports the diagnosis. Early CSF protein and early electrodiagnostics can be normal. Significant CSF pleocytosis or strongly atypical features should prompt a search for alternatives.
  • Consider anti-GQ1b testing when ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and areflexia suggest Miller Fisher syndrome. Urgently image when the presentation could localize to the brainstem or spinal cord.
  • Discuss elective ventilation with ICU when FVC approaches 20 mL/kg, falls quickly, or airway protection deteriorates. Use the trajectory and bedside exam together. ICU escalation can be appropriate with higher FVC if there is bulbar weakness, dysautonomia or rapid progression.

Step 3 — Treat GBS and prevent complications

  • IVIG 0.4 g/kg IV daily for five days for patients unable to walk unaided, preferably within two weeks of weakness onset. The guideline also supports considering IVIG at two to four weeks. Coordinate early treatment with neurology for ambulatory patients with rapid progression, bulbar or respiratory involvement, or other high-risk features.
  • Plasma exchange is an alternative, typically four to five exchanges over one to two weeks for patients unable to walk unaided presenting within four weeks. Choose with neurology and apheresis based on access, contraindications and clinical stability. See infusion and exchange protocols.
  • Use aspiration and thrombosis precautions as indicated, monitor autonomic instability, and start rehabilitation in hospital. Corticosteroids are ineffective for classic GBS. Avoid routine sequential IVIG and exchange or a second IVIG course for predicted poor outcome. Reassess new deterioration after stabilization with neurology. Worsening beyond eight weeks from onset or three or more treatment-related fluctuations should raise acute-onset CIDP.

docs.title: Disposition and handoff
docs.text:
Admit suspected GBS for serial neurologic and respiratory assessment. Escalate to ICU for respiratory, bulbar or autonomic risk. If the facility cannot provide monitoring or respiratory support, call early for transfer. Send onset and progression, last safe ambulation, cough and swallowing status, respiratory trends, and hemodynamic events.

TRICARE — IVIG and apheresis

Acute treatment and transfer take priority. For subsequent infusions, confirm the exact product, treatment site and medical or pharmacy benefit. Use the TRICARE authorization guide and Formulary Search for covered pharmacy products.

Military medicine

Record premorbid function, onset, exposure or duty context for EPTS/LOD, and residual endurance, gait and respiratory limits. In a deployed facility with limited monitoring, coordinate early consultation and evacuation. For recovery, use the profile, retention and MEB/IDES guide and deployment screen for the actual theater and duty.

docs.title: Acute dizziness and vertigo
docs.text:
Last reviewed: November 2026

One-liner: Ask when it started, whether it stops, and what brings on a new episode. “Spinning” alone will send you down several corridors.

Think posterior circulation early

New focal deficits, severe gait or truncal instability, sudden head/neck pain with neurologic symptoms, or new unilateral hearing loss with continuous acute vertigo warrant urgent assessment for a central cause. Activate the stroke pathway when indicated. A negative head CT cannot clear a suspected posterior circulation infarct.

docs.title: The bedside flow
docs.text:
Step 1 — Classify the syndrome

  1. Document last known well, episode duration, symptoms at rest, and whether turning the head starts a discrete attack or merely worsens ongoing dizziness. Check vitals, ocular movements, hearing, coordination and safe gait.
  2. Continuous, still symptomatic with nausea or gait instability: acute vestibular syndrome. Assess for stroke versus a peripheral vestibulopathy.
  3. Brief episodes triggered by position with relative baseline between them: test for BPPV. If standing is the trigger and the patient feels faint, assess orthostasis and use the blackout pathway as appropriate.
  4. Spontaneous episodes: use the history and focal exam to assess TIA, vestibular migraine, Ménière disease or a nonvestibular cause. Examine between attacks, but remember a resolved episode can leave a normal exam.

Step 2 — Choose the bedside test and imaging

  • Continuous syndrome with spontaneous nystagmus: HINTS is for trained clinicians in this setting. A normal head impulse, direction-changing gaze-evoked nystagmus, or skew is concerning for a central cause. Check for new unilateral hearing loss as well.
  • No spontaneous nystagmus: do not use HINTS to clear stroke. Assess gait and truncal stability, and use the focal exam and clinical risk to guide the stroke workup.
  • Central or equivocal HINTS, or stroke concern without a trained examiner: involve the stroke team and pursue appropriate imaging. GRACE-3 recommends MRI/MRA for central or equivocal HINTS. In a stroke activation, follow the local acute imaging pathway without waiting for elective MRI. With persistent concern after early negative MRI, reassess with neurology.
  • Triggered positional spells: use Dix–Hallpike for suspected posterior canal BPPV. Brief, characteristic upbeat-torsional nystagmus supports that diagnosis. If compatible, use the Epley maneuver on the affected side, adapting or deferring positional maneuvers when neck mobility or injury makes them unsafe. With a compatible history and horizontal or absent positional nystagmus on Dix–Hallpike, use the supine roll test or refer for lateral canal assessment.
  • Spontaneous episodic symptoms with TIA concern: use the TIA pathway and discuss CTA or MRA for large-vessel pathology. The scan should answer the vascular question.

docs.title: Treatment and disposition
docs.text:
Use repositioning for typical posterior canal BPPV and review fall precautions. Routine imaging and vestibular suppressants are unnecessary in a characteristic, confirmed case. Arrange reassessment within one month, sooner for ongoing disability or atypical findings. For probable vestibular neuritis after a central cause has been addressed, review hydration, symptom support and vestibular rehabilitation. GRACE-3 treats corticosteroids in the first three days as a shared decision with very low certainty of benefit. Use local prescribing guidance if considering them.

Observe, admit, or transfer when stroke remains plausible, walking is unsafe, oral intake is inadequate, or timely evaluation cannot be completed locally. For a secure peripheral diagnosis, document gait and reassessment, arrange follow-up, and give return instructions for new neurologic symptoms or worsening imbalance. For symptoms after head injury, use post-TBI vestibular care.

Military medicine

Document whether symptoms impair safe driving, climbing, weapons handling, or flight duties. Record onset and exposure or injury history for EPTS/LOD. Use profile, retention and MEB/IDES guidance and the deployment medication screen. Review sedating medications and involve flight medicine for covered duties.

docs.title: Discover
docs.text: GRACE-3 organizes adult ED dizziness by timing and triggers. Its bedside eye-movement recommendations depend on examiner training and syndrome selection. The positional BPPV recommendations support a maneuver-first workflow for the characteristic presentation.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• SAEM GRACE-3 adult ED dizziness guideline.
  • AAO-HNS BPPV clinical practice guideline update.

Evidence/policy audit: 22 November 2026. Syndrome selection, imaging and bedside maneuvers checked against GRACE-3 and the BPPV guideline.

docs.title: Focused neuro exam and localization
docs.text:
Last reviewed: November 2026

One-liner: Find the deficit that changes what you do next, then write it down so the next clinician can tell whether it changed.

Move before you finish the exam

  • Sudden focal deficit, including new aphasia, visual field loss, or inability to walk: activate the stroke pathway. Establish last known well and check bedside glucose in parallel.
  • Falling consciousness, new pupil asymmetry with deterioration, ongoing convulsions, or respiratory/bulbar weakness: get help and stabilize immediately. See coma, status epilepticus, and acute weakness.
  • New bilateral limb deficits with a sensory level or bladder symptoms: pursue cord or cauda equina evaluation urgently. Early cord injury can be flaccid.

docs.title: The bedside pass
docs.text:
Examine, localize, repeat

  1. Set the clock. Establish onset, last known normal, baseline deficits, and whether the change was abrupt, progressive, episodic, or fluctuating. Record sedatives, glucose, pain, and anything that limits the exam.
  2. Attention and language. Check alertness, orientation, and attention, then ask the patient to name an object, repeat a phrase, and follow a command. Describe language separately from articulation. Account for language barriers and hearing loss.
  3. Eyes and face. Compare pupils in light and dark, test fields in each eye, examine gaze and alignment, and check facial movement. Add acuity, color comparison and a swinging flashlight test when vision is the complaint. Assess speech, voice and secretion handling.
  4. Motor and reflexes. Compare arm drift, finger taps, and strength at proximal and distal joints. Grade and name the muscles if weak. Compare tone, tendon reflexes and plantar responses as indicated.
  5. Sensation and coordination. Compare sides for touch and pin, test vibration and joint position when needed, and look for a truncal level or extinction. Check finger–nose and heel–shin with weakness accounted for.
  6. Stance and gait, when safe. Watch the patient stand, start, turn and walk. Use assistance and document when testing is unsafe. If gait is the symptom, a normal supine exam leaves the key question unanswered.

docs.title: Where is the lesion?
docs.text:
Pattern to look for Likely level or next question Aphasia, neglect, gaze preference, field cut, or face/arm/leg weakness on one side Hemisphere. Acute onset goes to the stroke pathway, even with few findings. A pure motor deficit can be subcortical or brainstem. Diplopia or dysarthria with long-tract findings; cranial nerve signs on one side and body findings on the other Brainstem. Look for dysphagia, nystagmus, ataxia and other subtle findings. Dysmetria, truncal instability or lateral veering out of proportion to weakness or sensory loss Cerebellar or vestibular pathways. Sudden severe imbalance can be a stroke. Compare with acute dizziness. Bilateral limb findings below a level, back pain or new bladder dysfunction Cord or cauda equina. Compare upper and lower limb findings, and check for sacral symptoms. Myotomal weakness with reflex change, or weakness crossing roots within a single named nerve Root versus peripheral nerve. Map weak and spared muscles. See radiculopathy and neuropathy. Fluctuating ocular or bulbar symptoms, or symmetric proximal weakness Consider neuromuscular junction or muscle. Check sensation, reflexes, fatigability, respiratory function and time course.

Handoff example: “Last known well 01:10. Awake, follows two-step commands. New right lower facial weakness, right arm drift and word-finding difficulty. Baseline walks independently. Glucose checked. Stroke team activated.” Use observed findings, laterality and times. Repeat the same exam after a clinical change or before transfer.

docs.title: Disposition
docs.text:
New or progressing focal deficits, declining alertness, unsafe swallowing or breathing, inability to walk safely, and suspected cord compression need emergency evaluation. For stable outpatient findings, document the working localization, the test or referral that would change it, and the escalation instructions.

Military medicine

Record observable function such as gait, hand dexterity, visual fields and fatigability. Document onset and duty or injury context for EPTS/LOD. Use the profile, retention and MEB/IDES guide and deployment and medication screen for the confirmed diagnosis, task limitations and applicable theater or special-duty standards.

docs.title: Discover
docs.text: The AAN clinical neurology curriculum ties the exam to localization, time course and urgent management. This page adapts that framework for a short handoff. Expand the exam where the deficit points, and use the disease-specific pathway when a time-critical syndrome is suspected.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• AAN core curriculum for a required clinical neurology experience.
  • AHA/ASA guideline for early management of acute ischemic stroke.

Evidence/policy audit: 22 November 2026. Exam structure and urgent routing checked against the linked curriculum and stroke guidance.

docs.title: Vision loss, double vision, and facial palsy
docs.text:
Last reviewed: November 2026

One-liner: Check acuity, fields, pupils and eye movements before a reassuring label gets attached to a dangerous exam.

Protect sight and act on vascular clues

Presentation Immediate route Sudden painless monocular loss, including transient loss suspicious for retinal ischemia Emergency stroke evaluation with ophthalmology. Record last known well. Coordinate acute options with the receiving team. New visual loss with jaw claudication, scalp tenderness or other features of giant cell arteritis in an adult over 50 Send ESR, CRP and CBC with platelets when feasible. Call ophthalmology and the treating team for immediate glucocorticoid treatment when suspicion is high. Draw tests without delaying treatment for threatened vision. New third nerve palsy, especially painful or with an enlarged pupil Urgent vascular imaging for aneurysm. Pupil sparing alone cannot clear an acute third nerve palsy. New ptosis and small pupil with ipsilateral head or neck pain or after trauma Evaluate for carotid dissection with emergency vascular imaging. Painful red eye with reduced vision, halos or vomiting, or vision loss after eye trauma Emergency ocular assessment. Consider acute angle closure or an injury requiring immediate ophthalmology. Suspected papilledema with declining vision, severe headache or altered alertness Emergency imaging and ophthalmology/neurology assessment. See raised ICP and venous thrombosis. Facial weakness plus dysarthria, diplopia, ataxia or limb deficits Activate the stroke pathway. A pontine lesion can affect the entire hemiface.

docs.title: What to do in order
docs.text:
Step 1 — Document the minimum eye exam

  1. Test acuity in each eye with correction when possible, then pinhole if reduced. Compare confrontation fields, pupils in light/dark, relative afferent pupillary defect and color perception. Record eye pain, redness, trauma and onset. A painful red eye with reduced vision needs urgent ocular assessment.
  2. Check alignment, lids and motility in all directions. Ask whether double vision clears when either eye is covered. Examine the fundus if able. If the disc cannot be assessed reliably, document that and arrange an appropriate exam.
  3. For facial weakness, compare forehead, eye closure and smile. Check other cranial nerves, ear canal and pinna, and assess for limb findings, hearing change or vertigo.

Step 2 — Match workup to the pattern

  • Monocular visual loss: localize to the eye or optic nerve. Flashes, floaters or a curtain suggest retinal tear or detachment and need urgent ophthalmology. Pain with eye movement, reduced color vision and an afferent defect suggest optic neuropathy. Use dedicated orbit MRI with and without contrast when optic neuritis is suspected, with brain imaging as indicated. Route severe or atypical cases promptly to the demyelination workup.
  • Binocular diplopia: map the movement defect and accompanying signs. Ptosis with impaired adduction, elevation or depression suggests III. Vertical diplopia worse in downgaze can suggest IV. Abduction weakness suggests VI. Multiple nerve deficits, proptosis, or pain with fever require urgent orbital/cavernous sinus evaluation. Fluctuating ptosis or diplopia with normal pupils can suggest myasthenia.
  • Suspected papilledema: document acuity and fields, measure blood pressure, and arrange urgent brain imaging with venography to exclude structural disease and CVST. If imaging permits and LP is appropriate, measure opening pressure in lateral decubitus and check CSF composition. Worsening fields or acuity require urgent specialist management.
  • Isolated peripheral-pattern facial palsy: look for vesicles, ear infection, exposure compatible with Lyme disease, recurrence, bilateral involvement or gradual progression. Those findings change the workup. Typical new Bell palsy usually needs neither routine imaging nor routine labs.

Step 3 — Treat typical adult Bell palsy and protect the cornea

  • Prednisolone 25 mg PO twice daily for 10 days is one trial-supported adult regimen when started within 72 hours. Review contraindications and glycemic risk. This regimen is for idiopathic Bell palsy after evaluation for alternative causes.
  • Eye protection: start preservative-free lubricating drops during the day and lubricating ointment at bedtime if closure is impaired. Demonstrate gentle taping with the lid fully closed or use a moisture chamber. Eye pain, redness, photophobia or blurred vision needs prompt ophthalmology.
  • Antiviral monotherapy has no role in idiopathic Bell palsy. An adjunct can be discussed with selected patients. Vesicles or other evidence of zoster warrants a separate diagnosis and treatment plan.

docs.title: Disposition
docs.text:
Send acute sight-threatening or vascular presentations for emergency workup. For uncomplicated Bell palsy, confirm that the patient can protect the eye, arrange follow-up, and reassess with any new neurologic findings or ocular symptoms. Refer for incomplete recovery at three months.

TRICARE — outpatient treatment and follow-up

Verify the exact product through the TRICARE Formulary Search and route specialty visits or infusions through the correct benefit. See the prior authorization guide.

Military medicine

Document acuity, fields, diplopia in primary gaze, and ability to close the eye. Record onset and any injury for EPTS/LOD. Apply profile, retention and MEB/IDES guidance and destination-specific deployment standards. Refer flight and other vision-critical duties to the applicable authority.

docs.title: Discover
docs.text: AAO treats acute symptomatic retinal arterial occlusion as an emergency stroke referral. The Bell palsy steroid recommendation rests on randomized trials. Pupil sparing is less reassuring in a new third nerve palsy than older bedside rules suggest, so let vascular imaging answer the aneurysm question.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• AAO retinal and ophthalmic artery occlusions preferred practice pattern.
  • ACR vision loss imaging criteria and ACR Horner syndrome imaging criteria.
  • Patel and Burdon on third nerve palsy imaging and IIH consensus guidance on papilledema.
  • ACR/Vasculitis Foundation giant cell arteritis guideline.
  • AAO-HNS Bell palsy guideline and Sullivan et al. steroid trial.

Evidence/policy audit: 22 November 2026. Emergency routing, imaging, steroid regimen and corneal protection checked against the linked specialty guidance and trial.

docs.title: Peripheral neuropathy and entrapment
docs.text:
Last reviewed: November 2026

One-liner: Draw the distribution before you order the panel. Burning feet, a numb thumb and a new foot drop are different consults.

Move the workup up the calendar

  • Rapidly progressive weakness, bulbar symptoms, dyspnea or major dysautonomia: use the acute weakness pathway.
  • New bladder dysfunction, saddle symptoms or a sensory level: urgent spinal evaluation.
  • Painful, asymmetric, stepwise deficits in multiple nerves or new motor loss: expedite neurology assessment for vasculitic, inflammatory, compressive or other treatable causes. After trauma or with severe limb pain/swelling, evaluate for a surgical emergency.

docs.title: What to do in order
docs.text:
Step 1 — Map the pattern

Check pin and vibration, ankle reflexes, distal strength, gait and foot skin. In a focal complaint, compare muscles supplied by different nerves but the same root. Check occupational pressure, training load, weight loss, diabetes, alcohol, supplements such as B6, and neurotoxic medications.

Pattern Useful next step Slow, symmetric symptoms starting at the toes with reduced distal sensation Evaluate distal symmetric polyneuropathy. Foot protection and falls prevention can start today. Burning, allodynia or pin/temperature loss with preserved vibration and strength Consider small-fiber neuropathy. Normal routine NCS can occur. Refer for targeted testing when the result will affect management. Nocturnal thumb, index and middle finger paresthesia, sometimes with thenar weakness Median neuropathy at the wrist. Use the clinical pattern or CTS-6 in typical cases. Assess for proximal disease or other neuropathy when findings are atypical. Ring/small finger symptoms with elbow flexion or pressure and weak finger abduction Consider ulnar neuropathy. Compare dorsal ulnar sensation and proximal muscle findings to help localize. Foot drop with weak dorsiflexion and eversion Consider common fibular neuropathy. Weak inversion or hip abduction raises concern for L5 or a more proximal lesion. Inspect around the fibular head and see root and plexus patterns.

Step 2 — Order tests that answer the question

  • Unexplained distal symmetric polyneuropathy: check glucose or A1c, vitamin B12 with methylmalonic acid when indicated, and serum protein immunofixation. Add CBC and metabolic testing to look for systemic contributors as appropriate. Consider glucose tolerance testing when routine glucose tests are unrevealing in a compatible sensory phenotype.
  • EMG/NCS: order when localization is uncertain, a new motor deficit is unexplained, or axonal versus demyelinating physiology would change the plan. Ask a specific question, such as fibular neuropathy versus L5 radiculopathy. If an early study is unrevealing after acute injury, discuss timing and repeat testing with the lab.
  • Typical carpal tunnel: the AAOS supports the CTS-6 as a clinical diagnostic tool in lieu of routine ultrasound or EMG/NCS. Atypical symptoms, competing localization and motor loss can change the testing or referral decision.

Step 3 — Protect function and treat the cause

  • Correct a documented deficiency or remove a likely toxic or compressive exposure as appropriate. Address diabetes care and foot surveillance. Use PT or OT for balance, strength and adaptations.
  • For mild typical carpal tunnel, try a neutral wrist splint at night. For ulnar symptoms at the elbow, reduce direct pressure and prolonged flexion. For foot drop, address fall risk and consider an ankle-foot orthosis while clarifying the cause. Progressive weakness or atrophy warrants prompt referral.
  • For painful diabetic neuropathy in a suitable adult, duloxetine 60 mg PO daily is one labeled option. A lower starting dose can improve tolerability. Avoid in chronic liver disease, substantial alcohol use or GFR under 30 mL/min. Review interactions and orthostatic symptoms. If benefit is inadequate or adverse effects limit therapy, consider a different evidence-supported class. Avoid opioids for this indication.

docs.title: Disposition
docs.text:
Arrange expedited workup for motor, asymmetric, rapidly evolving or systemic features. For stable sensory symptoms or mild entrapment, make a follow-up plan around gait, pain interference, skin integrity and objective strength. Give clear instructions to return for progression, falls, new weakness or foot wounds.

TRICARE — drugs and testing

Check the exact drug and strength in the TRICARE Formulary Search. For EMG/NCS, orthoses, therapy or surgery, confirm referral and authorization through the applicable benefit. See the TRICARE guide.

Military medicine

Document falls, gait on uneven ground, boot and orthosis tolerance, grip and dexterity. Record onset and exposure or injury details for EPTS/LOD. Tie profile limitations to the task and use the retention and MEB/IDES guide and deployment medication screen to assess the condition and any sedating therapy.

docs.title: Discover
docs.text: The AAN laboratory evidence favors a focused initial workup for distal symmetric polyneuropathy. AAOS supports clinical diagnosis in typical carpal tunnel. For painful diabetic neuropathy, several drug classes help on average. Choose by comorbidity, adverse effects and the patient’s functional goals.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• AAN/AANEM/AAPM&R practice parameter on laboratory evaluation of distal symmetric polyneuropathy.
  • AAOS carpal tunnel guideline.
  • AAN painful diabetic polyneuropathy guideline and duloxetine label, sections 2.3 and 5.14.

Evidence/policy audit: 22 November 2026. Initial testing, CTS diagnosis, painful diabetic neuropathy treatment and duloxetine precautions checked against the linked guidance and label.

docs.title: Spells, syncope, and functional neurologic disorder
docs.text:
Last reviewed: November 2026

One-liner: Reconstruct the minute before, during and after the spell. Get the witness and the ECG before the chart decides it was epilepsy.

First exclude a time-critical cause

  • Ongoing convulsions for five minutes, or recurrent convulsions without return to baseline: stabilize and use the convulsive status pathway. Persistent impaired awareness after a spell needs reassessment for ongoing seizure, toxic/metabolic illness or other acute causes.
  • Collapse during exertion, chest pain or palpitations around the spell, abnormal ECG, known structural heart disease or a family history of early sudden death: urgent cardiac assessment.
  • New focal deficit, severe headache, significant injury, major bleeding, pregnancy/postpartum with concerning features, or unstable vitals: route to emergency evaluation for the suspected cause.

docs.title: What to do in order
docs.text:
Step 1 — Reconstruct the event

  1. Check vitals and bedside glucose when indicated. Obtain a 12-lead ECG after transient loss of consciousness. Consider orthostatic vitals once safe when the story suggests orthostasis. Review medicines, substances and missed doses.
  2. Get a witness account or consented video. Ask about posture, trigger, prodrome, color, movement timing, eye position, injuries, duration and the recovery clock. Clarify what the person remembers.
  3. Determine whether loss of awareness or posture actually occurred. Ask whether recurrent event types differ. Time the event rather than relying on “it lasted forever.”
Clues Next route Standing, pain or heat trigger; warmth, nausea or tunnel vision; rapid recovery Reflex syncope is plausible after assessment and ECG. Brief jerks can occur with syncope. Abrupt collapse with exertion, supine, or with palpitations; abnormal ECG or structural heart disease Consider arrhythmia or structural cardiac disease. Arrange monitoring and urgent evaluation as appropriate. Stereotyped onset, lateral tongue injury, sustained head turning, or prolonged confusion Consider epileptic seizure. Use the first-seizure workup, including EEG and imaging when indicated. Recurrent events with features suggestive of functional seizures Obtain specialist confirmation. Review the full semiology, ideally with video-EEG of each typical event type where feasible. Functional seizures and epilepsy can coexist.

Step 2 — Order for the leading risk

  • With unexplained or high-risk transient loss of consciousness, prioritize cardiac evaluation and select ambulatory ECG monitoring according to event frequency and suspicion. Routine EEG has little value when the presentation clearly fits uncomplicated syncope.
  • With suspected epilepsy, arrange timely specialist evaluation. A normal interictal EEG cannot rule out epilepsy. For persistent altered awareness, use the altered mental status and EEG pathway.
  • For other possible FND presentations, look for positive findings specific to the symptom. In functional leg weakness, Hoover’s sign is weak voluntary hip extension that improves during resisted flexion of the opposite hip. Interpret in context, including pain and comprehension. New objective findings still deserve evaluation. A history of trauma, psychiatric symptoms or normal imaging alone cannot establish FND.

docs.title: Give the diagnosis and the next step
docs.text:
When functional seizures are established, name them and explain the evidence: “These are real, involuntary episodes. The findings we saw during your usual spell support functional seizures. We can work on a plan to help you manage them.” Provide a clear event safety plan, review coexisting epilepsy and other conditions, and arrange neurology continuity and an appropriate psychological intervention. For motor FND, consider rehabilitation with clinicians familiar with functional symptoms.

Benzodiazepines and antiseizure medicines have no role for established functional seizures alone. If they were prescribed solely for functional seizures, arrange a supervised taper. Treat coexisting epilepsy on its own plan. During a typical confirmed event, protect from injury, observe breathing, and coach witnesses to stay calm and avoid restraint. If a future spell differs or emergency features arise, reassess.

docs.title: Disposition
docs.text:
Urgent evaluation or observation when a cardiac or neurologic emergency remains plausible, the patient has not returned to baseline, or safe follow-up cannot be secured. Confirm follow-up and discuss applicable driving rules and precautions around water, heights, machinery and other safety-sensitive activity.

Military medicine

Document the episode, known triggers, recovery, recurrence and functional impact. Record onset and duty or injury context for EPTS/LOD. Specify temporary profile restrictions by task while the cause is clarified. Use retention and MEB/IDES guidance and the deployment and medication screen for the established diagnosis. Coordinate flight or other special-duty decisions with the relevant authority.

docs.title: Discover
docs.text: NICE emphasizes the witness history and ECG in blackouts. The AAN functional seizures guideline emphasizes respectful explanation, evaluation for coexisting epilepsy, and continuity of care. The treatment plan follows the confirmed diagnosis and the individual event types.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• NICE transient loss of consciousness guideline.
  • AAN functional seizures practice guideline.
  • Hoover sign in suspected stroke, prospective cohort.
  • American Epilepsy Society convulsive status epilepticus guideline.

Evidence/policy audit: 22 November 2026. Blackout triage, functional seizure diagnosis and treatment boundaries checked against the linked guidelines.

docs.title: Seizure & status epilepticus
docs.text:
Last reviewed: July 2026

One-liner: a seizure is sudden, hypersynchronous cortical firing; status epilepticus is the neurologic code — treat it on a clock, escalate on schedule, and don't under-dose the benzo (the single most common mistake). This page covers the code, the first-seizure work-up, and picking an antiseizure medication (ASM).

The ER consult usually sounds like: "Known-or-unknown epileptic, two witnessed seizures, got 4 of Ativan, now not responding — should I load them with something, and you're admitting, right?" The answer to "load them?" is yes, now — and check whether that "not responding" is postictal or ongoing nonconvulsive status.

🚩 Status epilepticus — recognize it and start the clock

  • Definition (ILAE two-timepoint): treat at t1 (the seizure won't self-terminate) — 5 min for a generalized tonic-clonic seizure, but 10 min for focal SE with impaired awareness and 10–15 min for absence; or ≥2 seizures without recovery between them. t2 (risk of long-term injury) is ~30 min for GTC. Bottom line: GTC at 5 min = treat now, and don't wait 30 minutes for anything.
  • "Stopped but won't wake up" = nonconvulsive status until proven otherwise — get urgent cEEG. Persistent altered consciousness after visible convulsions stop is NCSE in up to ~20%.
  • Under-dosing benzodiazepines (and then blaming the "refractory" seizure) is the classic error — give the full weight-based dose.
  • Find and fix the cause in parallel — a seizure from hypoglycemia, hyponatremia, a toxin, or eclampsia won't stop on ASMs until the cause is corrected.

docs.title: Status epilepticus — the timed escalation ladder (the code)
docs.text:
Step 0 — Stabilize (0–5 min)

  • ABCs, O₂, position, suction; IV access ×2; continuous ECG, BP, SpO₂.
  • Point-of-care glucose — if low, D50W 50 mL IV (or local IV dextrose protocol), with prompt glucose recheck. Give thiamine promptly in malnutrition/alcohol-use risk, but never delay correction of hypoglycemia while waiting for thiamine.
    • 100 mg IV is prophylaxis. If Wernicke encephalopathy is suspected rather than merely being prevented, that dose is inadequate — give the treatment regimen instead: thiamine 500 mg IV over 30 min every 8 h. See rapidly progressive dementia.
  • STAT labs: CBC, BMP, Ca, Mg, glucose, ASM levels, ± LFTs, tox screen (blood + urine), ABG, β-hCG, PO₄; ECG.

Step 1 — First-line benzodiazepine (5–20 min) — give the FULL dose

Pick by access; these are frequently under-dosed — use the real weight-based dose and repeat once if still seizing.

  • IV lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg (max 4 mg/dose), may repeat ×1 — first choice if IV is in.
  • No IV? IM midazolam 10 mg (>40 kg) — RAMPART showed IM midazolam is at least as good as IV lorazepam and faster to give; also intranasal/buccal midazolam.
  • IV diazepam 0.15–0.2 mg/kg (max 10 mg), or rectal diazepam 0.2 mg/kg if no IV.

Step 2 — Second-line ASM (20–40 min) — the three are EQUIVALENT (ESETT)

ESETT (NEJM 2019) found levetiracetam, fosphenytoin, and valproate stop ~45–47% of benzo-refractory status — no winner. So pick by the patient, give the full load IV:

  • Levetiracetam 60 mg/kg IV (max 4500 mg) — fewest interactions/contraindications; a good default (esp. cardiac/hepatic disease, pregnancy).
  • Fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg IV (ESETT maximum 1500 mg PE; ≤150 mg PE/min) — avoid in hypotension/arrhythmia; watch the BP and QT.
  • Valproate 40 mg/kg IV (ESETT maximum 3000 mg) — avoid in hepatic disease and pregnancy/childbearing potential.
  • (Phenobarbital 15 mg/kg IV if none of the above is available.)
  • Broadening landscape: IV lacosamide and brivaracetam are increasingly used as second-line (lacosamide was non-inferior to fosphenytoin for nonconvulsive seizures in TRENdS, with a favorable hemodynamic profile) — reasonable alternatives, though the formal evidence base still rests on the ESETT triad.
  • Continue the second-line agent as you escalate; arrange cEEG.

Step 3 — Refractory status (>40 min, or 2 lines failed) — anesthetize + cEEG

Intubate, admit to ICU, start continuous cEEG, and begin a continuous anesthetic infusion. Target seizure suppression, not routine burst-suppression — induced burst suppression wasn't associated with better outcomes (Fisch 2023), and seizure suppression alone tracked with better function; reserve burst-suppression for seizures recurring despite adequate anesthetic dosing.

  • Midazolam — load 0.2 mg/kg, then 0.05–2.9 mg/kg/h.
  • Propofol — load ~1–2 mg/kg, then 1–15 mg/kg/h (watch propofol-infusion syndrome — avoid in suspected mitochondrial disease or on a ketogenic diet; limit dose/duration).
  • Ketamine — increasingly used (NMDA-mediated late status), usually with a GABAergic agent.
  • Keep the second-line ASM on board for maintenance.

Step 4 — Super-refractory (>24 h, or recurs on weaning)

  • Pentobarbital/thiopental infusion (load 5 mg/kg → titrate; hypotension is expected — pressors ready), titrated to seizure/burst suppression.
  • Hunt hard for the cause — autoimmune/paraneoplastic (NORSE/FIRES), CNS infection, PRES/RCVS, toxic-metabolic; consider immunotherapy (steroids/IVIg/PLEX) empirically in NORSE.
  • Ketogenic diet is used adjunctively in super-refractory SE (especially FIRES/NORSE).
  • Don't reach for unproven add-ons: hypothermia adds nothing beyond standard therapy, and the allopregnanolone (brexanolone) RCT was negative — no proven pharmacologic agent exists for super-refractory SE beyond anesthetics (+ immunotherapy for autoimmune causes).
  • Wean anesthetics slowly once seizure-free ~24–48 h; neurology + epileptology on board.

Copy-paste — first 20 minutes

  • Glucose now; D50 + thiamine if low.
  • Lorazepam 4 mg IV (or midazolam 10 mg IM if no IV) — repeat ×1 if seizing at ~5 min.
  • Levetiracetam 60 mg/kg IV (or fosphenytoin/valproate by patient) as the seizure continues.
  • cEEG, ICU, and treat the cause. No sub-therapeutic benzos, no delay to second-line.

Toxin-driven seizures — the antidote matters

  • INH (isoniazid): benzodiazepine + pyridoxine (vitamin B6) ~70 mg/kg, max 5 g.
  • Tricyclic antidepressants: wide QRS → sodium bicarbonate.
  • Organophosphates: atropine + pralidoxime (+ benzodiazepine).
  • Alcohol/benzo withdrawal: escalating benzodiazepines. Eclampsia: magnesium (+ deliver).

docs.title: Is it actually a seizure? (mimics)
docs.text:
Before you commit to lifelong ASMs, exclude the imitators — syncope (convulsive syncope after a faint; get an ECG/cardiac workup — cardiac syncope can kill), psychogenic non-epileptic seizures (PNES), TIA, transient global amnesia, migraine, and sleep disorders.

  • PNES tells (not diagnostic alone; confirm with video-EEG): side-to-side head shaking, eye closure (epileptic seizures usually have eyes open), pelvic thrusting, asynchronous flailing, a waxing–waning course, prolonged duration, crying/stuttering, preserved awareness despite bilateral movements, and resistance to eye opening. Manage with diagnosis delivery + behavioral health, not more ASMs.

docs.title: First seizure — work-up & whether to treat
docs.text:
First unprovoked seizure — the work-up (outpatient is OK if back to baseline, no deficits, low infection concern)

  • Labs: CBC, BMP, Ca/Mg, glucose, LFTs, tox, ± ESR/CRP; β-hCG.
  • Imaging: MRI brain (with & without contrast) is the study of choice; CT in the ED (and before LP) to exclude a bleed/mass.
  • EEG — best within 48 h (raises yield); urgent if consciousness stays altered.
  • LP only if infection/SAH suspected.

Start an ASM after a first seizure? — individualize (AAN/AES 2015)

Immediate ASM reduces recurrence over the first 2 years but does NOT improve long-term remission or quality of life. Recurrence after a first unprovoked seizure is ~21–45% at 2 years.

  • Treat now if recurrence risk is high: a prior brain insult (stroke/tumor/trauma), an epileptiform EEG, a relevant lesion on MRI, or a nocturnal seizure.
  • Reasonable to wait in a low-risk, normal-work-up first seizure — with a shared decision (weigh ASM adverse effects, ~7–31%).
  • An acute provoked (symptomatic) seizure — fix the provocation; long-term ASM usually isn't needed.

docs.title: Picking an ASM (by seizure type & the patient)
docs.text:
Match the drug to the seizure and the person

SANAD II reset the defaults (Lancet 2021): lamotrigine is first-line for focal epilepsy (beat levetiracetam on treatment failure, tolerability, and cost), and valproate is the most effective for generalized epilepsy (with the childbearing caveat). Levetiracetam is the alternative when you need rapid titration (lamotrigine must be titrated slowly for rash) — e.g., the ED first seizure of unknown type.

Situation Preferred → alternative Focal (most adults) Lamotrigine (best tolerated/cost) → levetiracetam (when rapid titration needed) or lacosamide; oxcarbazepine/carbamazepine Generalized (GTC) Valproate (most effective) → lamotrigine or levetiracetam (avoid valproate when clinically feasible in people who could become pregnant; involve an epilepsy specialist and do not abruptly stop effective therapy during pregnancy) Absence Ethosuximide, valproate, lamotrigine Myoclonic (e.g., JME) Valproate, levetiracetam (avoid carbamazepine/oxcarbazepine/phenytoin — worsen myoclonus/absence) Childbearing potential Lamotrigine or levetiracetam — avoid valproate (neural-tube defects, low IQ) Older adults Lamotrigine or levetiracetam (fewer interactions, better tolerated) Comorbid depression/mood Lamotrigine (avoid levetiracetam's irritability); renal → lamotrigine; hepatic → levetiracetam/gabapentin
  • Screen HLA-B*15:02 before carbamazepine/oxcarbazepine in at-risk (Southeast/East Asian) ancestry (SJS/TEN); some guidelines also screen HLA-A*31:01 (European/Japanese ancestry — DRESS/SJS).

Drug-resistant focal epilepsy — cenobamate is the standout newer ASM

Among the newer adjuncts, cenobamate gives the best chance of seizure freedom (~32% at 12 months; out-performs brivaracetam, lacosamide, and perampanel on 50%-responder rate even after many failed ASMs). The trade-offs: titrate slowly (DRESS risk with fast titration) and a higher overall adverse-effect rate. Worth it for refractory focal epilepsy.

  • Refractory (failed 2 appropriate ASMs) = drug-resistant epilepsy → refer to an epilepsy center. The 2022 ILAE surgical-referral consensus is emphatic: offer a surgical evaluation to every drug-resistant patient up to age 70, regardless of epilepsy duration, seizure type, localization, or comorbidity (including psychiatric disease or comorbid PNES) — plus consider VNS/RNS/DBS and video-EEG.

docs.title: Classify it (ILAE 2025 update)
docs.text: Describe seizure type → epilepsy type → epilepsy syndrome. The 2025 seizure classification uses focal, generalized, unknown whether focal or generalized, and unclassified. For focal and unknown seizures, document preserved or impaired consciousness, assessed through awareness (recall) and responsiveness; describe the chronological semiology. Translate older records using 2017 “aware/impaired-awareness” terms rather than treating them as new diagnoses. Seizure type still drives ASM choice: some sodium-channel agents aggravate generalized/myoclonic syndromes.

docs.title: Counseling, rescue plan & driving
docs.text:
• Driving is restricted after a seizure — the seizure-free interval is state/country-specific (commonly ~3–12 months; 6 months is typical); some states have mandatory physician reporting. Document the counseling.
  • Safety: no swimming/bathing alone, heights, or operating dangerous machinery until controlled; sleep, alcohol moderation, adherence.

Give a seizure action plan with a rescue medication (for cluster-prone patients)

Prescribe an outpatient rescue benzodiazepine and a written action plan — standard of care for epilepsy at risk of clusters/prolonged seizures. FDA-approved options:

  • Midazolam nasal spray (Nayzilam), age ≥12: 5 mg in one nostril. If prescribed and needed, 5 mg in the other nostril after 10 minutes. Maximum 2 doses per cluster. Do not give the second dose with trouble breathing or unusually excessive sedation. FDA labeling on DailyMed
  • Diazepam nasal spray (Valtoco), age ≥2: use the labeled age/weight device table (0.5 mg/kg age 2–5, 0.3 mg/kg age 6–11, 0.2 mg/kg age ≥12, rounded to the dispensed device dose). If prescribed, a second dose is at least 4 h later. Maximum 2 doses per episode. FDA prescribing information
  • Rectal diazepam gel, age ≥2: use its own age/weight prescribing table and caregiver action plan. Do not substitute nasal device strengths or redosing rules.

Write the EMS trigger explicitly. A convulsion lasting 5 minutes, recurring without recovery, or associated with breathing difficulty needs emergency care. The interval before a repeat outpatient rescue dose does not justify waiting to call EMS.

SUDEP — discuss it early, not just when uncontrolled

Sudden unexpected death in epilepsy is ~1/1,000 adults with epilepsy per year, rising to ~6–9/ 1,000 in drug-resistant epilepsy. Per the ILAE SUDEP task force, offer SUDEP communication to every patient at diagnosis and revisit it periodically (not only the uncontrolled). Modifiable risk factors: uncontrolled generalized tonic-clonic seizures (the biggest), nocturnal seizures, medication non-adherence, and lack of nocturnal supervision — target each.

docs.title: Disposition
docs.text:
Status epilepticus → ICU with cEEG. A first seizure back to baseline with a reassuring work-up can be discharged with urgent neurology follow-up, safety/driving counseling, and a decision on ASM. Admit for a prolonged postictal state, an unremitting/nonconvulsive picture, a concerning cause, or an unsafe home situation.

TRICARE — verified rules and the current form

Use the exact ASM, strength and formulation in the live formulary. This review did not establish a blanket PA requirement for newer ASMs or unrestricted coverage for every generic. Document seizure type, previous trials and the rescue plan for any requested exception. Do not delay status treatment for outpatient PA.

Current PA/MN details, benefit routing and packet · Live Formulary Search. Check the exact product, beneficiary and venue on the prescribing date.

Military medicine — duty, retention and deployment

  • Profile / function: Restrict driving and duties involving weapons, heights, water, flight or isolated operations after a seizure until the appropriate clinician/authority clears them. Record state-specific driving advice separately.
  • Retention / MEB–MAR2: Diagnosed epilepsy: DoDI V2 5.26.k, action on diagnosis; provoked seizures: 5.26.j. Army 3-31i applies. Distinguish acute symptomatic events, epilepsy and nonepileptic attacks. Use the retention framework; permanent P3/4 does not by itself select DES versus MAR2.
  • Deployment / medications: CENTCOM seizure activity in the preceding year is not waiverable; stable treatment with a year seizure-free may be considered. ASM indication and controlled-substance status matter separately. See the disease AND drug screen for the current CENTCOM rules and waiver packet.
  • Special duty: flight, diving and other special assignments have separate standards and waiver authorities; a general duty profile does not clear them.
  • LOD / EPTS: document onset, duty status, exposures and aggravation objectively. The designated authority determines LOD/EPTS; neither in-service diagnosis nor a genetic finding settles it automatically.

docs.title: 📚 Discover — evidence brief
docs.text:
• Treat status on a clock, not on a hunch. The AES 2016 algorithm: stabilize (0–5 min) → full-dose benzo (5–20 min) → second-line ASM (20–40 min) → anesthetize + cEEG (>40 min).
  • The second-line three are equivalent (ESETT 2019) — levetiracetam ≈ fosphenytoin ≈ valproate (~45–47% each); choose by comorbidity, and give the full weight-based load. Levetiracetam is the cleanest default.
  • Benzos are under-dosed — that's the commonest "refractory status" that wasn't. RAMPART: IM midazolam ≥ IV lorazepam when there's no IV.
  • "Won't wake up" → cEEG for nonconvulsive status.
  • First seizure: immediate ASM cuts early recurrence but not long-term remission (AAN/AES 2015) — treat when recurrence risk is high (lesion, epileptiform EEG, nocturnal), otherwise a shared decision.
  • Second-line is broadening — lacosamide (non-inferior to fosphenytoin, TRENdS; kinder hemodynamics) and brivaracetam are increasingly used alongside the ESETT triad.
  • Refractory SE: target seizure suppression, not routine burst-suppression (Fisch 2023); no proven drug beyond anesthetics (allopregnanolone RCT negative; hypothermia adds nothing); ketogenic diet in FIRES/NORSE.
  • SANAD II reset the maintenance defaults — lamotrigine first-line for focal epilepsy, valproate most effective for generalized (levetiracetam is the rapid-titration alternative). For drug-resistant focal epilepsy, cenobamate gives the best seizure-freedom odds (slow titration, DRESS risk).
  • Two failed ASMs = drug-resistant → refer for surgical evaluation — the 2022 ILAE consensus: offer it to every such patient up to 70, regardless of type/duration/comorbidity.
  • Give a rescue plan (Nayzilam/Valtoco/Diastat) and discuss SUDEP at diagnosis (biggest modifiable factor: uncontrolled GTC seizures).

Key sources: AES 2016 status-epilepticus guideline (Glauser et al.); Gettings et al., Lancet Neurol 2025 SE review; ESETT (Kapur, NEJM 2019); TRENdS (lacosamide); RAMPART (Silbergleit, NEJM 2012); Fisch et al. (burst-suppression, Neurology 2023); AAN/AES 2015 first-seizure guideline; SANAD II (Marson, Lancet 2021); cenobamate comparative-effectiveness (JAMA Neurol 2026); ILAE 2022 surgical-referral consensus; ILAE SUDEP task force (Epilepsia 2026); ILAE 2025 seizure classification (2017 terminology retained in older records).
