docs.title: Traumatic brain injury (TBI)
docs.text:
Last reviewed: July 2026

One-liner: brain injury from an external force — the signature injury of the post-9/11 military, and mostly a mild TBI (concussion) problem. The acute event is usually the easy part; the value is in managing the long tail of comorbidities — headache, sleep, mood/PTSD, cognition, dizziness, vision, and the ones people forget (neuroendocrine, autonomic, suicide risk). Treat them by domain (each has its own page in the sidebar under TBI), and the patient gets better.

🚩 Acute TBI — exclude a structural emergency first

  • Image (non-contrast CT) for red flags: worsening/severe headache, vomiting, ↓ or fluctuating consciousness, focal deficit, seizure, anticoagulation, or a high-risk mechanism (use a validated head-CT rule within its validated population). Suspect cervical-artery dissection with neck trauma/pain.
  • Second-impact syndrome: a second head impact before the first concussion has recovered can be catastrophic (diffuse cerebral edema) — remove from activity and do not return to play/duty while symptomatic.
  • Moderate/severe TBI → trauma/neurosurgery, ICP management, and the ICH/increased-ICP pathways; this page focuses on the post-acute and chronic course.

docs.title: Classify the severity
docs.text:
Severity GCS LOC Post-traumatic amnesia Imaging Mild (concussion) 13–15 ≤30 min <24 h Normal (or complicated-mild if abnormal) Moderate 9–12 >30 min–24 h 1–7 days Often abnormal Severe ≤8 >24 h >7 days May be normal or abnormal

Confirming an mTBI diagnosis — 2023 ACRM criteria

Severity grading and diagnosis are separate. Under the 2023 ACRM criteria, a plausible injury mechanism plus one of these pathways supports mTBI: a clinical sign attributable to brain injury; at least two acute symptoms plus an examination/laboratory finding; or trauma-related intracranial imaging evidence. Exclude competing explanations. You do not need a sign, two symptoms, and an objective finding in every patient. LOC >30 min, GCS <13 after 30 min, or PTA >24 h excludes the mild qualifier. A normal CT does not exclude concussion.

docs.title: Which patient is in front of you? — pick the pathway
docs.text:
The work-up is completely different by phase. Sort the patient into one of three before anything else:

Presentation Setting Pathway Acute head injury, just happened ER / aid station / field Work-up 1 — Acute TBI (ER) Recent concussion, still symptomatic (days–weeks) clinic / concussion cell Work-up 2 — Acute-phase mTBI (outpatient) Symptoms persisting >~4 wks, or moderate–severe TBI in the chronic phase, or repeated concussions TBI/neuro clinic Work-up 3 — Long-term TBI follow-up

docs.title: Work-up 1 — Acute TBI in the ER
docs.text:
The acute head-injury evaluation

  1. ABCs + C-spine precautions; GCS, pupils, focal exam; glucose; note anticoagulation/ antiplatelet use, LOC, and post-traumatic amnesia.
  2. Decide on CT with a validated rule (e.g., Canadian CT Head Rule). CCHR applies to eligible adults with minor head injury and LOC, amnesia, or disorientation; it is not a universal clearance tool, particularly with anticoagulation or an unreliable examination. Get a non-contrast head CT for any high-risk feature: GCS <15 at 2 h, suspected open/depressed skull fracture, any basilar-skull-fracture sign (hemotympanum, raccoon eyes, Battle's sign, CSF oto/ rhinorrhea), ≥2 episodes of vomiting, age ≥65; or medium-risk: retrograde amnesia ≥30 min, dangerous mechanism. Anticoagulation/coagulopathy or post-traumatic seizure → image regardless. Add CTA neck if dissection is a concern. GFAP/UCH-L1 testing may assist a CT decision in a selected adult under the specific assay’s instructions; see below.
  3. If there's a bleed: reverse anticoagulation (specifics in the box below, or the ICH reversal table), avoid hypoxia and hypotension, and obtain neurosurgery for a surgical lesion (EDH/SDH/contusion) or raised ICP. Do not import spontaneous-ICH BP-lowering targets into TBI. In deployed moderate–severe TBI, follow JTS/TCCC TXA guidance within 3 h (below). Moderate/severe → trauma bay + ICP pathway.
  4. Disposition: admit/observe for an abnormal CT, GCS <15, persistent vomiting, or an unsafe home; a normal CT with a normal exam and improving symptoms can go home with a reliable observer, written return precautions, and no return to play/duty the same day. ACEP does not recommend routine repeat CT or admission solely for anticoagulant/antiplatelet use after a negative CT and baseline exam when no other monitoring indication exists.
  5. In uniform: after a potentially concussive event, MACE2 and the mandated recovery period apply (military box).

GFAP / UCH-L1 — an adjunct, not a CT permission slip

Use the specific device, specimen, age range, and time window in its cleared instructions. The i-STAT whole-blood TBI assay was cleared in 2024 for selected adults with suspected mTBI within 24 h; other assays use a 12-h window. Do not transplant cutoffs between platforms. A not-elevated result lowers the likelihood of a CT-visible traumatic lesion; it does not exclude concussion, diagnose recovery, or authorize return to duty. Follow the JTS biomarker pathway in deployed care. Red flags or another established CT indication still require imaging/evacuation regardless of the biomarker.

Anticoagulation reversal & TXA (acute bleed) — dosed

Reversal (2024 ACS Best Practices / Neurocritical Care Society):

  • Warfarin → 4-factor PCC (Kcentra), INR-based, dosed on actual body weight capped at 100 kg: INR 2–3.9 → 25 units/kg (max 2500), INR 4–6 → 35 units/kg (max 3500), INR >6 → 50 units/kg (max 5000). (Many trauma centers use a fixed 1500–2000 units to save time — give it, then check INR.) Plus vitamin K 10 mg IV by slow infusion over 10–30 min (sustains reversal; PCC alone wears off). Recheck INR at 15–60 min, target <1.5.
  • Dabigatran → idarucizumab 5 g IV (two 2.5 g / 50 mL vials, consecutive boluses). If unavailable: activated PCC (FEIBA) 50 units/kg and consider hemodialysis.
  • Factor Xa inhibitors (apixaban/rivaroxaban) → 4-factor PCC 50 units/kg (or a fixed 2000 units) — andexanet alfa has been withdrawn from the US market.
  • Antiplatelet (aspirin/clopidogrel): do not routinely transfuse platelets for spontaneous/traumatic ICH (PATCH-signal harm) unless a neurosurgical procedure is planned; consider desmopressin (DDAVP) 0.4 µg/kg IV ×1.
  • Repeat CT at 6–24 h to check for hematoma progression before starting VTE prophylaxis.

TXA — follow the setting-specific trauma pathway. JTS recommends 2 g IV/IO within 3 h for evidence of moderate–severe TBI. The civilian CRASH-3 trial used 1 g over 10 min then 1 g over 8 h; benefit was clearest in mild–moderate injury, without a clear benefit in the most severe subgroup. Lack of subgroup benefit is not a blanket contraindication. Do not withhold indicated TXA for accompanying major hemorrhage because the patient also has severe TBI. Use the current trauma protocol and avoid duplicate prehospital/hospital dosing.

VTE prophylaxis timing (2024 ACS Best Practices) — dosed

Balance re-bleeding against clot risk. Agent — LMWH preferred over UFH: enoxaparin 30 mg SC q12h or 40 mg SC daily (reduce to 30 mg daily if CrCl <30), or UFH 5000 units SC q8–12h when LMWH is contraindicated. Start mechanical prophylaxis (SCDs) on admission in the meantime.

  • Low-risk nonoperative TBI: start within 24 h if follow-up CT shows no ICH progression.
  • Moderate/high-risk nonoperative TBI: within 24–48 h if follow-up CT is stable.
  • Post-craniotomy/craniectomy: within 24–48 h if the postoperative CT is stable.

A 2025 Military TBI Initiative meta-analysis found no increase in ICH progression with prophylaxis started within 72 h.

Moderate–severe TBI — ICP / PbtO₂ / CPP targets (with doses)

Prevent secondary injury: JTS targets SBP >110 mmHg in adult deployed TBI; support oxygenation and perfusion, accounting for concurrent hemorrhage. For GCS <9 with an abnormal CT, place ICP monitoring (Brain Trauma Foundation, 4th ed.); treat ICP >22 mmHg. Target CPP 60–70 mmHg — avoid driving CPP >70 (increased ARDS risk). PbtO₂ monitoring target >20 mmHg is an emerging complement: OXY-TC (Lancet Neurol 2023) cut brain-hypoxia time with dual ICP + PbtO₂ monitoring, though 6-month extended-GOS was not significantly improved. Where invasive monitoring is unavailable (austere/deployed), the 2025 Brussels (B-ICONIC) consensus guides non-invasive ICP.

Tiered ICP control — head of bed 30°, normocarbia (PaCO₂ 35–40), sedation/analgesia first; then for a surge:

  • Hyperosmolar bolus (either): hypertonic saline 3% 250 mL (or 23.4% 30 mL via central line) or mannitol 0.5–1 g/kg IV — mannitol needs a normal BP (osmotic diuresis) and serum osm <320; hypertonic saline is preferred if hypotensive.
  • Brief hyperventilation (PaCO₂ 30–35) only as a temporizing bridge to the OR/definitive care.
  • Refractory: neurosurgery for decompressive craniectomy / CSF drainage; not routine steroids (harmful in TBI — CRASH).

docs.title: Work-up 2 — Acute-phase outpatient mTBI (days–weeks out, still symptomatic)
docs.text:
The concussion-clinic / aid-station work-up

  1. History: mechanism, LOC/PTA, and a symptom inventory across domains (headache, dizziness, cognitive, sleep, mood), prior concussions, and persistence risk factors (cognitive symptoms, pre-existing anxiety/depression or sleep disorder, female sex, high acute symptom burden — see box below).
  2. Targeted exam: neuro + cervical spine, a vestibular/ocular-motor screen (VOMS), and a balance check (BESS). Use the right tool for the phase — SCAT6 on the sideline/≤72 h, SCOAT6 in the office at 3–30 days (or MACE2 in uniform) — plus a symptom scale (PCSS / Neurobehavioral Symptom Inventory). Cutoffs in the box below.
  3. Imaging is usually NOT needed — a normal exam with improving symptoms doesn't warrant it (AHS/ACR); image only for red flags, focal deficits, or worsening/atypical course.
  4. Manage: brief relative rest (24–48 h) → early sub-threshold aerobic exercise, sleep hygiene, and symptom-targeted treatment (treat the headache phenotype; avoid opioids/ butalbital). Reassure — most recover in days–weeks.
  5. Graded return to activity/duty; step back a stage on symptom recurrence. Treat the high-persistence-risk patient aggressively and early.
  6. Follow up; if not recovering by ~4 weeks → escalate to Work-up 3 / a multidisciplinary concussion clinic.

Concussion assessment tools — which, and when

  • SCAT6 — sideline/acute, within 72 h of injury.
  • SCOAT6 — office-based subacute assessment at 3–30 days; the 6th Amsterdam Consensus (2023) created it specifically for the clinic-follow-up gap.
  • VOMS — positive if symptom provocation ≥2 on any item or NPC ≥5 cm (AUC 0.89 for concussion identification).
  • mSIT Plus (2026 NCAA–DoD CARE, n=59,901) — a streamlined 6-question index + modified VOMS, AUC 0.94; built for time-limited field/military screening.
  • MACE2 — the mandated DoD sideline tool after a concussive event.

Persistence risk factors — who won't recover fast (treat early, aggressively)

2025 evidence (JAMA Netw Open meta-analysis, McIntosh et al.; NCAA–DoD CARE Consortium):

  • Cognitive symptoms (difficulty concentrating) — strongest predictor (OR >3).
  • Pre-existing anxiety/depression or a sleep disorder.
  • Acute clinical signs (LOC, amnesia).
  • Female sex — significant but a smaller effect.
  • High acute symptom burden (SCAT total >45), prior concussion history, and delayed reporting predict symptoms persisting >29 days.

docs.title: Work-up 3 — Long-term TBI follow-up (persistent — the common military clinic visit)
docs.text:
Structured multi-domain review (persistent post-concussive / chronic / repeated TBI)

  1. Re-confirm the diagnosis and rule out a new/secondary process if the pattern changed.
  2. Systematically screen and treat every comorbidity domain — work the domain pages below (headache, sleep, mood/PTSD, cognition, vestibular, vision, neuroendocrine, autonomic, seizures, pain/substance). This is where persistent TBI is won or lost.
  3. Don't miss the quiet ones: neuroendocrine (hypopituitarism), OSA, and suicide risk — screen deliberately.
  4. Refer to a multidisciplinary TBI clinic (neuro + rehab + behavioral health + sleep + vestibular/PT + endocrine + neuropsych) for refractory/complex cases.
  5. Own the disposition: profile, MEB/DES, VA rating documentation, and — for a repeated- impact history — honest TES/CTE counseling (below). Track longitudinally with a symptom inventory and treat to target.

docs.title: Manage the comorbidities — by domain
docs.text:
Persistent post-TBI symptoms are multidomain and overlapping — treat each explicitly (this is the engine of Work-up 3, and drives symptom care in Work-up 2); improving one (sleep, mood, headache) lifts the others. Each domain has its own page (nested under TBI in the sidebar):

  • Headache — the commonest symptom; phenotype-directed (full detail on the post-traumatic headache page).
  • Sleep — fix it first; CBT-I, screen for OSA.
  • Mood & PTSD — CBT + SSRI/SNRI, prazosin; screen suicide every visit.
  • Cognitive — treat the contributors first; cognitive rehab.
  • Vestibular / dizziness — BPPV/Epley; vestibular rehab.
  • Vision / oculomotor — convergence insufficiency; vision therapy.
  • Neuroendocrine — hypopituitarism screening — the quiet, treatable miss.
  • Autonomic — dysautonomia; exercise reconditioning.
  • Post-traumatic seizures — 7-day prophylaxis ≠ epilepsy prevention.
  • Pain & substance — opioid-sparing; screen substances.

docs.title: Return to activity / duty
docs.text:
Brief relative rest → early sub-threshold aerobic exercise → graded, supervised return (school/ work/cognitive load before full contact/duty); step back a stage on symptom recurrence. In uniform, follow the Progressive Return to Activity stages (military box). The headache-specific detail is on the post-traumatic headache page.

Sub-threshold aerobic exercise prescription

After 24–48 h of relative rest, introduce light symptom-limited activity and an individualized sub-threshold exercise plan. In DoD care, honor the mandatory initial 24-h recovery period and the PRA stages; do not skip clearance stages because the patient feels better. Keep exercise below the symptom-exacerbation threshold (a >2-point rise on a 0–10 symptom scale = "more than mild" = went too hard):

  1. Find the threshold with the Buffalo Concussion Treadmill Test (BCTT) — the HR at which symptoms rise >2 points.
  2. No treadmill? Prescribe at ~50% of age-predicted max HR (max = 220 − age).
  3. Dose ~20 min/day below that threshold; advance as tolerated, backing off on a >2-point rise.

RCT evidence: early aerobic exercise cut median recovery 17 → 13 days (p=0.009) and persistent symptoms 32% → 21% (p=0.04). Strong for in both the Amsterdam 2023 consensus and the 2025 AAPM&R guideline (2025 NEJM review, Leddy).

docs.title: Long-term: CTE / neurodegeneration & suicide risk
docs.text:
Traumatic encephalopathy syndrome (TES) — counsel carefully, don't over-diagnose

Chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) is a neuropathological diagnosis (perivascular p-tau at sulcal depths) — only confirmable at autopsy. In life, the 2021 NINDS consensus criteria define Traumatic Encephalopathy Syndrome (TES): substantial repetitive head-impact exposure (contact sport, military blast), progressive cognitive impairment (memory/executive) and/or neurobehavioral dysregulation (explosivity, impulsivity), not fully explained by another disorder. It is a clinical syndrome, not a confirmed CTE diagnosis — counsel honestly about uncertainty, treat the modifiable comorbidities, and avoid nihilism.

The 2021 NINDS TES criteria are explicitly research criteria — use them cautiously in clinical and medicolegal settings. Do not disclose provisional "levels of certainty" for underlying CTE pathology to patients: it can produce a nocebo effect — worsening mental health and deterring pursuit of treatable conditions. Keep counseling focused on the modifiable comorbidities.

Suicide risk is elevated after TBI — screen and act

TBI (especially with mood/PTSD, chronic pain, and repeated injury) independently raises suicide risk. Screen for suicidal ideation at every visit, treat depression/PTSD/pain/sleep aggressively, restrict means, and connect to behavioral health / the Veterans Crisis Line.

TRICARE — verified rules and the current form

Most drugs here treat a specific comorbid symptom, often off label after TBI. Document that diagnosis, the trial and functional response. Do not promise coverage for stimulants, sleep drugs, devices, SGB or rehabilitation from the TBI label alone; obtain the current drug/service-specific rule.

Current PA/MN details, benefit routing and packet · Live Formulary Search. Check the exact product, beneficiary and venue on the prescribing date.

Military medicine — duty, retention and deployment

  • Profile / function: Use TBICoE progressive return-to-activity with documented symptom, balance, vision and cognitive recovery. A normal scan or biomarker does not clear return to hazardous duty.
  • Retention / MEB–MAR2: DoDI V2 5.26.h and Army 3-31j address residual TBI impairment; associated epilepsy, sleep, psychiatric or visual disorders may invoke separate standards. Use the retention framework; permanent P3/4 does not by itself select DES versus MAR2.
  • Deployment / medications: CENTCOM has specific repeat-TBI evaluation rules. Assess the syndrome AND medication (controlled stimulants/hypnotics, injections, anticonvulsant exceptions); do not treat completion of a single recovery interval as deployment clearance. See the disease AND drug screen for the current CENTCOM rules and waiver packet.
  • Special duty: flight, diving and other special assignments have separate standards and waiver authorities; a general duty profile does not clear them.
  • LOD / EPTS: document onset, duty status, exposures and aggravation objectively. The designated authority determines LOD/EPTS; neither in-service diagnosis nor a genetic finding settles it automatically.

docs.title: 📚 Discover — evidence brief
docs.text:
• Sort by phase first — the work-up is different for acute TBI in the ER (CT-rule triage, reversal, neurosurgery/disposition), acute-phase outpatient mTBI (symptom inventory + VOMS/balance, usually no imaging, exercise + graded return), and long-term follow-up (systematic multi-domain comorbidity review — the common military clinic visit).
  • TBI is mostly a mild-TBI, chronic-comorbidity problem — the acute event resolves; the persistent symptoms (headache, sleep, mood/PTSD, cognition, dizziness, vision) are what disable, and they're multidomain and interlinked.
  • Treat by domain and fix sleep + mood first — they gate everything else; headache-specific CBT, CBT-I, and vestibular/vision rehab are the highest-value non-drug tools.
  • Don't miss the quiet ones: post-traumatic hypopituitarism (screen moderate–severe/blast TBI in the first year — treatable), OSA, and suicide risk (screen every visit).
  • Rest is not the treatment — brief relative rest then early sub-threshold aerobic exercise (within 24–72 h; BCTT threshold or ~50% max HR) and graded return; avoid opioids/butalbital.
  • GFAP/UCH-L1 can assist selected CT decisions under the specific assay’s cleared instructions and JTS pathway; it does not override red flags or clear someone for duty.
  • Acute bleed management has specifics — agent-specific reversal, TXA per the trauma/JTS pathway within 3 h, VTE prophylaxis within 24–48 h once the follow-up CT is stable (LMWH preferred), and for GCS <9 ICP >22 mmHg / CPP 60–70 / PbtO₂ >20 targets.
  • Confirm mTBI with the 2023 ACRM criteria (mechanism plus a qualifying sign, symptom/finding combination, or imaging evidence) — the 2025 AAPM&R-preferred standard, beyond the GCS/LOC/PTA severity grade.
  • CTE is a post-mortem diagnosis; TES (2021 NINDS) is a research clinical syndrome — counsel with honesty about uncertainty, don't disclose provisional CTE-certainty levels (nocebo), treat the modifiable.
  • Post-traumatic seizure prophylaxis is 7 days for early seizures in moderate–severe TBI — it does not prevent epilepsy.

Key sources: VA/DoD mTBI CPG (2021); DoDI 6490.11 + TBICoE Progressive Return to Activity; 2024 ACS Best Practices in the Management of TBI; 2025 AAPM&R Action Collaborative TBI guideline + 2023 ACRM mTBI diagnostic criteria; 2025 NEJM sport-related concussion review (Leddy); 6th Amsterdam concussion consensus (2023); CRASH-3; Brain Trauma Foundation guidelines + OXY-TC (2023); post-TBI hypopituitarism guidance (British Neurotrauma Group); 2021 NINDS Traumatic Encephalopathy Syndrome criteria.

docs.title: TBI comorbidity — Autonomic
docs.text:
Last reviewed: July 2026

Part of the TBI work-up & comorbidities hub.

One-liner: two very different problems live under "autonomic." (A) mTBI autonomic dysfunction — orthostatic and exercise intolerance, palpitations, temperature dysregulation — is an outpatient issue, very treatable with graded reconditioning. (B) Paroxysmal sympathetic hyperactivity (PSH) is a severe-TBI ICU emergency — different population, setting, and drugs. Keep them separate.

Why it happens — and why exercise is both test and treatment

mTBI causes diffuse axonal injury of brainstem autonomic centers and impairs cerebrovascular autoregulation, so the brain can't hold steady perfusion when blood pressure or metabolic demand changes. During exertion this creates a demand–perfusion mismatch → headache, dizziness, fog. Standardized testing shows blunted sympathetic baroreflex and reduced HR/BP variability in the first two weeks. Graded exercise restores autonomic function and autoregulation — which is exactly why exercise is both diagnostic (BCTT) and therapeutic.

docs.title: (A) mTBI autonomic dysfunction / exercise intolerance / POTS
docs.text:
Assess — orthostatic vitals + the Buffalo Concussion Treadmill Test

  • Symptoms: orthostatic intolerance/lightheadedness, exertional symptom exacerbation, palpitations/tachycardia, sweating and temperature dysregulation.
  • Orthostatic vitals / POTS: sustained HR rise ≥30 bpm (≥40 in adolescents) within 10 min of standing/tilt, without orthostatic hypotension, with orthostatic symptoms ≥3 months and no alternative cause such as dehydration, anemia, hyperthyroidism, medication effects, or prolonged bed rest. Acute post-concussion tachycardia alone is not established POTS. Concussion is a recognized POTS trigger, and POTS resolution tends to parallel return to activity — reinforcing exercise as treatment.
  • Buffalo Concussion Treadmill Test (BCTT) — an exercise-tolerance assessment, not a standalone diagnostic test for concussion: walk at 3.3 mph / 0% incline, increase incline 1° per minute, rate symptoms every minute; stop at a ≥3-point symptom rise (0–10 scale) or volitional exhaustion. In community (non-athlete) adults, ~56% show exercise intolerance at 1 week and ~48% at 1 month.

Sub-symptom-threshold aerobic exercise (SSTAE) — the prescription

The HR at the BCTT symptom threshold is the target (if no treadmill, use ~50% of age-predicted max HR, max = 220 − age):

  1. Exercise at 80% of the symptom-threshold HR, 20 min/day, 5–6 days/week.
  2. Retest every 2–3 weeks and advance the target HR upward as tolerance improves.
  3. Stay sub-threshold — a >2–3-point symptom rise means back off.

Adult RCT evidence: the 2026 Valaas trial (n=81, persistent PCS 3–24 mo) improved exercise tolerance at 12 weeks (sustained at 6 mo); the ACTBI trial (n=52) improved quality of life vs stretching (p=0.047), no adverse events. Nuance: SSTAE reliably improves exercise tolerance, but its effect on overall symptom burden in adults is less robust than in adolescent athletes — both treatment and control groups tend to improve over time.

Orthostatic intolerance / POTS pharmacotherapy — non-drug first

Drugs here are borrowed from the general OH/POTS literature, not TBI-specific. Exhaust non-pharmacological measures first (they are the cornerstone):

  • First-line (non-drug): fluids 2–3 L/day, salt up to 10–12 g/day when appropriate (not 10–12 g sodium; avoid indiscriminate loading in hypertension, cardiac, or renal disease), compression garments, and the graded exercise program above.
  • If insufficient, symptom-directed: beta-blocker or ivabradine (palpitation-dominant); midodrine (hypotension-dominant); pyridostigmine as an adjunct. Avoid atomoxetine as routine POTS treatment: a randomized crossover trial found worse standing tachycardia and symptoms. NRI use in selected neurogenic orthostatic hypotension is a different indication. Fludrocortisone for refractory volume support.

Temperature dysregulation — practical, and military-relevant

Post-TBI thermoregulatory dysfunction can present as heat intolerance, excessive sweating, or impaired sweating — a real hazard for troops exercising in the heat. Use graded heat acclimatization and modified PT standards during recovery; document heat intolerance as a duty/deployability consideration.

docs.title: (B) Paroxysmal sympathetic hyperactivity (PSH) — severe-TBI ICU
docs.text:
PSH — recognize, standardize, and treat the storm

Who: 10–30% of moderate–severe TBI; ~80% of all PSH follows TBI. Definition: simultaneous paroxysmal, transient surges in sympathetic activity (↑HR, ↑BP, ↑RR, hyperthermia, sweating) and motor activity (posturing) in survivors of severe acquired brain injury.

Diagnose with the PSH Assessment Measure (PSH-AM, 2014 consensus): a Clinical Feature Scale (grading HR, BP, RR, temperature, sweating, posturing) + an 11-item Diagnosis Likelihood Tool — standardizes diagnosis and tracks response.

PSH management ladder (2017 Lancet Neurology / 2024 ACS)

  • Find and treat triggers first — ~80% of paroxysms are allodynic (pain, urinary retention, movement, suctioning). Minimize noxious stimuli.
  • Abort/suppress: opioids (morphine) are the most-used first-line agent for allodynic responses.
  • Prevent/blunt: propranolol has the most evidence (low-quality data suggest lower mortality in severe TBI with PSH); alpha-2 agonists (clonidine, dexmedetomidine). A 2026 RCT found propranolol + gabapentin cut PSH incidence to 10% (vs 33% propranolol alone, 60% standard care) — though gabapentin prolonged recovery time.
  • Adjuncts/refractory: benzodiazepines, bromocriptine, baclofen (intrathecal for refractory cases), dantrolene.
  • Feed the storm: resting energy expenditure can rise up to 3× baseline during paroxysms — weight loss of 25–29% is reported. Prioritize nutritional support.

Military note: exercise intolerance directly limits return-to-duty fitness — the BCTT + SSTAE progression doubles as a documentable recovery metric; heat intolerance is a deployability consideration. See the TBI hub and the exercise prescription on the hub Return-to-activity section.

docs.title: TBI comorbidity — Cognitive
docs.text:
Last reviewed: July 2026

Part of the TBI work-up & comorbidities hub.

One-liner: post-TBI complaints of attention, processing speed, memory, and executive function are common — but much of it is treatable contributors, not fixed damage. Fix those first, then rehabilitate what remains. TRACK-TBI found 13.5% of mTBI patients had a poor cognitive outcome at 1 year (vs 4.5% of controls), memory and processing speed most affected.

Impairment profiles are heterogeneous — treat the profile, not a label

At 6 months (TRACK-TBI), the dominant deficit in moderate–severe TBI was processing speed (42%), then memory (27%) and executive function (20%); in mTBI, processing speed (17–19%) and memory (14–17%) predominated. Global impairment across all domains is uncommon — which argues for personalized rehabilitation, not one-size-fits-all. A large cohort (n=15,764) found attention and executive function are the most TBI-sensitive domains (≈2× the effect of processing speed/working memory), and that lasting deficits track with ≥3 lifetime mTBIs — a key counseling point for service members continuing high-risk activity.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Neuropsychological testing — when, and why

  • Not routinely within the first 30 days (VA/DoD) — first-48-hour deficits usually resolve in days–weeks; early testing mislabels normal recovery.
  • Most useful at >30 days when symptoms persist and functional impact needs documenting.
  • In the military, it drives disposition: RBANS significantly predicted return-to-duty vs medical retirement (p=0.001), and 25% of members cleared on symptom-resolution alone had not yet achieved neurocognitive recovery — so use testing as an adjunct to symptom-based clearance, not an afterthought.

Performance validity testing (PVT) — include it in every evaluation

Include appropriate validity measures and interpret the whole pattern with the neuropsychologist. A failed validity measure does not by itself diagnose malingering or invalidate every cognitive result. Selected forensic-cohort failure rates should not be applied to every injured service member. Consider the instrument, severe impairment, literacy, language, pain, fatigue, medications, and psychiatric factors. This is directly load-bearing for MEB/VA ratings, where cognitive documentation drives the outcome — a report without validity testing is incomplete.

docs.title: Manage
docs.text:
Step 1 — treat the treatable drivers first

A large share of "cognitive impairment" resolves once these are addressed — review all meds at every visit (polypharmacy is the rule in multi-comorbid TBI):

  • Treat: sleep, mood/PTSD, pain, and substances.
  • Avoid (cognition-toxic): benzodiazepines, anticholinergics, bupropion and traditional antipsychotics (seizure threshold), lithium (confusion).
  • Minimize: opioids, topiramate (word-finding), sedating antihistamines, gabapentin/pregabalin (sedation).

Step 2 — non-drug: cognitive rehab + exercise

  • Cognitive rehabilitation is clinician-directed (SLP/OT-led). Clinician-directed beats self-administered computerized "brain training" — self-directed computer training was less effective and associated with worse outcomes (VA/DoD).
  • Compensatory strategy instruction has the strongest functional effect (SMD ~0.58, ASHA 2022) — calendars, checklists, routines, reduced multitasking.
  • Trial 4–6 sessions to confirm benefit; prolonged treatment without gains fosters a "sick role" and is discouraged.
  • Assistive tech should be familiar/commercial (smartphone apps, alarms, calendars) — custom devices have higher abandonment.
  • Early sub-threshold aerobic exercise aids neuroplasticity and has cognitive (not just headache) benefit (2025 AAPM&R Good Practice) — see the exercise prescription on the TBI hub.

Step 3 — pharmacotherapy (dosed, specialist-guided)

  • Methylphenidate — best-evidenced, domain-specific (2026 ACRM guideline). Start 5 mg BID, titrate toward ~0.3 mg/kg BID (commonly 10–20 mg BID); monitor BP/HR. Usually well tolerated, no increased seizure risk in the evidence base.
    • Should be offered → sustained attention & processing speed (d 0.39–0.45).
    • May be offered → selective attention (d 0.33).
    • Should NOT be offered → executive function or working memory (no benefit).
    • Should be offered → depressive symptoms when rapid response and/or cognitive impairment are priorities (d 1.06; overlaps mood/PTSD).
    • A 2024 meta-analysis (14 RCTs, n=4,434) confirms a small but real cognitive effect (d 0.34).
  • Amantadine 100–200 mg BID, adjusted for renal function — the strongest recommendation is for adults with traumatic vegetative/unresponsive wakefulness or minimally conscious states 4–16 weeks after injury, to accelerate recovery during treatment. The pivotal trial did not establish that starting in week 1 is best. This is not routine treatment of chronic mTBI cognitive complaints.
  • Donepezil 5 mg daily, then 10 mg if tolerated — off-label, specialist-guided. The 2025 MEMRI-TBI-D randomized trial supports benefit in selected adults with persistent, functionally limiting verbal-memory impairment after TBI. Balance nausea/diarrhea, bradycardia/syncope, and uncertain generalizability; pair with rehabilitation and measured goals.

Long-term: repeated exposure & dementia risk

mTBI is an emerging dementia risk factor, and TRACK-TBI shows some patients decline after an apparent recovery. Risk concentrates with repeated exposure (≥3 lifetime mTBIs) — fold this into honest counseling about continuing high-risk activity, and connect it to the TES/CTE discussion on the TBI hub.

TRICARE — verified rules and the current form

Most drugs here treat a specific comorbid symptom, often off label after TBI. Document that diagnosis, the trial and functional response. Do not promise coverage for stimulants, sleep drugs, devices, SGB or rehabilitation from the TBI label alone; obtain the current drug/service-specific rule.

Current PA/MN details, benefit routing and packet · Live Formulary Search. Check the exact product, beneficiary and venue on the prescribing date.

Military note: objective neuropsych findings (with PVTs) carry weight in retention/DES decisions, and RBANS predicts return-to-duty vs medical retirement — document them. See the TBI hub for the retention/aeromedical framing.

docs.title: TBI comorbidity — Headache
docs.text:
Last reviewed: July 2026

Part of the TBI work-up & comorbidities hub.

One-liner: Headache is the most common post-TBI symptom. The rule is treat the phenotype, start early, and cap acute-medication days — PTH is a high-risk medication-overuse setting.

Name the phenotype (it drives treatment)

  • Migraine-like — most common (variable by cohort); the migraine acute/preventive ladders apply.
  • Tension-type-like.
  • Cervicogenic — neck-driven; manual therapy (2025 AAPM&R Good Practice) and occipital/ cervical nerve blocks.
  • Occipital neuralgia — occipital nerve blocks.
  • Vestibular migraine — commonly missed; overlaps the vestibular/dizziness domain — screen for it.

ICHD-3 framing: acute PTH = onset within 7 days of injury, resolving by 3 months; persistent PTH = beyond 3 months. With a pre-existing headache disorder, call it PTH only if it clearly worsened (≈ doubled frequency/severity) in temporal relation to the injury — the distinction drives escalation and VA/MEB documentation.

  • Acute: stratified by severity (NSAID → triptan, or a gepant/lasmiditan where triptans are unsuitable); a gepant may help when appropriate (follow label exposure limits). The only positive acute-PTH RCT is IV metoclopramide 10 mg + diphenhydramine 25 mg (n=81; 1.4 pts greater pain relief vs placebo). Scheduled (not PRN) analgesics in the first 72 h post-injury are an emerging way to blunt acute-phase severity.
  • Preventive (start at ≥8 monthly headache days if acute therapy is optimized and headaches remain disabling — Lancet Neurol 2021; >10 days/mo or disabling — 2025 AAPM&R): amitriptyline/nortriptyline (also helps sleep/mood), venlafaxine, candesartan, propranolol; botulinum toxin A has a small positive PTH trial; this does not establish every formulation/regimen or TRICARE coverage for PTH. OnabotulinumtoxinA chronic-migraine criteria remain a separate clinical and coverage question. Nerve blocks are high-yield — consider early.
  • CGRP agents: used by extrapolation from migraine — PTH-specific data are weak. The one completed placebo-controlled CGRP-mAb RCT in PTH (fremanezumab) was negative; erenumab has only open-label support. "Receptor- vs ligand-targeting preferred" is not established in PTH.
  • Non-drug: headache-specific CBT (McGeary 2022 RCT in post-9/11 veterans: HIT-6 −3.4, and PTSD −6.5 — the strongest non-drug PTH evidence, ideal for this population), aerobic exercise, sleep, cervical PT.
  • Emerging — neuromodulation: Devices cleared for certain migraine indications (eTNS, nVNS, REN, sTMS) may be considered by extrapolation for migraine-phenotype PTH, useful when MOH risk or drug access is limited; small rTMS/TMS pilots are promising but preliminary.
  • Watch MOH: cap analgesics-with-caffeine, triptans, or opioids/butalbital at <10 days/mo (simple analgesics <15); avoid opioids and butalbital outright.

Full detail — doses, the acute/preventive ladders, the CBT and aerobic-exercise evidence, and the military/TRICARE specifics — are on the dedicated post-traumatic headache page.

docs.title: TBI comorbidity — Mood & PTSD
docs.text:
Last reviewed: July 2026

Part of the TBI work-up & comorbidities hub.

One-liner: depression, anxiety, and PTSD track tightly with TBI in service members and drive outcome more than seizure/symptom counts do — treat them explicitly, screen with validated tools, and screen for suicide every visit. In military/veteran TBI, PTSD runs ~36–37% (≈4× the odds vs non-TBI military), depression ~30% in the first year (~80% of episodes begin within 6 months), and anxiety 11–24%. A 2024 JAMA Netw Open cohort showed both mild and moderate–severe TBI carry a decade-long, non-plateauing excess risk of depression, anxiety, and suicidal ideation/attempt.

Screen for suicidal ideation at every visit

TBI independently raises suicide risk (amplified by mood/PTSD, chronic pain, and repeated injury). Screen (C-SSRS or PHQ-9 item 9), treat the drivers aggressively, restrict means, and connect to behavioral health / the Veterans Crisis Line (dial 988, then 1). (Also flagged on the TBI hub.)

Screen and measure — validated tools, standard cutoffs (2025 AAPM&R, Strong for)

Standard primary-care cutoffs apply without modification in TBI. Screen early (~1 month) and again in anyone still symptomatic — peak onset is 2–6 months post-injury.

  • Depression — PHQ-2 → PHQ-9.
  • Anxiety — GAD-2 → GAD-7.
  • PTSD — PCL-5.
  • Suicidality — C-SSRS or PHQ-9 item 9.
  • Alcohol misuse — AUDIT-C.

docs.title: Depression & anxiety
docs.text:
Treat by target — CBT + an antidepressant (dosed)

  • Psychotherapy: CBT / behavioral activation is first-line and combines well with medication.
  • SSRI/SNRI (depression evidence base is broad): sertraline 50 mg/day → 50–200, escitalopram 10 → 20 mg, or venlafaxine XR 75 → 225 mg. Avoid highly anticholinergic/sedating agents (worsen cognition).
  • Methylphenidate — strongest TBI-specific evidence for depressive symptoms. The 2026 ACRM practice guideline (Should be offered) recommends it when rapid response and/or co-occurring cognitive impairment are priorities: start 5 mg BID, titrate toward ~0.3 mg/kg BID (commonly 10–20 mg BID); monitor BP/HR. (Overlaps the cognitive domain.)
  • Early prevention (not yet guideline-endorsed): sertraline 50 mg/day started soon after TBI reduced incident depression (NNT ~6 in one RCT).

docs.title: PTSD
docs.text:
PTSD — trauma-focused therapy first (VA/DoD 2023, Strong for)

TBI does not preclude trauma-focused therapy — these work in comorbid TBI. Offer a first-line trauma-focused psychotherapy:

  • Cognitive Processing Therapy (CPT), Prolonged Exposure (PE), or EMDR.
  • Written Exposure Therapy (WET) — 2025 APA-suggested alternative: fewer sessions, no homework, lower dropout — feasible in primary care / deployed settings. A 2025 JAMA Psychiatry RCT (n=700) found WET and SSRIs comparably effective in primary care; for SSRI non-responders, switching to venlafaxine beat WET augmentation.

PTSD — pharmacotherapy (dosed)

Guideline-recommended agents are specific — not all SSRIs qualify:

  • First-line (VA/DoD 2023, Strong for): paroxetine 20 → 60 mg, sertraline 50 → 200 mg, or venlafaxine XR 75 → 225 mg. Escitalopram has insufficient evidence for a VA/DoD recommendation for PTSD, and fluoxetine was dropped from the recommended list on updated evidence.
  • Prazosin — nuance the evidence. The large PACT trial (NEJM 2018, n=304 veterans) was negative for nightmares/PTSD at 26 weeks. But a 2025 meta-analysis (10 RCTs, n=648) found prazosin improves nightmares (SMD −0.64) and insomnia (SMD −0.65) — not overall PTSD. VA/DoD suggests against it for overall PTSD but gives a Weak for specifically for nightmares/sleep. Use it targeted: 1 mg qhs, titrate slowly (to ~5–15 mg) by orthostatic-BP tolerance — a two-for-one with post-traumatic headache.

docs.title: Irritability / aggression
docs.text:
Post-TBI agitation/aggression (dosed) — and what to avoid

  • Amantadine 100 mg BID — best TBI-specific evidence (multiple RCTs) for irritability/ aggression.
  • Beta-blockers (propranolol, pindolol) — reduce the intensity of agitation (titrate from a low dose as BP/HR allow).
  • Methylphenidate — improves anger measures (dose as above), doubles for depression/cognition.
  • Avoid haloperidol — may hinder neurocognitive recovery and prolong post-traumatic amnesia.
  • Avoid benzodiazepines for agitation — cognitive impairment and paradoxical disinhibition.

docs.title: Emerging & adjunctive
docs.text:
Stellate ganglion block (SGB) — relevant to the military population

A local-anesthetic block of the cervical sympathetic chain. A 2020 JAMA Psychiatry RCT (n=113 active-duty) found two right-sided SGBs cut CAPS-5 by −12.2 points vs sham; a 2026 VA series (n=579) reported 68% clinically meaningful improvement at 1 week. Hyperarousal symptoms respond best, effects last ~3–6 months, and it can be repeated. The VA actively offers SGB in selected settings; VA/DoD finds insufficient evidence for or against it. Discuss uncertainty, procedural risk, and coverage with a specialist.

MDMA-assisted therapy — not FDA-approved

The FDA declined to approve MDMA-assisted psychotherapy for PTSD in August 2024 (trial- validity, expectancy, and functional-unblinding concerns); an additional Phase 3 trial is required. Both the 2025 APA and 2023 VA/DoD CPGs rate psychedelics as insufficient evidence to recommend for or against — don't adopt prematurely.

Moral injury — distinct from PTSD (a military-specific concept)

Distress from acts (or failures to act) that violate one's moral code — presenting with shame, guilt, and existential distress rather than fear-based symptoms. It may not respond to standard trauma-focused therapies built around fear extinction. Emerging treatments include Adaptive Disclosure and Impact of Killing. Recognize it; screen when the narrative is about transgression, not threat.

Treat the domains together — they're bidirectional

  • Venlafaxine may serve both mood and migraine prevention. Do not assume every SSRI is an established headache preventive; select each drug for its supported indication and the patient.
  • Treating sleep (CBT-I; prazosin for nightmares) substantially improves mental health — treat concurrently or prioritize by severity.
  • Refer for headache-specific CBT, not just PTSD care: it improved both the headache and PTSD in veterans (McGeary 2022), whereas treating PTSD alone did not fix the headache (see the PTH page).

TRICARE — verified rules and the current form

Most drugs here treat a specific comorbid symptom, often off label after TBI. Document that diagnosis, the trial and functional response. Do not promise coverage for stimulants, sleep drugs, devices, SGB or rehabilitation from the TBI label alone; obtain the current drug/service-specific rule.

Current PA/MN details, benefit routing and packet · Live Formulary Search. Check the exact product, beneficiary and venue on the prescribing date.

Military note: PTSD, depression, and suicide risk are central to deployability, profile, and MEB/DES decisions — document screening, diagnosis, treatment trials, and response. See the TBI hub for the retention/aeromedical framing.

docs.title: TBI comorbidity — Neuroendocrine (hypopituitarism)
docs.text:
Last reviewed: July 2026

Part of the TBI work-up & comorbidities hub.

One-liner: the quiet, high-yield miss. Post-traumatic hypopituitarism is common, and its symptoms — fatigue, low mood, low libido, cognitive fog, weight change — mimic the rest of the TBI picture, so it gets blamed on "post-concussive syndrome" and never screened. It is treatable, and it changes disposition. Pooled prevalence of any pituitary-axis dysfunction is ~33% (higher <3 months, much of it transient; persistent ~15% on strict criteria with repeat testing). By axis: GH ~18%, gonadal ~16%, ACTH ~10%, TSH ~6%.

Why the pituitary is vulnerable

Its blood supply runs through long hypophyseal portal vessels — shearing, raised ICP, and hypotension cause ischemic necrosis; basal skull fracture can directly injure the gland or transect the stalk; and anti-pituitary/anti-hypothalamic antibodies appear after TBI and predict delayed-onset deficiency. The GH-secreting somatotrophs sit laterally, fed by the most vulnerable portal vessels — which is why GH is the axis most often lost.

docs.title: Who to screen
docs.text:
Screen the right patients — not every mTBI

  • Screen prospectively: complicated mild TBI (clinically mild but an intracranial abnormality on imaging), moderate, and severe TBI.
  • Uncomplicated mTBI: screen only if suggestive symptoms persist (fatigue, low mood, low libido, cognitive fog, weight change, poor recovery) — testing all mTBI is neither realistic nor cost-effective.
  • Lower the threshold with: basal skull fracture, diffuse axonal injury, raised ICP, prolonged ICU stay, older age, female sex, multiple acute-phase hormone deficiencies, radiological abnormalities.

docs.title: When to screen — the timeline matters
docs.text:
Screening timeline (what to test when)

  1. Acute phase (ICU) — test only two things:
    • Adrenal insufficiency — random cortisol; treat empirically if hemodynamically unstable (below).
    • Diabetes insipidus / SIADH — follow sodium and urine output.
    • Do NOT test GH, gonadal, or thyroid axes acutely — critical illness confounds the results and acute replacement of these doesn't improve outcome.
  2. 3–6 months — first comprehensive screen (morning): cortisol (± ACTH-stimulation if borderline), IGF-1, testosterone/estradiol + LH/FSH, TSH + free T4, prolactin. Watch for loss of secondary hair, new oligo/amenorrhea, sexual dysfunction, weight change, polydipsia, poor recovery.
  3. 12 months — repeat if deficiencies were found at 3–6 months (some recover, some worsen) or if new symptoms appear.
  4. Beyond 12 months — stay alert: new deficiencies can emerge even 5 years out — re-test on new symptoms.

docs.title: Don't-miss emergencies
docs.text:
Acute adrenal insufficiency — treat before you confirm

Life-threatening in the ICU: refractory hypotension, hyponatremia, hemodynamic instability. Draw cortisol/ACTH before treatment if this causes no delay, but random critical-illness cortisol thresholds are not interchangeable with stable outpatient morning testing. Suspected adrenal crisis: hydrocortisone 100 mg IV/IM immediately, then 200 mg/24 h infusion or 50 mg q6h, with isotonic fluid resuscitation and glucose/electrolyte monitoring. Do not await confirmation. Chronic central adrenal insufficiency may present with fatigue, weight loss, orthostasis, and hyponatremia; arrange endocrine testing and a sick-day/emergency steroid plan.

Sodium disorders — DI, SIADH, and cerebral salt wasting

  • Central DI (~2.9% acutely, more in severe TBI): polyuria >3 L/day, polydipsia, hypernatremia, dilute urine. Usually transient (hours–days); ~7% permanent.
  • SIADH (commoner than DI acutely): hyponatremia, concentrated urine, euvolemia — usually self-limited; specialist-guided fluid/electrolyte management. Do not reflexively restrict fluid in an unstable brain-injured patient; exclude cortisol deficiency and hypovolemia first.
  • Triphasic response (classic, rare): DI → SIADH → permanent DI over days as the posterior pituitary necroses and dumps stored AVP.
  • Distinguish SIADH from cerebral salt wasting — euvolemic vs hypovolemic hyponatremia; treatment is opposite (fluid restriction vs saline replacement). Get this right.

docs.title: Individual axes
docs.text:
GH axis — most affected, hardest to diagnose

  • IGF-1 is a screening test, not diagnostic — a normal IGF-1 does not exclude GH deficiency (sensitivity ~50%).
  • Confirm with dynamic testing: the insulin tolerance test (ITT) is gold standard; glucagon stimulation or macimorelin are alternatives. GHRH-arginine is no longer recommended (arginine supply).
  • Confirmed GH deficiency warrants endocrinology-directed replacement after dynamic testing and contraindication review. Small heterogeneous post-TBI studies suggest benefits in selected deficient patients, but GH is not an established general treatment for post-concussion fatigue or cognitive symptoms. Treatment above traditional deficiency thresholds remains investigational; do not prescribe from a low-normal IGF-1 alone.

Gonadal axis — relevant to the military population

Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism is the 2nd commonest deficiency (~16%): low libido, erectile dysfunction, fatigue, mood change, oligo/amenorrhea.

  • Acute phase: low testosterone is expected (critical illness) — do not treat.
  • Chronic (>3–6 months): persistent hypogonadism warrants replacement — testosterone in men, estrogen/progesterone in premenopausal women.
  • Confirm it's central (low/inappropriately normal LH/FSH) before attributing low testosterone to TBI rather than a primary gonadal cause — relevant given how often testosterone is prescribed in TBI veterans.

The symptom-overlap trap — the practical rule

Fatigue, disrupted sleep, altered cognition, weakness, exercise intolerance, and declining mental health can come from either TBI or hypopituitarism — you cannot tell them apart clinically. The rule: if a TBI patient isn't improving despite appropriate multi-domain treatment (sleep, mood, cognitive), check the pituitary.

Treat the confirmed deficiency (endocrinology)

Refer for targeted hormone replacement — replacing the deficient axis can dramatically improve fatigue, mood, and cognition that resisted everything else. Replace glucocorticoid before thyroid hormone (thyroxine can precipitate adrenal crisis in undiagnosed cortisol deficiency).

Military note: a screenable, treatable cause of "persistent post-concussive symptoms" that changes the disposition — document the axis, the confirmatory test, and the replacement. See the TBI hub for the retention/aeromedical framing.

docs.title: TBI comorbidity — Pain & substance use
docs.text:
Last reviewed: July 2026

Part of the TBI work-up & comorbidities hub.

One-liner: chronic pain and substance use are common, bidirectional with TBI, and both are worsened by the reflex reach for opioids — keep the plan opioid-sparing, multimodal, and mechanism-based, and screen actively. Chronic pain affects ~40–51% after complicated mild-to-severe TBI (≈2× the general population), with a median of 4 pain locations and pain interference in ~55%. Predictors: female sex, military service, pre-injury migraine, penetrating injury, and poor sleep/mood/PTSD.

docs.title: Classify the pain by mechanism — it drives the drug
docs.text:
Post-TBI pain phenotypes (IASP framework)

Mixed phenotypes are common (neuroinflammation + central sensitization) — which is why treatment must be multimodal.

  • Nociceptive (tissue injury/inflammation — musculoskeletal, cervicogenic, fracture) → NSAIDs, physical therapy, targeted injections.
  • Neuropathic (nerve lesion — occipital neuralgia, peripheral nerve injury, central pain) → TCA/SNRI, gabapentinoid, nerve blocks.
  • Nociplastic (altered processing without clear tissue/nerve damage — central sensitization, fibromyalgia-like) → SNRI, exercise, CBT, neuromodulation (drugs alone underperform).

docs.title: Treat — multimodal and opioid-sparing
docs.text:
Pharmacologic ladder (dosed, with TBI-specific caveats)

  • TCA — nortriptyline (preferred) or amitriptyline 10–75 mg qHS — first-line neuropathic (NNT ~4.6) and a two-for-one with sleep/headache prevention. Use nortriptyline (less anticholinergic) and start low — anticholinergic load worsens cognition.
  • SNRI — duloxetine 60–120 mg/day (strongest evidence) or venlafaxine XR 150–225 mg/day — first-line neuropathic (NNT ~7.4); also treats comorbid depression.
  • Gabapentinoid — titrate gabapentin or pregabalin from a low dose, with renal adjustment and an indication-specific maximum; those are target ranges, not starting doses — effective for neuropathic pain, but sedation/cognitive effects are a real problem in TBI — weigh against the cognitive comorbidity, titrate slowly.
  • NSAIDs — for nociceptive/musculoskeletal pain; limit duration and cap acute-medication days when headache coexists (MOH, below).
  • Topicals — lidocaine 5% patch, capsaicin — for localized neuropathic pain, minimal systemic/cognitive effect — underutilized in TBI.

Every acute analgesic is a potential MOH contributor

Medication-overuse headache sits at the pain–headache intersection: ~27% of moderate–severe PTH patients have probable MOH at 2–4 months (88% on simple analgesics, only 7% on a preventive). Cap acute-medication days (<10–15/month by agent) and start preventive therapy early in anyone with coexisting headache (see headache).

Non-drug — the disease-specific evidence

  • Collaborative care is the only RCT-proven chronic-pain treatment in TBI. The TBI Care RCT (JAMA Netw Open 2024, n=158) — up to 12 sessions over 16 weeks with a care manager delivering CBT for pain plus weekly expert-team review — cut pain interference (3.46 vs 5.03), sustained at 8 months, and improved pain severity, depression, and anxiety.
  • Graded aerobic exercise — treats pain, autonomic dysfunction, and mood together (see autonomic).
  • Cervical PT — for the very common cervicogenic component.
  • Nerve blocks (greater/third occipital, cervical medial branch) — high-yield for cervicogenic/occipital pain (also on the headache page).
  • Neuromodulation (rTMS, peripheral nerve stimulation) — emerging; rTMS carries a weak recommendation for neuropathic pain.

Opioids — VA/DoD 2022 CPG framework, and a TBI mortality signal

  • Strong recommendation against initiating long-term opioid therapy for chronic pain.
  • Already on opioids? Use a collaborative, patient-centered taper — gradual (5–20% every 4 weeks) while optimizing non-opioid therapy. Rapid tapering is harmful (destabilizes patients, worsens depression, increases suicidal ideation, drives illicit use).
  • Suspect OUD at any point → treat it (buprenorphine, or methadone through an opioid treatment program; extended-release naltrexone is an option only after an adequate opioid-free interval to avoid precipitated withdrawal).
  • TBI-specific: strong opioids carry the highest hazard for 30-day mortality after TBI (HR 1.41), and CNS-affecting drugs are far commoner in TBI patients than controls (37% vs 24%) — another reason to stay opioid-sparing.

docs.title: Screen the substances
docs.text:
Substance-use screening — tools, timing, and the numbers

New-onset SUD affects ~4.2% within 5 years (global cohort, n≈1.89 M): nicotine 2.4%, alcohol 1.1%, cannabis 0.9%, opioids 0.4% — and ~50% of eventual SUD is diagnosed within 3 years. In active-duty airmen, mTBI raised the hazard for alcohol and nicotine dependence and drug abuse (highest early); among post-9/11 veterans with TBI, 26.9% received opioids (of those, 30% also benzodiazepines, 36% sedative-hypnotics).

  • Tools: AUDIT / AUDIT-C (use the validated cutoff for that instrument and population; do not raise screening thresholds solely because the patient has TBI), DAST-10 (drugs), or TAPS (tobacco, alcohol, prescription misuse, illicit — one instrument). All validated in TBI.
  • When: at intake and follow-up, with particular attention in the first 3 years (highest risk).
  • Then: treat and involve behavioral health (see mood/PTSD).

Why TBI and substance use feed each other

TBI → SUD: reward-circuit neuroplasticity, chronic neuroinflammation / microglial priming (a "two-hit" vulnerability), impaired white-matter integrity in reward pathways, and frontal disinhibition/impulsivity. SUD → TBI/worse recovery: substances raise injury risk (falls, MVCs, assaults) and impair neuroplasticity, sleep, and medication adherence.

Cannabis — an explicit military caveat

Cannabis is the 3rd most common new-onset SUD after TBI (~0.9%) and is increasingly used for chronic pain by veterans. For active-duty service members it remains prohibited — a fitness-for-duty / UCMJ issue regardless of state law. The VA cannot prescribe or recommend cannabis but should discuss it openly with transitioning/veteran patients.

Military note: opioid/substance issues carry fitness-for-duty, drug-testing, and readiness implications — an added reason to stay opioid-sparing and screen early. See the TBI hub.

docs.title: TBI comorbidity — Post-traumatic seizures
docs.text:
Last reviewed: July 2026

Part of the TBI work-up & comorbidities hub.

One-liner: distinguish early provoked seizures from post-traumatic epilepsy (PTE), and know the one rule that trips people up — prophylaxis is a 7-day intervention that does not prevent epilepsy.

docs.title: Know the risk — it stratifies sharply by severity
docs.text:
Prevalence: early PTS vs post-traumatic epilepsy

  • Early PTS (≤7 days): up to 15% in severe TBI (down to <5% with prophylaxis); only 0–4% in mild/moderate (mostly <2%).
  • Subclinical (nonconvulsive) seizures: ~25% of moderate–severe TBI on continuous EEG — the main reason to monitor.
  • Post-traumatic epilepsy (late, unprovoked): ~⅓ of severe TBI survivors; 4–15% in moderate–severe; 45–53% in penetrating injury; mTBI roughly triples baseline risk (absolute ~1–4%).
  • 10-year epilepsy risk (Swedish registry, n≈112,000): 12.9% focal cerebral, 8.1% diffuse, 7.3% extracerebral, 2.6% mild — vs 0.9% in controls.
  • Repeated TBI doubles it: a Danish cohort (n≈2.5 M) found HR 2.04 after a first TBI and HR 4.45 after a second, staying elevated for decades.

Risk factors for PTE (2024 ACS Best Practices) — who to watch long-term

Evacuated SDH, contusion + SDH, evacuated intraparenchymal hematoma; GCS 3–8; early seizures (especially delayed); LOC/amnesia >1 day; >7 days to follow commands; skull fracture, unelevated depressed fracture, dural penetration; nonreactive pupil(s), parietal lesions; age >65, female sex, family history of epilepsy, history of depression.

docs.title: Acute management
docs.text:
Early-seizure prophylaxis — a 7-day intervention

  • Who gets it: moderate–severe TBI with intracranial bleeding / risk factors → 7 days of prophylaxis. Not recommended in TBI without intracranial bleeding or in isolated traumatic SAH (2024 ACS).
  • Agent — levetiracetam is preferred: levetiracetam 500–1000 mg IV/PO q12h (or ~20 mg/kg load) or phenytoin (20 mg/kg load then maintenance with levels). Meta-analyses show equivalent efficacy (OR ~0.85), but levetiracetam has fewer interactions, no drug-level monitoring, and shorter ICU stays — but the penetrating-TBI guideline does not establish a superior agent.
  • Blunt injury without a seizure: start early, usually stop at 7 days. A clinical/electrographic seizure changes the question from prophylaxis to treatment; discuss duration with neurology. AAN (Level A) — start ASAP after severe TBI to reduce early PTS; do not continue beyond 7 days (Level B).
  • Mild/moderate TBI: the benefit is small — a 2024 JAMA Neurology meta-analysis found an absolute risk reduction of 0.6% (NNT 167) — weigh against ASM harms and the real risk of inappropriate continuation past 7 days.

The rule: prophylaxis does NOT prevent epilepsy

The landmark Temkin RCT showed phenytoin cut early PTS from 14.2% → 3.6% but had no effect on late PTS/PTE — replicated across meta-analyses and the basis of every current guideline. Early PTS are associated with later PTE, but treating early seizures does not reduce PTE risk — so an early seizure should prompt closer long-term surveillance, not indefinite prophylaxis.

Continuous EEG — the 'won't wake up' after TBI

Nonconvulsive seizures occur in ~25% of moderate–severe TBI and are tied to worse outcomes and hippocampal atrophy. Consider cEEG in any moderate–severe TBI with unexplained altered consciousness ("won't wake up" → cEEG). The 2024 ACS guideline supports cEEG for seizure detection (and emerging detection of secondary ischemia); in the multicenter INTREPID study, EEG background features (absent posterior-dominant rhythm, absent sleep transients, predominant delta, discontinuous background) were independently associated with functional outcome.

Penetrating TBI — highest risk, least certainty

Penetrating TBI carries the highest PTE risk (45–53%), and frontal/temporal injuries are likely more epileptogenic. The 2026 Brain Trauma Foundation penetrating-TBI guideline flags pTBI as higher-risk than blunt. Expert consensus recommends prophylaxis for 7 days or longer, with no superior drug established. Optimal longer duration and cessation remain uncertain; agree a documented neurosurgical plan rather than automatically stopping all penetrating cases on day 7.

docs.title: Late seizures & follow-up
docs.text:
Late (>7-day) unprovoked seizure = post-traumatic epilepsy

  • A late unprovoked seizure warrants urgent neurology review, MRI/EEG, and a treatment decision. Epilepsy can be diagnosed after one seizure when the estimated 10-year recurrence risk is ≥60% (often after severe structural TBI); do not presume that every remote mild concussion meets that threshold. Risk is highest after penetrating or severe TBI and can emerge months–years later.

  • Driving: stop driving and document counseling. The 2025 AAN/AES/EFA statement ordinarily supports at least 3 seizure-free months, with individualized exceptions for exclusively provoked events whose cause is unlikely to recur. State law and licensing decisions govern; this is not a universal national legal interval. Sleep deprivation is not a reassuring one-off cause, and alcohol withdrawal requires recurrence/substance-risk assessment.

  • Full management — the status-epilepticus ladder, first-seizure work-up, and ASM selection — is on the seizure & status epilepticus page and the antiseizure medications page.

Horizon — antiepileptogenesis (no proven therapy yet)

The key unmet need: current ASMs prevent early seizures but do not modify epileptogenesis. The 2026 Epilepsia consensus roadmap (Zanier et al.) targets neuroinflammation (IL-1β/NLRP3), blood-brain-barrier dysfunction, and mTOR signaling. Preclinical candidates — IL-1 receptor antagonist (anakinra), mTOR inhibitor (rapamycin), glutamate modulator (ceftriaxone) — reduce seizures in animals but are unvalidated in humans. Candidate biomarkers: early epileptiform EEG (≈3× PTE risk within 14 days), serum S100B (HR ~2.12 in complicated mTBI), and neuroinflammatory markers. Military relevance: PTE is ~5% of all epilepsy and TBI is the signature military injury — moderate–severe/penetrating cohorts are a natural population for future prevention trials.

Military note: post-traumatic epilepsy is handled as any seizure disorder (AR 40-501 3-31i / DoDI 6130.03 Vol 2 5.26.k → action on diagnosis of epilepsy; separate flying-duty standards apply) — see the TBI hub and seizure page.

docs.title: TBI comorbidity — Sleep
docs.text:
Last reviewed: July 2026

Part of the TBI work-up & comorbidities hub.

One-liner: sleep disruption sustains every other TBI symptom (headache, mood, cognition, fatigue) — fix it first. Sleep–wake disturbance affects 30–70% of mTBI and ~46% of chronic TBI patients (insomnia the commonest), and a VA cohort of ~200,000 veterans confirmed TBI independently raises the risk of insomnia, hypersomnia, and sleep apnea years after injury.

Sleep gates recovery — the relationship is bidirectional

Poor sleep worsens post-traumatic headache (OR ~2.9 in the first 6 weeks), cognition, and mood/anxiety; conversely, treating sleep improves outcomes across every other domain. The 2025 AAPM&R guideline explicitly prioritizes sleep as a treatment target because it gates recovery. Improving sleep often unmasks how much of the "post-concussive" picture was sleep-driven.

Screen and measure — validated instruments

  • ISI (Insomnia Severity Index) — 7 items, validated in TBI; ≥10 = clinical insomnia.
  • PSQI (Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index) — global sleep quality; >5 = poor sleep.
  • ESS (Epworth Sleepiness Scale) — daytime sleepiness; ≥10 = excessive.
  • STOP-Bang — OSA risk (below).
  • Actigraphy — objective sleep–wake/circadian patterns when PSG isn't indicated.
  • PSG ± MSLT — for suspected OSA, narcolepsy, or hypersomnia (MSLT confirms objective sleepiness and separates it from fatigue).

docs.title: Name the disorder — it's not all insomnia
docs.text:
The post-TBI sleep differential (with rough prevalence)

  • Insomnia — most common; onset and/or maintenance difficulty.
  • Obstructive sleep apnea — 20–77% across studies; drives "refractory" fatigue/cognitive complaints (work-up below).
  • Post-traumatic hypersomnia (~11–22%) — sleep need ≥2 h/day above pre-injury, from hypothalamic injury / reduced hypocretin (orexin) signaling.
  • Narcolepsy / narcolepsy-like (~6%) — loss of hypocretin neurons → excessive daytime sleepiness, occasionally cataplexy. Exclude before starting a DORA (contraindicated).
  • Periodic limb movement disorder (~7%).
  • Parasomnias — nightmares, REM sleep behavior disorder — especially with comorbid PTSD.
  • Fatigue ≠ sleepiness. Fatigue is daytime tiredness without objective sleepiness on MSLT and needs different management (activity pacing, mood/pain treatment) — do not reach for a wake-promoting agent for pure fatigue.

docs.title: Insomnia
docs.text:
Step 1 — CBT-I is first-line (Strong for)

CBT-I before drugs. VA/DoD 2025 Insomnia/OSA CPG gives it a Strong for recommendation; a 2026 network meta-analysis (22 RCTs, n=1,299 TBI patients) found CBT the most consistently effective intervention across ISI/PSQI/ESS — supporting CBT-I; indirect comparisons do not prove superiority to every drug in every patient. 70–80% get enduring benefit and ~50% reach remission.

  • No in-person CBT-I? Use internet-delivered CBT-I (eCBT-I / SHUTi) — a 2024 JAMA Netw Open RCT in military TBI patients showed feasibility and efficacy, and it fixes the access barrier (military CBT-I referrals rose 372% over 2005–2014).
  • Pair with sleep-hygiene / circadian measures: fixed wake time, morning light, evening screen/caffeine limits — relevant to shift work and deployment.

Step 2 — pharmacotherapy if CBT-I is insufficient (dosed)

Adjunct to CBT-I, not a substitute. Match the drug to onset vs maintenance; reassess and taper.

  • Melatonin (prolonged-release) 2–5 mg, ~2 h before bedtime — best TBI-specific evidence: an RCT (n=33) improved PSQI (−1.79 vs placebo, p≤0.0001), sleep efficiency, anxiety, and fatigue; a 2023 scoping review found benefit in 8/9 studies, well tolerated. Sleep-onset benefit mainly — less for maintenance.
  • Dual orexin receptor antagonists (DORAs) — suvorexant 10–20 mg, lemborexant 5–10 mg, or daridorexant 25–50 mg qhs. Work for both onset and maintenance, less cognitive impairment than benzodiazepines, low abuse potential; a 2025 network meta-analysis shows all three beat placebo. Mechanistically apt (TBI disrupts the orexin system) — but contraindicated in narcolepsy (exclude first). Current drug-specific TRICARE criteria were not obtained; check the exact form.
  • Low-dose doxepin 3–6 mg qhs — FDA-approved for sleep-maintenance insomnia; the only sedating antidepressant with consistent insomnia efficacy (2024 NEJM review).
  • Trazodone is suggested against for chronic insomnia in the 2025 VA/DoD guideline. It is used off-label in practice, but low hypnotic doses are not adequate antidepressant treatment. No TBI-specific RCT and "inconsistent efficacy evidence" for general insomnia; a head-to-head vs melatonin vs combination trial is underway (2026).
  • Avoid: chronic benzodiazepines / Z-drugs (cognition, dependence, fall/duty risk) and antihistamines (diphenhydramine, hydroxyzine — anticholinergic/cognitive load, weak evidence).

docs.title: Excessive daytime sleepiness / hypersomnia
docs.text:
Wake-promoting agents — for objective sleepiness, not fatigue (dosed)

First exclude and treat OSA and confirm objective sleepiness (ESS/MSLT). Then, for post-traumatic hypersomnia (AASM 2021 Conditional recommendation):

  • Modafinil 100–200 mg each morning, or armodafinil 150–250 mg each morning. A 2025 meta-analysis (3 RCTs, n=158) showed reduced ESS (MD −1.65, p=0.04); armodafinil 250 mg gave the clearest objective sleep-latency benefit (+7.2 vs +2.4 min). Watch for treatment- emergent insomnia (RR ~3.7).
  • Schedule IV controlled substances — relevant for military prescribing and deployability.

docs.title: Obstructive sleep apnea
docs.text:
OSA — screen, test in tiers, treat (Strong for PAP)

  • Screen with STOP-Bang (Snoring, Tiredness, Observed apnea, Pressure, BMI, Age, Neck, Gender): ≥3 intermediate, ≥5 high risk. Have a low threshold — OSA prevalence in TBI is 20–77%.
  • Phased, cost-effective work-up: STOP-Bang → home sleep apnea (portable) testing → lab PSG if portable testing is negative/discordant but suspicion remains.
  • PAP therapy is first-line (VA/DoD 2025 Insomnia/OSA CPG). Set expectations: CPAP reliably improves AHI but may not fully resolve daytime sleepiness in TBI — reassess for a coexisting central hypersomnia if sleepiness persists on adherent PAP.

Light therapy — non-drug, no interactions, deployable

Useful for circadian misalignment, sleepiness, and comorbid low mood — attractive in the military setting. Morning blue-wavelength light (~469 nm, 30 min) phase-advanced sleep, cut daytime sleepiness, and improved executive function in an mTBI RCT (n=32); a 2022 meta-analysis (6 RCTs, n=278) found reduced sleep disturbance (SMD −0.63) and depression (SMD −1.00). Morning bright light ~10,000 lux, 60 min improved insomnia, mood, and pain in a veteran cohort.

TRICARE — verified rules and the current form

Most drugs here treat a specific comorbid symptom, often off label after TBI. Document that diagnosis, the trial and functional response. Do not promise coverage for stimulants, sleep drugs, devices, SGB or rehabilitation from the TBI label alone; obtain the current drug/service-specific rule.

Current PA/MN details, benefit routing and packet · Live Formulary Search. Check the exact product, beneficiary and venue on the prescribing date.

Military note: untreated OSA, chronic hypnotics, and Schedule IV wake-promoting agents are duty/deployability considerations — document the work-up, diagnosis, and PAP adherence. See the TBI hub for the retention/aeromedical framing.

docs.title: TBI comorbidity — Vestibular / dizziness
docs.text:
Last reviewed: July 2026

Part of the TBI work-up & comorbidities hub.

One-liner: dizziness is the second most common post-mTBI symptom after headache — 50–80% acutely, persisting in 25–30% beyond 3 months. The highest-yield moves are to catch the curable causes (BPPV), name the specific diagnosis (many have specific treatments), and refer for vestibular rehabilitation — not to reach for a vestibular suppressant. In blast mTBI, the otolith organs (utricle/saccule) are more vulnerable to overpressure than the semicircular canals, which shifts testing and rehab.

docs.title: Name the diagnosis — it's not all "post-concussive dizziness"
docs.text:
Differential of post-traumatic dizziness (each treats differently)

  • BPPV — commonest and curable; post-traumatic BPPV is distinct (below).
  • Labyrinthine concussion — direct inner-ear injury → acute vestibular hypofunction without fracture; looks like vestibular neuritis but with a trauma history.
  • Vestibular migraine — a major driver of persistent post-traumatic dizziness, especially with a migraine-phenotype PTH; responds to migraine preventives, not suppressants.
  • PPPD (persistent postural-perceptual dizziness) — Bárány Society 2017 diagnosis: chronic non-spinning dizziness/unsteadiness ≥3 months, worse upright, with self-motion, and with complex visual stimuli; mTBI is a recognized trigger. Treat with SSRI/SNRI + CBT + vestibular rehab, not suppressants (below).
  • Superior semicircular canal dehiscence (SSCD) — trauma unmasks a thin superior canal → sound/pressure-induced vertigo, autophony, pulsatile tinnitus (~45% report a preceding traumatic event). Diagnose with high-res CT temporal bone + VEMP.
  • Perilymph fistula — oval/round-window disruption after barotrauma/impact → fluctuating hearing loss + positional vertigo.
  • Secondary endolymphatic hydrops — post-traumatic Ménière-like: episodic vertigo, hearing loss, tinnitus.
  • Central vestibular dysfunction — diffuse axonal injury of vestibular nuclei/cerebellum/ vestibulo-thalamic pathways; may coexist with peripheral disease.

Acute — exclude a central cause first

New acute vestibular syndrome after trauma: exclude posterior-circulation stroke or vertebral/carotid dissection. HINTS requires a trained examiner and the appropriate continuous acute vestibular syndrome with nystagmus; it is not a rule-out test for all dizziness or for dissection. A normal head impulse, direction-changing nystagmus, or skew is concerning in that setting. Neck pain/headache, focal signs, or uncertainty → stroke/vascular imaging pathway. Don't call new dizziness "concussion" until the central cause is excluded.

docs.title: Assess
docs.text:
Screening & bedside tools (with cutoffs)

  • VOMS (Vestibular/Ocular-Motor Screening) — smooth pursuit, saccades, VOR, visual-motion sensitivity, near-point convergence. Abnormal = symptom provocation ≥2 points on any item, or NPC >5 cm.
  • Dix-Hallpike (posterior canal) and supine roll test (horizontal canal) — positional BPPV.
  • Dynamic visual acuity (DVA) — VOR during head movement; ≥2-line drop from static acuity is abnormal.
  • DHI (Dizziness Handicap Inventory) — 25 items; >30 = moderate handicap; tracks response.
  • BESS (Balance Error Scoring System) — the SCAT6/MACE2 balance test.
  • FGA (Functional Gait Assessment) — 10-item dynamic gait; more sensitive than the Berg Balance Scale in mTBI (head turns, eyes-closed walking).

docs.title: Treat
docs.text:
BPPV — post-traumatic BPPV is harder than idiopathic

  • Reposition, don't suppress. Dix-Hallpike → Epley for posterior canal; supine roll → Lempert (barbecue) roll for horizontal canal.
  • Check all canals: post-traumatic BPPV is multi-canal in ~50–67% (vs ~10% idiopathic) and more often bilateral — a Dix-Hallpike alone will miss horizontal-canal disease.
  • Expect higher recurrence and more maneuvers. Diagnose early — median time to first repositioning is ~13.5 days in polytrauma, and earlier treatment improves outcomes.

Vestibular rehabilitation therapy (VRT) — first-line for persistent symptoms

  • Refer for VRT for persistent dizziness/imbalance/oculomotor symptoms. A 2024 meta-analysis (6 RCTs) showed improved DHI (SMD −0.33) and VOMS (SMD −0.40) at end of treatment; individually tailored multimodal (cervical + vestibular + oculomotor) therapy had a moderate effect (SMD 0.63) and made patients ~3× more likely to return to sport by 8 weeks.
  • Goal-based reassessment: VA/DoD recommends vestibular/balance therapy beyond the acute phase but discourages prolonged therapy without improvement — reassess against functional goals.
  • Provider matters — ideally a therapist with post-graduate vestibular-rehab training.

Cervicogenic dizziness — identify and treat the neck

A diagnosis of exclusion considered after whiplash/blast. Neck symptoms alone are not diagnostic, and no single bedside test confirms it. Consider it when dizziness is provoked by neck movement, with neck pain and restricted cervical ROM. Support assessment with the cervical joint-position-error test and smooth-pursuit neck-torsion test. Treat with cervical manual therapy + proprioceptive retraining (Langevin 2022 RCT improved cervical and vestibular measures).

PPPD — break the dizziness→anxiety→avoidance cycle

Persistent dizziness often becomes maladaptive: dizziness → anxiety → movement avoidance → deconditioning → worse dizziness (the mechanism behind PPPD) — high-yield to catch in service members, where avoidance degrades duty performance. Use an individualized multimodal plan: SSRI/SNRI (sertraline, venlafaxine), CBT targeting dizziness-related anxiety/avoidance (see mood/PTSD), and graded vestibular exposure via rehab. Suppressants make it worse. Evidence for these PPPD interventions remains limited; explain that uncertainty and measure response rather than promising a proven three-part cure.

Vestibular suppressants — mostly a don't after concussion

  • Not recommended routinely (VA/DoD) — they delay central compensation and promote counterproductive adaptation.
  • If symptoms are severe enough to limit function, a brief (<1 week) trial of meclizine 25 mg is the preferred agent. Avoid benzodiazepines (clonazepam/diazepam/lorazepam — sedation, cognitive impairment, dependence).
  • Never treat BPPV with a suppressant — reposition instead.

When to refer for formal vestibular lab testing

Escalate beyond bedside (VNG, calorics, rotary chair, VEMP, posturography) for:

  • Persistent dizziness >4 weeks despite initial management.
  • Atypical nystagmus not consistent with BPPV.
  • Suspected SSCD (order high-res CT temporal bone + VEMP) or perilymph fistula (fluctuating hearing loss + positional vertigo).
  • Failure to respond to vestibular rehab.
  • Need for objective documentation (MEB/VA rating).

Military note: persistent vestibular dysfunction is deployment- and (with the vision/oculomotor overlap) special-duty-limiting; blast exposure favors otolith injury (VEMP-testable). Document objective testing for the TBI hub retention/aeromedical framing.
